On 889 held-out requests, in an analysis fixed before generation, truncation raises harmful compliance by 5.8 to 21.4 points, and SafeStart leaves a rise of 0.6 to 2.6 points, non-inferior to the original model on two of the three models. Our results show that faster MoE serving need not cost safety: a serving system can keep most of the gain from running fewer experts by running all of them at the start of each response, and it should test refusal, not only accuracy, before it enables such a method.

AI.tldr: SafeStart restores most of the refusal behavior that is weakened when MoE serving runs fewer experts per token, by running all experts for the prompt and the first eight generated tokens. It keeps at least 85% of the offline decode speedup at batch sizes 8 and 32.
AI.motivation: Serving methods that run fewer experts per token speed up MoE language models and are validated on accuracy benchmarks, but the paper shows that they can weaken the model's refusal of harmful requests.
AI.method: SafeStart runs all experts for the prompt and the first eight generated tokens and the reduced expert set afterwards, implemented as a fused kernel in vLLM.
AI.result: On one RTX A6000, keeping about two thirds of the selected experts speeds up offline decoding by 15 to 28% at batch size 8. Under a jailbreak, the rise in harmful compliance is 18.4 percentage points on Qwen1.5-MoE, 9.5 on OLMoE and 6.6 on DeepSeek-V2-Lite, the three of nine models where it rises significantly, while MMLU drops by less than two points. With SafeStart the change is between -2.1 and +1.3 points for three expert-reduction methods on those three models; on 889 held-out requests, truncation raises harmful compliance by 5.8 to 21.4 points while SafeStart leaves a rise of 0.6 to 2.6 points, non-inferior to the original model on two of the three models.
AI.conclusion: Faster MoE serving need not cost safety: running all experts at the start of each response keeps most of the gain, and refusal should be tested alongside accuracy before such a method is enabled.

title: CARM: Conformal Adaptive Risk Masking for Reliable Scientific Super-Resolution
summary: Deep learning-based super-resolution (SR) can reconstruct fine-scale Earth-observation fields from coarse observations, but reconstruction accuracy alone does not provide a calibrated rule for identifying reliable spatial regions. Conformal Mask Calibration (CMC), built on conformal risk control, converts a spatial uncertainty score into a trust mask and controls the expected worst-case local distortion under exchangeability. However, its fixed threshold can become miscalibrated in Earth-observation streams affected by seasonality and episodic events. We propose $\textit{CARM}$ (Conformal Adaptive Risk Masking), a statistical framework for adaptive spatial risk control under temporal distribution shift. CARM maintains experts with heterogeneous update rates and aggregates their threshold proposals online using an asymmetric surrogate loss, balancing rapid adaptation to distribution changes against stability during relatively stationary periods. All updates are causal and use only mature feedback available after a fixed delay, allowing CARM to operate with any SR model that provides a spatial uncertainty score. We prove that the time-averaged mask-conditioned risk converges to at most $\alpha$ at an $O(1/T)$ rate, without distributional assumptions and for any choice of aggregation weights across experts. On a daily South China Sea chlorophyll-$\textit{a}$ SR stream, CARM reduces the empirical violation rate from $43.49\%$ to $9.38\%$ and the moving-average exceedance frequency from $47.29\%$ to $1.22\%$ at $\alpha=0.10$, while retaining a non-trivial trusted region. Experiments on ERA5 wind and OSTIA sea-surface temperature further show consistent relative improvements across multiple SR backbones.

AI.tldr: CARM extends conformal mask calibration to temporal distribution shift by aggregating experts with different update rates through an asymmetric online surrogate loss, keeping the time-averaged mask-conditioned risk below alpha. On a daily South China Sea chlorophyll-a stream at alpha = 0.10 it reduces the empirical violation rate from 43.49% to 9.38%.
AI.motivation: A fixed conformal threshold becomes miscalibrated in Earth-observation streams affected by seasonality and episodic events, so reconstruction accuracy alone does not give a calibrated rule for identifying reliable spatial regions in super-resolution.
AI.method: CARM maintains experts with heterogeneous update rates and aggregates their threshold proposals online using an asymmetric surrogate loss, balancing rapid adaptation to distribution change against stability in stationary periods; all updates are causal and use only mature feedback available after a fixed delay, and the method works with any SR model that provides a spatial uncertainty score.
AI.result: On a daily South China Sea chlorophyll-a SR stream, the empirical violation rate falls from 43.49% to 9.38% and the moving-average exceedance frequency from 47.29% to 1.22% at alpha = 0.10, while a non-trivial trusted region is retained. The authors prove that the time-averaged risk converges to at most alpha at an O(1/T) rate without distributional assumptions; experiments on ERA5 wind and OSTIA sea-surface temperature show consistent relative improvements across multiple SR backbones.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive conformal risk masking gives a distribution-free, theoretically supported way to keep super-resolution trust masks calibrated under temporal distribution shift.

title: A Definition of Catastrophic Performance
summary: A central challenge in AI is specifying objectives that align with human preferences. While existing theoretical results elucidate how misspecification impacts performance, they typically do not distinguish between merely suboptimal and catastrophic outcomes. To enable rigorous analysis of catastrophic risk from AI misalignment, we introduce a formal definition of catastrophic performance. Our definition is based on two reference values. The first, baseline value, captures the value attained if no agent is deployed. The second, orthogonal value, captures the value of a trajectory that is unrelated to human preferences, in a sense we describe. Orthogonal value is typically far worse than baseline value. We interpret these reference values through examples in which past human activity has altered the state of the environment to human benefit. Starting at the resulting state, an AI agent is deployed with the goal of accelerating further progress. Catastrophic performance represents this agent's undoing of benefits afforded by human activity.

AI.tldr: The paper gives a formal definition of catastrophic performance based on two reference values: a baseline value, attained if no agent is deployed, and an orthogonal value, the value of a trajectory unrelated to human preferences. Catastrophic performance is an agent undoing benefits that past human activity has created.
AI.motivation: Existing theoretical results on objective misspecification show how misspecification affects performance but typically do not distinguish merely suboptimal outcomes from catastrophic ones, which limits rigorous analysis of catastrophic risk from AI misalignment.
AI.method: The definition is built on a baseline value, the value attained if no agent is deployed, and an orthogonal value, the value of a trajectory unrelated to human preferences, which is typically far worse than baseline; the two reference values are interpreted through examples in which past human activity altered the environment to human benefit.
AI.result: The abstract reports no empirical results; it offers a formal definition illustrated through examples.
AI.conclusion: Catastrophic performance is framed as an AI agent, deployed from a state that human activity has improved, undoing those benefits while pursuing further progress.

title: HarnessFlow: MCTS-Guided Harness Optimization for LLM Agents
summary: The performance of large language model (LLM) agents depends on both the underlying model and the harness that governs interaction with tools and the environment. Yet harness design remains largely manual, and automating it requires navigating an open-ended search space through costly end-to-end evaluations. We introduce HarnessFlow, a framework for optimizing complete executable harnesses under a limited candidate-evaluation budget, with the model and task environment held fixed. HarnessFlow organizes candidates and their evaluation histories in a refinement tree, using a Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)-based policy to balance exploitation and exploration. A coding agent refines selected harnesses using archived code, execution feedback, and a library of reusable harness mechanisms. With 15 refinement attempts per benchmark, HarnessFlow achieves the highest mean test scores among the compared methods on six benchmarks spanning agentic tasks, coding, and web interaction. The optimized harnesses achieve an average score of 69.48%, outperforming the initial harnesses and Meta-Harness by 10.89 and 3.95 percentage points, respectively, while incurring lower average per-task execution costs than hand-engineered baselines. These results suggest that structured harness search offers a promising route toward automating the design of capable and efficient LLM agents.

AI.tldr: HarnessFlow optimizes complete executable LLM-agent harnesses under a limited candidate-evaluation budget, using Monte Carlo Tree Search over a refinement tree. The optimized harnesses average 69.48% across six benchmarks, outperforming the initial harnesses by 10.89 points and Meta-Harness by 3.95 points.
AI.motivation: Harness design, which governs how an LLM agent interacts with tools and the environment, remains largely manual, and automating it requires navigating an open-ended search space through costly end-to-end evaluations.
AI.method: Candidates and their evaluation histories are organized in a refinement tree; a Monte Carlo Tree Search policy balances exploitation and exploration; a coding agent refines selected harnesses using archived code, execution feedback and a library of reusable harness mechanisms, with the model and task environment held fixed.
AI.result: With 15 refinement attempts per benchmark, HarnessFlow achieves the highest mean test scores among the compared methods on six benchmarks spanning agentic tasks, coding and web interaction; the optimized harnesses average 69.48%, outperforming the initial harnesses and Meta-Harness by 10.89 and 3.95 percentage points, at lower average per-task execution cost than hand-engineered baselines.
AI.conclusion: Structured harness search is presented as a promising route to automating the design of capable and efficient LLM agents.

title: A Systematic Benchmark for Evaluating Multimodal Personalized Reasoning of Vision-Language Models
summary: People often make decisions by holistically reasoning over heterogeneous forms of personal information. In this paper, we study the relatively underexplored capability of multimodal personalized reasoning in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). To this end, we introduce \texttt{MPRBench}, a novel and comprehensive benchmark specifically designed to evaluate personalized reasoning across a wide range of tasks and real-world challenges. \texttt{MPRBench} consists of 12 sub-tasks and additionally supports interpretable analysis of representative error cases. Through extensive experiments, we find that current personalized MLLMs still struggle with personalized reasoning due to several key challenges, including inaccurate recognition of personalized concepts and sensitivity to irrelevant personal information. We hope that MPRBench will stimulate further research on personalized reasoning in MLLMs. Code and data are available at this https URL

AI.tldr: MPRBench is a benchmark of 12 sub-tasks for evaluating personalized reasoning in multimodal large language models, with support for interpretable analysis of error cases. Experiments show that current personalized MLLMs still struggle with it.
AI.motivation: People make decisions by reasoning holistically over heterogeneous personal information, yet multimodal personalized reasoning in MLLMs is relatively underexplored.
AI.method: The authors introduce MPRBench, a benchmark of 12 sub-tasks designed to evaluate personalized reasoning across a wide range of tasks and real-world challenges, which also supports interpretable analysis of representative error cases.
AI.result: Current personalized MLLMs still struggle with personalized reasoning, mainly because of inaccurate recognition of personalized concepts and sensitivity to irrelevant personal information.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark is intended to stimulate further research on personalized reasoning in MLLMs, and its code and data are released.

title: DyPSI: Dynamic Physics Sensing via Joint Field and Sensor-Trajectory Generation
summary: Physics sensing in evolving environments requires reconstructing dense spatiotemporal fields from sparse observations while adapting where future observations should be collected. Existing reconstruction and sensor-placement methods have made substantial progress, but they typically rely on static sensing assumptions: they either use a single layout across all frames or optimize placements independently at each frame, which limits their ability to produce temporally coherent sensing trajectories. We introduce DyPSI, a dynamic physics sensing framework that formulates this problem as the joint generation of future fields and sensor trajectories conditioned on historical observations. DyPSI lifts discrete sensor coordinates into continuous Sensor Position Fields, encodes fields and sensing configurations with a shared Functional Tucker representation, and trains a joint diffusion model to generate future fields and sensing trajectories simultaneously in the resulting latent space. A Gaussian-process temporal kernel correlates the perturbation injected during diffusion training, biasing the denoiser toward temporally smooth recoveries, and we further provide an analysis linking the EDM training objective to a sequence-aggregated A-optimality criterion and a kernel-induced bound on discrete trajectory variation. Experiments on turbulent flow, GLORYS12 sea-surface temperature, and 3D car aerodynamics show that DyPSI consistently outperforms static and frame-wise placement strategies, with substantial error reduction under tight sensor budgets. The code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: DyPSI jointly generates future fields and sensor trajectories with a diffusion model in a shared Functional Tucker latent space, outperforming static and frame-wise sensor placement under tight sensor budgets. It is evaluated on turbulent flow, GLORYS12 sea-surface temperature and 3D car aerodynamics.
AI.motivation: Existing reconstruction and sensor-placement methods either use a single layout across all frames or optimize placements independently at each frame, which limits their ability to produce temporally coherent sensing trajectories in evolving environments.
AI.method: DyPSI lifts discrete sensor coordinates into continuous Sensor Position Fields, encodes fields and sensing configurations with a shared Functional Tucker representation, and trains a joint diffusion model conditioned on historical observations; a Gaussian-process temporal kernel correlates the diffusion perturbation to bias the denoiser toward temporally smooth recoveries, and the EDM objective is linked to a sequence-aggregated A-optimality criterion and a kernel-induced bound on discrete trajectory variation.
AI.result: Experiments on turbulent flow, GLORYS12 sea-surface temperature and 3D car aerodynamics show that DyPSI consistently outperforms static and frame-wise placement strategies, with substantial error reduction under tight sensor budgets.
AI.conclusion: Jointly generating fields and sensor trajectories yields temporally coherent sensing plans for physics sensing in evolving environments.

title: Multi-Resident Data Association in Smart Homes via MDP Modeling and Behavior Cloning
summary: Ambient sensors offer a privacy-preserving solution for activity recognition in smart homes, yet they face a critical challenge in multi-resident environments known as Data Association, which aims to identify the resident triggering a specific anonymous sensor event. Existing approaches fundamentally fail to maintain global consistency by often yielding conflicting associations for silent residents. Additionally, these methods frequently suffer from severe trajectory fragmentation caused by the ontological mismatch of applying continuous physical motion models to discrete logical behaviors. To address these limitations, we propose a novel framework that reformulates data association as a sequential decision-making task within a Markov Decision Process (MDP). We solve the defined MDP via Behavior Cloning (BC) to avoid complex reward engineering by directly learning from expert demonstrations. We instantiate the policy using two complementary architectures, including a lightweight Transformer that treats association as a multi-label classification task over linearized event histories, and a fine-tuned Large Language Model (LLM) that reformulates the problem as conditional text generation to leverage pre-trained semantic knowledge. Extensive evaluations on three diverse datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, particularly in resolving concurrent multi-resident events. Furthermore, the LLM-based policy shows preliminary cross-environment transfer potential under benchmark settings, while its robustness in real deployments still requires further validation.

AI.tldr: The paper reformulates data association in multi-resident smart homes as a Markov Decision Process solved by behavior cloning, using a lightweight Transformer and a fine-tuned LLM as policies. It significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on three datasets, especially on concurrent multi-resident events.
AI.motivation: Ambient-sensor activity recognition in multi-resident homes suffers from data association failures, which yield conflicting associations for silent residents, and from trajectory fragmentation caused by applying continuous physical motion models to discrete logical behaviors.
AI.method: Data association is cast as sequential decision-making in an MDP and solved by behavior cloning from expert demonstrations, avoiding complex reward engineering; a lightweight Transformer treats association as multi-label classification over linearized event histories, and a fine-tuned LLM reformulates it as conditional text generation.
AI.result: Evaluations on three diverse datasets show significant outperformance over state-of-the-art baselines, particularly in resolving concurrent multi-resident events; the LLM policy shows preliminary cross-environment transfer potential under benchmark settings, while its robustness in real deployments still requires validation.
AI.conclusion: Behavior cloning over an MDP formulation is a viable route to globally consistent data association in smart homes, although the LLM-based transfer is still preliminary.

title: STEK: Structural-Terrain-Enhanced Koopman-Inspired Cross-Channel Regularization for Retrospective Battery Multi-Target Estimation
summary: Retrospective battery characterization across heterogeneous cells is challenging because cycling records vary substantially with chemistry, protocol, cell format, capacity, and operating conditions. An endpoint charge--discharge curve captures the local condition of an evaluated cycle, while a cell-level lifecycle terrain summarizes structural evolution across the archived trajectory. We propose STEK, a structural-terrain-enhanced framework for retrospective battery multi-target estimation. STEK combines a cell-level lifecycle (dQ/dV) terrain with an endpoint-derived structural proxy through quality-proxy-conditioned gating. Bounded FiLM and a validity-gated residual head refine the endpoint-curve representation while preserving a curve-based prediction pathway. Battery-type and optional material-text representations further condition an identity-centered low-rank linear map, providing a Koopman-inspired cross-channel consistency objective without modeling temporal dynamics or performing rollout. Under the fixed seven-output MIX-battery protocol, the full retrospective setting improves aggregate performance over endpoint-only learned baselines across multiple temporal backbones; this comparison reflects both the additional archived context and the modeling design. Under matched auxiliary inputs, STEK outperforms direct concatenation and quality-unaware FiLM, while descriptor-removal tests show graceful fallback to the endpoint pathway. Deterministic rules remain preferable for directly recoverable capacity summaries. The method targets retrospective archive harmonization rather than online estimation from cycle t alone.

AI.tldr: STEK is a framework for retrospective multi-target battery estimation that combines a lifecycle dQ/dV terrain with an endpoint-derived structural proxy and a Koopman-inspired cross-channel consistency objective. Under the fixed seven-output MIX-battery protocol it improves aggregate performance over endpoint-only learned baselines across multiple temporal backbones.
AI.motivation: Retrospective characterization of heterogeneous battery cells is difficult because cycling records vary with chemistry, protocol, cell format, capacity and operating conditions, and an endpoint charge-discharge curve alone describes only the evaluated cycle.
AI.method: STEK fuses a cell-level lifecycle dQ/dV terrain with an endpoint-derived structural proxy through quality-proxy-conditioned gating, refines the endpoint-curve representation with bounded FiLM and a validity-gated residual head, and adds battery-type and material-text conditioning to an identity-centered low-rank linear map trained with a Koopman-inspired cross-channel consistency objective, without temporal rollout.
AI.result: Under the fixed seven-output MIX-battery protocol, the full retrospective setting improves aggregate performance over endpoint-only learned baselines across multiple temporal backbones. Under matched auxiliary inputs, STEK outperforms direct concatenation and quality-unaware FiLM, and descriptor-removal tests show graceful fallback to the endpoint pathway. Deterministic rules remain preferable for directly recoverable capacity summaries.
AI.conclusion: The method targets retrospective archive harmonization rather than online estimation from cycle t alone, and the abstract notes that the gains reflect both the additional archived context and the modeling design.

title: EnzymeRSI: A dual-loop recursive self-improvement system for enzyme design
summary: Improvement in enzyme engineering is usually pursued by optimising which candidates to assay within a fixed model and workflow; when the bottleneck arises from a mismatched method or a failing workflow, that route is difficult to escape. We present EnzymeRSI, a dual-loop system for recursive self-improvement (RSI). The outer loop evolves harness assets without changing model weights, the inner loop develops prediction and selection algorithms under controlled conditions, and a cloud laboratory system is specified to close the physical loop with quality-controlled feedback. By updating its prediction strategy through iterative comparison, the outer loop raised the mean development-set Spearman correlation on ProteinGym by 0.044 across five assays, reaching 0.335 on CD19 and 0.683 on OPSD (rhodopsin); of the two first places, only CD19 was produced by the outer loop itself. In the self-improvement of the ThermoMPNN algorithm the inner loop reached a PCC of 0.849, and on TadA-Bench it reached a Spearman correlation of 0.307 in 1.13 h. In three prospective wet-lab tests of the system's experimental decision-making, 10 of the 32 candidates that had not been pre-specified for the luciferase RLuc showed at least twice the wild-type activity; a recommended variant of the cytidine deaminase A3A raised 5mC conversion to 90.2%; and path selection in evolution raised the catalytic efficiency of the DNA polymerase KOD-E on a modified substrate to 31.1 times that of the parent. By treating the organisation of the research workflow and the development of algorithms as a single falsifiable dry-to-wet loop, this work offers an evolutionary paradigm for moving beyond the blind spots of a fixed method and for autonomous enzyme engineering.

AI.tldr: EnzymeRSI is a dual-loop recursive self-improvement system for enzyme design in which an outer loop evolves harness assets and an inner loop develops prediction and selection algorithms, with a cloud laboratory specified to close the physical loop. Prospective wet-lab tests produced several improved enzyme variants.
AI.motivation: Enzyme engineering usually optimises which candidates to assay within a fixed model and workflow, so when the bottleneck is a mismatched method or a failing workflow, that route is difficult to escape.
AI.method: The outer loop evolves harness assets without changing model weights, updating its prediction strategy through iterative comparison. The inner loop develops prediction and selection algorithms under controlled conditions. A cloud laboratory system is specified to close the physical loop with quality-controlled feedback.
AI.result: The outer loop raised mean development-set Spearman correlation on ProteinGym by 0.044 across five assays, reaching 0.335 on CD19 and 0.683 on OPSD (rhodopsin). The inner loop reached a PCC of 0.849 on ThermoMPNN self-improvement and a Spearman correlation of 0.307 on TadA-Bench in 1.13 h. In three prospective wet-lab tests, 10 of 32 unpre-specified RLuc candidates showed at least twice wild-type activity, a recommended A3A variant raised 5mC conversion to 90.2%, and path selection raised KOD-E polymerase catalytic efficiency on a modified substrate to 31.1 times the parent.
AI.conclusion: Treating research workflow organisation and algorithm development as a single falsifiable dry-to-wet loop is presented as an evolutionary paradigm for moving beyond the blind spots of a fixed method and for autonomous enzyme engineering.

title: Corralling AI Risks with Grassroots Contracts
summary: AI's inflection point is a fountain of alarming risks. Digital platforms in particular are vulnerable to three major AI risks, as those in control of global platforms cede control to AI, of the algorithms, of membership and of content: (1) AI control of global platforms, social and economic, used by the majority of humanity, resulting in the majority of humanity becoming vulnerable to AI control. (2) Unaccountable AI agents operating anonymously on social and economic digital platforms, side-by-side with humans, possibly masquerading as humans, serving unknown masters with unknown goals, operating under unknown restraints without accountability or culpability. (3) Unattributed deepfakes generated by anonymous AI, with people unable to distinguish them from genuine content and with their producers evading accountability and culpability. Here, we propose to corral these AI risks with grassroots contracts, a digital incarnation of a two-centuries old notion of Pierre-Joseph Proudhon. We present grassroots contracts for a social graph with accountable AI agents and for a social network with digital provenance, and working smartphone apps that implement the two and show how they corral these major AI risks: (1) AI control of global platforms. (2) Unaccountable AI agents. (3) Unattributed deepfakes.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes grassroots contracts, a digital form of a two-centuries-old notion of Pierre-Joseph Proudhon, to corral three AI risks on digital platforms, and presents two designs as working smartphone apps: a social graph with accountable AI agents and a social network with digital provenance.
AI.motivation: AI creates risks on digital platforms: AI control of global platforms used by most of humanity, unaccountable AI agents operating anonymously alongside humans, and unattributed deepfakes that people cannot tell apart from genuine content.
AI.method: Grassroots contracts are applied in two designs, one for a social graph with accountable AI agents and one for a social network with digital provenance, each implemented as a working smartphone app.
AI.result: The abstract claims that the two implemented apps show how grassroots contracts corral each of the three named risks, but it reports no quantitative evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Grassroots contracts are presented as a practical route to making AI agents accountable and digital content attributable on social and economic platforms.

title: Does Context Compression Preserve Refusal Alignment?
summary: Context compression reduces inference cost by encoding inputs into compact representations while preserving semantic content. An open question is whether semantic preservation alone is sufficient to maintain downstream behaviours such as refusal alignment. We investigate this question and find that encoder-based compression systematically weakens refusal behaviour in instruction-tuned language models, despite high reconstruction fidelity. This effect persists across model families and compression architectures. Mechanistic analysis shows that compression attenuates activation along the decoder's learned refusal direction. We further explore Memory Steering, a lightweight inference-time intervention that restores refusal rates to near-baseline levels without retraining and operates entirely in compressed representation space. These results demonstrate that semantic preservation does not guarantee behavioural preservation under compression, highlighting the need to explicitly preserve alignment-relevant features in compression-aware systems.

AI.tldr: Encoder-based context compression systematically weakens refusal behaviour in instruction-tuned language models despite high reconstruction fidelity. The authors also propose Memory Steering, an inference-time intervention that restores refusal rates to near-baseline levels.
AI.motivation: Context compression reduces inference cost by encoding inputs into compact representations, but it was an open question whether preserving semantic content alone is enough to maintain downstream behaviours such as refusal alignment.
AI.method: The authors evaluate encoder-based compression across model families and compression architectures and perform mechanistic analysis of activations along the decoder's learned refusal direction. They introduce Memory Steering, a lightweight inference-time intervention that operates entirely in compressed representation space without retraining.
AI.result: Compression attenuates activation along the refusal direction and weakens refusal across model families and compression architectures despite high reconstruction fidelity. Memory Steering restores refusal rates to near-baseline levels.
AI.conclusion: Semantic preservation does not guarantee behavioural preservation under compression, so alignment-relevant features need to be explicitly preserved in compression-aware systems.

title: LegalEvolver: Agentic Legal Judgment Prediction via Rubric-Guided Self-Evolution
summary: As LLM-based agents develop, they have been increasingly applied in the legal domain. Legal Judgment Prediction~(LJP) requires models to conduct multi-step reasoning and external legal evidence retrieval. Existing legal search agents' performance is often constrained by the quality of retrieval queries. They often formulate queries directly from the initial user request, overlooking latent legal issues and legally salient details. To address this issue, we propose \emph{LegalEvolver}, a query optimization framework specifically designed to generate legally informative queries for LJP-oriented retrieval. Sampling high-quality optimized queries and their corresponding search trajectories is challenging, as relying solely on unguided high-temperature rollouts is both inefficient and constrained by the model's initial capabilities. We therefore heuristically optimize queries as seeds, improving the efficiency of trajectory generation. Furthermore, we summarize rollout experience into rubrics and use them to guide multi-round iterative self-evolution. Iteratively performing rubric optimization and rubric-guided RL enables the model to surpass its initial performance ceiling. End-to-end performance on extensive benchmarks demonstrates the effectiveness of query optimization on LJP. Comparisons with direct SFT followed by RL demonstrate the effectiveness of rubric guidance. Evolving rubrics further outperform fixed rubrics, confirming the benefits of self-evolution.

AI.tldr: LegalEvolver is a query optimisation framework for agentic legal judgment prediction that generates legally informative retrieval queries and uses rubrics distilled from rollout experience to guide iterative self-evolution with RL.
AI.motivation: Existing legal search agents are limited by retrieval queries formed directly from the initial user request, which overlook latent legal issues and salient details, while unguided high-temperature rollouts are inefficient and bounded by the model's initial capability.
AI.method: Queries are heuristically optimised to seed trajectory generation, rollout experience is summarised into rubrics, and multi-round iterative self-evolution alternates rubric optimisation with rubric-guided RL.
AI.result: The abstract reports end-to-end effectiveness of query optimisation on extensive LJP benchmarks, that rubric guidance outperforms direct SFT followed by RL, and that evolving rubrics outperform fixed rubrics. It gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Iterating rubric optimisation with rubric-guided RL lets the model surpass its initial performance ceiling, with both query optimisation and self-evolving rubrics contributing to the gains.

title: MA-Mesh: Resilient Multi-Agent Collaboration via Role-based Self-Healing
summary: Effective collaboration in multi-agent systems requires mechanisms for coordination and adaptability in dynamic and uncertain environments. However, existing multi-agent systems rarely model resilience explicitly, instead relying on ad-hoc output correction that limits systematic, runtime management of robustness. In this work, we propose Multi-Agent Mesh (MA-Mesh), a framework that constructs a role-based self-healing layer on top of a collaboration pattern. Specifically, MA-Mesh generates resilience-aware system specifications and synthesizes them into executable multi-agent policy code. To enhance resilience, we introduce two self-healing mechanisms: Cross-agent reflection, a mechanism that allows agents to evaluate not only their own outcomes but also the performance of their peers, enabling informed behavioral adjustments and collective policy refinement; Role-based failover, a strategy which dynamically reassigns roles and enables agents to substitute for one another when sub-tasks fail or agents underperform, ensuring continuity of task execution. Experimental results across diverse tasks (e.g., software development, tool use, scientific reasoning) demonstrate that MA-Mesh significantly outperforms existing multi-agent systems in both task performance and robustness under system uncertainty.

AI.tldr: MA-Mesh adds a role-based self-healing layer to multi-agent collaboration, combining cross-agent reflection and role-based failover to improve task performance and robustness under system uncertainty.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-agent systems rarely model resilience explicitly and rely on ad hoc output correction, which limits systematic runtime management of robustness.
AI.method: MA-Mesh generates resilience-aware system specifications, synthesises them into executable multi-agent policy code, and adds two mechanisms. Cross-agent reflection lets agents evaluate peers' performance as well as their own, and role-based failover dynamically reassigns roles so agents can substitute for one another when sub-tasks fail or agents underperform.
AI.result: The abstract reports that MA-Mesh significantly outperforms existing multi-agent systems in task performance and robustness under system uncertainty across diverse tasks, including software development, tool use and scientific reasoning. It gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modelled resilience through role-based self-healing is presented as a route to more robust multi-agent collaboration.

title: GIST: Gibbs-Targeted Hierarchical Data Selection for Offline RLVR
summary: Offline reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) trains on a fixed pool of sampled responses and typically supervises every token of every response, although responses and tokens are not equally informative. We study which ones to supervise through the Gibbs-optimal policy of KL-regularized RLVR, which offline training targets, and measure the mismatch between a policy and this target with a bidirectional KL divergence. At the reference policy, this mismatch factorizes exactly and separates the two outcomes: correct responses contribute mainly through the forward term, concentrated on their low-probability tokens, and incorrect responses through the reverse term, concentrated on the responses the policy generates often and on their high-probability tokens. Based on this analysis, we propose GIST (Gibbs-Targeted Hierarchical Data Selection), a two-level selection method that approximates these principles with signals available before training. GIST uses the sampling temperature to select correct responses on-policy and incorrect responses near the policy's mode, and it uses the initial policy's token probabilities to supervise only the tokens where the mismatch lies. Applied to two offline training objectives, GIST raises the average accuracy over GSM8K, MATH-500, and MBPP for all three models under both objectives. In a controlled comparison on Qwen3-0.6B/GSM8K, it outperforms seven selection baselines that choose from the same candidates while supervising 66.6% fewer tokens than training on all candidates of the same prompts.

AI.tldr: GIST is a two-level data selection method for offline RLVR that chooses which responses and tokens to supervise, guided by the Gibbs-optimal policy target. It raises average accuracy on GSM8K, MATH-500 and MBPP while supervising 66.6% fewer tokens than training on all candidates in a controlled comparison.
AI.motivation: Offline RLVR supervises every token of every response in a fixed pool, although responses and tokens are not equally informative, and it was unclear which ones matter for the Gibbs-optimal policy that offline training targets.
AI.method: The mismatch between a policy and the Gibbs-optimal target is measured with a bidirectional KL divergence, which at the reference policy factorises into a forward term for correct responses, concentrated on their low-probability tokens, and a reverse term for incorrect responses, concentrated on frequently generated, high-probability tokens. GIST uses sampling temperature to select correct responses on-policy and incorrect responses near the policy mode, and the initial policy's token probabilities to supervise only the tokens where the mismatch lies.
AI.result: Applied to two offline training objectives, GIST raises average accuracy over GSM8K, MATH-500 and MBPP for all three models. On Qwen3-0.6B with GSM8K, it outperforms seven selection baselines that choose from the same candidates while supervising 66.6% fewer tokens than training on all candidates of the same prompts.
AI.conclusion: Signals available before training are enough to approximate the Gibbs-targeted selection principles, improving accuracy while reducing the number of supervised tokens.

title: D3D: Decoupled Diffusion Drafting for Asynchronous Speculative Decoding
summary: Target-conditioned diffusion drafters predict candidate tokens in parallel, yet each new block must wait for updated target-model hidden states. This forces drafting and verification to run sequentially, limiting speedup even though each block is generated in one pass. We introduce D3D, a standalone diffusion drafter that removes this inter-round dependency. D3D combines blockwise denoising with auxiliary autoregressive supervision to achieve long accepted prefixes without target hidden states. This independence lets D3D draft successor blocks during verification in one packed pass, enabling asynchronous speculative decoding. We progressively prune layers according to their effect on acceptance length to reduce the cost of packed drafting. Removing five of 36 layers retains over 99\% of mean acceptance length across three benchmarks with Qwen3-8B as the target. Across seven benchmarks, D3D averages 5.00$\times$ and 5.71$\times$ decoding speedup with Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B targets, compared with 4.03$\times$ and 3.67$\times$ for DFlash. On GSM8K with Qwen3-32B, speedup reaches 7.48$\times$. Code is publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: D3D is a standalone diffusion drafter for speculative decoding that removes the dependence on updated target hidden states, enabling asynchronous drafting and verification. It averages 5.00x and 5.71x decoding speedup with Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B targets, versus 4.03x and 3.67x for DFlash.
AI.motivation: Target-conditioned diffusion drafters must wait for updated target-model hidden states before each new block can be drafted, so drafting and verification run sequentially, which limits speedup even though each block is generated in one pass.
AI.method: D3D combines blockwise denoising with auxiliary autoregressive supervision to reach long accepted prefixes without target hidden states, so it can draft successor blocks during verification in one packed pass. Layers are progressively pruned according to their effect on acceptance length to reduce the cost of packed drafting.
AI.result: Removing five of 36 layers retains over 99% of mean acceptance length across three benchmarks with Qwen3-8B as the target. Across seven benchmarks D3D averages 5.00x and 5.71x speedup with Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B, compared with 4.03x and 3.67x for DFlash, and reaches 7.48x on GSM8K with Qwen3-32B.
AI.conclusion: Removing the inter-round dependency on target hidden states enables asynchronous speculative decoding with higher speedups than DFlash, and the code is publicly available.

title: EviSeek: An Evidence-Centric Agentic Framework for Embodied Active Information Seeking
summary: Active embodied question answering requires agents to acquire evidence through viewpoint changes and physical interaction. The central challenge is to avoid undirected interaction: taking plausible actions without specifying what evidence they should reveal for answering the question. Action plans and accumulated histories alone can leave the informational purpose of an interaction implicit. We introduce EviSeek, a training-free framework that makes question-derived evidence demands explicit acquisition objectives, linking observation-conditioned actions and selectively retained evidence to the information the agent seeks. On 3,436 ESI-Bench questions, EviSeek improves accuracy over the Single-model agent by 7.1 percentage points with Qwen3-VL-32B and 3.7 points with Gemini 3.1 Pro, while improving visual-support-weighted accuracy and reducing mean token usage. These findings support making the informational purpose of interaction explicit, with action selection and evidence retention organized around what the agent needs to learn to answer the question.

AI.tldr: EviSeek is a training-free agentic framework for embodied active question answering that turns question-derived evidence demands into explicit acquisition objectives. On 3,436 ESI-Bench questions it improves accuracy over a single-model agent by 7.1 points with Qwen3-VL-32B and 3.7 points with Gemini 3.1 Pro.
AI.motivation: Active embodied question answering requires evidence acquisition through viewpoint changes and physical interaction, but action plans and accumulated histories leave the informational purpose of an interaction implicit, which leads to undirected interaction.
AI.method: EviSeek makes question-derived evidence demands explicit acquisition objectives, linking observation-conditioned actions and selectively retained evidence to the information the agent needs in order to answer the question.
AI.result: On 3,436 ESI-Bench questions, EviSeek improves accuracy over the single-model agent by 7.1 percentage points with Qwen3-VL-32B and 3.7 points with Gemini 3.1 Pro, while improving visual-support-weighted accuracy and reducing mean token usage.
AI.conclusion: Making the informational purpose of interaction explicit, and organising action selection and evidence retention around it, supports more effective active information seeking.

title: SUMONE: A Simple and Efficient Summarizer for Plug-and-Play Agent Memory
summary: Long-horizon language-model agents accumulate increasingly large interaction histories, making context compaction essential for efficient execution. Existing learned compaction methods often rely on downstream task outcomes or solver behavior, coupling training to specific tasks or agents. We introduce SumOne, a standalone summarizer trained to preserve information in agent histories through masked reconstruction. Given a summary of the expired history, a frozen reconstructor recovers randomly masked portions of the original trajectory; reconstruction quality, combined with a length penalty, provides a task-agnostic reward for optimizing the summarizer with GRPO. This yields self-supervision directly from raw trajectories, without reference summaries or downstream task execution. At inference time, only the lightweight summarizer is retained, enabling plug-and-play context compression for otherwise unchanged agents. We conduct a systematic evaluation of SumOne in long-horizon search and software-engineering tasks. SumOne reduces estimated inference cost by approximately 78\% on DeepSearchQA and 75\% on SWE-bench Verified relative to operating with full context, with absolute decreases of 0.04. The same checkpoint also transfers across downstream models and agent harnesses without additional fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: SumOne is a standalone summariser for agent histories, trained with GRPO against a task-agnostic reward from masked reconstruction. It reduces estimated inference cost by about 78% on DeepSearchQA and 75% on SWE-bench Verified, and the same lightweight checkpoint transfers across downstream models and harnesses.
AI.motivation: Learned context compaction methods often rely on downstream task outcomes or solver behaviour, which couples training to specific tasks or agents.
AI.method: The summariser is trained to preserve information in agent histories through masked reconstruction. A frozen reconstructor recovers masked portions of the original trajectory from the summary of the expired history, and reconstruction quality combined with a length penalty gives a reward for GRPO optimisation. This needs no reference summaries or downstream task execution, and only the lightweight summariser is kept at inference.
AI.result: SumOne reduces estimated inference cost by approximately 78% on DeepSearchQA and 75% on SWE-bench Verified relative to full context, with absolute decreases of 0.04. The same checkpoint transfers across downstream models and agent harnesses without additional fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: The summariser offers task-agnostic, plug-and-play context compression for long-horizon search and software-engineering agents without modifying the agents themselves.

title: AmbiHTMLBench: A Benchmark for HTML-based Visually Rich Document parsing
comment: Check latest benchmark info on this https URL
summary: Traditional document parsing systems use Markdown as their output representation, which is effective for linear text but does not fully preserve fine-grained spatial structure, table geometry, visual hierarchy, or rendering semantics. We show that HTML is advantageous for heterogeneous and layout-sensitive documents whose representations must remain editable, inspectable, and reusable, and introduce AmbiHTMLBench to systematically study this setting. In this benchmark, given a real-world document, a model must recover executable HTML that preserves its content, organization, and visual appearance. The benchmark contains 1,115 diverse pages with structured annotations and evaluates predictions in two different ways: The objective protocol aligns ground-truth and predicted rendered blocks and measures table fidelity, page-level text error, and a two-dimensional layout consistency; a complementary reference-anchored protocol measures perceived fidelity by aligning LLM judges with human preferences. Across ten primary multimodal systems, the best objective score is 0.8092, while the subjective winner is different, demonstrating that automatic decomposition and human-perceived fidelity capture complementary properties. We further fine-tune a small-parameter expert model and find that task-specific adaptation yields good performance on document-to-HTML reconstruction task. These results position AmbiHTMLBench as a diagnostic testbed for building smarter and more logical document parsing systems.

AI.tldr: AmbiHTMLBench is a benchmark of 1,115 pages for parsing visually rich documents into executable HTML, scored by an objective layout protocol and a human-aligned LLM-judge protocol. The best objective score is 0.8092, and the best subjective system is a different one.
AI.motivation: Markdown-based document parsing does not fully preserve fine-grained spatial structure, table geometry, visual hierarchy or rendering semantics, whereas HTML can keep heterogeneous, layout-sensitive documents editable, inspectable and reusable.
AI.method: Given a real-world document, a model must recover executable HTML that preserves its content, organisation and visual appearance. The objective protocol aligns rendered blocks and measures table fidelity, page-level text error and two-dimensional layout consistency, while a reference-anchored protocol measures perceived fidelity with LLM judges aligned to human preferences. The authors also fine-tune a small-parameter expert model.
AI.result: Across ten primary multimodal systems, the best objective score is 0.8092, and the subjective winner is a different system. Task-specific adaptation of the small expert model yields good performance on document-to-HTML reconstruction.
AI.conclusion: The objective and subjective protocols capture complementary properties, and the benchmark is positioned as a diagnostic testbed for building more capable document parsing systems.

title: FPTR: Feasibility-Preserving Transactional Refinement for Deadline-Constrained Joint Beam and Resource Allocation
comment: 14 pages, 4 figures; includes appendix. Code: this https URL
summary: Short-interval wireless schedulers must return a complete, feasible beam-and-resource allocation before each execution deadline, and a late or invalid output gives no utility in the current control cycle. Searching longer can increase transmitted traffic, but it may also miss the deadline or leave only an infeasible intermediate solution. We propose Feasibility-Preserving Transactional Refinement (FPTR), which always keeps a validated feasible allocation, the incumbent. Each refinement stage builds a separate candidate and leaves the incumbent unchanged. A candidate replaces the incumbent only if it is complete, passes the feasibility validator before its stage cutoff, and strictly improves the objective; otherwise it is discarded. Four refinement stages use this rule: buffer-aware resource selection, compatibility-group (CG) user sharing, beam-mask rebuilding from remaining demand, and joint reassignment of two resources. On 150 fixed synthetic instances, the full pipeline (Full) raises traffic by 3.83% on average over a lightweight beam-first reference and by 1.79% over its Base constructor. In a separate suite with matched inputs, Full exceeds six independent search baselines (ALNS, tabu search, GA, simulated annealing, iterated local search, and GRASP) by 6.68-8.35%, where outputs later than 100 ms receive zero utility. All 750 Full runs in the internal suite returned feasible allocations, and none exceeded 100 ms. Separating mandatory output construction from optional refinement lets spare computation time improve the allocation without endangering the incumbent. The open-source implementation supports independent reproduction.

AI.tldr: FPTR is a deadline-constrained beam and resource allocation method that always keeps a validated feasible incumbent and accepts a candidate only if it is complete, feasible and strictly better. The full pipeline outperforms six search baselines by 6.68-8.35% in traffic when late outputs receive zero utility.
AI.motivation: Short-interval wireless schedulers must return a complete, feasible allocation before each deadline, and a late or invalid output has no utility, while longer search can miss the deadline or leave only an infeasible intermediate solution.
AI.method: FPTR keeps a validated feasible incumbent. Four refinement stages (buffer-aware resource selection, compatibility-group user sharing, beam-mask rebuilding from remaining demand, and joint reassignment of two resources) each build a separate candidate, which replaces the incumbent only if it is complete, passes the feasibility validator before its stage cutoff and strictly improves the objective.
AI.result: On 150 fixed synthetic instances, the full pipeline raises traffic by 3.83% over a lightweight beam-first reference and by 1.79% over its Base constructor. Against six independent search baselines (ALNS, tabu search, GA, simulated annealing, iterated local search and GRASP) it is 6.68-8.35% higher in a suite with matched inputs, where outputs later than 100 ms receive zero utility. All 750 full runs in the internal suite returned feasible allocations, and none exceeded 100 ms.
AI.conclusion: Separating mandatory output construction from optional refinement lets spare computation time improve the allocation without endangering the incumbent.

title: Tools Need Not Speak in Text: Latent Context Compression for Agents
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents typically append raw tool outputs to their context. Over multi-step interactions, long and noisy observations incur substantial context overhead and dilute the agent's attention to task-relevant information. Existing token pruning and summarization methods remain constrained by discrete text representations, limiting the achievable compression ratios. In this work, we challenge the prevailing assumption that agents must consume tool observations as explicit text tokens. To this end, we propose Coca-Cola, a continuous latent context compression model for LLM agents. Coca-Cola compresses tool observations into latent tokens and embeds them into the input embedding space of the agent. We further introduce Action-Preserving Training, which aligns the agent's next-action distributions under full and compressed observations. This trains the compression model to learn action-sufficient latent tokens that retain decision-critical information. Experiments with web-search agents on four QA benchmarks and two model families show that Coca-Cola reduces the agent's token consumption by 70.01%-89.24% and end-to-end runtime by 24.45%-55.97%, while consistently improving task performance. These results suggest that Coca-Cola offers a promising approach for context compression in agents. Our code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Coca-Cola compresses LLM agent tool observations into continuous latent tokens embedded in the agent's input embedding space. On web-search agents it reduces token consumption by 70.01%-89.24% and end-to-end runtime by 24.45%-55.97% while consistently improving task performance.
AI.motivation: Agents append raw tool outputs as text, and long, noisy observations add context overhead and dilute attention to task-relevant information, while discrete text pruning and summarisation limit the achievable compression ratio.
AI.method: Coca-Cola is a continuous latent context compression model that compresses tool observations into latent tokens embedded in the agent's input embedding space. Action-Preserving Training aligns the agent's next-action distributions under full and compressed observations, so the compressor learns action-sufficient latent tokens that keep decision-critical information.
AI.result: Experiments with web-search agents on four QA benchmarks and two model families show that Coca-Cola reduces token consumption by 70.01%-89.24% and end-to-end runtime by 24.45%-55.97%, while consistently improving task performance.
AI.conclusion: Agents need not consume tool observations as explicit text, and continuous latent tokens are a promising approach to context compression for agents.

title: ElecLoad: Adaptive Electricity Load Forecasting Guided by Multiple Events
summary: Accurate electricity load forecasting provides critical decision support for energy procurement, generation scheduling, and supply-demand balancing, contributing to the economic efficiency and operational reliability of power systems. However, future electricity demand can be affected by the complex interplay of multiple events described in Web notices, weather alerts, and event schedules. Their effects vary over time and can reinforce or offset one another, making electricity load difficult to forecast accurately. While existing methods can incorporate context as additional input, how to use the effects of multiple events and their interactions to guide the load forecasting process itself remains to be explored. To address this gap, we propose ElecLoad, a context-aware agent for multi-event electricity load forecasting that adaptively organizes the forecasting process. Specifically, we train ElecLoad to combine historical load with context to analyze each event's relevance to the target load, the timing of its effects, and potential interactions among events. Guided by this analysis, ElecLoad adaptively chooses to forecast the entire forecast horizon directly or to partition it into segments according to changes in event effects. When the horizon is partitioned, sub-agents independently generate initial forecasts for each segment. The main agent then reviews these forecasts, and the sub-agents perform selective refinement guided by its feedback. Experiments on multiple electricity load datasets show that ElecLoad achieves state-of-the-art performance in most evaluation scenarios. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: ElecLoad is a context-aware agent for electricity load forecasting that analyses multiple events and adaptively chooses between direct and segmented forecasting with sub-agents. It achieves state-of-the-art performance in most evaluation scenarios on multiple electricity load datasets.
AI.motivation: Future demand is shaped by interacting events described in web notices, weather alerts and schedules, whose effects vary over time and can reinforce or offset one another, while existing methods use context only as extra input rather than to guide the forecasting process itself.
AI.method: ElecLoad trains an agent to combine historical load with context to analyse each event's relevance, the timing of its effects and interactions among events. Guided by this analysis it either forecasts the whole horizon directly or partitions it by changes in event effects, in which case sub-agents forecast each segment, the main agent reviews the forecasts, and sub-agents refine selectively under its feedback.
AI.result: ElecLoad achieves state-of-the-art performance in most evaluation scenarios on multiple electricity load datasets. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Using the effects of multiple events to guide the forecasting process itself is presented as an improvement over treating context as additional input.

title: Using Experience Twice: Dynamic Process Rubrics for Privileged Token-Level Credit Assignment
summary: Agent trajectories often contain both successful decisions and failed attempts, yet optimization with sparse trajectory-level rewards struggles to identify which critical decisions should be reinforced or suppressed. We observe that meaningful distinctions among on-policy trajectories can be distilled into natural-language process rubrics and used as process supervision signals. Based on this insight, we propose Online Rubric Self-Distillation (ORSD), which leverages self-derived process rubrics for dense token-level supervision, thereby augmenting outcome-centric reinforcement learning. Specifically, the current policy independently generates multiple rubric bundles at each step according to the same group of trajectories, extracting candidate process rubrics from cross-trajectory behavioral differences. A frozen verifier then evaluates all rubric items against each trajectory in the group, and selects one candidate bundle based on bundle-level alignment between rubric satisfaction and task success. ORSD treats the selected rubric bundle as privileged information during training, then compares the log-likelihoods of the original tokens with and without the rubric. The resulting likelihood gap provides token-specific process credit, which is added to the original trajectory-level GRPO advantage through additive advantage shaping. ORSD thus bridges trajectory-level outcome supervision and fine-grained process supervision, enabling token-level credit assignment using process signals. Extensive experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop show that ORSD accelerates policy improvement and boosts final task performance for both Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B under the same environment-interaction budget. Our code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: ORSD, Online Rubric Self-Distillation, derives natural-language process rubrics from cross-trajectory differences and turns their likelihood gap into token-level credit added to GRPO advantages. It boosts final task performance on ALFWorld and WebShop for Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B under the same interaction budget.
AI.motivation: Sparse trajectory-level rewards make it hard to identify which critical decisions in trajectories containing both successes and failed attempts should be reinforced or suppressed.
AI.method: At each step the current policy generates multiple rubric bundles from a group of on-policy trajectories, extracting candidate process rubrics from cross-trajectory behavioural differences. A frozen verifier scores rubric items against each trajectory and selects the bundle whose satisfaction best aligns with task success. The selected bundle is treated as privileged information, and the log-likelihood gap of the original tokens with and without the rubric gives token-specific process credit, added to the trajectory-level GRPO advantage through additive advantage shaping.
AI.result: Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop show that ORSD accelerates policy improvement and boosts final task performance for both Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B under the same environment-interaction budget.
AI.conclusion: ORSD bridges trajectory-level outcome supervision and fine-grained process supervision, enabling token-level credit assignment from process signals within outcome-centric reinforcement learning.

title: Addition by Subtraction: Toward Mitigating Fragile Safety Alignment in Large Language Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) undergo safety alignment to prevent harmful generations, yet they remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks. Recent work reveals a deeper structural weakness: safety alignment can be highly sparse, such that pruning a small number of safety-critical neurons or ablating a single refusal direction can substantially undermine aligned behavior. In this work, we take the first steps toward strengthening safety alignment such that it is less dependent on sparse model components. We propose Addition by Subtraction, which gradually removes identified safety-critical neurons during finetuning and uses preference optimization to re-establish safety-aligned behavior through other parts of the model. Our results show that the resulting models are substantially more robust to pruning-based attacks. Remarkably, these benefits generalize beyond the white-box attacks motivating our design: Addition by Subtraction improves robustness against other sparsity-based interventions, including refusal-direction ablation, as well as a broad range of black-box jailbreak attacks. The finetuned models also exhibit improved truthfulness while largely preserving general capabilities. Comprehensive experiments across four models from three vendors demonstrate consistent improvements in safety robustness, reducing attack success rates by up to 90% for some attacks.

AI.tldr: Addition by Subtraction removes identified safety-critical neurons during finetuning and uses preference optimisation to re-establish safety through other parts of the model. The resulting models are substantially more robust to pruning-based attacks and reduce attack success rates by up to 90% for some attacks.
AI.motivation: Safety alignment can be highly sparse, so pruning a few safety-critical neurons or ablating a single refusal direction can substantially undermine aligned behaviour, and the authors seek alignment that depends less on sparse components.
AI.method: The method gradually removes identified safety-critical neurons during finetuning and uses preference optimisation to restore safety-aligned behaviour through other parts of the model.
AI.result: The resulting models are substantially more robust to pruning-based attacks, and the benefits extend to refusal-direction ablation, other sparsity-based interventions and a broad range of black-box jailbreak attacks. The finetuned models also show improved truthfulness while largely preserving general capabilities. Across four models from three vendors, attack success rates fall by up to 90% for some attacks.
AI.conclusion: Reducing reliance on sparse safety-critical components yields broader robustness to jailbreaks and sparsity-based interventions while largely preserving general capability.

title: RAGAM-AI: A Hybrid Reinforcement Learning based Agentic approach powered by Generative AI for Edge Resource Management
summary: Resource management for distributed edge networks hosting different services has been handled efficiently using Reinforcement learning (RL). Reward generalization in complex workflows is still an open issue within the RL realm. Therefore, this work proposes RAGAM-AI, a hybrid framework that combines the capabilities of RL algorithms and Generative-AI (Gen-AI) for powering an Agentic AI workflow that optimizes resource allocation at the Multi-access Edge Computing (MEC) units. This framework further resolves the reward generalization issue by utilizing Large Language Model (LLM) for feedback. A Multi- Agent Soft-Actor Critic (MASAC) using Math{\Sigma}tral as a reward oracle is implemented for managing resource allocations at the MEC. RAGAM-AI interprets system state information and evaluates multi-objective trade-offs guiding the resource orchestration loop over distributed edge server agents. The complexity of the framework is further brought down by incorporating surrogate reward model. The overall performance is evaluated against the single agent SAC, REINFORCE and random policies for benchmarking. On using RAGAM-AI, lower allocation deviations for CPU, memory and bandwidth resources are reported while minimizing the latency and data rate costs. A scalable AI as a feedback (AIAF) solution optimizing network resources with significant performance improvement is thus presented.

AI.tldr: RAGAM-AI is a hybrid RL and generative-AI framework for edge resource management in which a multi-agent soft actor-critic uses the LLM Mathstral as a reward oracle. It reports lower allocation deviations for CPU, memory and bandwidth while reducing latency and data rate costs.
AI.motivation: RL-based resource management for distributed edge networks has the open problem of reward generalisation in complex workflows.
AI.method: A Multi-Agent Soft Actor-Critic (MASAC) manages resource allocation across edge server agents, using Mathstral as a reward oracle that interprets system state and multi-objective trade-offs to provide LLM feedback. A surrogate reward model is used to reduce the complexity of the framework.
AI.result: Evaluated against single-agent SAC, REINFORCE and random policies, RAGAM-AI reports lower allocation deviations for CPU, memory and bandwidth while minimising latency and data rate costs. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Using AI as feedback is presented as a scalable solution for optimising network resources with significant performance improvement.

title: One Scale, Four Texts: Gaps, Overlaps and Silent Repairs in Published Grading Schemes
summary: Category systems often reach their users as text, and readers apply them with tacit repairs. We ask what such a text determines once the repairs are removed, using diabetic retinopathy grading, where one international scale circulates in several documents. We transcribe four texts (the English screening definitions of 2025, the international scale as tabulated in 2017 and as published in 2003, and an Italian guideline of 2015) into one rule language over 24 finding variables, and make every point a text leaves open a named precisification. Exhaustive enumeration of 1,425,807,360 finding profiles, re-derived by an SMT solver and spot-checked by an OWL reasoner, shows that every text that assigns actions leaves some eyes without a category under every reading; that the 2017 tabulation has a proliferative class that is empty when read literally and a macular gap that the 2003 text lacks, so that no function maps the 2003 grades onto the 2017 grades; and that on image findings alone the English and Italian texts order some pairs of eyes in opposite ways. On 927 annotated photographs from three public datasets, with retinal thickening assumed absent, the English text and the 2017 tabulation disagree on referral for 26.8% of the eyes of one dataset (DDR) on which both decide, and in a pre-registered experiment classifiers trained on each text's labels side with their own text. Thickening cannot be seen on a colour photograph; left free, every disagreement involving England becomes undecidable, so it rests on what the camera cannot show. In a second pre-registered study, language models that answered without deliberating repaired most gap and overlap items even when told to read literally, while Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Opus 5.5 reported the defects far more often; within two models, deliberation reduced silent repair without removing it.

AI.tldr: Using diabetic retinopathy grading as a case, the paper shows that four published texts of one scale leave gaps and overlaps that readers repair silently. The English 2025 text and the 2017 tabulation disagree on referral for 26.8% of eyes in one dataset, DDR, where both decide.
AI.motivation: Category systems reach users as text, and readers apply them with tacit repairs, so the question is what a text determines once those repairs are removed.
AI.method: The four texts (the 2025 English screening definitions, the international scale as tabulated in 2017 and as published in 2003, and a 2015 Italian guideline) are transcribed into one rule language over 24 finding variables, and every point a text leaves open is made a named precisification. Exhaustive enumeration of 1,425,807,360 finding profiles is re-derived with an SMT solver and spot-checked with an OWL reasoner. On 927 annotated photographs from three public datasets, referral decisions are compared, and two pre-registered studies are run.
AI.result: Every text that assigns actions leaves some eyes without a category under every reading. The 2017 tabulation has a proliferative class that is empty when read literally and a macular gap that the 2003 text lacks, so no function maps 2003 grades onto 2017 grades. On image findings alone the English and Italian texts order some pairs of eyes in opposite ways. Classifiers trained on each text's labels side with their own text. In the second study, language models that answered without deliberating repaired most gap and overlap items, while Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Opus 5.5 reported the defects far more often, and within two models deliberation reduced silent repair without removing it.
AI.conclusion: Thickening cannot be seen on a colour photograph, so disagreements involving England become undecidable from images, and published grading texts carry silent repairs that readers and models apply without noticing.

title: Time-Division Multiplexing: The Operational Rhythm and Temporal Organization Layer of Digital Life
summary: Continual agents must handle urgent interaction while retaining alternatives, replaying errors, and committing safe long-term changes. A previous digital-life framework distinguishes online (busy) and offline (idle) channels, but leaves open whether these are separate programs or phases of a common process and how their operations should be ordered. Motivated by recent observations of rapidly alternating perceptual representations in primate cortex, we develop a temporal organization layer with phase-tagged micro-epochs, an observable duty cycle, independent content and resource controls, and three nested clocks separating candidate exploration from durable commitment. We give a projected duty-cycle update, state its deterministic descent guarantee and the additional noise term required for a stochastic guarantee, and specify coupled busy/idle execution contracts. Five synthetic experiments (64 seeds each) examine descent and noise, objective misalignment, gain asymmetry, resource coupling, and dropped replay logs. In the gain/noise model the best tested gain ratio is 1.55; decoupled scheduling yields 26.6% versus 11.1% success on a constructed urgent/high-load subset. A frozen-backbone Qwen3-8B prototype further checks orchestration, but its proxy outcomes are not task-benchmark evidence. The results establish a testable scheduling design and identify its conditions of validity, not machine consciousness or general-purpose agent superiority.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a temporal organisation layer for continual agents that alternates online and offline work through phase-tagged micro-epochs and a projected duty-cycle update. Decoupled scheduling reaches 26.6% success versus 11.1% on a constructed urgent/high-load subset.
AI.motivation: Continual agents must handle urgent interaction while retaining alternatives, replaying errors and committing safe long-term changes, and a prior digital-life framework left open whether online and offline channels are separate programs or phases of one process and how their operations should be ordered.
AI.method: The authors develop a temporal organisation layer with phase-tagged micro-epochs, an observable duty cycle, independent content and resource controls, and three nested clocks that separate candidate exploration from durable commitment. They give a projected duty-cycle update with a deterministic descent guarantee, the additional noise term needed for a stochastic guarantee, and coupled busy/idle execution contracts.
AI.result: Across five synthetic experiments with 64 seeds each, the best tested gain ratio in the gain/noise model is 1.55, and decoupled scheduling yields 26.6% versus 11.1% success on a constructed urgent/high-load subset. A frozen-backbone Qwen3-8B prototype checks orchestration, but its proxy outcomes are not task-benchmark evidence.
AI.conclusion: The results establish a testable scheduling design and its conditions of validity, without claims of machine consciousness or general-purpose agent superiority.

title: Interactive World Simulation with Cosmos for Physical AI
summary: We present a shared framework that adapts Cosmos world foundation models for real-time interactive world simulation in Physical AI. By streaming visual observations in response to actions and scene controls, the framework enables users and embodied agents to interact with evolving virtual environments. It supports both predicting the visual consequences of actions and generating observations from physical state maintained by an external simulator. We demonstrate this approach across camera navigation and robot manipulation, controllable video transfer, and multi-view autonomous vehicle (AV) simulation. These examples provide a shared foundation for developing interactive virtual environments for Physical AI training and evaluation. Our code and model checkpoints are available at this https URL and this https URL. The project website is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a shared framework that adapts Cosmos world foundation models for real-time interactive world simulation, streaming visual observations in response to actions and scene controls. It is aimed at Physical AI training and evaluation.
AI.motivation: The abstract states no explicit gap in existing work; it motivates the framework by the need for a shared foundation for interactive virtual environments for Physical AI training and evaluation.
AI.method: The framework adapts Cosmos world foundation models to stream visual observations in response to actions and scene controls. It supports both predicting the visual consequences of actions and generating observations from physical state maintained by an external simulator.
AI.result: The approach is demonstrated across camera navigation and robot manipulation, controllable video transfer, and multi-view autonomous vehicle simulation. The abstract reports no quantitative results.
AI.conclusion: The framework is offered as a shared foundation for developing interactive virtual environments for Physical AI training and evaluation, with code and model checkpoints released.

title: From Certified Pairs to a Certified Hub: Reasoner-Checked Crosswalks for the Information Exchange Standard
summary: A national digital twin was conceived as an ecosystem of twins connected through mappings to a common foundation, but the roadmap that promises to confirm those mappings are valid never says what valid means. We give the test a precise form, coherence and conservativity of the merged ontology, borrowed from logic-based alignment repair, and apply it to the Information Exchange Standard (IES), first pair by pair and then to whole hubs. Crosswalks from IES into thirteen ontologies across seven sector groups, anchored on the building ontologies BOT, Brick, and SAREF4BLDG, pass through separate stages of matching, human review, certification of each SKOS correspondence against the two class hierarchies, and reasoning with HermiT. Pair by pair, the stages catch different failures: certification alone removed all 526 conservativity violations of the raw crosswalks, review alone left 73, and together they made eleven of twelve overlapping pairs coherent and conservative. Pairwise certification does not compose.
