Merging the three certified building crosswalks into one hub made five Brick classes unsatisfiable, through a homonym between the IES and Brick notions of a floor that only BOT's disjointness axioms expose; rejecting that one row gave a coherent and conservative hub that entails 290 cross-ontology links nobody wrote down. The core hub is inconsistent before any crosswalk is added, because two published standards, the Open Energy Ontology and BFO 2020, contradict each other; with either one left out it is coherent and conservative. A hub, not a pair, is the unit an ecosystem of twins has to certify.

AI.tldr: The paper gives a precise test for crosswalks in a national digital twin, namely coherence and conservativity of the merged ontology, and applies it to the Information Exchange Standard (IES) pair by pair and as whole hubs. Pairwise certification does not compose, and the core hub is inconsistent before any crosswalk is added because the Open Energy Ontology and BFO 2020 contradict each other.
AI.motivation: The national digital twin roadmap promises to confirm that mappings between twins are valid but never says what valid means, so an ecosystem of twins lacks a defined certification test.
AI.method: Coherence and conservativity of the merged ontology are borrowed from logic-based alignment repair. Crosswalks from IES into thirteen ontologies across seven sector groups, anchored on BOT, Brick and SAREF4BLDG, pass through matching, human review, certification of each SKOS correspondence against the two class hierarchies, and reasoning with HermiT.
AI.result: Certification alone removed all 526 conservativity violations of the raw crosswalks, review alone left 73, and together they made eleven of twelve overlapping pairs coherent and conservative. Merging the three certified building crosswalks made five Brick classes unsatisfiable through an IES and Brick homonym for floor, exposed only by BOT's disjointness axioms; rejecting that one row gave a coherent and conservative hub that entails 290 cross-ontology links nobody wrote down.
AI.conclusion: Pairwise certification does not compose, so the hub rather than the pair is the unit that an ecosystem of twins has to certify.

title: Where Search Agents Go Off the Rails: Graph-Grounded Step-Level Verification
summary: Search-augmented reasoning systems can reach correct answers while making errors in intermediate steps. Reliable auditing must check whether evidence $D$ covers the question $Q$, reasoning $T$ addresses $Q$, and $T$ is grounded in $D$. We introduce GraphRail, which represents requirements, evidence, and reasoning as structured claims and compares them without a generative judge or gold answer. Across three multi-hop QA benchmarks and three reasoning frameworks, GraphRail improves error recall over generative verifiers while remaining stable under stochastic extraction. Its diagnoses can also guide online reasoning, providing a traceable way to detect and correct intermediate errors.

AI.tldr: GraphRail audits search-augmented reasoning step by step by representing requirements, evidence and reasoning as structured claims and comparing them, with no generative judge or gold answer. Across three multi-hop QA benchmarks and three reasoning frameworks it improves error recall over generative verifiers.
AI.motivation: Search-augmented reasoning can reach correct answers while making errors in intermediate steps, so auditing must check whether the evidence covers the question, whether the reasoning addresses it, and whether the reasoning is grounded in the evidence.
AI.method: GraphRail represents requirements, evidence and reasoning as structured claims and compares them without a generative judge or gold answer. Its diagnoses can also be used to guide online reasoning.
AI.result: Across three multi-hop QA benchmarks and three reasoning frameworks, GraphRail improves error recall over generative verifiers while remaining stable under stochastic extraction.
AI.conclusion: The structured diagnoses give a traceable way to detect and correct intermediate errors in search agents.

title: LifeVal: Evaluating AI Model Performance on Personalized Agentic Consumer Tasks
summary: We introduce LifeVal, a benchmark evaluating AI model performance on personalized agentic consumer tasks. LifeVal covers the most valuable life tasks that a personalized digital superassistant could automate, representing over 1.7 trillion US dollars in annual willingness-to-pay across 148 consumer task categories (e.g., managing finances, moving apartments, searching for a job, finding childcare). To construct our activity distribution, we conducted a new survey of willingness-to-pay for a digital superassistant across a demographically representative sample of over 3,800 consumers, cross-referencing our results against the American Time Use Survey (Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025) and the Multinational Time Use Study (Fisher et al., 2025). For the most valuable consumer activities, we recruited task creators to create AI evaluation tasks personalized using real ChatGPT conversations and memories, reference files, and personal context. Task creators had to pass our expertise threshold (including personally completing the task multiple times and seeing the results through in their real lives for over a year) and also write a rubric, ensuring that our evaluation measured the best personalized completion for that task. All tasks had to pass at least three rounds of human quality-control before acceptance into our final evaluation sets.

AI.tldr: LifeVal is a benchmark of personalized agentic consumer tasks across 148 task categories, covering life tasks that a personalized digital superassistant could automate. Its tasks are written by expert task creators using real ChatGPT conversations, memories and personal context, and each task passes at least three rounds of human quality control.
AI.motivation: The benchmark targets consumer tasks worth over 1.7 trillion US dollars in annual willingness-to-pay for a personalized digital superassistant, which the abstract presents as the value that evaluation should cover.
AI.method: A survey of willingness-to-pay across a demographically representative sample of over 3,800 consumers, cross-referenced with the American Time Use Survey and the Multinational Time Use Study, sets the activity distribution. Task creators who pass an expertise threshold, including completing the task several times and seeing it through in real life for over a year, write personalized tasks and rubrics.
AI.result: The abstract reports no model results; it describes the benchmark's construction over 148 consumer task categories.
AI.conclusion: LifeVal supplies an expert-built, personalized evaluation set whose task weighting is grounded in survey and time-use data.

title: ConceptARC at Scale: Studying Conceptual Understanding in Reasoning Models
summary: Large reasoning models (LRMs) perform well on challenging benchmarks, yet it remains unclear whether they form generalizable abstractions across conceptually related reasoning tasks. The Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC) provides a controlled testbed for studying abstraction, requiring solvers to infer transformation rules over two-dimensional grids from a small set of examples. While ARC evaluates rule abstraction within individual tasks, different tasks may share higher-level structure despite requiring different transformations$\unicode{x2014}$for example, several tasks may involve reasoning about objects contained within other objects. Benchmarks such as ConceptARC capture this structure by grouping ARC-style tasks into recurring spatial and semantic concepts, but they often contain only a few manually constructed tasks per concept. We introduce ConceptARC at Scale, a generator for creating thousands of ARC-style tasks targeting a specific concept. Using this generator, we construct ConceptARC-100, a dataset of 1,600 new, manually reviewed tasks, with 100 tasks for each of the 16 concepts defined by ConceptARC$\unicode{x2014}$ten times the size of the original benchmark. We evaluate a range of recent LRMs and models trained from scratch on ConceptARC-100 to characterize which concepts they solve reliably and where they struggle. We further analyze the models' internal representations and find clear semantic structure: task representations cluster according to the operations applied to objects, such as recoloring, removal, or translation, even when realized through substantially different rules and scenarios. Together, our results suggest that models form stable abstractions of transformation operations that generalize across diverse tasks.

AI.tldr: ConceptARC at Scale is a generator of ARC-style tasks that yields ConceptARC-100, 1,600 manually reviewed tasks covering the 16 ConceptARC concepts. Evaluations suggest that reasoning models form stable abstractions of transformation operations that generalize across tasks.
AI.motivation: It is unclear whether large reasoning models form generalizable abstractions across conceptually related ARC tasks, and the original ConceptARC contains only a few manually constructed tasks per concept.
AI.method: A generator creates thousands of ARC-style tasks targeting a specific concept. The authors build ConceptARC-100 with 100 tasks for each of the 16 concepts, evaluate recent reasoning models and models trained from scratch on it, and analyse their internal representations.
AI.result: Models solve some concepts reliably and struggle with others. Task representations cluster by the operation applied to objects, such as recoloring, removal or translation, even when the operation is realized through substantially different rules and scenarios.
AI.conclusion: The results suggest that models form stable abstractions of transformation operations that generalize across diverse tasks.

title: Task-Efficient Agent Evaluation Using Cached Traces
summary: Efficient benchmarking estimates a system's full benchmark performance from a small number of task executions. Standard approaches rely solely on the binary correctness of executions from a collection of already-evaluated reference systems. An agentic system, however, produces a rich trace for each execution that can reveal substantially more about its capabilities. Leveraging this information requires useful trace representations. We propose representing a trace by extracting a structured summary of it with an LLM and embedding the summary with a standard text encoder. These representations preserve correctness- and task-related signal while minimizing the presence of system identity-, model family- and harness-related signals that dominate raw trace embeddings. Given this representation for each task execution from all reference systems, we construct low-dimensional representations of the systems and predict a new system's score from its position among the reference systems. On SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench 2.0, augmenting an item-response model with this geometry-based prediction reduces mean absolute error from 0.13 to 0.08 (Wilcoxon $p < 10^{-4}$) and from 0.14 to 0.12 (Wilcoxon $p < 10^{-3}$), respectively, when provided a single random executed task. Further, given access to the full set of reference systems, our approach dominates baselines for any given number of executed tasks on both benchmarks.

AI.tldr: The paper represents each agent trace by an LLM-extracted structured summary embedded with a text encoder, and uses these representations to predict a new system's benchmark score from few executed tasks. With a single random executed task, mean absolute error falls from 0.13 to 0.08 on SWE-bench Verified and from 0.14 to 0.12 on Terminal-Bench 2.0.
AI.motivation: Efficient benchmarking usually relies only on the binary correctness of executions by reference systems, which ignores the rich traces agentic systems produce, while raw trace embeddings are dominated by system identity, model family and harness signals.
AI.method: Each trace is summarised by an LLM into a structured summary, which a standard text encoder embeds, keeping correctness and task signals while reducing identity signals. Systems are positioned among the reference systems, and a new system's score is predicted from its position, augmenting an item-response model.
AI.result: With a single random executed task, mean absolute error falls from 0.13 to 0.08 on SWE-bench Verified (Wilcoxon p < 0.0001) and from 0.14 to 0.12 on Terminal-Bench 2.0 (p < 0.001). Given the full set of reference systems, the approach dominates baselines for any number of executed tasks on both benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Structured trace summaries offer a more task-efficient way to estimate the benchmark performance of agentic systems.

title: Rules, Traces and Routing Statistics: Training and Calibration Data for Open Models on ARC-AGI-2
summary: We study which training and calibration data help three open models solve ARC-AGI-2 tasks when the solver runs offline on four L4 GPUs for at most 12 hours. We compare data offline on public tasks and report 189 runs on the 120 hidden semi-private tasks. For the NVARC Qwen3-4B grid model, we built a corpus of 12,000 executable rules in a typed language and 95,993 tasks; a rule is admitted only if its behaviour on a fixed probe set differs from that of every admitted rule, and a task only if its pairs refute a shortlist of nearest competing rules and defeat 12 shortcut solvers. Continued fine-tuning on 1,920 real task records with revised four-GPU scheduling raised the semi-private score from 28.96 (mean of the released model) to 33.06 (mean of five runs, best 34.86); no checkpoint trained with synthetic tasks, even all 95,993 of them, improved on the real-task model. For the Qwen3.8-27B reasoning model, we fine-tuned on 1,036 of its own reasoning traces with correct final answers and compared sets that add traces of other models and synthetic tasks. With an inference procedure built around the model (a thinking cap enforced in the serving engine, a Python program checked on the demonstrations after each answer, a long first attempt per input), the score rose from 26.81 to 44.03, the level the ARC Prize Foundation measured for the base model without a time limit (42.36); most of the gain came from the inference procedure. For the Qwen3.8-Flash-Next mixture-of-experts model (125B parameters, 6B active), GPU memory limited concurrency. Pruning from 512 to 384 experts per layer by router-weighted activation saliency grew the key-value cache from 0.55M to 1.39M tokens; a 296-expert list adapted with ARC routing statistics, keeping experts for program tokens, plus an FP8 indexer cache, reached 1.96M. With a tool that checks programs, the model scored 56.67, our best result.

AI.tldr: The paper studies which training and calibration data help three open models solve ARC-AGI-2 tasks when the solver runs offline on four L4 GPUs for at most 12 hours. Real-task fine-tuning outperformed synthetic tasks, and most of the reasoning model's gain came from its inference procedure.
AI.motivation: Open models must solve ARC-AGI-2 tasks under a limited offline budget, and it is unclear which training and calibration data help them do so.
AI.method: Data are compared on public tasks, and 189 runs are reported on the 120 hidden semi-private tasks. For NVARC Qwen3-4B, a corpus of 12,000 executable rules and 95,993 tasks was built and fine-tuning used 1,920 real task records with revised four-GPU scheduling. For Qwen3.8-27B, fine-tuning used 1,036 of its own correct reasoning traces with a thinking cap, a Python program checked on demonstrations, and a long first attempt per input. For Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, expert pruning and a program-checking tool were used.
AI.result: The semi-private score of NVARC Qwen3-4B rose from 28.96 to 33.06 (mean of five runs, best 34.86), and no checkpoint trained on synthetic tasks, even all 95,993 of them, improved on the real-task model. For Qwen3.8-27B the score rose from 26.81 to 44.03, close to the 42.36 measured for the base model without a time limit, with most of the gain from the inference procedure. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next with the program-checking tool scored 56.67, the paper's best result.
AI.conclusion: Under a fixed compute budget, real task data and inference procedure design mattered more than synthetic tasks for these open models.

title: ServerBench: How can your coding agents design specialized LLM serving systems?
summary: Large language model (LLM) coding agents develop software through experimentation, offering an opportunity to design the serving systems supporting their own operation. Effective serving requires coordinating implementation and operating decisions under session dependencies, latency constraints, and correctness requirements. We introduce ServerBench, a benchmark for agentic design of complete, specialized LLM serving systems. Agents experiment against a common objective, dollars per dollar: latency-qualified token value per dollar of GPU cost. Stateful replay preserves session dependencies, and independent verification checks the submitted system. Across 11 coding-agent models and three deployments, Claude Sonnet 5.5 achieves 2.97 dollars per dollar on Gemma E4B, $4.87\times$ the vLLM reference; 22 of 33 runs yield verified systems, and 13 exceed the strongest baseline. Our analysis identifies three findings: high-value designs coordinate capacity improvements with load selection; agents interpret performance feedback through workload-relevant experiments; and reliable delivery requires verification of the execution paths introduced by optimization. Overall, ServerBench supports systematic study of how agents translate service objectives and feedback into effective, verified serving systems for given task specifications.

AI.tldr: ServerBench is a benchmark in which coding agents design complete, specialized LLM serving systems against a dollars-per-dollar objective. Claude Sonnet 5.5 reaches 2.97 dollars per dollar on Gemma E4B, 4.87 times the vLLM reference, and 22 of 33 runs yield verified systems.
AI.motivation: Effective LLM serving requires coordinating implementation and operating decisions under session dependencies, latency constraints and correctness requirements, which coding agents could handle through experimentation.
AI.method: Agents experiment against a common objective, latency-qualified token value per dollar of GPU cost. Stateful replay preserves session dependencies, and independent verification checks each submitted system.
AI.result: Across 11 coding-agent models and three deployments, Claude Sonnet 5.5 achieves 2.97 dollars per dollar on Gemma E4B, 4.87 times the vLLM reference; 22 of 33 runs yield verified systems, and 13 exceed the strongest baseline.
AI.conclusion: High-value designs coordinate capacity improvements with load selection, agents interpret feedback through workload-relevant experiments, and verification of the execution paths introduced by optimization is needed for reliable delivery.

title: CompressionBench: How can your coding agents compress LLMs?
summary: Recursive self-improvement requires AI systems to improve the models and infrastructure used by subsequent systems. LLM compression offers a concrete efficiency objective: retain a pretrained model's behavior within a smaller model storage budget. We study whether coding agents can carry out this step autonomously. We formulate compression as a terminal task in which an agent receives a source checkpoint, storage limit, inference environment, and time budget, then constructs compressed weights and executable inference code. The agent controls its algorithm and experiments; perplexity feedback guides search, and independent verification checks the final model. Across six agents and six model--size settings, 29 of 36 submissions pass verification. Selecting the lowest-perplexity agent design per task yields an average 3.4% perplexity increase over BF16 and 77.33% downstream accuracy, compared with 79.56% for BF16. Recorded experiments reveal how agents achieve these outcomes and where improvement breaks down. Agents lower PPL in 21 of 24 revisions at nearly fixed storage; complete-model feedback reverses 17 of 79 prior local rankings; and generation and inference tests expose failures that likelihood alone misses. The results identify representation design, experimental judgment, and capability validation as central to agent-driven model compression, a measurable component of efficiency-oriented self-improvement.

AI.tldr: CompressionBench tests whether coding agents can compress a pretrained LLM autonomously within a storage budget. Across six agents and six model-size settings, 29 of 36 submissions pass verification, and the lowest-perplexity design per task averages a 3.4% perplexity increase over BF16.
AI.motivation: Recursive self-improvement requires AI systems to improve the models and infrastructure used by later systems, and LLM compression offers a concrete, measurable efficiency objective.
AI.method: Agents receive a source checkpoint, a storage limit, an inference environment and a time budget, and construct compressed weights and executable inference code. Perplexity feedback guides the search, and independent verification checks the final model.
AI.result: Selecting the lowest-perplexity agent design per task gives an average 3.4% perplexity increase over BF16 and 77.33% downstream accuracy, against 79.56% for BF16. Agents lowered perplexity in 21 of 24 revisions at nearly fixed storage, complete-model feedback reversed 17 of 79 prior local rankings, and generation and inference tests exposed failures that likelihood alone missed.
AI.conclusion: Representation design, experimental judgment and capability validation are central to agent-driven model compression, a measurable component of efficiency-oriented self-improvement.

title: On Turn-Level Best-of-N Sampling for Scaling LLM Agents
summary: In this work, we evaluate a simple inference-time scaling approach based on \textit{turn-level best-of-N sampling} (\method) for large language model (LLM) agents on complex, long-horizon tasks. We instantiate this using a \textit{generator-selector} framework with two LLMs; at each turn, a \emph{generator} model generates $N$ candidate actions and a \emph{selector} model selects one of them, which is then executed in the environment. This paper is closely related to the work of \cite{zainullina2025guided} who used critic models for guided search at inference time. Different from their work, we evaluate if off-the-shelf, open-weight LLMs can be effective at comparing different candidate actions directly. Experiments on long-horizon terminal tasks show that \method can lead to significant performance improvements, both in terms of accuracy (5--10\%) and consistency across repeated attempts. Analysis of agent trajectories reveal a shift in agent behaviour towards desirable patterns such as reduction in number of attempts to solve the task, improved task instruction following, debugging and testing.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates turn-level best-of-N sampling for LLM agents on long-horizon terminal tasks, where a generator proposes N candidate actions per turn and a selector picks one to execute. Using off-the-shelf open-weight LLMs, it improves accuracy by 5-10% and consistency across repeated attempts.
AI.motivation: Prior work used critic models for guided search at inference time, and this paper asks whether off-the-shelf open-weight LLMs can compare candidate actions directly.
AI.method: A generator-selector framework with two LLMs: at each turn the generator produces N candidate actions and the selector chooses one, which is then executed in the environment.
AI.result: On long-horizon terminal tasks the method gives accuracy gains of 5-10% and better consistency across repeated attempts. Trajectory analysis shows fewer attempts to solve a task, better task instruction following, and more debugging and testing.
AI.conclusion: Simple turn-level best-of-N selection with open-weight models is an effective inference-time scaling approach for LLM agents.

title: Learning to Decode Linear Codes with Generalized Belief Propagation Network
summary: Error correcting codes are a fundamental component of communication systems, enabling reliable data transmission over noisy channels. Recently, neural decoders have demonstrated notable performance gains over classical iterative algorithms. In this paper, we propose a Generalized Belief Propagation Network (GBPNet) that preserves message-passing symmetry while enhancing the decoder's learning capability. The architecture uses cascaded variable-node updates and learned element-wise message scaling while retaining the Tanner graph structure. We also introduce two training strategies, progressive training and high-SNR training, that improve decoding accuracy. Experimental results on several linear codes show that GBPNet achieves lower bit error rates than conventional belief propagation and the evaluated state-of-the-art neural decoders.

AI.tldr: GBPNet is a neural decoder for linear codes that preserves message-passing symmetry and the Tanner graph while adding cascaded variable-node updates and learned element-wise message scaling. It achieves lower bit error rates than conventional belief propagation and the evaluated neural decoders on several linear codes.
AI.motivation: Neural decoders have already shown gains over classical iterative algorithms, and this work aims to increase the learning capability of the decoder without breaking the symmetry of message passing.
AI.method: GBPNet uses cascaded variable-node updates and learned element-wise message scaling on the Tanner graph. Two training strategies, progressive training and high-SNR training, are introduced to improve decoding accuracy.
AI.result: On several linear codes GBPNet achieves lower bit error rates than conventional belief propagation and the evaluated state-of-the-art neural decoders.
AI.conclusion: A message-passing neural decoder with learned scaling and tailored training can outperform conventional belief propagation on the codes tested.

title: Dull, Dirty, Dangerous? Working Conditions and the Limits of Occupational AI Exposure
summary: Automation is often justified as relief from dull, dirty, and dangerous work. I examine how these conditions relate to occupational AI exposure using 21 O*NET items across 754 US occupations. Higher exposure is associated with lower condition scores under a large language model (LLM) measure and AI Occupational Exposure (AIOE), with equal occupation weights and employment weights. Adjustment for physical demands, required education, training and experience, and wages reduces the composite association. The adjusted confidence intervals include zero for LLM exposure and remain below zero for AIOE. Separating repetition from restricted discretion also changes what the combined Dull score conveys. These comparisons show how item groupings and occupational characteristics shape the interpretation of exposure estimates. Occupational profiles offer a starting point for selecting contrasting research settings. Establishing desired automation or realized relief requires evidence about workers' preferences and specific interventions.

AI.tldr: Using 21 O*NET items across 754 US occupations, the paper finds that higher AI exposure is associated with lower dull, dirty and dangerous condition scores. Adjusting for occupational characteristics shrinks the composite association, and for the LLM measure the adjusted confidence interval includes zero.
AI.motivation: Automation is often justified as relief from dull, dirty and dangerous work, and the paper examines how these conditions relate to occupational AI exposure.
AI.method: Uses 21 O*NET items across 754 US occupations and two exposure measures, an LLM measure and AI Occupational Exposure (AIOE), with equal occupation weights and employment weights. Adjusts for physical demands, required education, training and experience, and wages, and separates repetition from restricted discretion.
AI.result: Higher exposure is associated with lower condition scores under both measures. Adjustment reduces the composite association, with adjusted confidence intervals that include zero for LLM exposure and remain below zero for AIOE. Separating repetition from restricted discretion changes what the combined Dull score conveys.
AI.conclusion: Item groupings and occupational characteristics shape how exposure estimates are read, and establishing realized relief requires evidence about workers' preferences and specific interventions.

title: FrontierPhysics: Evaluating Agents for End-to-End Physics Research
comment: 41 pages (10 pages main text), 19 figures, 11 tables
summary: AI agents are playing an increasingly important role in physics research. However, existing physics benchmarks only evaluate fixed questions, isolated sub-tasks, or paper reproduction with given solutions, and rarely check research quality alongside correctness. We introduce FrontierPhysics, an end-to-end benchmark with 56 tasks made by 42 physicists based on their own research, covering nine domains across theoretical, computational, and experimental physics. Each task requires agents to review the literature, develop a research plan, conduct research and experiments, and produce structured outputs and scientific manuscripts. Combining deterministic verifiers with expert-authored rubrics, FrontierPhysics evaluates whether agents' research is correct and publishable. Across 22 models in 26 configurations, no configuration passes more than 46 of its 168 rollouts. Manual review of agent trajectories shows that frontier agents' main weaknesses are insufficiently rigorous reasoning and limited expert intuition, rather than gaps in physics knowledge or execution errors.

AI.tldr: FrontierPhysics is an end-to-end benchmark of 56 research tasks written by 42 physicists from their own research, spanning nine domains of theoretical, computational and experimental physics. Across 22 models in 26 configurations, no configuration passes more than 46 of its 168 rollouts.
AI.motivation: Existing physics benchmarks evaluate fixed questions, isolated sub-tasks, or paper reproduction with given solutions, and rarely check research quality alongside correctness.
AI.method: Each task requires agents to review the literature, develop a research plan, conduct research and experiments, and produce structured outputs and scientific manuscripts. Deterministic verifiers are combined with expert-authored rubrics to judge correctness and publishability.
AI.result: Across 22 models in 26 configurations, no configuration passes more than 46 of its 168 rollouts. Manual review of trajectories shows that the main weaknesses of frontier agents are insufficiently rigorous reasoning and limited expert intuition, rather than gaps in physics knowledge or execution errors.
AI.conclusion: Current agents fall short of correct, publishable physics research, and their weaknesses lie in rigour and expert intuition rather than in knowledge or execution.

title: BEAKER: An Expert-Curated Benchmark for Embodied Brains in Self-Driving Chemical Laboratories
comment: Accepted by NeurIPS 2026 (Track on Evaluations and Datasets, Spotlight)
summary: Self-Driving Chemical Laboratories (SDCLs) are moving chemical experimentation toward embodied automation, where machines must perceive laboratory scenes, reason about experimental states, and act under physical, procedural, and safety constraints. Although Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly considered as embodied brains for such systems, existing laboratory benchmarks mainly focus on safety, anomaly detection, or general scientific understanding, leaving their execution-oriented embodied capabilities underexplored. To fill this gap, we introduce BEAKER, a Benchmark for evaluating Embodied Actionability, Knowledge, Experimentation, and Reasoning in SDCLs. BEAKER contains 1,000 expert-curated question-answer samples across 11 image and video task types, covering key judgments required for chemical laboratory execution, including affordance grounding, trajectory planning, equipment, state, and safety recognition, apparatus setup, operation and step reasoning, and temporal procedure reasoning. All questions and annotations are manually created and reviewed by chemistry and embodied Artificial Intelligence (AI) experts, without AI-assisted generation or annotation. We evaluate 28 general-purpose, science-oriented, chemistry-specialized, and embodied MLLMs in an offline, single-turn setting. Results show that current models can follow coarse experimental procedures in videos, but still struggle to ground actions into operable regions and feasible trajectories, to recognize fine-grained laboratory apparatus, states, and safety norms, and to order steps in mid-length procedures. BEAKER thus reveals a clear gap between coarse procedural understanding and the precise, action-grounded perception required for laboratory execution, providing a diagnostic benchmark for future MLLMs in SDCLs.

AI.tldr: BEAKER is an expert-curated benchmark of 1,000 question-answer samples across 11 image and video task types, testing embodied capabilities of multimodal LLMs in self-driving chemical laboratories. Evaluating 28 MLLMs, the paper finds that models can follow coarse procedures in videos but struggle with action grounding, fine-grained apparatus and safety recognition, and ordering steps in mid-length procedures.
AI.motivation: Existing laboratory benchmarks focus on safety, anomaly detection or general scientific understanding, leaving execution-oriented embodied capabilities underexplored in self-driving chemical laboratories.
AI.method: 1,000 question-answer samples across 11 image and video task types cover affordance grounding, trajectory planning, equipment, state and safety recognition, apparatus setup, operation and step reasoning, and temporal procedure reasoning. All questions and annotations were manually created and reviewed by chemistry and embodied AI experts, without AI-assisted generation or annotation, and models are evaluated offline in a single-turn setting.
AI.result: Of the 28 general-purpose, science-oriented, chemistry-specialized and embodied MLLMs evaluated, current models can follow coarse experimental procedures in videos but struggle to ground actions into operable regions and feasible trajectories, to recognize fine-grained apparatus, states and safety norms, and to order steps in mid-length procedures.
AI.conclusion: BEAKER reveals a gap between coarse procedural understanding and the precise, action-grounded perception needed for laboratory execution, and serves as a diagnostic benchmark for future MLLMs in self-driving laboratories.

title: Behavior Graphs: Unsupervised Graph Structures for Interpreting Robot Deployment Data
comment: 8 pages, 6 figures, 3 tables. Project website: this https URL
summary: Data flywheels promise continuous improvement via insights from deployment data. Understanding how the deployed model succeeds and fails can steer subsequent data collection towards patching failures and reinforcing successes. However, robot deployments create large volumes of high-dimensional rollout data, which is challenging to understand and confidently ground data collection decisions in. To make deployment data easier to analyze and act on, we propose behavior graphs, which compress policy rollouts into a single interpretable, directed graph. We construct the graphs by learning to identify similar behavior modes across rollouts, connecting the behaviors temporally, and finally linking them to outcomes. In a user study on three real-world tasks, where participants analyzed rollouts to choose a data collection strategy, 16 of 18 preferred behavior graphs to rollout videos, reaching comparable conclusions with 40.3% lower perceived temporal demand and 37.6% lower effort. Beyond interpretability for deployment data, behavior graphs are capable progress predictors: across 43 datasets, they improve the rank correlation between predicted progress and true temporal order by 22.9% and reduce mean absolute error by 53.5% relative to the strongest baseline. As the number of deployed robots grows, behavior graphs lend structure to high-dimensional policy rollouts and make deployment data easier to interpret and reason about.

AI.tldr: Behavior graphs compress robot policy rollouts into a single interpretable directed graph of behavior modes linked to outcomes. In a user study on three real-world tasks, 16 of 18 participants preferred them to rollout videos, and across 43 datasets they improve progress prediction over the strongest baseline.
AI.motivation: Robot deployments produce large volumes of high-dimensional rollout data that are hard to analyze, which makes it difficult to ground data collection decisions confidently in deployment data.
AI.method: Behavior graphs are built by learning to identify similar behavior modes across rollouts, connecting the behaviors temporally, and finally linking them to outcomes.
AI.result: In the user study, 16 of 18 participants preferred behavior graphs to rollout videos, reaching comparable conclusions with 40.3% lower perceived temporal demand and 37.6% lower effort. Across 43 datasets, behavior graphs improve the rank correlation between predicted progress and true temporal order by 22.9% and reduce mean absolute error by 53.5% relative to the strongest baseline.
AI.conclusion: Behavior graphs make deployment data easier to interpret and reason about, and give structure to high-dimensional policy rollouts as the number of deployed robots grows.

title: Do agents need to sleep?
summary: LLM-based agents, which increasingly operate persistently across sessions and accumulate memory through interaction, already exhibit the familiar symptoms of unchecked plasticity: semantic drift, degraded retrieval precision, propagation of stored errors, and saturation of memory capacity. Drawing on the selectionist "ringing, resonance and renormalization" (RRR) account of sleep, we propose that each of its three phases maps onto an operation feasible in digital memory architectures. Engineers building stateful agents, meanwhile, are independently rediscovering the problems sleep evolved to solve: what to forget, and when to do the forgetting. From this we derive the falsifiable prediction that selectionist consolidation will outperform instructionist alternatives as memory stores grow large. The core claim concerns the nature of continuous learning itself: plasticity has a price, and for any system that learns continuously under finite capacity while coupled to its environment, that price is sleep.

AI.tldr: The paper maps the three phases of sleep in the selectionist ringing, resonance and renormalization (RRR) account onto operations feasible in digital memory architectures for persistent LLM agents. It derives a falsifiable prediction that selectionist consolidation will outperform instructionist alternatives as memory stores grow large.
AI.motivation: Persistent LLM agents accumulate memory through interaction and show semantic drift, degraded retrieval precision, propagation of stored errors and saturated memory capacity, while engineers are independently rediscovering what to forget and when to forget.
AI.method: Drawing on the selectionist RRR account of sleep, each of its three phases is mapped onto an operation that is feasible in digital memory architectures.
AI.result: The paper reports no experiments; it derives a falsifiable prediction that selectionist consolidation will outperform instructionist alternatives as memory stores grow large.
AI.conclusion: Plasticity has a price, and for any system that learns continuously under finite capacity while coupled to its environment, that price is sleep.

title: AI-Driven SaaS Platform Integration: AI Express for Unified Generative AI Services with Pay-As-You-Go Credit Systems and Scalable Microservice Architecture
summary: Generative AI is currently fragmented, with separate subscriptions required for text generation, image synthesis, and code assistance, leading to high costs and workflow disruptions. AI Express is a SaaS platform that consolidates these capabilities into a unified pay-as-you-go service. The platform provides a range of AI tools, including a Core Code Reviewer that evaluates GitHub repositories, a Text-to-Website generator that converts text into fully functional websites, script generation, grammar checking, data analysis, and watermark removal, all accessible through a single interface without requiring technical expertise.

AI.tldr: AI Express is a SaaS platform that consolidates text generation, image synthesis, code assistance and related tools into one pay-as-you-go service with a credit system and a microservice architecture.
AI.motivation: Generative AI is fragmented across separate subscriptions for text generation, image synthesis and code assistance, which leads to high costs and workflow disruptions.
AI.method: The platform uses a scalable microservice architecture and pay-as-you-go credits, and offers a Core Code Reviewer that evaluates GitHub repositories, a Text-to-Website generator, script generation, grammar checking, data analysis and watermark removal through a single interface.
AI.result: The abstract reports no evaluation results.
AI.conclusion: The platform offers unified access to several generative AI services without requiring technical expertise.

title: A Training-Free Socket for DNA in Frozen Language Models
summary: Connecting a DNA foundation model to a large language model (LLM) usually requires training a connector, and often the LLM too. We show that a closed-form map is enough for gene-level questions. Our method, the socket, fits one ridge regression (the plug) from frozen Evo 2 features to the host LLM's own representation of the gene's symbol, name, and description at an early layer. The plug's output replaces the hidden state at placeholder positions, and no gradient passes through the host. We test it on GeneHop, a five-way multiple-choice benchmark split by homology. In a single run on the held-out test set, under a frozen analysis plan, real DNA beats shuffled DNA on all four hosts: by +22.2 points [19.8, 25.0] on Qwen3.5-4B, +26.1 [24.3, 27.9] on Qwen3.6-27B, +16.7 [14.2, 19.7] on Mistral-7B, and +18.4 [16.2, 21.0] on OLMo-2-7B. All four survive Holm correction, every null control stays within two points of the sham level, and the development results agree within 2.3 points. A layer rule that uses no task items was selected on three hosts; it predicted the working layer of the fourth before any DNA-plug scoring on it. A text-only linear map lets one plug feed any other host, at a cost of at most 0.9 points on test. The socket conveys gene identity: nearest-neighbour retrieval recovers 72-84% of the effect, but the plug beats it on every host by 3.0-5.2 points and keeps most of its effect without training homologs.

AI.tldr: The socket is a training-free, closed-form ridge-regression map from frozen Evo 2 DNA features into a host LLM's representation of a gene, so that gene-level questions can use DNA without any gradient through the host. On GeneHop, real DNA beats shuffled DNA by 16.7 to 26.1 points across four hosts.
AI.motivation: Connecting a DNA foundation model to a large language model usually requires training a connector, and often the LLM as well.
AI.method: One ridge regression, called the plug, maps frozen Evo 2 features to the host LLM's own representation of the gene's symbol, name and description at an early layer. The plug's output replaces the hidden state at placeholder positions, and no gradient passes through the host. It is tested on GeneHop, a five-way multiple-choice benchmark split by homology.
AI.result: In a single run on the held-out test set, real DNA beats shuffled DNA on all four hosts, by 22.2 points on Qwen3.5-4B, 26.1 on Qwen3.6-27B, 16.7 on Mistral-7B and 18.4 on OLMo-2-7B, and all four survive Holm correction. Nearest-neighbour retrieval recovers 72-84% of the effect, but the plug beats it by 3.0-5.2 points on every host.
AI.conclusion: A closed-form map conveys gene identity without training, and a text-only linear map lets one plug feed other hosts at a cost of at most 0.9 points on test.

title: VenusGenome: Genome-Aware Masked Autoencoding for Microbial Genome Representation Learning
summary: Genomic-context models have shown that contextualizing protein embeddings can improve predictions of microbial function. We observe that a gene's protein embedding is partially predictable from the embeddings of neighboring genes in the genome, motivating high-ratio masking that requires reconstruction from sparser genomic context. Genomic modeling must also distinguish biological relationships from assembly conventions, since the ordering of separate contigs does not imply adjacency and strand labels depend on the reference orientation. We therefore introduce VenusGenome, a gene-resolution masked autoencoder that combines visible-only encoding with genome-aware attention incorporating contig boundaries, relative strand orientations, and gene positions. We pretrain this model on a curated corpus of over 1.7 million microbial genome assemblies from isolate and metagenomic sources, using frozen protein embeddings as gene-level inputs. Across genome-level phenotype prediction and gene-level tasks, the resulting frozen representations achieve the highest mean performance among the evaluated models on nine of eleven primary metrics. An exploratory gene-input perturbation analysis further links representation sensitivity to experimentally measured fitness defects. Ablations support the contribution of genome-aware attention and show the benefits of masked autoencoding over BERT-style masked modeling, with further gains from higher masking ratios.

AI.tldr: VenusGenome is a gene-resolution masked autoencoder for microbial genomes that uses genome-aware attention with contig boundaries, relative strand orientations and gene positions. Pretrained on over 1.7 million microbial genome assemblies, its frozen representations achieve the highest mean performance on nine of eleven primary metrics among the evaluated models.
AI.motivation: Contextualizing protein embeddings with genomic neighbours improves predictions of microbial function, and genomic modelling must separate biological adjacency from assembly conventions such as contig ordering and strand labels.
AI.method: A visible-only encoder with genome-aware attention, trained with high-ratio masking on frozen protein embeddings as gene-level inputs, using a curated corpus of over 1.7 million microbial genome assemblies from isolate and metagenomic sources.
AI.result: Across genome-level phenotype prediction and gene-level tasks, the frozen representations achieve the highest mean performance among the evaluated models on nine of eleven primary metrics. Ablations support the contribution of genome-aware attention and show that masked autoencoding beats BERT-style masked modelling, with further gains from higher masking ratios.
AI.conclusion: Genome-aware masked autoencoding yields useful frozen representations of microbial genomes, and an exploratory perturbation analysis links representation sensitivity to experimentally measured fitness defects.

title: When Does Sharing Work? Scaling a Shared SigLIP2 Across Image, Video, Audio, and Audio-Visual Representations
summary: Contrastive pretraining has advanced image-text understanding, yet image, video, and audio encoders are still trained independently, with cross-modal alignment realized mainly through post-hoc binding to a frozen anchor space. We present Omni-Encoder, a general multimodal encoder that processes image, video, audio, and audio-visual inputs within a single SigLIP-2 Vision Transformer with fully shared parameters. Unlike anchor-centric binding or per-modality adapters, all modalities are optimized jointly end-to-end, and the framework is organized from input to training. A modality-native input stage first maps each signal into the shared embedding space, including a 1D-convolutional audio tokenizer that converts mel-spectrograms into tokens aligned with visual patches. A multimodal rotary position embedding parameterized by absolute timestamps then places visual frames and audio segments in a unified spatiotemporal coordinate system. Finally, alternating-modality training interleaves image, video, audio, and temporally aligned audio-visual batches and accumulates their gradients into one update, which we find central to stable joint optimization. Omni-Encoder achieves competitive results on 16 benchmarks across all four modalities with one shared parameter set, and joint training improves each modality over its separately trained counterpart. Code and models will be publicly released.

AI.tldr: Omni-Encoder processes image, video, audio and audio-visual inputs with one fully shared SigLIP-2 Vision Transformer, trained jointly end-to-end. It achieves competitive results on 16 benchmarks across the four modalities with one parameter set, and joint training improves each modality over its separately trained counterpart.
AI.motivation: Image, video and audio encoders are still trained independently, with cross-modal alignment realized mainly through post-hoc binding to a frozen anchor space.
AI.method: A modality-native input stage maps each signal into the shared embedding space, including a 1D-convolutional audio tokenizer that turns mel-spectrograms into tokens aligned with visual patches. A multimodal rotary position embedding parameterized by absolute timestamps places frames and audio segments in one spatiotemporal coordinate system, and alternating-modality training accumulates gradients from image, video, audio and temporally aligned audio-visual batches into one update.
AI.result: The model achieves competitive results on 16 benchmarks across all four modalities with one shared parameter set, and joint training improves each modality over its separately trained counterpart.
AI.conclusion: Fully shared joint training across modalities is feasible, with alternating-modality gradient accumulation central to stable optimization; code and models are to be publicly released.

title: PEEK: One-Step-Look-Ahead Exposure Bias Correction for Diffusion Sampling
summary: Diffusion image generators are successful due to accurate denoising networks and strong numerical samplers. Yet the two components are not fully matched. During sampling, the denoiser predicts for the next step based on flawed input that differ much from the real data. This train-test gap, or exposure bias, caps image generation quality (i.e., blurry, lacking in details or awkward in shape). To mitigate the problem, we propose PEEK, a novel training-free deterministic sampler plugin. At each eligible denoising step, PEEK first performs a provisional one-step update, evaluates the denoiser once at the look-ahead state, and interpolates it with the one-step-later prediction to form the next noisy state. By taking the additional step, we obtain a generally more-image-like prediction from the higher-signal noisy state, mitigating the exposure bias. To optimize the interpolation positions, PEEK searches for an interpolation schedule search made efficient by the prefix and baseline noise-schedule-rebasing caches. On 8 pixel-space and latent-space diffusion models with unconditional, label-guided, and text-guided settings across various output resolutions, PEEK consistently improves over NFE-matched baselines, with FID improvements up to 49.3\% at minimal extra computation cost (e.g., the one-time-per-model calibration takes at most 2.2 minutes across our experiments.). Project website is at this https URL.

AI.tldr: PEEK is a training-free deterministic sampler plugin for diffusion models that corrects exposure bias with a one-step look-ahead and an optimized interpolation schedule. It improves over NFE-matched baselines on 8 diffusion models, with FID improvements up to 49.3% at minimal extra computation cost.
AI.motivation: During sampling the denoiser predicts the next step from flawed inputs that differ from real data, and this train-test gap, or exposure bias, caps image generation quality.
AI.method: At each eligible denoising step PEEK performs a provisional one-step update, evaluates the denoiser at the look-ahead state, and interpolates that prediction with the one-step-later prediction to form the next noisy state. The interpolation positions are chosen by a search made efficient with prefix and baseline noise-schedule-rebasing caches.
AI.result: On 8 pixel-space and latent-space diffusion models with unconditional, label-guided and text-guided settings across various resolutions, PEEK consistently improves over NFE-matched baselines, with FID improvements up to 49.3% at minimal extra computation; the one-time calibration per model takes at most 2.2 minutes.
AI.conclusion: PEEK mitigates exposure bias as a plug-in sampler that needs no retraining and adds little computation.

title: CAST-Bench: Tracing Every Sound to Its Source in Multi-Shot Audio-Video Generation
summary: Existing benchmarks for joint text-to-audio-video (T2AV) generation evaluate perceptual quality and audiovisual alignment, but balanced sound-source sam?pling and separate reporting by shot structure remain limited. This makes it dif?ficult to determine whether a specific sound is missing, attributed to the wrong source, or lost across shot transitions. To address this, we introduce CAST?BENCH, a benchmark designed to trace every generated sound back to its in?tended source in multi-shot audio-video generation. The core idea is to formu?late T2AV correctness as an audiovisual contract in which each requested sound must be emitted by the right source, synchronized with the corresponding visual action, and carry the right semantic content. Concretely, the benchmark orga?nizes 900 prompts into 9 sound-source categories, with 100 prompts per cate?gory, spanning speech, animals, instruments, ambient sounds, and other emitter types. The prompts include 439 single-shot and 461 multi-shot narratives, each derived from a structured specification that links every audio event to its emit?ter, subject, and temporal slot. The benchmark provides an 18-metric evaluation suite covering three dimensions: Visual Performance, Content Consistency, and Audio & Semantic Alignment. We further benchmark 12 representative gen?erators and find that visual quality is nearly saturated across leading systems, yet audio semantic scores still differ markedly. Across the nine shared mod?els, multi-shot prompts receive lower aggregate scores under the subset-specific scoring rules and yield different model rankings. Multi-person speech, con?sistent speaker identity across shots, and cross-shot event retention remain the main unresolved challenges. All prompts and evaluation code are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: CAST-Bench is a benchmark of 900 prompts in nine sound-source categories for checking whether each requested sound comes from the right source, is synchronized with the visual action, and has the right semantic content in multi-shot audio-video generation. Across 12 generators, visual quality is nearly saturated while audio semantic scores still differ markedly.
AI.motivation: Existing joint text-to-audio-video benchmarks assess perceptual quality and audiovisual alignment but offer limited balanced sound-source sampling and separate reporting by shot structure, so it is hard to tell whether a sound is missing, misattributed, or lost across shot transitions.
AI.method: The 900 prompts (100 per category; 439 single-shot and 461 multi-shot) are derived from structured specifications that link each audio event to its emitter, subject, and temporal slot. An 18-metric suite covers Visual Performance, Content Consistency, and Audio and Semantic Alignment.
AI.result: Among the nine shared models, multi-shot prompts receive lower aggregate scores under subset-specific scoring rules and yield different model rankings. Multi-person speech, consistent speaker identity across shots, and cross-shot event retention remain the main unresolved challenges.
AI.conclusion: Correct sound attribution across shots is still an open problem for audio-video generators, and the prompts and evaluation code are released to track progress on it.

title: LLM-based NPCs in Video Games: A Systematic Mapping Study
comment: 12 pages. Accepted manuscript. Published in IEEE Transactions on Games (Early Access)
summary: For decades, non-player characters (NPCs) have been driven by rule-based systems whose personalities and interactions are scripted before release. Large language models (LLMs) promise NPCs that converse openly, adapt to new situations, and behave in ways developers did not fully author, prompting a wave of research and commercial experimentation. Yet the field lacks a unified picture of what has been built, how well it works, and at what cost. We address this gap with a systematic mapping study of 377 papers from the academic literature, yielding 42 papers analysed against a main research question and ten sub-questions across four thematic axes. We provide the first quantitative characterisation of component adoption, latency, safety coverage, and reproducibility: short-term memory and world-state grounding are near-universal (60% and 69%), whereas long-term memory (31%), reflection (38%), and retrieval-augmented generation (14%) remain rare, and response times span 2.6 to 15 seconds. Finally, we identify six structural barriers to commercial adoption and offer evidence-based recommendations for developers and researchers.

AI.tldr: A systematic mapping study of 42 papers (selected from 377) on LLM-based NPCs in video games, quantifying component adoption, latency, safety coverage, and reproducibility, and identifying six barriers to commercial adoption.
AI.motivation: NPCs in games are still scripted by rule-based systems, and the literature on LLM-driven NPCs lacks a unified picture of what has been built, how well it works, and at what cost.
AI.method: A systematic mapping study of 377 academic papers, yielding 42 analysed against a main research question and ten sub-questions across four thematic axes.
AI.result: Short-term memory (60%) and world-state grounding (69%) are near-universal, while long-term memory (31%), reflection (38%), and retrieval-augmented generation (14%) remain rare. Response times span 2.6 to 15 seconds.
AI.conclusion: Six structural barriers to commercial adoption are identified, and the paper offers evidence-based recommendations for developers and researchers.

title: Constraint-Preserving Flow Matching for Spectral Graph Generation
summary: Spectral graph generation models graphs through the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of their Laplacians, providing a compact and continuous alternative to direct graph construction. However, these eigensystems must retain the structural properties of graph Laplacians. Existing approaches preserve eigenvector orthonormality but do not enforce the Laplacian nullspace constraint, potentially producing eigensystems inconsistent with Laplacian structure. To address this, we introduce Laplacian-Constrained Stiefel Flow Matching (LaSFM), which preserves the nullspace condition alongside eigenvector orthonormality and positive eigenvalues during generation. We characterize the underlying constrained Stiefel manifold and formulate flow matching on it. We further extend LaSFM to property-guided generation, steering samples toward desired graph properties while maintaining these constraints. Experiments demonstrate improved performance on both spectral and graph-level metrics, along with better alignment with target properties.

AI.tldr: LaSFM is a flow matching method for spectral graph generation that keeps generated eigensystems on the constrained Stiefel manifold, enforcing the Laplacian nullspace condition alongside eigenvector orthonormality and positive eigenvalues. It also extends to property-guided generation.
AI.motivation: Spectral graph generation builds graphs from Laplacian eigenvalues and eigenvectors, but existing approaches preserve orthonormality without enforcing the nullspace constraint, so the generated eigensystems can be inconsistent with Laplacian structure.
AI.method: Laplacian-Constrained Stiefel Flow Matching characterises the constrained Stiefel manifold and performs flow matching on it. An extension steers samples toward desired graph properties while keeping the constraints.
AI.result: Experiments show improved performance on both spectral and graph-level metrics, along with better alignment with target properties.
AI.conclusion: Respecting the full Laplacian structure during generation improves spectral and graph-level quality and property alignment over methods that omit the nullspace constraint.

title: SurgTransfer: Multi-Step Latent Action Modeling for Action Transfer in Surgical World Model
summary: Surgical world models have the potential to provide intra-operative guidance, accelerate risk-free training and facilitate transfer of expert surgical maneuvers. However, the use of world models for transferring surgical expertise has been largely unexplored. Moreover, recent approaches in this domain have mainly relied on ground truth kinematics actions or expert annotations for specific tasks, limiting their applicability beyond the narrow range of tasks with ground-truth annotations. In contrast, existing works in the natural domain have shown promising results in learning latent actions solely from unlabeled videos and transferring the learned actions across contexts. We observe that this paradigm is short-sighted for the surgical domain, failing to capture the hierarchical and goal-directed structure of surgical procedures. Thus, we propose a novel multi-step action learning framework to learn context-invariant latent actions that are easily transferable across various surgical contexts. We perform extensive experiments on the publicly available datasets, SurgToolLoc-2022 and PitVis-2023, verifying our approach with both quantitative metrics and qualitative evaluation by surgical experts. We have published our code and the implementation details at this https URL.

AI.tldr: SurgTransfer proposes a multi-step latent action learning framework that learns context-invariant latent actions for transferring expert maneuvers in a surgical world model. It is evaluated on SurgToolLoc-2022 and PitVis-2023.
AI.motivation: Surgical world models that transfer expertise have relied on ground-truth kinematic actions or expert annotations for specific tasks, which limits them to narrow task ranges. Natural-domain latent action methods are short-sighted for surgery because they miss the hierarchical, goal-directed structure of procedures.
AI.method: A multi-step action learning framework that learns latent actions intended to be context-invariant and easily transferable across surgical contexts.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on the public SurgToolLoc-2022 and PitVis-2023 datasets, verified with quantitative metrics and qualitative evaluation by surgical experts.
AI.conclusion: The approach aims to transfer surgical actions beyond tasks with ground-truth annotations, and the code and implementation details are published.

title: LIBRA: Programmatic Induction of Executable Tool Libraries
comment: 10 pages, 5 figures. Introduces LIBRA, a query-agnostic tool library built via execution-validated prerequisites in a sandbox (avg ARR review score: 3.5/5). Demonstrates consistent performance gains across three benchmarks while discussing sandbox dependencies and library construction trade-offs
summary: Large language model agents increasingly retrieve tools from large catalogs, yet most retrievers rank each tool independently by request similarity. For multi tool tasks, this recovers the goal matching tool while omitting prerequisite tools required by the this http URL introduce LIBRA, a framework for Library Induction by Runtime Assembly that turns a flat tool catalog into an executable tool library. An LLM proposes per tool contracts of candidate invocations, reusable outputs and state changes, and success conditions; LIBRA then tests these compositions in a sandbox and retains the relations supported at runtime. Constructed before user queries, the library requires no dependency annotations, tool use trajectories, or task specific training, and supports both one-shot and agentic retrieval. On AppWorld, BFCL, and SciToolEval, LIBRA improves one-shot Recall and NDCG over the same dense retriever by 7.9 and 3.7 percentage points on average. Within ToolReAGt, it yields corresponding gains of 4.5 and 2.9 points after ten retrieval iterations.

AI.tldr: LIBRA turns a flat tool catalog into an executable tool library by having an LLM propose tool contracts that are tested in a sandbox, keeping only the relations supported at runtime, so retrieval can also surface prerequisite tools for multi-tool tasks.
AI.motivation: LLM agent retrievers rank each tool independently by request similarity. For multi-tool tasks they find the goal-matching tool but omit the prerequisite tools it needs.
AI.method: Library Induction by Runtime Assembly. An LLM proposes per-tool contracts (candidate invocations, reusable outputs, state changes, and success conditions), and LIBRA tests these compositions in a sandbox. The library is built before user queries, needs no dependency annotations, trajectories, or task-specific training, and supports one-shot and agentic retrieval.
AI.result: On AppWorld, BFCL, and SciToolEval, one-shot Recall and NDCG improve over the same dense retriever by 7.9 and 3.7 percentage points on average. Within ToolReAGt, gains are 4.5 and 2.9 points after ten retrieval iterations.
AI.conclusion: Runtime-validated tool relations let retrieval account for prerequisites without extra annotation or training, with gains in both one-shot and agentic settings.

title: Jev with Foresight: Safe Language-Guided Autonomous Driving via a Language World Model
summary: Large language models understand passengers' driving commands, but as driving agents they reason in generated text for seconds and must infer each action's consequences implicitly from the scene. We present Jev-AD, which pairs Jev, a typed decision model that answers predefined questions with probabilities, not generated text, with a language world model that predicts for every candidate action how nearby vehicles move over the next two seconds. Code turns these predictions into foreseen consequences, which Jev compares instead of inferring them from coordinates. In simulated highway merging (500 car-episodes), this foresight lowers the same decision model's collision rate from 26.0% to 2.4% at 0.25 seconds per decision, and Jev-AD achieves the passenger's intent in 93% of free-form command trials. In 500 replayed real-world NGSIM episodes, foresight lowers the collision rate from 48.2% to 2.8%, and the world model, learned from this traffic, foresees 93% of dangerous actions. Project page: this https URL.

AI.tldr: Jev-AD pairs a typed decision model that outputs probabilities over predefined questions with a language world model that predicts nearby vehicle motion for each candidate action, so the agent compares foreseen consequences before acting. It sharply lowers collision rates in simulated highway merging and in replayed NGSIM episodes.
AI.motivation: LLMs understand passengers' driving commands but reason in generated text over seconds and must infer each action's consequences implicitly from the scene, which is slow and risky for driving decisions.
AI.method: Jev, a typed decision model, is paired with a language world model that predicts, for every candidate action, how nearby vehicles move over the next two seconds. Code turns these predictions into foreseen consequences, which Jev compares.
AI.result: In simulated highway merging (500 car-episodes), foresight lowers the same decision model's collision rate from 26.0% to 2.4% at 0.25 seconds per decision, and Jev-AD achieves the passenger's intent in 93% of free-form command trials. In 500 replayed NGSIM episodes, the collision rate falls from 48.2% to 2.8%, and the world model foresees 93% of dangerous actions.
AI.conclusion: Explicit foresight from a learned world model makes a probability-based decision model much safer than inferring consequences alone, supporting fast, safe language-guided driving.

title: Hybrid LLM-Deterministic Pipelines for Enterprise-Scale Code Migration at Bloomberg
summary: Large organizations carry a long tail of infrastructure migrations that are worth doing but rarely urgent enough to compete with feature work, because each one costs significant engineering time per repository. This paper reports on our industrial experience from Automated Uplift, a multi-month initiative applying LLM-assisted migration pipelines across thousands of Bloomberg repositories. We examine two distinct production campaigns: a heterogeneous Python packaging migration (approx. 1,900 candidate repositories) and a uniform C++ build system migration (approx. 6,700 candidate repositories). Together, these campaigns generated 2,333 pull requests, resulting in 729 successful migrations. We detail our hybrid architectural solution which maximizes deterministic processing, confines the LLM to bounded file transformations within a pre-computed context, and incorporates runtime production telemetry (such as execution logs and usage traces). Our findings show that generating migrations turned out to be the easier part; the bottleneck was the cost, for owning teams, of reviewing, testing, and deploying them. These costs were lowered when changes could be verified directly in the pipeline before opening a PR (as with C++ compilation and test validation), and when the population was uniform enough for fixes to carry over from one repository to the next. We conclude by distilling our experience and findings into actionable, transferable patterns for architecting hybrid LLM-deterministic pipelines and scaling code migrations across the enterprise

AI.tldr: A Bloomberg report on Automated Uplift, a hybrid LLM-deterministic pipeline for migrating thousands of repositories, which produced 729 successful migrations from 2,333 pull requests. The main bottleneck was the owning teams' cost of reviewing, testing, and deploying changes, not generating them.
AI.motivation: Large organisations carry many worthwhile but low-urgency infrastructure migrations, each of which costs significant engineering time per repository.
AI.method: A hybrid architecture that maximises deterministic processing, confines the LLM to bounded file transformations within a pre-computed context, and uses runtime production telemetry such as execution logs and usage traces. It was applied to a Python packaging migration (about 1,900 candidate repositories) and a uniform C++ build system migration (about 6,700 candidates).
AI.result: The campaigns generated 2,333 pull requests and 729 successful migrations. Review cost was lower when changes could be verified in the pipeline (as with C++ compilation and test validation) and when the population was uniform enough for fixes to carry over between repositories.
AI.conclusion: The authors distil transferable patterns for architecting hybrid LLM-deterministic pipelines and scaling code migrations across an enterprise.

title: Objective-Conditioned Active Preference Learning for Multi-Objective Alignment
summary: Aligning large language models (LLMs) with several objectives, such as helpfulness, harmlessness, and honesty, typically relies on preference judgment for each objective, growing the annotation cost linearly with the number of objectives. Active preference learning can reduce this cost by selecting the comparisons whose labels are expected to change the policy most. Existing remedies either lack an objective-aware query selection mechanism for the multi-objective setting or regard conflicting preferences as harmful, therefore excluding them from the training data. We introduce OGC-DPO (Objective-conditioned Gradient Coverage DPO), an active learning framework that treats each (response pair, objective) combination as a separate query and measures its informativeness through the policy's own implicit gradient, without relying on an external reward model. OGC-DPO then selects the queries that most expand each objective's gradient coverage. Empirical experiments across varying numbers of objectives demonstrate the effectiveness of OGC-DPO over existing active preference learning methods under the same annotation cost. Further analysis demonstrates that informative conflicts, rather than being uniformly harmful, provide a useful policy training signal.

AI.tldr: OGC-DPO is an active preference learning framework for multi-objective LLM alignment. It treats each response pair and objective combination as a query, selects queries by the policy's implicit gradient coverage, and shows that informative conflicts between objectives are a useful training signal.
AI.motivation: Aligning LLMs to several objectives needs per-objective preference labels, so annotation cost grows linearly with the number of objectives. Existing active methods either lack objective-aware query selection or discard conflicting preferences as harmful.
AI.method: Objective-conditioned Gradient Coverage DPO treats each (response pair, objective) combination as a separate query and measures its informativeness through the policy's own implicit gradient, without an external reward model. It selects the queries that most expand each objective's gradient coverage.
AI.result: Across varying numbers of objectives, OGC-DPO outperforms existing active preference learning methods under the same annotation cost. Further analysis shows that informative conflicts provide a useful policy training signal rather than being uniformly harmful.
AI.conclusion: Objective-aware, reward-model-free query selection can reduce annotation cost in multi-objective alignment, and conflicting preferences should be kept as training signal.

title: TSFM Meets LLM: Context as Covariates
summary: Textual information is ubiquitous in real-world time series datasets, appearing as news, reports, and annotations that hold key predictive signals not deducible from numerical history alone. Large Language Models (LLMs) interpret text but lack numerical precision, while Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) are quantitatively accurate but cannot reason about the effects of text. Moreover, the lack of large-scale paired multimodal datasets limits progress in bridging this gap. In this work, we address this challenge by providing a scalable approach for generating realistic multimodal datasets by annotating real-world time series with LLMs. Building on this, we propose Context as Covariates (CoCo), a forecasting framework in which an LLM distills its textual reasoning into numerically grounded forecast and confidence covariates that guide a TSFM backbone, thereby exploiting the strengths of both LLMs and TSFMs. We align the two models in stages, first fine-tuning the LLM via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with a reward tied to covariate-induced improvement in forecasting performance, and then fine-tuning the TSFM on covariates generated by the aligned LLM. Our experiments show that models trained on our synthetic multimodal corpus generalize to real benchmarks spanning finance, economics, weather, traffic, and security. Notably, CoCo with Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 as the LLM and Chronos2 as the TSFM achieves up to 12% MAE improvement over state-of-the-art TSFMs and LLM forecasters, such as GPT-4o. Code, checkpoints, and the evaluation datasets are publicly available.

AI.tldr: CoCo (Context as Covariates) has an LLM distil its textual reasoning into numerical forecast and confidence covariates that guide a time series foundation model (TSFM). It reaches up to 12% MAE improvement over state-of-the-art TSFMs and LLM forecasters such as GPT-4o.
AI.motivation: Real time series come with predictive text that LLMs can interpret but cannot forecast precisely, while TSFMs are numerically accurate but cannot reason about text. Paired multimodal datasets are also scarce.
AI.method: A scalable pipeline annotates real-world time series with LLMs to generate realistic multimodal datasets. The LLM (Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507) is fine-tuned with GRPO, using a reward tied to covariate-induced forecasting improvement, and the TSFM (Chronos2) is then fine-tuned on covariates from the aligned LLM.
AI.result: Models trained on the synthetic multimodal corpus generalise to real benchmarks spanning finance, economics, weather, traffic, and security. CoCo achieves up to 12% MAE improvement over state-of-the-art TSFMs and LLM forecasters such as GPT-4o.
AI.conclusion: Passing LLM textual reasoning to a TSFM as numerically grounded covariates improves forecasting, and the code, checkpoints, and evaluation datasets are public.

title: When to Ask, When to Answer: Strategic Clarification for Ambiguous Reference Resolution in Dialogue
comment: 22 pages, 10 figures. Code and data: this https URL
summary: For humans, referential disambiguation is a collaborative process involving clarification questions asked when they will meaningfully change the outcome. However, large language models (LLMs) have been shown to be biased toward premature answering, preferring definite single-turn responses over more clarification exchanges. In this paper, we study the problem of "strategic clarification" -- asking clarification questions in a reference game when their answers will narrow the set of candidate referents. We construct a controlled test environment from the SIMMC 2.1 dataset that records how many questions each ambiguous reference needs to be successfully resolved, and examine how baseline LLM behavior and common post-training methods ask clarifying questions vs. attempt to answer the referent. We also propose BACE (Belief-Aware Critic with Epistemic tracking), a lightweight action chooser method on top of a frozen LM backbone, and show that BACE more consistently chooses the optimal number of clarifying questions than methods such as GRPO and ArCHer.

AI.tldr: The paper studies when LLMs should ask clarifying questions in referential disambiguation. It builds a controlled test environment from SIMMC 2.1 and proposes BACE, a lightweight action chooser on a frozen LM backbone, which more consistently picks the optimal number of clarifying questions than GRPO and ArCHer.
AI.motivation: LLMs are biased toward premature answering over asking clarification questions that would narrow the set of candidate referents, and common post-training methods do not fix this.
AI.method: A reference game built from SIMMC 2.1 records how many questions each ambiguous reference needs to be resolved. BACE (Belief-Aware Critic with Epistemic tracking) is a lightweight action chooser on top of a frozen LM backbone.
AI.result: BACE more consistently chooses the optimal number of clarifying questions than methods such as GRPO and ArCHer. Baseline LLM behaviour and common post-training methods are examined in the same environment.
AI.conclusion: BACE offers a lightweight way to choose between asking and answering on a frozen backbone, so questions are asked only when they will change the outcome.
