title: Decision Models as Scalable Economic Surrogates that Capture Human Variation
summary: Decision Models (DMs), a new class of AI models, give fast responses and return a probability distribution over a fixed set of options. These properties make them candidate human surrogates in economic simulations and surveys, a role increasingly filled by Large Language Models (LLMs), which are costly at scale and under-represent the variation in human behaviour. We present a first evaluation of DMs as human surrogates in economics, comparing 10 DMs with 8 LLMs in three economic settings: a household spending survey on consumption, several classic economic games and a labour-market field experiment. Frontier DMs, those that score highest on general decision-making benchmarks, reproduce the variation in human responses more closely than LLMs in all three settings. They capture the modal human response as well as LLMs in the spending survey, but less well in the economic games. Frontier DMs are also roughly ten times faster than the fastest LLM and can be over a hundred times cheaper. Together, these results suggest that DMs capture the heterogeneity of human behaviour better than LLMs and make large-scale economic simulations more feasible.

AI.tldr: The first evaluation of Decision Models (DMs), fast AI models that return probability distributions over fixed options, as human surrogates in economics. Frontier DMs reproduce human response variation more closely than LLMs in all three settings, while being roughly ten times faster than the fastest LLM and up to over a hundred times cheaper.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used as human surrogates in economic simulations and surveys, but they are costly at scale and under-represent variation in human behaviour.
AI.method: Ten DMs are compared with eight LLMs in three settings: a household spending survey on consumption, several classic economic games, and a labour-market field experiment.
AI.result: Frontier DMs (those scoring highest on general decision-making benchmarks) reproduce human variation more closely than LLMs in all three settings. They capture the modal human response as well as LLMs in the spending survey, but less well in the economic games.
AI.conclusion: DMs capture the heterogeneity of human behaviour better than LLMs and make large-scale economic simulations more feasible.

title: How Finely Can Vision-Language Models See Biology? Bio-VQA: A Benchmark for Taxonomic, Morphological, Spatial and Individual Reasoning
comment: Accepted to WACV 2027, 8 pages main paper; 4 figures, 4 tables
summary: In biodiversity monitoring, a single image raises several questions: which taxon, how many, which trait, and whether the individual has been seen before. Vision-language models (VLMs) could answer all of these from the image, but their ability is largely untested in biology, as existing benchmarks focus mostly on species identification within a few taxonomic groups. We present Bio-VQA, the largest biological visual question answering (VQA) benchmark and the only one to span four aspects of biological visual understanding: hierarchical taxonomic reasoning, fine-grained attribute grounding, quantitative spatial reasoning, and individual re-identification. Bio-VQA contains 1.86M questions over 217K images from 11 public datasets, and extends right-or-wrong scoring to graded scoring, so a near-miss counts for more than a distant one. Evaluating 18 open-weight models from 3.75B to 38.4B parameters, we find that general visual capabilities do not transfer to biological organisms: the best model counts animals exactly on 41.7% of images with 2 to 10 individuals, less than half its accuracy on everyday objects at the same counts. Taxonomic accuracy falls to one sixth, from 0.72 at phylum to 0.12 at scientific name, and scaling helps mostly at coarse ranks. The gap to a domain specialist widens accordingly, from 0.731 against BioCLIP-2's 0.874 at class (1.2x) to 0.269 against 0.544 at scientific name (2x). On trait size measurement, 15 of the 18 models do no better than an image-blind baseline that predicts one fixed number for every specimen, and on re-identification, 17 of the 18 models fall below chance under adversarial conditions. These failures persist across a tenfold range of model size. We hope Bio-VQA becomes a standard test of how well VLM capabilities transfer to the biological domain.

AI.tldr: Bio-VQA is a biological visual question answering benchmark of 1.86M questions over 217K images, covering taxonomic, morphological, spatial, and individual reasoning. Evaluating 18 open-weight VLMs shows that general visual capabilities do not transfer to biological organisms.
AI.motivation: VLMs could answer the questions biodiversity monitoring raises from a single image, but existing biology benchmarks focus mostly on species identification within a few taxonomic groups, so this ability is largely untested.
AI.method: Bio-VQA draws on 11 public datasets and spans four aspects. It extends right-or-wrong scoring to graded scoring so that near misses count for more than distant ones. Eighteen open-weight models from 3.75B to 38.4B parameters are evaluated.
AI.result: The best model counts animals exactly on 41.7% of images with 2 to 10 individuals, less than half its accuracy on everyday objects at the same counts. Taxonomic accuracy falls from 0.72 at phylum to 0.12 at scientific name. At class the best model scores 0.731 against BioCLIP-2's 0.874 (1.2x), and at scientific name 0.269 against 0.544 (2x). On trait size measurement, 15 of 18 models do no better than an image-blind baseline; on re-identification, 17 of 18 fall below chance under adversarial conditions.
AI.conclusion: These failures persist across a tenfold range of model size, and Bio-VQA is offered as a standard test of how well VLM capabilities transfer to the biological domain.

title: Discarded or Unreachable? Diagnosing and Repairing Spatial Relation Failure in Vision--Language Similarity
comment: Code, stimulus generators, and all result files: this https URL
summary: Contrastive vision-language models score left/right relations near chance, but the symptom has two causes that call for opposite repairs: the relation may survive in the pooled embedding yet be unreachable by native image-text similarity, or pooling may discard it while the dense features retain it. On clean two object photographs, across ten encoders, the lateral polarity is linearly decodable from the flip odd component of the pooled vector at 0.77-0.99, yet a search over a million captions leaves nine of the ten at chance under native scoring: an access failure. On controlled C4 orbits, where the relation is the only thing that varies, pooling keeps the arrangement axis at 0.998-1.000 and loses its polarity, which the patch grid retains: a pooling failure. Both sit downstream of the dense features, so one readout covers both. Our zero parameter, query conditioned spatial moment recomputes the geometry from the patch grid and stores it as a vector beside the native embedding. On a 118,287 image index it raises left/right pairwise accuracy against reversed geometry negatives from 0.51-0.53 to 0.81-0.96 and conditional R@1 among 21 category matched candidates from 0.05 to 0.37-0.75, at under a millisecond per batched query, while reproducing the native ranking exactly for queries that name no relation.

AI.tldr: The paper diagnoses why contrastive vision-language models score left/right relations near chance. The cause is either an access failure (the relation is decodable from the pooled vector but unreachable by native image-text similarity) or a pooling failure. A zero-parameter, query-conditioned spatial moment recomputed from the patch grid repairs both.
AI.motivation: Contrastive VLMs score left/right relations near chance, and the two possible causes call for opposite repairs: either the relation survives in the pooled embedding but cannot be reached, or pooling discards it while the dense features keep it.
AI.method: Diagnostics on clean two-object photographs across ten encoders, and on controlled C4 orbits where the relation is the only varying factor. The spatial moment recomputes the geometry from the patch grid and stores it as a vector beside the native embedding.
AI.result: Lateral polarity is linearly decodable from the flip odd component of the pooled vector at 0.77-0.99, yet nine of ten encoders stay at chance under native scoring over a million captions. On C4 orbits, pooling keeps the arrangement axis at 0.998-1.000 but loses polarity. On a 118,287-image index, left/right pairwise accuracy rises from 0.51-0.53 to 0.81-0.96, and conditional R@1 among 21 category-matched candidates rises from 0.05 to 0.37-0.75, at under a millisecond per batched query. Rankings for queries that name no relation are reproduced exactly.
AI.conclusion: Both failures sit downstream of the dense features, so one readout covers both, and it improves relational retrieval without changing non-relational rankings.

title: MESA: An Evaluation Framework for Compositional, Semantic, and Spatial Generalization in Robotics
comment: 51 pages, 12 figures, including appendices. Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL), 2026. Project website: this https URL
summary: Despite growing interest in foundation models for robotic manipulation, systematic evaluation of their capabilities remains elusive. Existing benchmarks are either narrow and saturated, offering little signal on SOTA methods, broadly scoped, providing diversity at the cost of controlled experimentation, or require training on large, messy open-source datasets. We introduce MESA, an evaluation framework designed for precise, reproducible measurement of language-conditioned policy generalization. MESA provides five evaluation suites that isolate in-distribution performance and four distinct axes of generalization: spatial configuration, object instance, object category, and subtask composition, enabling researchers to diagnose where and why policies fail, not just whether they fail. To populate these suites at scale, we develop MESA-Gen, a pipeline for task and demonstration generation built by improving MimicGen. We instantiate the framework on two platforms and release both: the single-arm MESA suite, and BiMESA, the first large-scale benchmark for bimanual generalization. We evaluate seven baseline methods spanning diffusion policies, VLM-based approaches, and pretrained VLAs, finding that the strongest model achieves only 52% on MESA and 49% on BiMESA, providing meaningful signal while leaving ample room for progress. MESA rankings are broadly consistent with RoboArena scores, suggesting that MESA captures method-level differences relevant beyond simulation. Project website: this https URL.

AI.tldr: MESA is an evaluation framework with five suites that isolate in-distribution performance and four axes of generalisation for language-conditioned robot manipulation policies. BiMESA, its bimanual benchmark, is described as the first large-scale benchmark for bimanual generalisation, and the strongest of seven baselines reaches only 52% on MESA and 49% on BiMESA.
AI.motivation: Existing robot manipulation benchmarks are narrow and saturated, broadly scoped at the cost of controlled experiments, or require training on large, messy open-source datasets.
AI.method: Suites isolate spatial configuration, object instance, object category, and subtask composition generalisation. They are populated by MESA-Gen, a task and demonstration generation pipeline built by improving MimicGen, and instantiated on a single-arm platform and a bimanual platform.
AI.result: Seven baselines spanning diffusion policies, VLM-based approaches, and pretrained VLAs are evaluated. The strongest reaches 52% on MESA and 49% on BiMESA. MESA rankings are broadly consistent with RoboArena scores.
AI.conclusion: The framework gives meaningful signal while leaving ample room for progress, and its rankings suggest it captures method-level differences relevant beyond simulation.

title: Just the Facts: How Dialogues with AI Reduce Conspiracy Beliefs
summary: Personalized dialogues with AI substantially reduce conspiracy beliefs. To identify why, we conducted two experiments with U.S. adults recruited online (total N = 2,193) that removed possible causes one at a time. The debunking effect was robust to disclosing the AI's persuasive goal, framing the exchange as a debate, instructing the AI to inform rather than persuade, halving its response length, altering how beliefs were measured, and replacing the dialogue with a single tailored message. Only instructing the AI to persuade without factual evidence and arguments substantially reduced the debunking effect. Content analyses of the AI's output and participants' own accounts linked larger reductions in conspiracy beliefs to factual argumentation rather than rapport, storytelling, or appeals to empathy. AI dialogues appear to reduce conspiracy beliefs primarily by supplying relevant, well-reasoned counterevidence. Our results suggest that humans might be similarly effective if they could supply comparable evidence.

AI.tldr: Two experiments with 2,193 US adults show that dialogues with AI reduce conspiracy beliefs mainly by supplying factual counterevidence and argumentation, rather than rapport, storytelling, or empathy.
AI.motivation: Personalised AI dialogues are known to reduce conspiracy beliefs, but the reason for the effect was unclear.
AI.method: Two online experiments removed possible causes one at a time. They tested robustness to disclosing the persuasive goal, debate framing, instructions to inform rather than persuade, halving response length, changing how beliefs were measured, and replacing the dialogue with a single tailored message. Content analyses covered the AI's output and participants' own accounts.
AI.result: The debunking effect survives every manipulation except instructing the AI to persuade without factual evidence and arguments, which substantially reduces it. Larger reductions in conspiracy belief are linked to factual argumentation rather than rapport, storytelling, or appeals to empathy.
AI.conclusion: AI dialogues appear to reduce conspiracy beliefs primarily by supplying relevant, well-reasoned counterevidence, suggesting humans could be similarly effective if they supplied comparable evidence.

title: Readable Is Not Steerable: Pre-Registered Tests of Physical Structure in Learned Fluid Representations
comment: 30 pages, 9 figures. Code, pre-registrations and checkpoints: this https URL
summary: Self-supervised world models are often said to organize their latents around physical quantities. We test this on 2D decaying Navier-Stokes flow in three pre-registered studies, each tested once on held-out data. In Study 1, a joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) trained to predict the flow fails the pre-registered criteria for organizing its latent around fluid quantities better than an untrained network of the same architecture (not supported); a JEPA trained on non-physical linear dynamics and a static invariance model that never sees time do as well or better. In Study 2, plain autoencoders that render the field make enstrophy prominent in their slowest unsupervised latent directions (best r 0.80-0.86 vs 0.38 untrained; fresh seeds, sealed data). Adding VICReg lowers this prominence in every comparison, though not by the pre-registered margin for vorticity, while raising the autoencoders' linear decodability (partially supported). In Study 3, we build steerable directions ("dials") by routing: the decoder gets overall scale only through a small conditioning code, while its other pathway carries a degraded copy of spectral shape. Label-free rules find a loudness dial in all 8 trained models and a shape dial in 3 of 5 fresh seeds on sealed data, against a pre-registered bar of 4; neither control shows a shape dial (partially supported). Across the studies, what a latent contains and what can be controlled through it come apart. In exploration, a supervised direction reading spectral shape almost perfectly moved nothing when steered. During the build, the loudness dial had to be found by its effect on the output (closest to a pure rescaling), not by data variance; for shape, a variance rule and an effect-constrained rule each worked in 3 of 5 seeds. The program used about 70 logged hours on one consumer GPU; all pre-registrations, deviations, code and outputs are public.

AI.tldr: Three pre-registered studies on 2D decaying Navier-Stokes flow find that learned world-model latents do not reliably organise around physical quantities or yield steerable controls. What a latent contains and what can be controlled through it come apart.
AI.motivation: Self-supervised world models are often said to organise their latents around physical quantities, and the paper tests this with pre-registered criteria on held-out data.
AI.method: Study 1 compares a JEPA trained to predict the flow against an untrained network and non-physical controls. Study 2 tests whether autoencoders and VICReg variants make enstrophy prominent in slow latent directions. Study 3 builds steerable dials by routing scale through a small conditioning code, with label-free rules searching for dials on sealed data.
AI.result: Study 1 is not supported: the JEPA does not beat an untrained network, and a non-physical linear-dynamics JEPA and a static model match or exceed it. Study 2 is partially supported: enstrophy prominence reaches r 0.80-0.86 against 0.38 untrained, and VICReg lowers it in every comparison while raising linear decodability. Study 3 is partially supported: a loudness dial is found in all 8 trained models and a shape dial in 3 of 5 fresh seeds, against a pre-registered bar of 4. A supervised spectral-shape direction moved nothing when steered.
AI.conclusion: A latent that reads physical structure does not imply that the structure can be steered. Controllable directions had to be found by their effect on the output rather than by data variance, all within about 70 logged GPU hours with public pre-registrations and code.

title: Multimodal Fusion Methods for Whole-Slide Images and Clinical Data in Inflammatory Bowel Disease
comment: 5 pages, 4 figures, Submitted to the 2027 IEEE 24th International Symposium on Biomedical Imaging (ISBI)
summary: Multimodal AI fusion of histology and clinical data is an active research area in computational pathology, but fusion methods are rarely compared under identical conditions and across different clinical endpoints. We present a modular framework in which slide-level embeddings, obtained by training an attention-based aggregator over patch embeddings from a frozen foundation model, and per-visit clinical embeddings are fed into 15 interchangeable fusion methods with a shared output dimension and prediction head (except decision-level methods). Using a prospective cohort of newly diagnosed inflammatory bowel disease patients, we predicted STRIDE-II-aligned remission outcomes from baseline or follow-up visits. The best fusion method reached macro-F1 of 0.57-0.75, outperforming both single-modality models in four of six scenarios, and differed by outcome and input. Image reliance, the drop in balanced accuracy when the slide embedding is removed, tended to follow the remission type - highest for histological and lowest for endoscopic remission; methods with similar accuracy relied on the slide to very different degrees.

AI.tldr: A modular comparison of 15 fusion methods that combine whole-slide image embeddings with clinical embeddings to predict remission in newly diagnosed inflammatory bowel disease. The best method reaches macro-F1 0.57-0.75 and beats both single-modality models in four of six scenarios.
AI.motivation: Histology-clinical fusion methods in computational pathology are rarely compared under identical conditions or across different clinical endpoints.
AI.method: Slide-level embeddings from an attention-based aggregator over a frozen foundation model's patch embeddings, and per-visit clinical embeddings, feed 15 interchangeable fusion methods with a shared output dimension and prediction head (except decision-level methods). Outcomes are STRIDE-II-aligned remission, predicted from baseline or follow-up visits in a prospective cohort.
AI.result: The best fusion method reaches macro-F1 0.57-0.75 and outperforms both single-modality models in four of six scenarios; the best method differs by outcome and input. Image reliance tends to follow remission type, highest for histological and lowest for endoscopic remission. Methods with similar accuracy rely on the slide to very different degrees.
AI.conclusion: Comparable accuracy can hide very different reliance on the image, so fusion methods should be judged on how they use each modality as well as on accuracy.

title: Whiel: A Neurosymbolic Platform for Certified Relational Program Verification
summary: We present the Whiel (a contraction of Whi(le-R)el) system for Lean-certified reasoning about imperative relational programs. The system can encode containment and equivalence problems for Datalog, its extensions with negation, and the core fragment of graph query languages. It can also represent optimized or incremental evaluation algorithms that are not expressible in the original query language, as well as first-order specifications of integrity constraints, schema mappings, and views arising in data integration, exchange, and sharing. Whiel's program states are database instances, and its imperative structure enables compositional Hoare-style reasoning with first-order relational specifications, using prophecy variables and leveled invariants to support inductive arguments. Whiel supports neurosymbolic discovery of loop invariants whose verification conditions can be checked using the Vampire first-order theorem prover. Counterexamples are fed back into the neurosymbolic pipeline, while proposed solutions are translated into Lean proof certificates. To validate the Whiel system, we evaluate its performance on a curated benchmark suite. In summary, we envision the Whiel system as a tool for tackling mathematically demanding, typically undecidable problems involving complex query and constraint languages, with a high degree of trust in its output.

AI.tldr: Whiel is a Lean-certified system for reasoning about imperative relational programs. It combines neurosymbolic loop invariant discovery, checked with the Vampire theorem prover, with translation of proof certificates into Lean.
AI.motivation: Containment and equivalence problems for Datalog, its extensions with negation, and graph query fragments are mathematically demanding and typically undecidable, and they need high-trust verification.
AI.method: Program states are database instances, and compositional Hoare-style reasoning uses first-order relational specifications, prophecy variables, and leveled invariants. Neurosymbolic discovery proposes loop invariants whose verification conditions are checked by Vampire, with counterexamples fed back into the pipeline and solutions translated into Lean proof certificates.
AI.result: The system is evaluated on a curated benchmark suite, but the abstract reports no quantitative results.
AI.conclusion: Whiel is envisioned as a high-trust tool for complex query and constraint language problems, including integrity constraints, schema mappings, and views in data integration, exchange, and sharing.

title: Spatio-Temporal Multi-Order Interaction for Video Recognition
summary: Many temporal approaches for video recognition rely on explicit cross-channel aggregation projections, which have quadratic complexity in the number of channels, introducing significant computational overhead. In addition, the spatio-temporal representation used for video recognition is biased either toward local order interactions (for CNNs) or toward global order interactions (for transformers). Starting from the multi-order spatial representation of MogaNet, our method introduces two complementary contributions to tackle these problems. First, for the temporal modelling, we introduce parallel multi-order processing with depthwise-only convolutions and implicit gating-based aggregation, which is linear in the number of channels, inducing a considerable computational reduction. Second, we propose a dual interaction between spatial and temporal dimensions, which allows a better spatio-temporal representation without increasing the computational cost. By combining these two contributions, our proposed VideoMogaNet achieves performance on par with or better than state-of-the-art action recognition approaches across multiple video benchmarks (UCF101, HMDB51, Kinetics-400, Diving48), while considerably reducing the cost of the temporal branch.

AI.tldr: VideoMogaNet reduces the cost of temporal modelling with parallel multi-order, depthwise-only convolutions and implicit gating that is linear in channels, and adds a dual spatio-temporal interaction. It is on par with or better than state-of-the-art action recognition on four benchmarks with a considerably cheaper temporal branch.
AI.motivation: Many temporal video recognition approaches use explicit cross-channel projections whose cost is quadratic in channels. Their spatio-temporal representations are also biased toward local interactions in CNNs or global ones in transformers.
AI.method: Starting from the multi-order spatial representation of MogaNet, the temporal branch uses parallel multi-order processing with depthwise-only convolutions and implicit gating-based aggregation. A dual interaction between the spatial and temporal dimensions is added on top.
AI.result: VideoMogaNet performs on par with or better than state-of-the-art action recognition approaches on UCF101, HMDB51, Kinetics-400, and Diving48, while considerably reducing the cost of the temporal branch.
AI.conclusion: The two contributions together give a better spatio-temporal representation without increasing computational cost.

title: VIPBench: A Human-Aligned Benchmark for Voice Identity Perception in the Age of Voice Cloning
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026, Track on Evaluations and Datasets (poster). 30 pages, 12 figures, 22 tables. Dataset and code: this https URL
summary: Speaker-recognition benchmarks test how accurately a model recovers the speaker label of a recording, treating voice identity as a property of the person who produced it. However, these benchmarks do not evaluate how humans perceive voice identity. Whether a listener hears two voices as the same person has consequences for intellectual property rights, cybersecurity, and everyday life. We introduce the Voice Identity Perception benchmark (VIPBench), which contains 124,876 same-or-different judgments from 1,290 listeners on 9,800 recording pairs from 100 public figures. The pairs include real recordings, voice clones generated by a text-to-speech system, and morphs between two speakers' voices. We also define four tasks that evaluate the alignment between speaker-representation models and human identity perception. The first two tasks measure how well a model's similarity score predicts the proportion of listeners who respond "same" and the majority response. The other two measure whether a model and listeners find the same speaker pairs similar, and whether a model's relationship to listener judgments holds equally for real and synthetic recordings. We evaluate eleven publicly available speech models. Listener judgments diverge from speaker labels most often for voice clones: in 41% of responses, listeners judged a clone and a real recording of the same speaker to be different people. No model reaches the noise ceiling; the best model explains 61% of the explainable variance. Models trained with speaker labels align with listeners better than self-supervised models do, yet a model with a 12% error rate on speaker labels aligns with listeners as well as models with error rates below 2%. VIPBench enables the evaluation of speaker models against human perception on real, cloned, and morphed speech, and our results motivate training speaker models directly on listener judgments.

AI.tldr: VIPBench is a benchmark of 124,876 human same-or-different judgments on 9,800 recording pairs (real recordings, text-to-speech clones, and morphs) for testing whether speaker models match human voice identity perception. No model reaches the noise ceiling, and listeners judged a clone and a real recording of the same speaker to be different people in 41% of responses.
AI.motivation: Speaker-recognition benchmarks measure how accurately a model recovers speaker labels and treat voice identity as a property of the speaker. They do not evaluate how humans perceive whether two voices belong to the same person, which matters for intellectual property, cybersecurity, and everyday life.
AI.method: 1,290 listeners judged 9,800 pairs from 100 public figures. Four tasks measure how well speaker-representation similarity aligns with listener responses, including whether the relationship holds equally for real and synthetic recordings. Eleven publicly available speech models are evaluated.
AI.result: Listener judgments diverge from speaker labels most for voice clones. The best model explains 61% of the explainable variance, and no model reaches the noise ceiling. Models trained with speaker labels align with listeners better than self-supervised models, yet a model with a 12% error rate on speaker labels aligns as well as models with error rates below 2%.
AI.conclusion: Speaker models should be evaluated against human perception on real, cloned, and morphed speech, and the results motivate training speaker models directly on listener judgments.

title: TACT: A Pragmatic Approach to Qualitative Analysis with an AI Council
summary: Qualitative data can tell software teams what their stakeholders need, yet rigorously analyzing thousands of qualitative responses takes expert time that few teams can afford or justify. Teams therefore often face a false choice: leave the responses unanalyzed, or hand them to a large language model and accept its interpretation and judgment. In this paper, we take a pragmatic approach to AI-assisted qualitative analysis and present TACT (Traceable AI Council for Thematic analysis), a procedure that enables such analysis at scale while keeping teams in control of interpretation and judgment. TACT comes in two variants: TACT-Lite, the core AI council procedure, and TACT-Full, which adds adversaries (models from other model families that critique each model's output) and a decision model that surfaces high-uncertainty code assignments. We evaluated TACT on an independent dataset of 256 Stack Overflow threads qualitatively coded by other researchers. Against their labels, TACT's candidate codebook achieved an F1 of 0.75-0.77 and its final coding an F1 of 0.71-0.72. On a held-out sample, agreement between our own manual coding and TACT's coding was Cohen's $\kappa$ of 0.79-0.85. TACT is also economical: model calls cost \$13.77 (TACT-Lite) to \$33.59 (TACT-Full) per 100 threads. Finally, drawing on our experience building and validating TACT, we identify pitfalls in AI-assisted qualitative analysis, describe safeguards to address them, and offer guidance for teams and researchers applying TACT in practice.

AI.tldr: TACT is a procedure for AI-assisted thematic analysis of qualitative data that uses a council of LLMs, cross-family adversaries and an uncertainty-flagging decision model. On 256 Stack Overflow threads it reaches F1 0.71-0.77 against other researchers' labels at $13.77-$33.59 per 100 threads.
AI.motivation: Teams cannot afford expert qualitative analysis of thousands of responses, and handing the responses to an LLM cedes interpretation and judgment to the model.
AI.method: TACT-Lite is the core AI council procedure. TACT-Full adds adversaries, models from other model families that critique each model's output, and a decision model that surfaces high-uncertainty code assignments. Safeguards are drawn from the authors' experience building and validating TACT.
AI.result: On an independent set of 256 Stack Overflow threads coded by other researchers, the candidate codebook reaches F1 0.75-0.77 and the final coding F1 0.71-0.72. On a held-out sample, agreement between the authors' manual coding and TACT's coding is Cohen's kappa 0.79-0.85. Model calls cost $13.77 (TACT-Lite) to $33.59 (TACT-Full) per 100 threads.
AI.conclusion: The pragmatic procedure lets teams scale qualitative analysis while keeping humans in control of interpretation and judgment, and the paper offers pitfalls, safeguards and practical guidance for applying it.

title: Do Language Models Know Which Constraints Belong Together?
comment: 23 pages, 4 figures, 15 tables. Code and data: this https URL
summary: Dantzig-Wolfe reformulation strengthens the linear relaxation of a mixed-integer program by convexifying a chosen set of constraint families, and every candidate costs a column generation run. The choice is hard when families strengthen the bound only together, because a search that adds one family at a time then stops at the linear relaxation. The classical inequalities of lot sizing, network design and facility location rest on such zero-marginal groups. We prove that when each evaluation convexifies at most $s$ of $k$ families, any method that observes only bounds needs a covering number of evaluations, of order $k^w$, to find a hidden group of $w$ families, also on actual Dantzig-Wolfe relaxations. A prediction that misses $e$ members reduces the cost to $\Theta(k^e)$, through one staged search that does not need to know $e$, so the evaluations a prediction saves measure what the predictor knows. We study two sources of predictions. A one-pass lookahead at an optimal LP dual is provably blind to groups whose families share no variable, and a language model reads the names and text of the model. JointDW verifies the prediction of the language model with the staged search and interleaves it with the lookahead at a bounded loss. Groups that strengthen the bound only jointly appear in a quarter of the MIPLIB-NL models whose bound can be improved. There the strongest language models identify them about as often as the lookahead, their predictions rest on the names for textbook models, and reasoning about doubles the accuracy of the same model. On larger models with distracting families, the lookahead finds the group in one evaluation of three families. Language models given only the text seldom name it, while one reasoning model given every coefficient names it in all but one answer and then needs fewer evaluations than the lookahead for pairs of families.

AI.tldr: The paper proves a query-complexity bound for finding groups of constraint families that strengthen the Dantzig-Wolfe bound only jointly, and proposes JointDW, which verifies language-model predictions with a staged search. On MIPLIB-NL models the strongest LLMs find such groups about as often as a one-pass lookahead.
AI.motivation: Choosing which constraint families to convexify is hard when families help only together, because adding one family at a time stops at the linear relaxation and each candidate costs a column generation run.
AI.method: The authors prove that bound-only methods need on the order of k^w evaluations to find a hidden group of w families out of k, and that a prediction missing e members reduces this to Theta(k^e) through a staged search that does not need to know e. Two prediction sources are compared: a one-pass lookahead at an optimal LP dual, and a language model that reads the names and text of the model. JointDW checks the LLM prediction with the staged search and interleaves it with the lookahead at bounded loss.
AI.result: Jointly strengthening groups appear in a quarter of the MIPLIB-NL models whose bound can be improved. There the strongest LLMs identify them about as often as the lookahead, and reasoning doubles the accuracy of the same model. On larger models with distracting families, the lookahead finds the group in one evaluation of three families. LLMs given only the text seldom name the group, while one reasoning model given every coefficient names it in all but one answer and needs fewer evaluations than the lookahead for pairs of families.
AI.conclusion: A prediction saves evaluations in proportion to what the predictor actually knows, and pairing a language model with a verified staged search is a practical way to choose constraint families for Dantzig-Wolfe reformulation.

title: OdorSpaces: Visual-Olfactory Embodied Navigation in 3D Environments
comment: Accepted at the 10th Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL 2026). 20 pages, 4 figures, 6 tables
summary: Olfaction provides critical information about airborne chemical cues, yet it remains largely underexplored in embodied AI, with limited prior machine olfaction work focusing primarily on semantic odor perception. We introduce OdorSpaces, a physics-based simulation platform and benchmark for visual-olfactory embodied navigation. OdorSpaces augments Habitat-Sim with 3D odor transport and dispersion simulated by Fire Dynamics Simulator (FDS), enabling agents to navigate photorealistic indoor environments using both visual and olfactory observations. The benchmark includes two representative source-seeking scenarios: invisible gas-leak localization and early-stage fire localization. We develop an initial multimodal reinforcement learning policy that integrates visual observations and olfactory measurements over time. Experiments show that the policy outperforms a diverse set of baselines, establishing a strong reference for future research on visual-olfactory embodied navigation.

AI.tldr: OdorSpaces is a physics-based simulation platform and benchmark for embodied navigation that uses both vision and smell. It couples Habitat-Sim with 3D odor dispersion from Fire Dynamics Simulator, and an initial multimodal RL policy outperforms a set of baselines on two source-seeking tasks.
AI.motivation: Olfaction is largely unexplored in embodied AI, and prior machine olfaction work focuses mainly on semantic odor perception rather than on navigating toward odor sources.
AI.method: The platform augments Habitat-Sim with 3D odor transport and dispersion simulated by FDS, so agents navigate photorealistic indoor scenes using visual and olfactory observations. The two scenarios are invisible gas-leak localization and early-stage fire localization. The initial policy integrates visual observations and olfactory measurements over time through multimodal reinforcement learning.
AI.result: The policy outperforms a diverse set of baselines on the two source-seeking scenarios. The abstract reports no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: OdorSpaces gives future visual-olfactory embodied navigation research a strong reference point.

title: Learning Hierarchical Patch Splitting Policies for Faster Vision Transformers
summary: Vision Transformers (ViTs) are bottlenecked by the length of their input token sequence. Standard patchification fixes this length with a single patch size applied across the image, regardless of regional content. Prior work on adaptive patch sizing reduces token count by assigning coarser patches to visually simple regions, but relies on noisy pixel-level heuristics such as local entropy to make patchification decisions. We argue that this compute allocation should be grounded in the model's interpretation of task relevant information, not in raw pixel statistics. We introduce Split Policy Learned Image Tokenization which learns to allocate token resolution based on what the model finds meaningful, producing shorter token sequences that are better matched to task-relevant content. SPLIT matches the accuracy of full-resolution ViT classification baselines while using 30% fewer tokens. The same gains hold on dense prediction: SPLIT achieves competitive accuracy on COCO and ADE20K, demonstrating that semantically aligned patchification generalises well beyond classification.

AI.tldr: SPLIT learns where to allocate fine and coarse patches in a Vision Transformer, using the model's own interpretation of task-relevant content rather than pixel heuristics. It matches full-resolution ViT classification accuracy with 30% fewer tokens and stays competitive on COCO and ADE20K.
AI.motivation: ViT cost grows with token count, and standard patchification applies one patch size across the whole image. Prior adaptive patch sizing reduces tokens but relies on noisy pixel-level heuristics such as local entropy.
AI.method: Split Policy Learned Image Tokenization learns to allocate token resolution according to what the model finds meaningful, producing shorter token sequences matched to task-relevant content.
AI.result: SPLIT matches the accuracy of full-resolution ViT classification baselines while using 30% fewer tokens. On dense prediction it achieves competitive accuracy on COCO and ADE20K.
AI.conclusion: Semantically aligned patchification cuts token count without losing accuracy, and the benefit extends beyond classification to dense prediction.

title: Text-Only Domain Adaptation for Low-Resource Medical ASR: Shallow Fusion and Density Ratio Rescoring for Hausa
summary: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems often struggle with specialised medical vocabulary, especially in low-resource languages where domain-specific speech data are scarce. We investigate text-only domain adaptation for Hausa medical ASR using the fixed MMS-1B-FL102 acoustic model and two decoding-time language-model fusion methods: Shallow Fusion (SF) and the Density Ratio Approach (DRA). A 4-gram KenLM trained on 19,421 Hausa health sentences serves as the medical target model, while a 75,372-sentence general-domain model provides the source prior for DRA. Evaluation uses 250 recordings of 25 physician-reviewed prompts from 10 speakers across six northern Nigerian states. Under prompt-disjoint five-fold cross-validation, SF and DRA reduce WER from 29.56% to 23.55% and 23.33%, respectively. Both significantly outperform greedy decoding (p < 0.001), while their difference is not significant (p = 0.423). However, general-LM-only SF achieves 23.96% WER, indicating that the medical LM's additional improvement over a general LM is modest. Medical Term Error Rate also improves under fusion, but does not establish a distinct medical-domain advantage. These findings demonstrate that lightweight, text-only language-model fusion can improve Hausa medical ASR without additional domain-specific speech collection.

AI.tldr: Shallow fusion and the density ratio approach, both text-only, improve Hausa medical ASR on the fixed MMS-1B-FL102 acoustic model, lowering WER from 29.56% to about 23.3-23.6%. The two methods do not differ significantly.
AI.motivation: Domain-specific speech data is scarce for low-resource languages, so medical ASR for Hausa struggles with specialised vocabulary.
AI.method: Two decoding-time language-model fusion methods are compared: Shallow Fusion and the Density Ratio Approach. A 4-gram KenLM trained on 19,421 Hausa health sentences serves as the medical target model, and a 75,372-sentence general-domain model supplies the source prior for DRA. Evaluation uses 250 recordings of 25 physician-reviewed prompts from 10 speakers across six northern Nigerian states, under prompt-disjoint five-fold cross-validation.
AI.result: SF and DRA reduce WER from 29.56% to 23.55% and 23.33% respectively, and both significantly outperform greedy decoding (p < 0.001), while their difference is not significant (p = 0.423). General-LM-only SF reaches 23.96% WER, so the medical LM adds only a modest gain over a general LM. Medical Term Error Rate also improves under fusion but does not establish a distinct medical-domain advantage.
AI.conclusion: Lightweight text-only LM fusion improves Hausa medical ASR without collecting domain-specific speech, although the extra benefit of medical-specific text over general text is modest.

title: Pairing Expert Critique with LLM-Driven Refinement: An Iterative Approach for Curating Quality AI Evaluation Datasets
summary: Evaluating and improving domain-specific LLM responses requires high-quality reference data and rubrics, yet expert authoring is slow and expensive, and synthetic datasets may fail to capture practitioner preferences unless they are grounded in expert judgment. We present SME-C (Subject Matter Expert Critique), a human-AI workflow that captures expertise through lightweight critiques of candidate responses and complements it with LLM-driven analysis and refinement to iteratively curate response datasets and evaluation rubrics. We validate SME-C in the domain of financial business briefs, collecting 3,853 critiques from 411 finance professionals on 520 queries across two survey rounds. We evaluate two LLM-driven refinement strategies: one guided by the experts' written critiques and one that infers critique solely from their preference votes. In a blind validation survey with 100 additional professionals, we found that both strategies significantly improved quality over the experts' top-ranked baseline responses. The gains were concentrated among weaker original responses, and the two strategies excelled in different ways: critique-based refinement produced more domain-grounded improvements, whereas vote-based refinement was more effective at identifying and removing irrelevant content. The resulting rubrics and refined dataset support reproducible offline evaluation and benchmarking of LLMs, suggesting that structured expert critique is a viable alternative to expert authoring for building high-quality, domain-specific evaluation resources more quickly, at scale, and at lower cost.

AI.tldr: SME-C is a human-AI workflow in which finance professionals give lightweight critiques of candidate LLM responses, and LLM-driven refinement curates better response datasets and rubrics. Both refinement strategies significantly improve on the experts' top-ranked baseline responses.
AI.motivation: Expert authoring of evaluation references and rubrics is slow and expensive, and synthetic datasets may miss practitioner preferences unless they are grounded in expert judgment.
AI.method: Experts critique candidate responses, and LLMs analyse and refine them iteratively to curate response datasets and evaluation rubrics. Two refinement strategies are compared: one guided by the experts' written critiques, and one that infers critique solely from their preference votes.
AI.result: Using 3,853 critiques from 411 finance professionals on 520 queries across two survey rounds, both strategies significantly improved quality over the top-ranked baseline responses in a blind validation survey of 100 further professionals. Gains were concentrated among weaker original responses. Critique-based refinement produced more domain-grounded improvements, while vote-based refinement was more effective at identifying and removing irrelevant content.
AI.conclusion: Structured expert critique is a viable, faster, scalable and cheaper alternative to expert authoring for building domain-specific evaluation resources, and the resulting rubrics and dataset support reproducible offline LLM evaluation.

title: Scheduling Data to Compute: Hierarchical Data Pipelining for LLM Training on AMD GPUs
summary: Large language models (LLM) have been the key focus of recent machine learning breakthroughs. As the model size grows exponentially, the computation needed for training is astronomical. A GPU can do a huge amount of arithmetic. However, the data its compute units need is not always available when they are ready. This data may still be in slow memory or on another GPU. While the chip waits, expensive compute sits idle, and at scale even a small drop in utilization translates into substantial cost. In this paper, we treat this waiting time as the primary bottleneck. We focus on hardware features designed for explicit data movement. These features load data from off-chip memory onto the chip, rearrange it into the layout the computation requires as it is loaded, and transfer it between GPUs. By orchestrating them, we keep a steady pipeline of data flowing to the compute units so that they remain busy. We present kernel and framework implementations that address this bottleneck using three key data-movement instructions and hardware features. The Tensor Data Mover (TDM) moves tensor data from high-bandwidth memory (HBM) into on-chip memory. Transpose-load instructions transpose tensor data into the layout that LLM computations require as it is loaded on-chip. Finally, System DMA (SDMA) and Remote DMA (RDMA) move data between GPUs over the scale-up and scale-out networks, respectively. Our results show that TDM and transpose-load provide on average 1.88x and 1.19x speedup at the kernel level, respectively. The SDMA and RDMA lead to on average 1.16x and 1.33x speedup for computation overlapped with communication. This is the first AMD LLM training system to utilize all the GPU data pipelining features. Our implementation has been integrated into open source framework and library for AMD GPUs. this https URL this https URL

AI.tldr: The paper presents AMD GPU LLM training kernels and framework integrations that use explicit data-movement hardware (TDM, transpose-load, SDMA and RDMA) to keep compute units fed. Reported kernel speedups are 1.88x for TDM and 1.19x for transpose-load, and 1.16x and 1.33x for computation overlapped with communication.
AI.motivation: Compute units often wait for data held in slow memory or on other GPUs, leaving costly compute idle, and at scale even small utilization losses are substantial.
AI.method: Three data-movement instructions and hardware features are orchestrated into a steady pipeline. The Tensor Data Mover moves tensors from HBM on-chip, transpose-load instructions rearrange data into the layout LLM computations need as it loads, and System DMA and Remote DMA move data across scale-up and scale-out networks.
AI.result: TDM and transpose-load give on average 1.88x and 1.19x speedup at the kernel level. SDMA and RDMA give on average 1.16x and 1.33x speedup for computation overlapped with communication. The implementation is integrated into an open-source framework and library for AMD GPUs.
AI.conclusion: The authors present this as the first AMD LLM training system to use all of the GPU data-pipelining features, showing that treating data waiting as the primary bottleneck pays off in practice.

title: BobFlow: Towards Human-Agent Collaborative Data Science Using Dataflows
summary: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have established human-agent collaboration as a promising paradigm for data science. Effective collaboration requires a shared computational abstraction that enables agents to reason about processing logic while allowing human analysts to understand, guide, and refine the analysis. Although scripts written in Python or SQL provide precise control, their syntax and execution details can be difficult for analysts to understand and modify. In this paper, we argue that dataflows are an effective abstraction for human-agent collaboration in data science. We introduce BobFlow, a system that combines the dataflow abstraction with the ReAct paradigm. It enables agents to iteratively construct and execute dataflows for data science tasks while allowing analysts to inspect the analysis and provide feedback. Our user study shows that BobFlow helps analysts understand, inspect, and verify agent-generated analyses. A thorough experimental evaluation across proprietary and open-weight LLMs shows accuracy score gains of up to 18.6 points at just over 1/3 of a script-based ReAct agent's inference cost.

AI.tldr: BobFlow lets LLM agents build and execute dataflows under the ReAct paradigm so that analysts can inspect and steer data science work. It improves accuracy by up to 18.6 points at just over one third of a script-based ReAct agent's inference cost.
AI.motivation: Human-agent collaboration in data science needs a shared abstraction, and Python or SQL scripts, though precise, are hard for analysts to understand and modify.
AI.method: The authors argue that dataflows are an effective abstraction and build BobFlow, which combines the dataflow abstraction with ReAct. Agents iteratively construct and execute dataflows while analysts inspect the analysis and give feedback.
AI.result: A user study shows that BobFlow helps analysts understand, inspect and verify agent-generated analyses. Across proprietary and open-weight LLMs, accuracy gains reach 18.6 points at just over 1/3 of the inference cost of a script-based ReAct agent.
AI.conclusion: Dataflows are a practical abstraction for human-agent collaborative data science, balancing agent reasoning with analyst oversight at lower cost.

title: How Well Can Large Language Models Impersonate Individual Authors? A Comparative Evaluation
summary: This study investigates the authorship impersonation capacity of six widely used large language models (LLMs): Gemini 3 Pro, Claude Opus, GPT 5.2, GPT 5.2 Pro, DeepSeek 3.2, and Grok 4.1 Fast. The evaluation was conducted using short product review texts selected to ensure high within author consistency in individual writing style. Two types of in context prompt were designed: a simple prompt with minimal instruction and a complex prompt incorporating explicit stylometric guidance for mimicry. Authorship mimicry was evaluated using a cosine distance based distance to training metric, supplemented by visual analyses of embedding distributions. The results indicate that authorship impersonation remained challenging for most LLMs, with Gemini 3 Pro showing the strongest apparent mimicry performance. However, subsequent overlap analysis revealed that Gemini 3 Pro extensively copied and reused sentences and phrases from the training texts, at levels far exceeding those observed among human authors. Follow up factor analyses showed that training set consistency was the most robust predictor of mimicry success across models, whereas author distinctiveness did not generalise as a reliable predictor. Global embedding visualisations further revealed a consistent macro level pattern: for most models, generated texts occupied regions of the embedding space that were largely separated from the corresponding human training clusters. This indicates limited convergence towards target author style and suggests the presence of model specific lexical and phraseological preferences. The findings highlight the importance of distinguishing genuine stylistic imitation from direct textual reuse and have implications for the forensic analysis of textual evidence involving potential LLM enabled impersonation.

AI.tldr: Six LLMs are tested on authorship impersonation from short product reviews. The most convincing mimicry, from Gemini 3 Pro, relies heavily on copying sentences from the training texts, and training-set consistency rather than author distinctiveness predicts mimicry success.
AI.motivation: Forensic analysis of textual evidence needs to know whether LLMs can convincingly imitate individual authors, and whether apparent imitation reflects genuine style rather than textual reuse.
AI.method: Six LLMs (Gemini 3 Pro, Claude Opus, GPT 5.2, GPT 5.2 Pro, DeepSeek 3.2 and Grok 4.1 Fast) are prompted with either a simple or a stylometrically guided in-context prompt. Mimicry is scored by a cosine-distance-based distance to training texts, supplemented by embedding visualisations, overlap analysis and factor analyses.
AI.result: Most models show limited mimicry. Gemini 3 Pro scores strongest but extensively copies and reuses sentences and phrases from the training texts, far beyond levels among human authors. Training-set consistency is the most robust predictor of mimicry success across models, while author distinctiveness does not generalise as a reliable predictor. For most models, generated texts lie largely apart from the human training clusters in embedding space.
AI.conclusion: Genuine stylistic imitation must be distinguished from direct textual reuse, and LLM-enabled impersonation has implications for the forensic analysis of textual evidence.

title: Unsupervised Neural Operators for Rotating Relativistic Stars: High-Fidelity Equation of State Inference and Pulsar Spin Evolution at Scale
summary: Observed populations of rotating neutron stars~(NSs) with millisecond-order periods are powerful probes of fundamental physics. Mass-radius measurements inform poorly constrained properties of degenerate nuclear matter, whereas high-fidelity population synthesis connects unknowns in NS formation and binary evolution to large radio-timing surveys. However, repeated structure calculations are prohibitive due to the computational cost of solving the highly coupled partial differential equations of axisymmetric general relativistic hydrostatic equilibrium that govern rotating NS interiors. Non-rotating calculations or approximate rotational corrections can bias equation of state inference and limit the fidelity of population synthesis in tracing the evolutionary history of progenitors and propagating equation of state uncertainties. In this \textit{Letter}, we develop physics-informed neural operators that can solve the axisymmetric problem with high accuracy and negligible computational cost. \textit{Our solvers are trained in a fully unsupervised setting, with the training objective informed solely by the partial differential equations, and achieve a $10^3\times$ speed-up with negligible accuracy loss}. These solvers enable scalable EoS inference that self-consistently accounts for rotation and repeated stellar-structure calculations during binary evolution, making spin predictions that account for rotational structure and EoS uncertainties computationally accessible to population synthesis.

AI.tldr: Physics-informed neural operators trained without labelled data solve the axisymmetric general relativistic equilibrium of rotating neutron stars about 10^3 times faster, with negligible accuracy loss. This makes scalable equation of state inference and rotation-aware population synthesis feasible.
AI.motivation: Rotating neutron star structure requires repeatedly solving coupled axisymmetric GR hydrostatic equilibrium PDEs, which is too costly. Non-rotating calculations or approximate rotational corrections bias EoS inference and limit population synthesis.
AI.method: Physics-informed neural operators are trained in a fully unsupervised setting, with the training objective defined solely by the governing partial differential equations.
AI.result: The solvers achieve a 10^3 speed-up with negligible accuracy loss, which allows repeated stellar-structure calculations during binary evolution and self-consistent EoS inference that accounts for rotation.
AI.conclusion: Spin predictions that account for rotational structure and EoS uncertainty become computationally accessible to population synthesis.

title: DARE: Difficulty Analysis for Repair Enhancement
summary: LLM-based coding agents are primarily evaluated by their solve rates. However, this metric does not reveal how difficult the solved tasks are or account for differences intask difficulty across benchmarks. Determining the difficulty of individual tasks by repeatedly running multiple agents is costly, while a predicted difficulty score alone provides limited guidance on what support an agent needs. To address these challenges, we propose DARE (Difficulty Analysis for Repair Enhancement), which integrates repair-task difficulty measurement, prediction, feature-group contribution analysis, and task-specific repair support. We define continuous task difficulty as the observed failure rate across multiple coding agents. The DARE difficulty model predicts this difficulty using 151 static features extracted from benchmark artifacts. The framework also analyzes the contributions of seven Repair-Task Feature Groups to identify the characteristics most salient to each task and uses this information to select task-specific agent support. We evaluate DARE on four benchmark partitions comprising 2,594 tasks. The difficulty model's aligned predictions achieve Spearman's $\rho$ = .476-.621 on held-out partitions, and the most salient Feature Groups vary across tasks and benchmarks. Furthermore, coding-agent experiments show improved repair success when support is matched to each task's salient Feature Group. These findings demonstrate that difficulty prediction and interpretation can lead to practical improvements in automated program repair (APR), while also providing a basis for difficulty-stratified agent evaluation, cross-benchmark comparisons, and identifying areas of repair capability that warrant further improvement.

AI.tldr: DARE measures repair-task difficulty as the observed failure rate across coding agents, predicts it from 151 static features, and uses feature-group analysis to select task-specific agent support. Support matched to each task's most salient feature group improves repair success.
AI.motivation: Solve rates hide how difficult the solved tasks are and ignore difficulty differences across benchmarks, and measuring difficulty by repeatedly running many agents is costly.
AI.method: DARE combines difficulty measurement, a difficulty predictor built from 151 static features extracted from benchmark artifacts, analysis of the contributions of seven Repair-Task Feature Groups, and selection of task-specific agent support based on the most salient group.
AI.result: On four benchmark partitions comprising 2,594 tasks, the difficulty model achieves Spearman rho of 0.476-0.621 on held-out partitions. The most salient feature groups vary across tasks and benchmarks. Coding-agent experiments show improved repair success when support is matched to each task's salient group.
AI.conclusion: Difficulty prediction and interpretation can yield practical gains in automated program repair and support difficulty-stratified evaluation, cross-benchmark comparison and the identification of repair capabilities that need improvement.

title: GREP: Grounding Generated Room Evaluation in Principles
comment: 24 pages. Project page: this https URL
summary: Recent LLM-centric advances can generate attractive furnished rooms by selecting and arranging assets. Yet evaluation remains limited to specific perspectives or predefined questions, failing to reflect overall scene quality. To address this pressing need, we introduce GREP. Its core is a focus shift from defining specific questions to establishing a three-tier evaluation philosophy: basic physical validity checks whether a scene obeys physical constraints; visual coherence concerns compatibility in object scale, style, and composition; and, at the highest level, human-use logic requires object arrangements to align with everyday human habits. Guided by these principles, an evaluation agent autonomously and adaptively identifies issues from scene context, gathers evidence, and produces scores and reports. This supports scene-specific issue discovery and reliable judgments. Experiments show that (1) GREP achieves 87% agreement with human majority preferences, substantially outperforming baseline evaluators. (2) GREP reports improve scene quality through refinement, whereas score-only and no-feedback baselines show slight declines. (3) GREP suggests that as planning ability improves, recent models such as GPT-5.6 Sol can move from relying on pipelines and harnesses to challenging their guidance and constraints, but still lack the ability to resolve the resulting conflicts. Stronger models are therefore expected not only to plan well, but also to adapt to external guidance and constraints more flexibly. Project page: this https URL

AI.tldr: GREP evaluates generated furnished rooms with a three-tier principle hierarchy and an autonomous evaluation agent, reaching 87% agreement with human majority preferences. Refinement guided by GREP reports improves scene quality, whereas score-only and no-feedback baselines decline slightly.
AI.motivation: Evaluation of LLM-generated furnished rooms is limited to specific perspectives or predefined questions, so it fails to reflect overall scene quality.
AI.method: The evaluation philosophy has three tiers: basic physical validity, visual coherence in object scale, style and composition, and human-use logic, meaning arrangements that match everyday human habits. Guided by these principles, an evaluation agent adaptively identifies issues from scene context, gathers evidence, and produces scores and reports.
AI.result: GREP achieves 87% agreement with human majority preferences, substantially outperforming baseline evaluators. GREP reports improve scene quality through refinement, whereas score-only and no-feedback baselines show slight declines. Recent models such as GPT-5.6 Sol can move from relying on pipelines and harnesses to challenging their guidance and constraints, but still cannot resolve the resulting conflicts.
AI.conclusion: Stronger models should adapt flexibly to external guidance and constraints as well as plan well.

title: Matching the Training-Time Weight Rule in Inference-Time Expert Deactivation
comment: Corresponding authors: Hanzhang Jia (lead corresponding) and Bo Ma
summary: Expert deactivation at inference time changes both token routing and expert weights, and its effect on performance depends on how these changes are implemented. We compare removal, freezing, remaining-expert renormalization, and unnormalized re-routing on identical disabled sets across five instruction-tuned checkpoints from four model families, with a base OLMoE checkpoint as an additional comparison. We develop a weight-sum model that relates the loss of expert contributions and changes in branch scale to the weight rule used during training. With half of the experts deactivated according to activation-based rankings, remaining-expert renormalization yields the highest perplexity in models trained with raw router probabilities, whereas unnormalized re-routing yields the highest perplexity in models trained with normalized weights. Perplexity ranges from 1.4 to 73 times the intact baseline when the training rule is retained, and from 14 to 28,740 times the baseline under a rule mismatch. Task outcomes vary across evaluation types: on OLMoE, GSM8K strict-match accuracy falls to zero under all four implementations. Extending the model to changes in the number of active experts yields a further prediction, supported by the OLMoE experiments: the perplexity penalty from additional renormalization increases as fewer experts are activated.

AI.tldr: Comparing four ways of deactivating experts at inference shows that perplexity depends on whether the implementation matches the weight rule used in training. Under a mismatch, perplexity rises to as much as 28,740 times the intact baseline.
AI.motivation: Inference-time expert deactivation changes both token routing and expert weights, and its effect on performance depends on how those changes are implemented.
AI.method: Removal, freezing, remaining-expert renormalization and unnormalized re-routing are compared on identical disabled sets across five instruction-tuned checkpoints from four model families, plus a base OLMoE checkpoint. A weight-sum model relates lost expert contributions and branch-scale changes to the weight rule used in training. Half of the experts are deactivated by activation rankings, and the number of active experts is also varied.
AI.result: With raw router probabilities in training, remaining-expert renormalization gives the highest perplexity; with normalized weights, unnormalized re-routing does. Perplexity is 1.4 to 73 times the intact baseline when the training rule is kept and 14 to 28,740 times under a rule mismatch. On OLMoE, GSM8K strict-match accuracy falls to zero under all four implementations. The model predicts that the perplexity penalty from additional renormalization grows as fewer experts are activated, and the OLMoE experiments support this.
AI.conclusion: The training-time weight rule should be matched when deactivating experts at inference, and the weight-sum model explains and predicts the resulting perplexity penalties.

title: When File Ingestion Misleads Language Models: Measuring and Mitigating Divergences in Office Documents
summary: Office documents are now routinely uploaded to large language models (LLMs) for processing. However, an LLM does not always see what a human sees, because it typically reads the text that an extractor produces from the document's underlying Office Open XML (OOXML) files. Depending on the implementation, extractors differ in which OOXML parts they read and how they interpret them, so their output can differ from what Office applications display. For example, by slightly shifting the positions of text boxes on a slide, an adversary can swap the order in which the model reads them while the slide looks unchanged. We show that this extraction divergence is an attack surface for LLM applications. In this work, we first measure what an adversary can exploit by analyzing the widely used extractors that LLM applications rely on. By combining static source code analysis with dynamic analysis, we identify 19 OOXML channels where extractors read content a human cannot see and 12 where they drop content a human can. We also find that widely used extractors ignore display formatting and reading order, so even visible content reaches the model in a different form. Building on these findings, we construct five attacks that lead the model to interpret a document differently from a human reviewer, without injecting any instruction. We test the attacks on four major chat assistants (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Microsoft 365 Copilot) and four coding agents (Codex, Claude Code, Antigravity, and GitHub Copilot CLI), and every one of them is misled by at least one attack. Finally, we propose Prism, a lightweight defense that reconstructs the human view from the OOXML specification before passing the text to the model. Prism also generalizes to unseen attack payloads.

AI.tldr: Measurement of Office document extractors finds 19 OOXML channels where extractors read content humans cannot see and 12 where they drop content humans can see. Five attacks mislead LLMs without injected instructions, every chat assistant and coding agent tested is fooled by at least one, and the Prism defense reconstructs the human view from the OOXML specification.
AI.motivation: LLMs read extractor output rather than what Office applications display, so extraction divergence is an attack surface, and its scope had not been measured.
AI.method: Static source code analysis combined with dynamic analysis of widely used extractors identifies divergent OOXML channels. Five attacks are built on these divergences. Prism reconstructs the human-visible view from the OOXML specification before passing the text to the model.
AI.result: The extractors ignore display formatting and reading order, so even visible content reaches the model in a different form. All four chat assistants (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Microsoft 365 Copilot) and all four coding agents (Codex, Claude Code, Antigravity, GitHub Copilot CLI) are misled by at least one attack. Prism generalises to unseen attack payloads.
AI.conclusion: Extraction divergence is a real attack surface, and reconstructing the human view from the specification is a lightweight defense.

title: Learning When Human Decisions Matter: Executor-Relative Consultation Value for LLM Agents
summary: Large language models increasingly automate complex tasks, but human decision capacity does not scale with their capabilities. In many applications, humans remain essential for providing private context, authority, or judgments unavailable to the agent. We formulate human decision capacity allocation: given multiple consultation opportunities and a limited budget, at which decisions should an LLM agent consult a human? The central challenge is estimating consultation value, which is executor-dependent because the same human input may benefit different downstream agents differently. We introduce Consultation Value Distillation (CVD), which estimates consultation values offline using Monte Carlo executor rollouts and distills these values into lightweight predictors for budgeted allocation, requiring no rollout-based value estimation at deployment. Across five batch and three sequential settings with two frontier executors, CVD improves allocation through joint and continuation-aware value learning, while independent consultation values remain competitive in several settings. CVD also broadly outperforms direct prompting and Value of Information where applicable, remains robust with substantially less rollout supervision, and enables nearly lossless approximate allocation at low search cost.

AI.tldr: CVD estimates the value of human consultation offline with Monte Carlo executor rollouts, distills these values into lightweight predictors, and allocates a limited consultation budget without rollouts at deployment. It improves allocation across five batch and three sequential settings with two frontier executors.
AI.motivation: Human decision capacity does not scale with agent capability, so an agent must decide where to consult a human under a limited budget, and the value of a consultation depends on which executor will use the input.
AI.method: Consultation Value Distillation estimates consultation values offline with Monte Carlo executor rollouts and distills them into lightweight predictors for budgeted allocation, using joint and continuation-aware value learning.
AI.result: Across five batch and three sequential settings with two frontier executors, CVD improves allocation, while independent consultation values remain competitive in several settings. CVD broadly outperforms direct prompting and Value of Information where applicable, stays robust with substantially less rollout supervision, and enables nearly lossless approximate allocation at low search cost.
AI.conclusion: Executor-relative, distilled consultation values make budgeted human consultation for LLM agents practical.

title: A Hybrid Approach for Automated Security Pattern Recovery
summary: Security-by-design emphasises integrating security into software design and development. Security pattern catalogues operationalise this principle by prescribing reusable architectural solutions to recurring security problems. However, recovering their implementations from source code remains challenging because security patterns are abstract, span multiple components, and admit many valid implementations. We present SecPatRec, a hybrid approach for automated security pattern recovery from source code repositories. We treat a security pattern as a reference architecture and frame its recovery as a deductive task: determining which prescribed roles are present, grounding them in code entities, and recovering their interaction sequences. SecPatRec pairs a ReAct-style LLM agent equipped with semantic and lexical code search for role detection and grounding with static code property graph analysis for interaction recovery. We curate a human-validated ground-truth dataset of 100 pattern instances covering five security patterns across 93 open-source Java and Python repositories, and introduce a three-level evaluation framework measuring recovery correctness against this ground truth. We evaluate SecPatRec using four LLMs, including proprietary and open-source models. Averaged over all models and pattern instances, SecPatRec achieves role-detection accuracy of 0.84, role-grounding similarity of 0.84, and an interaction-recovery score of 0.66. Compared to a one-shot end-to-end LLM baseline, SecPatRec achieves higher aggregate recovery scores and lower estimated LLM API costs per run, while processing repositories that exceed the baseline's configured input limit. The recovered role mappings and statically derived interaction sequences provide structural and behavioural evidence that can support inspection of security-pattern implementations.

AI.tldr: SecPatRec recovers security pattern implementations from Java and Python repositories by combining a ReAct-style LLM agent, for role detection and grounding, with static code property graph analysis, for interaction recovery. It beats a one-shot LLM baseline on aggregate recovery while costing less per run and handling repositories that exceed the baseline's input limit.
AI.motivation: Security patterns are abstract, span multiple components and admit many valid implementations, so recovering them from source code is hard.
AI.method: The pattern is treated as a reference architecture, and recovery is framed as determining which roles are present, grounding them in code entities, and recovering their interaction sequences. An LLM agent with semantic and lexical code search handles role detection and grounding, and static code property graph analysis recovers interactions.
AI.result: Over a human-validated ground truth of 100 pattern instances covering five patterns across 93 open-source repositories, averaged over four LLMs, SecPatRec achieves role-detection accuracy 0.84, role-grounding similarity 0.84 and interaction-recovery score 0.66. Compared with a one-shot end-to-end LLM baseline, it achieves higher aggregate recovery scores and lower estimated API costs per run.
AI.conclusion: The recovered role mappings and statically derived interaction sequences give structural and behavioural evidence that supports inspection of security-pattern implementations.

title: RACE: Calibrated Cumulative Scoring for Rollout-Free Robot Policy Checkpoint Selection
summary: Assessing the deployment performance of learned robot policies during training is challenging, as directly measuring task success requires costly real-world trials for each candidate checkpoint. Averaged validation loss offers a rollout-free alternative, but its checkpoint rankings can be inconsistent with deployment performance. We analyze two limitations of this criterion: it penalizes action deviations without considering whether the policy can recover from them, and gives later reference predictions equal weight even when earlier deviations may lead execution away from the reference. We propose RACE, a novel rollout-free metric for ranking checkpoints using a fixed set of held-out successful trajectories. RACE calibrates action deviations against state-conditional thresholds derived from action differences at similar states in these trajectories. We aggregate these scores through a running product, so that a substantial deviation reduces the contribution of subsequent reference predictions. Averaging the resulting cumulative scores over time and across trajectories yields the checkpoint score. In simulation, RACE outperforms baselines across validation sources, while several baselines degrade sharply when the validation set changes. On real robots, its rankings align with deployment success across the evaluated policy backbones and tasks of varying difficulty. Perturbation analyses further show that RACE distinguishes deviations with markedly different effects on task success, even when baselines respond similarly.

AI.tldr: RACE ranks robot policy checkpoints without rollouts by scoring action deviations against state-conditional thresholds and aggregating them as a running product over held-out successful trajectories.
