Its rankings track real-robot deployment success better than validation loss and stay stable when the validation set changes.
AI.motivation: Average validation loss is a rollout-free checkpoint criterion, but its rankings can disagree with deployment performance because it penalises deviations without considering whether the policy can recover from them, and weights later reference predictions equally.
AI.method: RACE calibrates each action deviation against thresholds derived from action differences at similar states in held-out successful trajectories. Scores are aggregated by a running product, so a substantial deviation reduces the contribution of subsequent reference predictions, and the cumulative scores are then averaged over time and across trajectories.
AI.result: In simulation RACE outperforms baselines across validation sources, while several baselines degrade sharply when the validation set changes. On real robots its rankings align with deployment success across the evaluated policy backbones and tasks of varying difficulty. Perturbation analyses show that it distinguishes deviations with markedly different effects on task success, where baselines respond similarly.
AI.conclusion: A calibrated cumulative criterion gives a rollout-free checkpoint selection signal that is more reliable than validation loss.

title: PEARL: Prediction Error-Adaptive Regularized Learning for Selective Forgetting under Partial Preference Drift
summary: User preferences shift as needs, context, and tastes evolve. This matters for personalized recommendation, LLM response generation, and RLHF-trained reward models, which can become miscalibrated as preferences drift. Existing non-stationary bandit methods forget uniformly across all dimensions, but real preference shifts are typically partial: some dimensions go stale while others remain valid. Neural contextual bandits accumulate confidence monotonically via the Gram matrix, with no mechanism to direct uncertainty where predictions have gone wrong. We propose PEARL (Prediction Error-Adaptive Regularized Learning), which reverses the Gram update along feature directions where predictions are surprisingly wrong, while leaving confidence intact elsewhere. We prove that (i) any non-adaptive policy suffers linear regret after a preference shift, (ii) no fixed exploration rate achieves low regret in both stationary and non-stationary regimes, and (iii) PEARL's cumulative regret scales with the number of shifted users N_s, not the total population N. On PRISM, a personalized LLM response selection benchmark (1,500 users, 21 LLMs), PEARL beats greedy by +4.0 points and the best neural bandit baseline by +2.5 points (p<0.001), while performing on par with greedy when preferences are stable. It beats sliding-window and discounted approaches by 3 to 10 points, showing that selective forgetting outperforms uniform forgetting. The selection policy is a ~100K-parameter MLP that runs in milliseconds on CPU, leaves LLM weights frozen, and works with any API-based model.

AI.tldr: PEARL is a neural contextual bandit that reverses Gram-matrix confidence along feature directions where predictions are wrong, so it forgets only the stale dimensions after partial preference drift. On PRISM it beats greedy by 4.0 points and the best neural bandit by 2.5 points, with a selection policy of about 100K parameters.
AI.motivation: Existing non-stationary bandits forget uniformly, while real preference shifts are partial. Neural contextual bandits accumulate confidence monotonically and have no mechanism to direct uncertainty to where predictions have gone wrong.
AI.method: PEARL reverses the Gram update along feature directions where predictions are surprisingly wrong and leaves confidence intact elsewhere. The selection policy is a roughly 100K-parameter MLP that runs in milliseconds on CPU, leaves LLM weights frozen, and works with any API-based model.
AI.result: The authors prove that any non-adaptive policy suffers linear regret after a preference shift, that no fixed exploration rate achieves low regret in both stationary and non-stationary regimes, and that PEARL's cumulative regret scales with the number of shifted users N_s rather than the total population N. On PRISM (1,500 users, 21 LLMs), PEARL beats greedy by +4.0 points and the best neural bandit baseline by +2.5 points (p<0.001), performs on par with greedy when preferences are stable, and beats sliding-window and discounted approaches by 3 to 10 points.
AI.conclusion: Selective forgetting outperforms uniform forgetting under partial preference drift, and regret is tied to the number of shifted users rather than the whole population.

title: Generative AI for urban planning: synthesizing land-use maps with satellite imagery via DualControlNet
summary: Various land-use models characterize land-use patterns and facilitate scenario planning. However, existing models are largely predictive, forecasting transitions based on numeric data without synthesizing new land-use maps from simple text prompts. Meanwhile, generative AI in urban systems remains unimodal, weakly controllable, and evaluated mostly by generic image quality rather than domain-specific metrics. To address these gaps, we introduce DualControlNet, a generative land-use model that jointly synthesizes high-resolution land-use maps and satellite imagery, addressing multimodality, controllability, and verification challenges. Trained on over 40,000 paired tiles from Orlando and Chicago, DualControlNet is evaluated using land-use, spatial consistency, and image quality metrics. Relative to unimodal baselines, DualControlNet improves land-use diversity consistency by 62.8% and building coverage ratio consistency by 16.3%, more than doubles cross-modal spatial consistency, and triples visual quality. Scenario-based experiments demonstrate that DualControlNet supports sustainable development through multidimensional controls, increasing density and diversity, and responding to text prompts like "high-density development." Overall, this work advances land-use modeling via a multimodal, controllable, and verifiable generative framework, lowering technical barriers and enabling intuitive exploration of urban futures.

AI.tldr: DualControlNet jointly generates high-resolution land-use maps and satellite imagery from text prompts and controls, trained on over 40,000 paired tiles from Orlando and Chicago. It improves land-use diversity consistency by 62.8% and building coverage ratio consistency by 16.3% over unimodal baselines.
AI.motivation: Land-use models are predictive rather than generative, and generative AI for urban systems is unimodal, weakly controllable and judged by generic image quality rather than domain-specific metrics.
AI.method: A generative land-use model jointly synthesises land-use maps and satellite images under multidimensional controls and text prompts. It is evaluated with land-use, spatial consistency and image quality metrics.
AI.result: Relative to unimodal baselines, DualControlNet improves land-use diversity consistency by 62.8% and building coverage ratio consistency by 16.3%, more than doubles cross-modal spatial consistency and triples visual quality. Scenario experiments show that it increases density and diversity and responds to text prompts such as "high-density development."
AI.conclusion: The multimodal, controllable and verifiable framework lowers technical barriers to intuitive exploration of urban futures and supports sustainable development scenarios.

title: AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust
summary: When does an AI assistant improve human decision-making, and when does it hurt? We argue that the answer depends not just on AI accuracy but also on how much its evidence overlaps with the human's and how the human combines the two. A worker makes a binary decision by observing her own signal and receiving a recommendation from an AI. We develop a human behavioral model with two primitives: her awareness of the overlap and her trust in the AI. Our analysis gives a closed-form phase diagram over AI capability and overlap, with regions of complementarity, impairment, and automation. A worker who neglects the overlap (correlation neglect) can be made less accurate by a more capable AI, double-counting the shared evidence. Trust reshapes the regions - undertrust may compensate for correlation neglect, so that the trust level maximizing accuracy depends on the deployment parameters. Empirically, we identify the two model parameters by pairing the same workers with different AIs, and break the accuracy loss into a correlation-neglect cost and an undertrust cost, one tied to reducing overlap on the AI side, the other to calibrating trust on the human side. On ChatBench, AI assistance raises accuracy by 21 points, yet workers apply only about a quarter of the Bayes-rational weight to AI information; GPT-4o falls in the automation region and Llama-3.1-8b stays at the complementarity boundary; and calibrating trust recovers about 2.6 points for GPT-4o but almost nothing for Llama-3.1-8b.

AI.tldr: A model of a worker combining her own signal with an AI recommendation shows that AI assistance can hurt when the worker neglects evidence overlap. On ChatBench, AI raises accuracy by 21 points, yet workers apply only about a quarter of the Bayes-rational weight to the AI's information.
AI.motivation: Whether AI helps depends not only on its accuracy but also on how much its evidence overlaps with the human's and how the human combines the two. Correlation neglect can make a more capable AI reduce accuracy by double-counting shared evidence.
AI.method: A behavioural model with two primitives, awareness of overlap and trust in the AI, gives a closed-form phase diagram over AI capability and overlap, with complementarity, impairment and automation regions. The two parameters are identified empirically by pairing the same workers with different AIs, and the accuracy loss is decomposed into a correlation-neglect cost and an undertrust cost.
AI.result: On ChatBench, AI assistance raises accuracy by 21 points, but workers apply only about a quarter of the Bayes-rational weight to AI information. GPT-4o falls in the automation region and Llama-3.1-8b stays at the complementarity boundary. Calibrating trust recovers about 2.6 points for GPT-4o but almost nothing for Llama-3.1-8b.
AI.conclusion: The trust level that maximises accuracy depends on deployment parameters, so reducing overlap on the AI side and calibrating trust on the human side are distinct levers.

title: CellCanon: An Agentic Cellular World Model for Prediction, Explanation, and Observation-Driven Updating
comment: 31 pages, 5 figures. Code: this https URL
summary: Biological discovery requires using molecular knowledge and new measurements to infer responses beyond the conditions already observed. We introduce CellCanon, the first agentic cellular world model to unify single-cell expression prediction, evidence-grounded explanation, and observation-driven updating. Its predictive core reuses condition-level biological evidence across gene-specific numerical readouts to guide single-cell expression generation. A shared world state links predictions, acquired measurements, and source-linked claims, supporting explanation and revision. On 339 held-out SciPlex3 conditions across three cell lines, CellCanon improves differential-expression AUPRC and Macro-F1 over the best baseline for each metric by 63.3% and 17.3%, respectively, and direction Macro-F1 by 7.2%. Relative to gene-wise reasoning on matched drug-cell cohorts, measured language-model token use falls by 99.77% for Predict and 98.41% for Explain. On the source-grounded benchmark, Explain correctly answers all answerable questions with supporting proofs and identifies all insufficient-evidence cases. In simulated experimental feedback, Update uses one measured source context per drug to exceed the best fine-tuned baselines in differential-expression AUPRC and Macro-F1 without changing model weights. Together, these capabilities support a cumulative account of cellular responses, with predictions and biological judgments that can be revised as evidence accumulates.

AI.tldr: CellCanon is an agentic cellular world model that unifies single-cell expression prediction, evidence-grounded explanation and observation-driven updating. On 339 held-out SciPlex3 conditions it improves differential-expression AUPRC and Macro-F1 over the best baseline for each metric by 63.3% and 17.3%.
AI.motivation: Biological discovery requires inferring cellular responses beyond the conditions already observed, combining molecular knowledge with new measurements, and existing approaches do not jointly predict, explain and revise such responses.
AI.method: A shared world state links predictions, acquired measurements and source-linked claims. The predictive core reuses condition-level biological evidence across gene-specific numerical readouts to guide single-cell expression generation, and the Explain and Update capabilities operate on the same world state.
AI.result: On 339 held-out SciPlex3 conditions across three cell lines, differential-expression AUPRC and Macro-F1 improve over the best baseline for each metric by 63.3% and 17.3%, and direction Macro-F1 by 7.2%. Relative to gene-wise reasoning on matched drug-cell cohorts, measured language-model token use falls by 99.77% for Predict and 98.41% for Explain. On the source-grounded benchmark, Explain answers all answerable questions with supporting proofs and identifies all insufficient-evidence cases. Update, using one measured source context per drug in simulated feedback, exceeds the best fine-tuned baselines in differential-expression AUPRC and Macro-F1 without changing model weights.
AI.conclusion: Taken together, the capabilities support a cumulative account of cellular responses in which predictions and biological judgments can be revised as evidence accumulates.

title: Does Your Trial Simulator Know What the Drug Does? An Intervention-Blind Test of Interventional Validity on 7,207 Registered Trials
comment: Oral presentation at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on World Models for High-Stakes Health. 31 pages, 5 figures. Code and data: this https URL
summary: Patient world models are increasingly proposed as simulators of clinical trials, and recent surveys rank their capabilities on a ladder from temporal prediction to counterfactual rollouts. Position on that ladder is currently assigned by reading papers rather than by measurement. We turn the counterfactual rung into a measured quantity. From 30,119 completed phase 2/3 trials with results posted to this http URL we construct 9,996 audited within-trial contrasts from 7,207 trials, and we score a simulator on how much of its accuracy depends on knowing which intervention was tested. The instrument is an intervention-blind reference: the same model, trained on the same trials, with every intervention-identifying field withheld. Interventional skill is the error the full model removes relative to that reference. On a temporal split (878 test contrasts from 655 trials) a registry-trained gradient-boosting simulator removes a fifth of the error of a trivial baseline, but its interventional skill is -0.12 (95% CI -0.21 to -0.05): withholding the intervention makes it better, and no alternative featurisation, stratum, temporal cut or same-molecule retrieval yields an interval above zero. A frontier language model reading only the registered protocol has interventional skill 0.20 [0.08, 0.31]; smaller and open-weight models sit at the limit of detection. Perturbation tests show the large model uses the intervention as such: swapping the arms reverses the sign of its prediction in 86% of contrasts. The blind reference is itself not drug-blind (a language model recovers the withheld drug class 45% of the time from the blind prompt), so interventional skill is a conservative lower bound. A reliability layer shows that ranking by predicted error lowers it but that calibrated error control does not transfer under temporal shift. Benchmark, code, prompts and per-call model outputs are released.

AI.tldr: The paper measures whether patient world models truly simulate interventions by scoring a registry-trained simulator against an intervention-blind reference on 9,996 audited within-trial contrasts from 7,207 registered trials. The gradient-boosting simulator has negative interventional skill of -0.12, while a frontier language model reading only the protocol reaches 0.20.
AI.motivation: Patient world models are proposed as clinical trial simulators and ranked by their counterfactual capability, but that position is currently assigned by reading papers rather than by measurement.
AI.method: From 30,119 completed phase 2/3 trials with posted results, the authors build within-trial contrasts and define interventional skill as the error a full model removes relative to an intervention-blind reference trained on the same trials with every intervention-identifying field withheld. They evaluate on a temporal split and run perturbation tests that swap trial arms, plus a reliability layer for error control.
AI.result: On a temporal split with 878 test contrasts from 655 trials, a registry-trained gradient-boosting simulator removes a fifth of the error of a trivial baseline, but its interventional skill is -0.12 (95% CI -0.21 to -0.05), and no alternative featurisation, stratum, temporal cut or same-molecule retrieval yields an interval above zero. A frontier language model reading only the registered protocol has interventional skill 0.20 [0.08, 0.31], while smaller and open-weight models sit at the limit of detection. Swapping arms reverses the sign of the large model's prediction in 86% of contrasts. A language model recovers the withheld drug class 45% of the time from the blind prompt, so the measure is a conservative lower bound. Ranking by predicted error lowers interventional skill, and calibrated error control does not transfer under temporal shift.
AI.conclusion: Interventional validity can be measured rather than asserted, and most registry-trained simulators do not yet use the intervention; the released benchmark, code, prompts and per-call outputs allow others to repeat the audit.

title: Do Saliency Maps Fail Dense Breasts? A Chance-Normalized, Confounder-Aware Audit of Explanation Fairness in Mammography
summary: Saliency maps, offered as evidence that mammography classifiers use the cancer, are untested in dense breasts, which can hide cancers. We tested whether they locate cancers worse there, and why. On 1,345 malignant CBIS-DDSM views, we scored three CNNs' Grad-CAM, Integrated Gradients and occlusion maps by whether their peak hits the lesion and a chance-normalized lesion-to-background saliency ratio (bits; +1 doubles it). Unadjusted gaps were large: Grad-CAM peaks hit 44% of dense vs. 58% of non-dense lesions. Case mix, chiefly more calcifications in dense breasts, explained about half or more of each gap. Occlusion kept a significant average of -0.56 bit gap. Controls also implicate the classifiers: unadjusted gaps exceeded an image-only conspicuity map's, and models relied less on dense-breast lesions. We recommend reporting density gaps before and after case-mix adjustment, per classifier, with conspicuity and lesion-reliance controls.

AI.tldr: A chance-normalized audit of saliency maps on 1,345 malignant mammography views finds that Grad-CAM peaks hit 44% of lesions in dense breasts versus 58% in non-dense breasts. Case mix, chiefly more calcifications in dense breasts, explains about half or more of each gap.
AI.motivation: Saliency maps are offered as evidence that mammography classifiers use the cancer, but they have not been tested in dense breasts, which can hide cancers.
AI.method: The authors score three CNNs' Grad-CAM, Integrated Gradients and occlusion maps on CBIS-DDSM malignant views by whether the peak falls on the lesion and by a chance-normalized lesion-to-background saliency ratio in bits. They adjust for case mix and use controls comparing against an image-only conspicuity map and measuring each classifier's reliance on dense-breast lesions.
AI.result: Unadjusted gaps are large, with Grad-CAM peaks hitting 44% of dense versus 58% of non-dense lesions. Case mix explains about half or more of each gap. Occlusion keeps a significant average gap of -0.56 bit. Unadjusted gaps exceed those of an image-only conspicuity map, and the models rely less on dense-breast lesions.
AI.conclusion: The authors recommend reporting density gaps both before and after case-mix adjustment, per classifier, together with conspicuity and lesion-reliance controls, since the classifiers themselves contribute to the gaps.

title: Autonomous ETL Pipelines for Salesforce M&A Consolidation: A Reference Framework, Jitterbit Mapping, and Reproducible Simulation Study
comment: 16 pages, 4 figures, 7 tables. Code and data: this https URL preprint also archived at this https URL
summary: Merging companies that each run Salesforce must consolidate their customer data into a single organization while both source systems remain in use. This requires reconciling different schemas and picklists, resolving duplicate customers across and within organizations, preserving relationships between records, and keeping the target current until cutover. This article proposes a reference framework for an autonomous extract-transform-load pipeline for this task. It combines partitioned bulk extraction, declarative mapping templates, rule-based and statistical quality gates, master data management with deterministic and blocked fuzzy matching, constrained loading with per-record error capture, and change data capture guarded by a data-health circuit breaker. Each stage is mapped to Jitterbit Integration Studio constructs. The framework was implemented as an open reference prototype and evaluated on synthetic two-organization scenarios with known ground truth at three scales, from 32,040 to 383,973 source records, over five random seeds. At a preset threshold, hybrid matching reached pairwise F1 scores of 0.918 for accounts and 0.885 for contacts; calibrating the threshold per object would raise these to 0.938 and 0.963. The quality gates prevented all load failures and all silent loss of unmapped picklist values without wrongly flagging any clean record, whereas removing them produced about 1,000 load failures per run. Over five simulated days of hourly incremental synchronization, replayed events were ignored, an injected upstream fault was contained in the batch in which it occurred, and the target agreed with a full rebuild on more than 99.3 percent of field values. Validation on a production deployment remains future work.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a reference framework for an autonomous Salesforce ETL pipeline for M&A customer data consolidation, implemented as an open prototype with Jitterbit mappings. On synthetic two-organization scenarios, hybrid matching reaches pairwise F1 of 0.918 for accounts and 0.885 for contacts, and the quality gates prevent all load failures.
AI.motivation: Merging companies that both run Salesforce requires consolidating customer data into one organization while both source systems stay in use, which involves reconciling schemas and picklists, resolving duplicates, preserving relationships and keeping the target current until cutover.
AI.method: The framework combines partitioned bulk extraction, declarative mapping templates, rule-based and statistical quality gates, master data management with deterministic and blocked fuzzy matching, constrained loading with per-record error capture, and change data capture guarded by a data-health circuit breaker. Each stage is mapped to Jitterbit Integration Studio constructs.
AI.result: Evaluated on synthetic scenarios with known ground truth at three scales, from 32,040 to 383,973 source records, over five random seeds. At a preset threshold, hybrid matching reaches pairwise F1 of 0.918 for accounts and 0.885 for contacts, rising to 0.938 and 0.963 with per-object threshold calibration. The quality gates prevent all load failures and all silent loss of unmapped picklist values without flagging any clean record, whereas removing them yields about 1,000 load failures per run. Over five simulated days of hourly synchronization, replayed events are ignored, an injected upstream fault is contained in its batch, and the target agrees with a full rebuild on more than 99.3 percent of field values.
AI.conclusion: The framework is shown to work on synthetic data, and validation on a production deployment is left as future work.

title: Deep Meets Classical: A CPU-Efficient Decision-Fusion Model for Automatic Modulation Classification
comment: 5 pages, 2 figures, 5 tables. Accepted at the 2026 6th International Conference on Artificial Intelligence, Automation and High Performance Computing (AIAHPC)
summary: Automatic modulation classification (AMC) underpins spectrum sensing and non-cooperative signal identification in cognitive radio, yet the two standard CPU-feasible approaches to it, a compact convolutional neural network (CNN) on raw in-phase and quadrature (I/Q) samples and a classical higher-order-cumulant feature classifier, are rarely compared against each other conditioned on signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). We show that they are, in fact, complementary: the CNN is markedly more robust at low SNR, where hand-crafted statistics collapse toward chance, while the cumulant classifier is more accurate at high SNR, where higher-order statistics cleanly separate dense constellations. We exploit this complementarity with FuseAMC, a lightweight decision-fusion model that trains a logistic-regression meta-combiner over the concatenated class-posteriors of an approximately 198k-parameter residual CNN and a gradient-boosted-tree cumulant classifier, on a validation split disjoint from test. On RadioML 2016.10a (5 seeds, 44k-frame held-out test set), FuseAMC reaches 55.8% overall accuracy, improving on the best cumulant-feature baseline by 5.1 points and on the CNN alone by 3.2 points (paired-bootstrap 95% confidence-interval lower bounds of 5.0 and 3.1 points, both positive), while matching the best classical baseline in its own strong high-SNR regime and the CNN in its strong low-SNR regime. With about 0.2 million parameters, a model footprint of a few megabytes, and roughly 3 MFLOPs per frame, the whole pipeline trains and runs on one CPU core, targeting general-purpose and embedded processors without hardware acceleration.

AI.tldr: FuseAMC combines a compact CNN on I/Q samples with a higher-order-cumulant classifier through logistic-regression decision fusion, reaching 55.8% overall accuracy on RadioML 2016.10a. The whole pipeline trains and runs on one CPU core with about 0.2 million parameters.
AI.motivation: The CNN and cumulant-feature classifier are the two standard CPU-feasible approaches to automatic modulation classification, but they are rarely compared conditioned on SNR, and their relative strengths across SNR regimes are unknown.
AI.method: FuseAMC trains a logistic-regression meta-combiner over the concatenated class posteriors of an approximately 198k-parameter residual CNN and a gradient-boosted-tree cumulant classifier, fitted on a validation split disjoint from the test set.
AI.result: On RadioML 2016.10a over 5 seeds with a 44k-frame held-out test set, FuseAMC reaches 55.8% overall accuracy, improving on the best cumulant-feature baseline by 5.1 points and on the CNN alone by 3.2 points, with paired-bootstrap 95% confidence-interval lower bounds of 5.0 and 3.1 points. It matches the best classical baseline in the high-SNR regime and the CNN in the low-SNR regime. The model has about 0.2 million parameters, a footprint of a few megabytes and roughly 3 MFLOPs per frame.
AI.conclusion: The two approaches are complementary across SNR, and the fused model gives a lightweight option for general-purpose and embedded processors without hardware acceleration.

title: BAM: Bivariate Additive Models for Interpretable Tabular Prediction
summary: Generalized Additive Models with pairwise interactions (GA$^2$Ms) are regarded as glass-box models, since each pairwise shape function can be visualized as a contour plot. In practice, the shape functions learned by methods such as EBM or NODE-GAM are so complex (irregular contours and sharp local fluctuations) that a practitioner cannot meaningfully interpret them or check them against domain knowledge. Auditability in this stronger sense requires substantially simpler shape functions. We argue that such simplification can match the accuracy of standard GAMs if the right feature pairs are captured. We propose Bivariate Additive Models (BAMs), a class of GA$^2$Ms in which every pairwise shape function is constrained to a simple parametric form, instantiated as an asymmetric bivariate Gaussian. Each component is visualizable as a unimodal contour map, and its feature pair is selected automatically during training. Experiments on six tabular benchmarks show that BAM attains predictive accuracy comparable to standard GAMs and approaches that of GA$^2$Ms. We also show the trade-off between accuracy and the number of components to inspect.

AI.tldr: Bivariate Additive Models (BAMs) constrain every pairwise shape function of a GA2M to an asymmetric bivariate Gaussian, so each component is a unimodal contour map that can be audited. Across six tabular benchmarks, BAM reaches accuracy comparable to standard GAMs and approaches that of GA2Ms.
AI.motivation: Pairwise shape functions in EBM and NODE-GAM are so irregular that practitioners cannot meaningfully interpret them or check them against domain knowledge, so stronger auditability requires simpler shapes.
AI.method: Each pairwise shape function is instantiated as an asymmetric bivariate Gaussian, giving a unimodal contour plot, and the feature pair for each component is selected automatically during training.
AI.result: On six tabular benchmarks, BAM attains predictive accuracy comparable to standard GAMs and approaches that of GA2Ms. The trade-off between accuracy and the number of components to inspect is also shown.
AI.conclusion: Simplifying pairwise shape functions can match the accuracy of standard GAMs when the right feature pairs are captured, making glass-box models more auditable.

title: Ray-Tracing-Based Dynamic Channel Sounding With Autoregressive Wi-Fi CSI Prediction
summary: Channel sounding in Wi-Fi multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems must balance channel state information (CSI) accuracy against CSI acquisition overhead. Device mobility causes channel aging, while autoregressive CSI prediction introduces errors that accumulate over sounding intervals. However, standardized statistical channel models cannot fully capture the environment-specific channel dynamics encountered in physical artificial intelligence (AI) applications, motivating the use of Sionna-based ray tracing to evaluate CSI prediction under device mobility and evolving propagation geometry. This paper develops a dynamic sounding framework that integrates autoregressive CSI prediction with signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR)-constrained interval selection. A Transformer with rotary position embedding that converts device positions into CSI sequences predicts CSI across multiple subcarriers for beamforming updates between sounding exchanges. We formulate sounding-interval selection as a predicted average-throughput maximization problem under per-stream SINR lower-bound constraints, including CSI acquisition and processing overhead. A prediction-error perturbation analysis provides the SINR bounds, and cumulative-sum enumeration globally solves the finite single-variable problem. Actual SINR feasibility holds whenever the prediction errors satisfy the bounds. Ray-tracing experiments assess channel prediction, trajectory transfer, and autoregressive prediction errors. In single-STA Wi-Fi 7 link-level simulations, predicted-CSI beamforming improves mean goodput by 67.3%, 112.7%, and 119.1% over stale CSI for linear, circular, and cosine trajectories, respectively.

AI.tldr: A dynamic channel sounding framework for Wi-Fi MIMO couples Transformer-based autoregressive CSI prediction with SINR-constrained selection of sounding intervals, evaluated in Sionna ray-tracing environments. In single-STA Wi-Fi 7 link-level simulations, predicted-CSI beamforming improves mean goodput by 67.3% to 119.1% over stale CSI, depending on the trajectory.
AI.motivation: Device mobility causes channel aging, and autoregressive CSI prediction accumulates errors over sounding intervals, while standardized statistical channel models cannot capture environment-specific dynamics for physical AI applications.
AI.method: A Transformer with rotary position embedding converts device positions into CSI sequences and predicts CSI across subcarriers for beamforming between sounding exchanges. Sounding-interval selection is formulated as predicted average-throughput maximization under per-stream SINR lower-bound constraints that include acquisition and processing overhead, with bounds from a prediction-error perturbation analysis and a cumulative-sum enumeration that solves the single-variable problem globally.
AI.result: In single-STA Wi-Fi 7 link-level simulations, predicted-CSI beamforming improves mean goodput over stale CSI by 67.3%, 112.7% and 119.1% for linear, circular and cosine trajectories, respectively. Actual SINR feasibility holds whenever the prediction errors satisfy the bounds.
AI.conclusion: Ray-tracing-based evaluation shows that autoregressive CSI prediction combined with constrained interval selection can substantially improve goodput under mobility, given that prediction errors remain within the derived bounds.

title: Clips2Story: Training-Free Video Storyboarding and Editing Using Multimodal Retrieval-Embedded Generation
summary: Video editors often work with large collections of fragmented footage and must select and organize relevant clips into a coherent story. However, many existing video editing and summarization methods assume a temporally ordered source video and aim to preserve its original narrative and temporal structure. In this paper, we introduce Clips2Story, a training-free, LLM-based pipeline that enables users to create keyword-specified short videos from a pool of video clips. Given a pool of clips and a user-specified keyword, we first extract text-based multimodal descriptors for each clip and retrieve the clips most relevant to the keyword. We then provide the textual descriptors of these candidate clips to an LLM, which selects and arranges them into an editable storyboard with connective narrations. Finally, we assemble the selected clips and retrieve accompanying visuals for the narrations to compose the output video. To evaluate the proposed pipeline, we construct a synthetic evaluation dataset from 100 long-form videos across five genres by segmenting each video into short clips using a scene-change detection model and shuffling the resulting clips to remove their temporal order. Through objective evaluation and qualitative examples, we demonstrate that Clips2Story can effectively retrieve keyword-relevant clips and compose coherent storyboards based on user-specified keywords. Human evaluation further shows that Clips2Story outperforms a strong baseline in terms of narrative coherence, keyword alignment, and overall realism.

AI.tldr: Clips2Story is a training-free LLM pipeline that retrieves keyword-relevant clips from an unordered pool and arranges them into an editable storyboard with narrations, then assembles a short video. On a synthetic dataset built from 100 long-form videos, it outperforms a strong baseline in narrative coherence, keyword alignment and realism.
AI.motivation: Existing video editing and summarization methods assume a temporally ordered source video and preserve its narrative, whereas editors often start from fragmented collections of clips with no order.
AI.method: Text-based multimodal descriptors are extracted for each clip, and the clips most relevant to a user keyword are retrieved. An LLM receives the descriptors of these candidates and selects and arranges them into a storyboard with connective narrations, and accompanying visuals are retrieved for the narrations before the output video is composed.
AI.result: The evaluation dataset is built from 100 long-form videos across five genres, segmented by scene-change detection and shuffled. Objective evaluation and qualitative examples show that the pipeline retrieves keyword-relevant clips and composes coherent storyboards. Human evaluation shows that it outperforms a strong baseline in narrative coherence, keyword alignment and overall realism.
AI.conclusion: Clips2Story shows that an LLM operating over text descriptors can turn an unordered clip pool into a coherent keyword-specified short video without any training.

title: Intra-Architecture Source Attribution for Stable Diffusion: A New Task with Benchmark Dataset and Baseline
comment: Accepted at IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision(WACV 2027)
summary: Designing systems that attribute a generated image to its source model has lately become a major area of AI research. Most existing datasets and systems related to image source attribution are targeted towards the detection of architectural signatures of the source models. Distinct from this, focusing on stable diffusion, we introduce a novel task, IntrAA-SD, Intra-Architecture source Attribution for Stable Diffusion, where the source models to be differentiated share the same architectural backbone and differ only due to fine-tuning. The proposed task aligns with the emergence of fine-tuned generators having the same architecture, like Juggernaut XL and RealVis XL, which are fine-tuned versions of Stable Diffusion XL (SDXL). We provide a first-of-its-kind $140$K-image benchmark dataset containing images generated from different fine-tunes of SDXL, along with in-domain and out-of-distribution prompts. We also provide a baseline framework for IntrAA-SD, which leverages a style-conditioned Mixture-of-Experts network. It uses a frozen CLIP backbone to capture the image style and gate the MoE, which processes fine-tuned trace features from a high-resolution LoRA-adapted DINOv2 network. The fine-tuned models used, the prompting strategies considered, and the formation details employed in the novel dataset are elaborated. Our baseline intra-architecture source attribution method is evaluated in terms of attribution accuracy on our dataset, and ablation studies are also performed. Code and dataset is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces IntrAA-SD, a task of attributing images to fine-tuned Stable Diffusion models that share one architecture, with a 140K-image benchmark built from SDXL fine-tunes and a style-conditioned Mixture-of-Experts baseline. The baseline is evaluated on attribution accuracy and ablations are reported.
AI.motivation: Existing image source attribution targets architectural signatures of different generator families, but fine-tuned generators such as Juggernaut XL and RealVis XL share one backbone and differ only through fine-tuning.
AI.method: The baseline uses a frozen CLIP backbone to capture image style and gate a Mixture-of-Experts network, which processes fine-tuned trace features from a high-resolution LoRA-adapted DINOv2 network.
AI.result: The authors provide a 140K-image benchmark generated from different SDXL fine-tunes, with in-domain and out-of-distribution prompts. Attribution accuracy of the baseline is evaluated on this dataset, and ablation studies are performed.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a new intra-architecture attribution task together with a benchmark and baseline, and code and dataset are made available.

title: How Unbalanced Must a Latin Rectangle Be?
summary: We view a $k\times n$ Latin rectangle as $n$ points in the grid $[n]^k$. Each symbol gives one point, whose coordinates are the columns it occupies. The rectangle is balanced when these points are pairwise equidistant in the $\ell_1$ metric. Its imbalance measures the distance from this ideal. We study the minimum imbalance from three sides. Constructively, we use a simulated annealing that moves symbols within rows and only penalises column clashes. Against the reference table of Voboril et al. (2025), it improves 33 of the 51 non-square values for $8\le n\le 13$, by up to 39.4%, and matches the rest. A cheap invariant, the row group, certifies that none of the 33 new rectangles is isotopic to rows of a group table, so the earlier column-swapping local search cannot reach any of them. Exactly, a computer-assisted branch and bound proves that the minimum imbalance of a $3\times 9$ rectangle is $56$. Díaz et al. found this value, but its optimality was open. A sharper pruning bound, derived from the identity $I=2\sum(d-t)^+$, reduces the search tree by a factor of $2.4$ to $3.3$ on the instances with $k\ge3$ that we solve. Asymptotically, the minimum imbalance is $\Theta(n^3)$ for every fixed $k$. A pigeonhole argument gives a lower constant of order $k\,4^{-k}$, and random rectangles give an upper constant of order $\sqrt k$. For $k=2$, the limit of $\min I/n^3$ exists, a permuton attains it, and it lies between $4/375$ and $0.1196$. Perfect balance is an $\ell_1$-equilateral problem, so it forces $k=\Omega(n/\log n)$ rows. For $2\times n$ rectangles, single two-minute annealing runs improve five of the seven six-hour MIP upper bounds for $14\le n\le 20$. Finally, the Lean 4 kernel checks every rectangle reported in this paper against a 74-line specification that imports only Lean's core library. We also prove the pigeonhole lower bound in Lean with Mathlib.

AI.tldr: The paper studies the minimum imbalance of k by n Latin rectangles, proving that the minimum is Theta(n^3) for fixed k and computing exact values with branch and bound and Lean verification. Simulated annealing improves 33 of 51 non-square reference values for 8 at most n at most 13.
AI.motivation: A balanced Latin rectangle has its n points in the grid pairwise equidistant in the l1 metric, and the minimum imbalance of such rectangles had been studied only partially, with some values open.
AI.method: The authors use simulated annealing that moves symbols within rows and penalises only column clashes, a branch and bound search with a sharper pruning bound derived from the identity I = 2 times the sum of (d - t) positive parts, a pigeonhole lower bound, random constructions for upper bounds, MIP upper bounds for 2 by n cases, and a Lean 4 kernel check of all reported rectangles against a 74-line specification.
AI.result: Against the reference table of Voboril et al. (2025), annealing improves 33 of the 51 non-square values for 8 at most n at most 13, by up to 39.4%, and matches the rest. The minimum imbalance of a 3 by 9 rectangle is proved to be 56, and the pruning bound reduces the search tree by a factor of 2.4 to 3.3. The minimum is Theta(n^3) for every fixed k, with a lower constant of order k times 4^(-k) and an upper constant of order sqrt(k). For k = 2, the limit of min I / n^3 lies between 4/375 and 0.1196. For 2 by n rectangles, short annealing runs improve five of seven six-hour MIP upper bounds for 14 at most n at most 20.
AI.conclusion: Combined constructive, exact and asymptotic results pin down the minimum imbalance from several sides, and the Lean kernel verification adds machine-checked guarantees for the reported rectangles and the pigeonhole bound.

title: Practical Estimation of the Bayes Optimal Fairness-Accuracy Tradeoff with Soft Labels
summary: There is a fundamental limit to the best prediction error of any model for a given data distribution. In classification, the Bayes error quantifies this limit and serves as both a benchmark for trained models and a criterion to detect overfitting. The state-of-the-art Bayes error estimation techniques for binary classification use only soft labels (positive class probabilities) and require no input features or auxiliary training. We extend such notions to constrained classification problems, such as fairness. Fair classification is an important case of constrained or multi-objective classification. It requires a model not only to be accurate but also to yield fair outcomes (equal or near-equal true positive rates) across different demographic groups (e.g., race and gender). This leads to an inherent fairness-accuracy tradeoff or a Pareto frontier that is used to compare fair classifiers against each other. The focus of our work is to estimate the fundamental limit for this fairness-accuracy tradeoff. We derive an explicit expression for the fair Bayes error rate (i.e., best achievable error rate subject to given fairness constraints), and construct consistent, instance-free estimators for it using only soft labels and group information. We provably bound the bias and the sample complexity of our estimators. Empirically, our method produces a robust, low-variance estimate of the optimal fairness-accuracy tradeoff curve, even when the soft labels are noisy and derived from a classification model on hard labels.

AI.tldr: The paper derives an explicit expression for the fair Bayes error rate and constructs consistent, instance-free estimators of the optimal fairness-accuracy tradeoff using only soft labels and group information. Empirically the estimator gives a robust, low-variance estimate of the Pareto frontier, even with noisy soft labels.
AI.motivation: Fair classifiers are compared along a fairness-accuracy Pareto frontier, but the fundamental limit of that tradeoff is unknown, and existing Bayes error estimators handle only unconstrained binary classification.
AI.method: The authors extend soft-label Bayes error estimation to constrained classification with equal or near-equal true positive rates across demographic groups, deriving the fair Bayes error and building estimators that use only soft labels and group membership, with no input features or auxiliary training.
AI.result: The authors prove bounds on the bias and sample complexity of the estimators. Empirically, the method produces a robust, low-variance estimate of the optimal fairness-accuracy tradeoff curve, even when soft labels are noisy and derived from a classifier trained on hard labels.
AI.conclusion: The estimators provide a practical reference for the best achievable fairness-accuracy tradeoff, against which fair classifiers can be judged.

title: Confucius4-R2T2: A Stable-Prefix Streaming ASR Model for Real Real-Time Transcription
comment: 30 pages, 6 figures, 8 tables. Code and model weights available at this https URL and this https URL
summary: Streaming speech recognition is increasingly consumed by machines, such as translators and voice agents, that act on each token as it appears. A token that is later revised costs wasted work or a wrong action. In this work, we present Confucius4-R2T2 (short for Real Real-Time Transcription), a stable-prefix streaming ASR model that never modifies its earlier output while maintaining high accuracy and low latency. R2T2 is obtained by post-training Qwen3-ASR-1.7B on 1,500 hours of Chinese and English audio while freezing its pre-trained audio encoder and projector. The adaptation is based on the concept of Longest Stable Prefix (LSP), a new notion that we introduce in this work. We prove that LSP is monotone under the prefix order, consistent with the full-audio output, and maximal among labels that equal a whole earlier output. Learning from LSP labels converts a full-context model into a stable-prefix streaming one without any architectural change. Extensive evaluations show that R2T2 brings streaming recognition close to the base model's full-context quality while delivering stable text with low emission lag. Its gains extend beyond the post-training languages, demonstrating a practical path from full-context ASR to stable streaming. We open-source the model weights and code at this https URL and this https URL.

AI.tldr: Confucius4-R2T2 post-trains Qwen3-ASR-1.7B on 1,500 hours of Chinese and English audio into a stable-prefix streaming ASR model that never revises earlier output. Its gains extend beyond the post-training languages, and the model weights and code are open-sourced.
AI.motivation: Streaming ASR is consumed by machines such as translators and voice agents that act on each token immediately, so later revisions of emitted tokens cost wasted work or wrong actions.
AI.method: The adaptation is based on the Longest Stable Prefix (LSP), a new notion for which the authors prove that LSP is monotone under the prefix order, consistent with the full-audio output and maximal among labels equal to a whole earlier output. Learning from LSP labels converts a full-context model into a stable-prefix streaming model, with the pre-trained audio encoder and projector frozen and no architectural change.
AI.result: The paper reports extensive evaluations showing that R2T2 brings streaming recognition close to the base model's full-context quality while delivering stable text with low emission lag, and that the gains extend beyond the post-training languages.
AI.conclusion: The LSP-based adaptation offers a practical path from full-context ASR to stable streaming recognition without changing the architecture.

title: TouchéWorld tech report : Towards Online Unified Camera--Hand Exploration in Generative Worlds
summary: Recent video world models allow users to explore generated environments through camera navigation. Continuous hand motion provides a fine-grained action channel for interacting with the people and objects encountered during exploration. We present TouchéWorld, a framework that integrates gesture-driven interaction into a camera-controlled video world model. Given an initial image and a scene-description prompt, the model generates video conditioned on temporally aligned camera and hand controls. We construct joint camera--hand training data from heterogeneous egocentric videos through annotation completion, consistency-based filtering, and temporal alignment. Building on a pretrained camera-controlled world model, we combine spatial hand-skeleton conditioning with numerical hand-motion features through parameter-efficient adaptation. Causal adaptation and few-step distillation support chunk-level online generation, allowing users to update their controls based on generated visual feedback. We further introduce TouchéBench to evaluate hand-motion following, camera--hand coordination, online interaction, and object response. Together, these components establish a framework for studying continuous exploration and hand-driven interaction within generative worlds.

AI.tldr: TouchéWorld integrates continuous hand-gesture control with camera control in a video world model, generating video conditioned on aligned camera and hand inputs and supporting chunk-level online generation. It also introduces TouchéBench to evaluate hand-motion following, camera-hand coordination, online interaction and object response.
AI.motivation: Camera-controlled video world models let users explore generated environments, but continuous hand motion, a fine-grained action channel for interacting with encountered people and objects, has not been integrated into them.
AI.method: Joint camera-hand training data is built from heterogeneous egocentric videos through annotation completion, consistency-based filtering and temporal alignment. Spatial hand-skeleton conditioning and numerical hand-motion features are combined on a pretrained camera-controlled world model through parameter-efficient adaptation, and causal adaptation with few-step distillation enables chunk-level online generation.
AI.result: The abstract does not report quantitative results; it states that the components establish a framework for studying hand-driven interaction within generative worlds and introduces the TouchéBench evaluation suite.
AI.conclusion: The framework is presented as a foundation for studying continuous exploration and hand-driven interaction in generative worlds, with users able to update controls from generated visual feedback.

title: SysPilot: Cross-Library Performance Autotuning via Library Performance Contracts
comment: SysPilot is open source at this https URL
summary: Modern scientific and machine-learning applications compose many independently developed libraries. When these libraries run together, their independently managed runtimes can oversubscribe shared resources: using the same CPU cores, fighting over GPUs, or contending for memory bandwidth. Avoiding such contention requires careful configuration across library boundaries. Existing autotuners do not directly investigate what resources are shared between libraries, which runtime signals correlate with interference. As a result, they are inefficient for finding optimal configurations to mitigate contention. This paper presents SysPilot, a cross-library performance autotuning system based on Library Performance Contract (LPC). A Library Performance Contract captures a library's resource demands, assumptions, controls, and observability signals in LPCL, a specification language for describing library resource requirements. SysPilot synthesizes contracts from documentation and code artifacts, composes contracts from the libraries used by an application, derives resource-conflict hypotheses, profiles the application to validate those hypotheses, and selects candidate configurations. This design makes the Library Performance Contract a reusable unit of performance knowledge: a contract for a library can be reused across many applications that depend on that library. We evaluate SysPilot on a benchmark suite of cross-library contention scenarios. The results show that SysPilot matches the performance of autotuners that rely on application-specific manual information while retaining cross-application reuse. Compared with general-purpose autotuners such as OpenTuner and SMAC3, SysPilot improves benchmark performance metrics by up to an additional 38% over the best configuration found by these autotuners, while using 3x fewer runs.

AI.tldr: SysPilot is a cross-library autotuning system built on Library Performance Contracts (LPCs), which describe each library's resource demands, controls and observability signals. On a benchmark of cross-library contention scenarios, it improves performance by up to an additional 38% over the best configurations found by OpenTuner and SMAC3, using 3x fewer runs.
AI.motivation: Independently managed library runtimes can oversubscribe shared CPU cores, GPUs and memory bandwidth, and existing autotuners do not investigate which resources are shared across libraries or which runtime signals correlate with interference.
AI.method: An LPC captures a library's resource demands, assumptions, controls and observability signals in LPCL, a specification language. SysPilot synthesizes contracts from documentation and code, composes the contracts of an application's libraries, derives resource-conflict hypotheses, profiles the application to validate them and selects candidate configurations.
AI.result: SysPilot matches autotuners that rely on application-specific manual information while retaining cross-application reuse. Compared with OpenTuner and SMAC3, it improves benchmark performance metrics by up to an additional 38% over the best configuration those tuners find, while using 3x fewer runs.
AI.conclusion: Library Performance Contracts act as reusable units of performance knowledge, so a contract written for a library can serve many applications that depend on it.

title: Drift-adaptive Representation Preservation for Domain-Incremental Learning
summary: Pretrained vision models provide strong general-purpose representations, but in Domain-Incremental Learning (DIL), where the input distribution changes sequentially, adapting to new domains often degrades performance on previously learned ones. We observe that forgetting is not uniform across domains and classes and is not explained by training order alone. This motivates us to track each past domain-class concept individually. We use representation drift, defined as the deviation of a past concept's current representation from a fixed anchor, as a measurable surrogate for forgetting risk. The measured drift then serves two complementary roles. A consolidation loss assigns stronger preservation to high-drift pairs, while prototype construction down-weights highly drifted domains to reduce their influence on the class reference. Preservation is thus allocated by measured drift rather than assumed importance. To obtain this signal during training without storing past raw data, we repurpose a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA). For each domain-class pair, we store only a compact context summary in the backbone feature space and rerun it through the learned context-to-target relation to measure its drift from the fixed anchor. Across DomainNet, Office-Home, CORe50, and CDDB-Hard, our method sustains a strong accuracy-forgetting balance on every benchmark, using substantially less training memory than accuracy-competitive methods and the smallest storage among compared methods.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a drift-adaptive method for domain-incremental learning that measures each past domain-class concept's representation drift from a fixed anchor and uses it to allocate preservation. Using a JEPA-based drift measure without storing raw past data, it sustains a strong accuracy-forgetting balance on DomainNet, Office-Home, CORe50 and CDDB-Hard.
AI.motivation: Adapting a pretrained vision model to new domains in domain-incremental learning degrades performance on earlier domains, and forgetting is not uniform across domains and classes or explained by training order alone.
AI.method: Representation drift, the deviation of a past concept's current representation from a fixed anchor, serves as a surrogate for forgetting risk. A consolidation loss gives stronger preservation to high-drift pairs, and prototype construction down-weights highly drifted domains. Drift is measured by repurposing a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture, storing only a compact context summary per domain-class pair in backbone feature space.
AI.result: Across DomainNet, Office-Home, CORe50 and CDDB-Hard, the method sustains a strong accuracy-forgetting balance on every benchmark, using substantially less training memory than accuracy-competitive methods and the smallest storage among the compared methods.
AI.conclusion: Allocating preservation by measured drift rather than assumed importance offers a memory- and storage-efficient route to balancing accuracy and forgetting in domain-incremental learning.

title: Reconciling Privacy with Provenance for Language Model Watermarks
summary: Watermarking has great potential for regulating the use of language models (LMs), but its deployment has been marred by controversy, as many users argue that fine-grained tracking of LM usage violates their privacy. This tension reduces the effectiveness of watermarks, as users engage in evasion strategies such as paraphrasing that can remove much of the watermark signal. We show that provenance and privacy can be reconciled if we shift the goal of watermark design from tracking individuals to estimating aggregate usage. We develop locally differentially private watermarks which provably limit the evidence that any individual text can contribute to detection, while still enabling accurate estimation of population frequencies. We introduce the Red-Green Sequence (RGS) watermark, a private and computationally efficient watermark that achieves accurate frequency estimation at high privacy levels across various models, sample sizes and generation entropies in settings that reflect realistic deployment scenarios. On C4 language modeling tasks, we attain $0.0019$ MSE with $0.0038$ mean absolute bias at a low $\varepsilon$ of 1, while in more challenging settings such as an essay writing task with only 100 text samples, we still find errors on the order of $0.0113$ MSE with $0.004$ mean absolute bias at $\varepsilon=2$.

AI.tldr: The paper reconciles privacy and provenance for LM watermarks by shifting the goal from tracking individuals to estimating aggregate usage, using locally differentially private watermarks. The Red-Green Sequence watermark gives an MSE of 0.0019 on C4 at epsilon 1, and about 0.0113 on a 100-sample essay task at epsilon 2.
AI.motivation: Fine-grained tracking of LM usage through watermarks conflicts with user privacy, which motivates evasion such as paraphrasing that removes much of the watermark signal.
AI.method: The authors develop locally differentially private watermarks that provably limit the evidence any individual text can contribute to detection while still permitting accurate estimation of population frequencies. They introduce the Red-Green Sequence (RGS) watermark, which is private and computationally efficient.
AI.result: On C4 language modeling at epsilon 1, RGS attains MSE 0.0019 with mean absolute bias 0.0038. In an essay writing task with only 100 text samples at epsilon 2, errors are on the order of 0.0113 MSE with 0.004 mean absolute bias. The method achieves accurate frequency estimation at high privacy levels across models, sample sizes and generation entropies.
AI.conclusion: Provenance and privacy can be reconciled when watermarks are designed to estimate aggregate usage rather than attribute text to individuals.

title: The Harness Is the Model: Agent Scaffolding Changes a Fixed LLM's Compliance with Banking Conduct Rules, Unevenly Across Models
comment: 16 pages, 4 tables. Pre-registered. Code, data and all 3120 episode traces: this https URL
summary: Banks validate language models, but they deploy systems: a model inside a harness that decides what it sees, which tools it can call and who checks its actions. We test whether that harness changes compliance with banking conduct rules when the model is held fixed. Four open-weight models each ran five harnesses (a pipeline that makes one structured decision, a ReAct-style tool loop, a loop in which the policy is reachable only through search, a loop with a long benign customer memory, and a loop with a same-model compliance reviewer) on 156 pre-registered cases in a simulated retail bank whose 11 rule families paraphrase EU consumer-credit, payments, investor-protection, data-protection and anti-money-laundering provisions. Every one of the 3120 two-turn episodes was scored deterministically from the executed tool trace, with violations and over-refusals counted separately. Pooled across models the harness moved the correct-case rate only between 87.3% and 92.1%, but within a model it mattered a great deal: for one model the spread between its best and worst harness was 11.5 percentage points, enough to move it from first to last place among the four models, while for another the harness made no detectable difference; the model x harness interaction itself was suggestive rather than conclusive. The same-model reviewer cut violations from 9.6% to 6.4% without raising over-refusals, contrary to our pre-registered prediction. Rules that require date arithmetic failed in every harness. In an exploratory analysis with two LLM judges and a blind human check, 26% of violations were accompanied by a customer message that denied the action the agent had just executed, which a transcript-only review would record as a correct refusal. For model-risk management the unit of validation should be the model-harness pair, and conduct testing should read the action log, not the conversation.

AI.tldr: On 156 pre-registered banking conduct cases with four fixed open-weight models, the choice of agent harness changes compliance substantially within a model, while pooled correct-case rates vary only from 87.3% to 92.1%. A same-model compliance reviewer lowers violations from 9.6% to 6.4% without raising over-refusals.
AI.motivation: Banks validate language models but deploy systems in which a model sits inside a harness that controls what it sees, which tools it can call and who checks its actions, so validation of the model alone may miss compliance differences.
AI.method: Four open-weight models each run five harnesses (a one-shot structured decision pipeline, a ReAct-style tool loop, a loop with policy reachable only through search, a loop with long benign customer memory, and a loop with a same-model compliance reviewer) on 156 cases in a simulated retail bank covering 11 rule families paraphrasing EU consumer-credit, payments, investor-protection, data-protection and anti-money-laundering provisions. All 3120 two-turn episodes are scored deterministically from the executed tool trace.
AI.result: Pooled across models, the harness moves the correct-case rate only between 87.3% and 92.1%, but for one model the spread between its best and worst harness is 11.5 percentage points, enough to move it from first to last place. For another model the harness makes no detectable difference, and the model-by-harness interaction is suggestive rather than conclusive. The reviewer cuts violations from 9.6% to 6.4% without raising over-refusals, contrary to the pre-registered prediction. Rules requiring date arithmetic fail in every harness. In an exploratory analysis, 26% of violations were accompanied by a customer message denying the action the agent had executed.
AI.conclusion: For model-risk management the unit of validation should be the model-harness pair, and conduct testing should read the action log rather than the conversation.

title: Ab Initio Accuracy Beyond the Cutoff: Distributed Message-Passing Equivariant Attention at Tens-of-Millions-of-Atom Scale
summary: Molecular dynamics predicts molecular motion from atomic forces and trajectory integration. Density functional theory (DFT) provides first-principles forces, but its $O(N^3)$ cost limits simulations to thousands of atoms; empirical force fields scale to millions but miss bond breaking and charge transfer. Equivariant message-passing Transformers learn the ab initio potential at linear cost. Stacked layers propagate information beyond a single cutoff, giving four layers a receptive field up to 23Å. At this frontier, scale is limited by communication: layers exchange boundary features across devices, force backpropagation repeats the exchange, and moving atoms change neighbor graphs and tensor shapes. We present Tessera, a distributed runtime that fixes workload shapes between rebuilds. It sorts atoms along a space-filling curve into equal-count shards, ensuring identical atom counts and tensor shapes per rank. Peer sets scale as $K^{0.5}$, not $K$. A conservative neighbor skin preserves topology across updates, enabling each rebuild interval to replay as one CUDA Graph. Fused kernels, three-level neighbor search, and overlapped All-to-All complete it. On 512 GPUs, Tessera sustains 30.7M atoms at 89.7% weak-scaling efficiency (77--90% across three per-GPU loads); per-step time rises 1.11--1.29x as machine and problem grow 16x. Graph reuse cuts full-step time $1.87\times$. Across an $8\times$ device increase, neighbor-search cost grows $1.7\times$, versus $3.0\times$ for Morton order. In a live $10.24$M-atom salt solution, NVE energy drift is $0.42\,\mu$eV/atom/ps over $10$ ps, and structure matches a serial reference. A 10.06M-atom Norovirus capsid sustains 100 ps of NVT at $\approx 8$ ps/day on 256 A100 GPUs. Over 200,000 steps, it has no broken bonds or anomalously close pairs and uses three compiled variants, with no graph breaks or eager fallbacks.

AI.tldr: Tessera is a distributed runtime for equivariant message-passing Transformers that makes tens-of-millions-atom ab initio-accuracy molecular dynamics feasible, sustaining 30.7M atoms on 512 GPUs at 89.7% weak-scaling efficiency. A 10.06M-atom Norovirus capsid runs 100 ps of NVT at about 8 ps per day on 256 A100 GPUs.
AI.motivation: DFT scales as O(N^3) and limits simulation to thousands of atoms, empirical force fields reach millions of atoms but miss bond breaking and charge transfer, and at the scale of equivariant Transformers with receptive fields up to 23 Å, communication across devices limits scaling.
AI.method: Tessera sorts atoms along a space-filling curve into equal-count shards so that each rank has identical atom counts and tensor shapes, limits peer sets to scale as K^0.5, and uses a conservative neighbor skin so that each rebuild interval replays as one CUDA Graph. It adds fused kernels, three-level neighbor search and overlapped All-to-All communication.
AI.result: On 512 GPUs, Tessera sustains 30.7M atoms at 89.7% weak-scaling efficiency (77 to 90% across three per-GPU loads), with per-step time rising 1.11 to 1.29 times as machine and problem grow 16 times. Graph reuse cuts full-step time by 1.87 times. Across an 8-fold device increase, neighbor-search cost grows 1.7 times versus 3.0 times for Morton order. In a live 10.24M-atom salt solution, NVE energy drift is 0.42 microeV per atom per ps over 10 ps and the structure matches a serial reference. Over 200,000 steps of the capsid simulation there are no broken bonds or anomalously close pairs, and no graph breaks or eager fallbacks.
AI.conclusion: Communication-aware sharding and graph reuse make ab initio-accuracy molecular dynamics practical at tens-of-millions-atom scale on commodity GPU clusters.

title: Grounding in the Dark: Text-Only Training for Zero-Shot Video Temporal Localization
summary: Video-LLMs are typically trained on paired video-text data for temporal tasks, yet collecting precise temporal annotations and training on large-scale video datasets are both costly. We investigate whether a text-only LLM, with no vision-language pretraining, can be trained on textual video descriptions alone to perform temporal grounding and receive video only at inference time. This setting removes paired video data from training altogether and is a step toward training multimodal models without paired annotations. We generate a 134K-example corpus of textual sequences with up to 100 time steps, adapt Qwen3-8B with LoRA on CLIP or LLM2CLIP text embeddings, and evaluate on Charades-STA and QV-Highlights without training on videos from either benchmark. LLM2CLIP, whose text encoder supports longer inputs, represents detailed descriptions better than CLIP (61.54 versus 53.86 mtIoU on Temporal-TextVid) and transfers them better to video. Still, replacing text with frame embeddings at inference yields only 4.99 mtIoU on Charades-STA and 11.12 on QV-Highlights, revealing a large modality gap. To bridge it, we propose Nearest Entity Replacement (NER), a training-free mapping that represents each video frame by the normalized mean of its nearest text-entity embeddings, so that the model receives the kind of input it was trained on. NER reaches 14.45 mtIoU on Charades-STA and 20.72 on QV-Highlights, outperforming the strongest of four families of modality-gap baselines by 5.00 and 1.71 points. NER thus enables partial transfer from text to video, while more reliable grounding will likely require encoders with better-aligned text and visual representations.

AI.tldr: A text-only LLM fine-tuned with LoRA on 134K textual temporal-grounding examples performs zero-shot video temporal localization at inference. The proposed Nearest Entity Replacement maps video frames to text-entity embeddings and reaches 14.45 mtIoU on Charades-STA and 20.72 on QV-Highlights.
AI.motivation: Video-LLMs usually need paired video-text data with precise temporal annotations, which are costly, and the paper asks whether a text-only LLM can learn temporal grounding without any paired video data during training.
AI.method: The authors generate a 134K-example corpus of textual sequences with up to 100 time steps and adapt Qwen3-8B with LoRA on CLIP or LLM2CLIP text embeddings, evaluating on Charades-STA and QV-Highlights without training on videos from either benchmark. They propose Nearest Entity Replacement (NER), a training-free mapping that represents each frame by the normalized mean of its nearest text-entity embeddings.
AI.result: LLM2CLIP represents detailed descriptions better than CLIP (61.54 versus 53.86 mtIoU on Temporal-TextVid) and transfers better to video. Replacing text with frame embeddings at inference yields only 4.99 mtIoU on Charades-STA and 11.12 on QV-Highlights, while NER reaches 14.45 and 20.72. NER outperforms the strongest of four families of modality-gap baselines by 5.00 and 1.71 points.
AI.conclusion: NER enables partial transfer from text to video, but the authors expect more reliable grounding to require encoders with better-aligned text and visual representations.

title: Reasoning-Aware Cross-Modal Association Unlearning in Multimodal Large Reasoning Models
summary: Multimodal large reasoning models (MLRMs) integrate visual inputs with textual and parametric knowledge, allowing sensitive information to be accessed through cross-modal associations during reasoning. This raises privacy concerns when a visual input should no longer provide access to such information. Machine unlearning can remove this influence without retraining the model from scratch. However, multimodal unlearning methods mainly target samples, concepts, or knowledge content, without separating the knowledge from the cross-modal association through which it is accessed. In reasoning models, target information may disappear from the final answer while remaining in intermediate reasoning, or be replaced by incorrect substitute knowledge. We therefore study cross-modal association unlearning, where the forget target is a designated visual-to-knowledge association: the model should suppress target-bearing behavior under the designated visual context while preserving access to the same knowledge in permitted contexts. We propose Visual-Keyed Counterfactual Rebinding (VKCR), a parameter-efficient framework for cross-modal association editing. VKCR first localizes the edit to a compact association-conditioned parameter subspace. It then reduces support for the designated target at task outputs and counterfactually rebinds the affected reasoning behavior by discouraging target-bearing or unsupported continuations while favoring valid non-sensitive alternatives. We further introduce CLEAR-R and MLLMU-R to evaluate target leakage, hallucinated reassociation, reasoning preservation, and modality-specific utility. Experiments show that VKCR substantially reduces image-conditioned target leakage and hallucinated reassociation, including across heterogeneous task formulations, while preserving non-sensitive visual reasoning and permitted text-only knowledge.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Visual-Keyed Counterfactual Rebinding (VKCR), a parameter-efficient method that unlearns a designated visual-to-knowledge association in multimodal large reasoning models while keeping the same knowledge available in permitted contexts. It substantially reduces image-conditioned target leakage and hallucinated reassociation.
AI.motivation: Sensitive knowledge in multimodal reasoning models can be reached through cross-modal associations, and existing multimodal unlearning targets samples, concepts or knowledge content without separating the knowledge from the association that accesses it, so the target can persist in intermediate reasoning.
AI.method: VKCR localizes the edit to a compact association-conditioned parameter subspace, reduces support for the designated target at task outputs, and counterfactually rebinds affected reasoning by discouraging target-bearing or unsupported continuations while favouring valid non-sensitive alternatives. The authors also introduce the CLEAR-R and MLLMU-R benchmarks.
AI.result: Experiments show that VKCR substantially reduces image-conditioned target leakage and hallucinated reassociation, including across heterogeneous task formulations, while preserving non-sensitive visual reasoning and permitted text-only knowledge.
AI.conclusion: Cross-modal association unlearning offers a way to remove visually triggered access to sensitive knowledge in reasoning models without broad loss of utility.

title: AssameseLM-E2B: An Open-Weight Assamese Language Model for Efficient Consumer-Grade Deployment
summary: While Large Language Models (LLMs) excel in high-resource languages, their performance often degrades in low-resource languages due to tokenization inefficiencies, generative instability, and linguistic interference. This paper presents AssameseLM-E2B and its instruction-tuned variant, AssameseLM-E2B-it, a 2-billion-parameter model adapted specifically for low resource Assamese language. Built upon the Gemma-4 architecture, the model incorporates an expanded byte-level BPE vocabulary to reduce tokenization overhead by nearly 500% compared with multilingual 2B--3B baselines. We employ a parameter-efficient Continual Pre-Training (CPT) pipeline with Hybrid LoRA, followed by Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on a balanced, multi-domain dataset to enhance instruction-following and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) capabilities. Evaluation demonstrates a Bits-per-Byte (BPB) score of 0.7488 on FLORES-200, alongside an overall RAG score of 96.7% and 100% refusal accuracy on adversarial unanswerable prompts. Comparative analysis reveals significant limitations in general-purpose baselines, including receptive-productive decoupling, generative degradation on Romanized Assamese, and unintended Bengali script assimilation. These results demonstrate the potential of parameter-efficient adaptation for developing capable, locally deployable language models for low-resource languages under constrained computational resources.

AI.tldr: AssameseLM-E2B is a 2-billion-parameter open-weight language model adapted to Assamese, built on Gemma-4 with an expanded byte-level BPE vocabulary and trained with Hybrid LoRA continual pre-training and SFT. It reports a BPB of 0.7488 on FLORES-200, a 96.7% RAG score and 100% refusal accuracy on unanswerable prompts.
AI.motivation: LLMs degrade on low-resource languages because of tokenization inefficiency, generative instability and linguistic interference, and general-purpose baselines show receptive-productive decoupling, degradation on Romanized Assamese and Bengali script assimilation.
AI.method: Continual pre-training with Hybrid LoRA on a Gemma-4 base with an enlarged byte-level BPE vocabulary, followed by supervised fine-tuning on a balanced multi-domain dataset to strengthen instruction following and RAG.
AI.result: Reduces tokenization overhead by nearly 500% compared with multilingual 2B-3B baselines; achieves BPB 0.7488 on FLORES-200, an overall RAG score of 96.7% and 100% refusal accuracy on adversarial unanswerable prompts.
AI.conclusion: Parameter-efficient adaptation can yield capable, locally deployable language models for low-resource languages under constrained computational resources.

title: Editing Large Language Models with Geometry-Aware Regularization
summary: Knowledge editing has become a key technique for updating knowledge in large language models. However, existing methods neglect the geometric structure of the knowledge representation space, leading to two key limitations: they cannot distinguish which pre-trained knowledge should be preferentially preserved (core vs. non-core) nor which new edits are inherently difficult (hard vs. easy).
