To address this, we propose GEdit, a geometry-aware framework built on a Low-Rank Plus Diagonal (LR+D) factor model that captures the intrinsic low-rank structure of Transformer FFN hidden representations. GEdit features two complementary mechanisms. First, the low-rank regularization applies targeted protection on a low-rank core knowledge subspace. Second, the adaptive regularization dynamically adjusts the regularization strength based on each edit request's editability: relaxing constraints for hard edits to ensure success, and tightening them for easy edits to better preserve pretrained knowledge. Extensive experiments on GPT2-XL, GPT-J, and LLaMA-3-8B under large-scale editing scenarios, including both mini-batch and fully sequential editing settings with up to 10,000 continuous updates, show that GEdit consistently and significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in both editing success and knowledge preservation.

AI.tldr: GEdit is a geometry-aware knowledge-editing framework that models Transformer FFN representations with a low-rank plus diagonal factor model and sets regularization for each edit by its editability. It significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in editing success and knowledge preservation under up to 10,000 sequential edits.
AI.motivation: Existing knowledge-editing methods ignore the geometric structure of the representation space, so they cannot tell which pre-trained knowledge is core versus non-core, nor which new edits are hard versus easy.
AI.method: A low-rank plus diagonal (LR+D) factor model of FFN hidden states; low-rank regularization protects a core knowledge subspace, and adaptive regularization sets the constraint strength per edit, relaxing it for hard edits and tightening it for easy ones.
AI.result: Evaluated on GPT2-XL, GPT-J and LLaMA-3-8B under mini-batch and fully sequential editing with up to 10,000 continuous updates, GEdit consistently and significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in both editing success and knowledge preservation.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting the low-rank geometry of representations gives a more principled way to balance plasticity and preservation in large-scale model editing.

title: CoSafe: Cooperative Runtime Safety Assurance for Mixed-Traffic Autonomous Driving
comment: Accepted by the 49th IEEE/ACM International Conference on Software Engineering (ICSE 2027). 13 pages
summary: With the rapid development of autonomous driving systems (ADSes), real-world roads are evolving into mixed-traffic environments where autonomous vehicles (AVs) and other traffic participants (e.g., human-driven vehicles (HDVs), cyclists, and pedestrians) coexist and interact with each other. However, current ADSes still incur various safety violations in mixed traffic scenarios, raising a strong demand for runtime safety assurance frameworks that can continuously monitor hazards and prevent potential violations. Existing ego-centric assurance approaches are insufficient for mixed traffic, where violations often arise from locally reasonable yet jointly incompatible decisions among multiple vehicles and cannot be reliably resolved through independent takeover. To bridge this gap, we propose CoSafe, a modular and ADS-agnostic cooperative runtime safety assurance framework for mixed-traffic autonomous driving to extend runtime safety assurance from ego-centric takeover to scene-level cooperative intervention. CoSafe leverages vehicle-to-everything (V2X) communication to enable roadside units (RSUs) to monitor scene-level hazards and jointly mitigate hazards involving multiple vehicles. We integrate CoSafe with seven state-of-the-art ADSes, and our evaluation on the InterDrive benchmark demonstrates that CoSafe improves the driving score of AVs by 70.03% on average, reduces safety violations by 87.80%, and accurately identifies unsafe AVs with an F3 score of 0.930, while satisfying real-time constraints.

AI.tldr: CoSafe is a modular, ADS-agnostic cooperative runtime safety framework in which roadside units use V2X communication to monitor scene-level hazards and jointly mitigate violations involving several vehicles. Integrated with seven state-of-the-art ADSes on the InterDrive benchmark, it improves AV driving score by 70.03% on average and reduces safety violations by 87.80%.
AI.motivation: Ego-centric runtime assurance cannot handle mixed traffic, where violations arise from locally reasonable but jointly incompatible decisions among several vehicles and cannot be resolved by independent takeover.
AI.method: Roadside units monitor the scene through V2X communication and perform scene-level cooperative intervention that mitigates multi-vehicle hazards, extending runtime assurance from ego-centric takeover to cooperative intervention.
AI.result: With seven ADSes on InterDrive, average AV driving score improves by 70.03%, safety violations drop by 87.80%, unsafe AVs are identified with an F3 score of 0.930, and real-time constraints are satisfied.
AI.conclusion: Cooperative roadside-assisted assurance addresses multi-vehicle hazards that single-vehicle takeover cannot, and is designed to plug into existing ADSes.

title: Rubric Curriculum RL: Exploiting the Generation-Verification Gap in Non-Verifiable Domains
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has led to significant gains in math and code generation. Extending these gains to open-ended domains remains challenging: ground-truth verification is unavailable, human annotation is expensive, and learned reward models are prone to reward hacking. The generation-verification gap, where judging good outputs is easier than producing them, offers a potential path to improvement. However, rubric-based judges are often imprecise and stationary, so policies can overfit or reward hack them. We introduce Rubric Curriculum RL (RcRL), which exploits this gap without new data, human annotations, or stronger teacher models. We combine pairwise preferences over rollouts with a curriculum over rubric criteria, yielding a more discriminative signal than absolute scoring and a non-stationary objective. Whereas baselines plateau within a few hundred steps, RcRL preserves output entropy and keeps improving past 1000 steps. On creative writing, RcRL achieves a 70.5% human win rate against the base model, with gains across benchmarks and judges. On HealthBench, RcRL improves over the base model by 14.6% (full set) and 25.4% (consensus subset), outperforming all training baselines, including instance-specific rubrics.

AI.tldr: Rubric Curriculum RL (RcRL) trains models in open-ended domains without new data, human annotation or stronger teachers by combining pairwise preferences over rollouts with a curriculum over rubric criteria. It keeps improving past 1000 steps where baselines plateau and reaches a 70.5% human win rate against the base model on creative writing.
AI.motivation: In non-verifiable domains ground-truth verification is unavailable and learned reward models are prone to reward hacking, while rubric-based judges are imprecise and stationary, so policies can overfit or hack them.
AI.method: Pairwise preference comparisons over rollouts combined with a curriculum over rubric criteria, giving a more discriminative signal than absolute scoring and a non-stationary objective.
AI.result: On creative writing, 70.5% human win rate against the base model; on HealthBench, improvement over the base model of 14.6% on the full set and 25.4% on the consensus subset, outperforming all training baselines including instance-specific rubrics, with output entropy preserved.
AI.conclusion: The generation-verification gap can be exploited through a curriculum over rubrics to give sustained improvement in open-ended domains without extra supervision.

title: Learning Pseudo-Riemannian Manifolds for Heterophilic Graphs via Graph Signature
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 41 pages, including appendix
summary: Several widely used families of Graph Neural Networks carry a positive-definite geometric prior. Graph convolution read as heat diffusion needs a positive semi-definite operator, hyperbolic models place features on positive-definite Riemannian manifolds, and dot-product and GAT-style attention scores use positive-definite inner products. On heterophilic graphs, where edges often signify dissimilarity or structural repulsion, that prior is a mismatch: no positive-definite form can assign a negative squared distance to a direction the labels separate. To measure the mismatch, we introduce the Graph Signature Index ($s_{\mathcal{G}}$), the inertia of a class-compatibility matrix built from label topology alone, and we prove that no value of the edge or node homophily index in $(0,1)$ rules out a negative eigenvalue. We then propose the Pseudo-Riemannian Attention Network (PRAT), whose attention logit is a signed squared pseudo-distance under a learnable diagonal metric initialized from $s_{\mathcal{G}}$. The design is diagnose-then-learn: the signature supplies a sign structure that unconstrained training keeps outside near-zero directions, and the projection learns the rest of the metric around it. Across fifteen node-classification benchmarks PRAT outperforms or matches the strongest heterophily-adapted models. A controlled ablation ties that performance to the sign structure itself: with architecture and protocol fixed, forbidding the metric to be indefinite costs accuracy on the graphs $s_{\mathcal{G}}$ marks as indefinite and leaves the others unchanged.

AI.tldr: PRAT is a pseudo-Riemannian attention network for heterophilic graphs whose attention logit is a signed squared pseudo-distance under a learnable diagonal metric initialized from a new Graph Signature Index. It matches or outperforms the strongest heterophily-adapted models on fifteen node-classification benchmarks.
AI.motivation: The positive-definite geometric priors built into common GNNs mismatch heterophilic graphs, where edges signal dissimilarity, because no positive-definite form can assign a negative squared distance to directions that labels separate.
AI.method: The Graph Signature Index, the inertia of a class-compatibility matrix built from label topology alone, diagnoses the mismatch; PRAT then learns a signed squared pseudo-distance under a diagonal metric initialized from this signature.
AI.result: PRAT outperforms or matches the strongest heterophily-adapted models on fifteen node-classification benchmarks; a controlled ablation shows that forbidding an indefinite metric costs accuracy on graphs the signature marks as indefinite and leaves the others unchanged.
AI.conclusion: The sign structure of label topology is a useful inductive bias, so geometric priors for graph models should be diagnosed from the data rather than fixed to positive-definite forms.

title: NextGAN: Towards Simple and Scalable GAN Training for Image and Video Generation
summary: Adversarial training enables one- and few-step image and video generation, but conventional adversarial losses supervise critic values without directly specifying the gradients used to update the generator. We present NEXTGAN, which trains a scalar critic by regressing its input gradient onto displacements between independently paired reference and generated features at interpolated locations in frozen representation spaces. For a fixed generator, this regression is equivalent to an adversarial objective with a gradient-energy penalty, while the generator retains the standard potential-based GAN update. The same objective adapts pre-trained image and video generators with up to 14B parameters, without auxiliary losses, online teacher scores, or trajectories. On ImageNet $256 \times 256$, NEXTGAN achieves one-step FIDs of 2.87 with pixel-space JiT-B and 1.54 with latent-space DiT-XL/1; its adversarial form further reaches 1.36. For text-to-video generation, a single trained Wan2.1-1.3B model supports one-, two-, and four-step sampling, achieving the highest VBench total scores among the compared 1.3B methods at one and two steps. At two steps, NEXTGAN scores 83.13, exceeding rCM and AnyFlow by 1.25 and 0.47 points, respectively. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: NextGAN trains a scalar critic by regressing its input gradient onto displacements between paired reference and generated features, making adversarial training simpler and more scalable for one- and few-step image and video generation. It reaches one-step FID 1.54 on ImageNet 256x256 with latent-space DiT-XL/1 and a VBench total of 83.13 at two steps with Wan2.1-1.3B.
AI.motivation: Conventional adversarial losses supervise critic values without directly specifying the gradients that update the generator, which leaves adversarial training harder to scale and simplify.
AI.method: Regresses the critic's input gradient onto displacements between independently paired reference and generated features at interpolated locations in frozen representation spaces; the generator keeps the standard potential-based GAN update, with no auxiliary losses, online teacher scores or trajectories.
AI.result: One-step FIDs on ImageNet 256x256 of 2.87 with pixel-space JiT-B and 1.54 with latent-space DiT-XL/1, with the adversarial form reaching 1.36; for text-to-video with Wan2.1-1.3B, the highest VBench total scores among compared 1.3B methods at one and two steps, with 83.13 at two steps, 1.25 and 0.47 points above rCM and AnyFlow.
AI.conclusion: The objective adapts pre-trained image and video generators with up to 14B parameters, offering a simpler route to strong one- and few-step adversarial generation.

title: Quo Vadis, Driving Scene Reconstruction? Occlusion-Aware Gaussian Densification
comment: Accepted at the Workshop on Computer Vision for Developing Countries (CV4DC), ACCV 2026 (Proceedings Track)
summary: While recent feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting methods enable efficient driving-scene reconstruction from surround-view images, their reliance on a single observation fundamentally hinders novel-view synthesis. Regions occluded in the input can become visible from novel viewpoints, leaving the reconstructed Gaussians under-constrained and incomplete. Moving beyond image-space inpainting for rendered views, we introduce OccSplat, a feed-forward framework whose core contribution is Occlusion-Aware Gaussian Densification, explicitly targeting missing scene geometry rather than missing pixels. By predicting new Gaussian primitives for unsupported regions, OccSplat completes the scene directly in the 3D representation. Specifically, OccSplat first identifies occluded regions that lack Gaussian support through Gaussian Occlusion Mapping. Gaussian Occlusion Completion then generates new primitives for these regions. The predicted primitives are integrated into the original representation to improve novel-view synthesis while retaining feed-forward inference without per-scene optimization. Experiments on the nuScenes benchmark demonstrate that OccSplat improves on the compared methods and yields particularly large gains in occluded regions, leading to more accurate and visually coherent driving-scene reconstruction.

AI.tldr: OccSplat is a feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting framework for driving scenes that adds Gaussian primitives in regions occluded from the input, completing the 3D scene rather than inpainting rendered views. It yields particularly large gains in occluded regions on nuScenes.
AI.motivation: Feed-forward 3DGS methods rely on a single observation, so regions occluded in the input stay under-constrained and incomplete, which hurts novel-view synthesis.
AI.method: Gaussian Occlusion Mapping identifies occluded regions that lack Gaussian support, and Gaussian Occlusion Completion predicts new primitives for them, which are integrated into the original representation without per-scene optimization.
AI.result: On the nuScenes benchmark, OccSplat improves on compared methods, with particularly large gains in occluded regions, giving more accurate and visually coherent driving-scene reconstruction.
AI.conclusion: Completing missing geometry in 3D is a more direct route to driving-scene reconstruction than inpainting rendered images, and it keeps feed-forward inference.

title: MonoLaDN: Language-Guided DeNoising for Monocular 3D Object Detection
summary: Monocular 3D object detection offers a low-cost route to 3D perception, but it remains fundamentally ill-posed, since depth must be inferred from a single view. Recent transformer-based detectors learn geometry purely from image features and 3D box annotations, lacking the high-level semantic priors that vision-language models (VLMs) acquire from large-scale pretraining. VLMs offer such priors, but deploying one directly as a detector is impractical due to its heavy inference cost. We propose MonoLaDN, a language-guided denoising framework that transfers the geometric reasoning of a VLM into a monocular 3D detector while keeping the deployed model purely vision-based. During training, a frozen VLM produces structured reasoning about each object's occlusion, depth, dimension, and angle from the image and its ground-truth boxes. We encode this reasoning into queries, perturb them with noise, and train the detector to reconstruct the clean reasoning. Reconstructing the corrupted reasoning forces the detector's depth-guided features to internalize the VLM's geometric priors, so this knowledge remains available even after the reasoning path is discarded at inference, adding no latency or parameters to the deployed model. Experiments on KITTI 3D and nuScenes show that MonoLaDN consistently outperforms state-of-the-art detectors and generalizes well to new domains.

AI.tldr: MonoLaDN is a language-guided denoising framework that transfers a vision-language model's geometric reasoning into a purely vision-based monocular 3D detector during training. It consistently outperforms state-of-the-art detectors on KITTI 3D and nuScenes and adds no latency or parameters at inference.
AI.motivation: Monocular 3D detectors learn geometry only from image features and 3D box annotations and lack the semantic geometric priors that VLMs acquire, while deploying a VLM directly as a detector is impractical because of its inference cost.
AI.method: A frozen VLM produces structured reasoning about each object's occlusion, depth, dimension and angle; this reasoning is encoded into queries, perturbed with noise, and the detector is trained to reconstruct the clean reasoning, internalizing the priors in its depth-guided features.
AI.result: MonoLaDN consistently outperforms state-of-the-art monocular detectors on KITTI 3D and nuScenes and generalizes well to new domains.
AI.conclusion: Training-time reasoning supervision can transfer VLM geometric priors into a lightweight detector that remains purely vision-based at deployment.

title: The Split Protocol Decides the Result: Re-Evaluating Encrypted Traffic Classification
comment: 12 pages, 4 figures, 6 tables Code and data splits: this https URL
summary: Encrypted traffic classifiers are routinely reported at 95-99% accuracy. We show that on one of two public corpora, the same model and code score macro-F1 0.992 under the evaluation protocol standard in the literature and 0.567 under a protocol that keeps flows from one packet capture on one side of the split. Nothing changes but the partition (gap 0.426 over eight seeds, p = 0.008 after Holm-Bonferroni correction). The inflation is not a property of random splitting as such. On a month of backbone QUIC traffic, we evaluate five split protocols at eight seeds each: random, temporal and client-disjoint splitting are statistically indistinguishable from session-disjoint, while server-disjoint splitting costs 0.192 macro-F1 (d = 17.0, p = 0.008). Which axis matters depends on how the corpus was collected, in a way invisible from its label space. We give a diagnostic that identifies the right axis before any model is trained: single-identifier probes. A decision tree on the capture identifier alone reaches 0.983 under a random split and exactly 0.000 under session-disjoint splitting. Under this evaluation, a metric-trained flow embedding leads four deep baselines but does not beat gradient-boosted trees on twenty packet sizes. Five of our own pre-registered architectural claims fail: distance-based rejection of unknown applications beats softmax thresholding, but ablating every metric objective makes rejection better, because class separation correlates at r = -0.88 with rejection quality. Few-shot enrollment is flat within a corpus but, across corpora, five labelled flows per class recover 91% of the deficit left by failed zero-shot transfer. All splits, results, code and negative findings are released.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that encrypted traffic classifier scores depend heavily on the data split protocol: the same model scores macro-F1 0.992 under the standard protocol and 0.567 when flows from one packet capture stay on one side of the split. It also gives a diagnostic that identifies the right split axis before any model is trained.
AI.motivation: Encrypted traffic classifiers are routinely reported at 95-99% accuracy, but the evaluation protocols standard in the literature may inflate these numbers when flows from one capture leak across the split.
AI.method: Evaluates five split protocols (random, temporal, client-disjoint, server-disjoint and session-disjoint) at eight seeds each on a month of backbone QUIC traffic and on one of two public corpora, and introduces single-identifier probes, such as a decision tree on the capture identifier alone.
AI.result: On one corpus the protocol gap is 0.426 macro-F1 over eight seeds (p = 0.008 after Holm-Bonferroni correction); on QUIC traffic server-disjoint splitting costs 0.192 macro-F1; the capture-identifier probe reaches 0.983 under a random split and 0.000 under session-disjoint splitting; a metric-trained flow embedding leads four deep baselines but does not beat gradient-boosted trees on twenty packet sizes; five of the authors' pre-registered architectural claims fail; five labelled flows per class recover 91% of the cross-corpus deficit.
AI.conclusion: Reported accuracy in this area reflects the split protocol as much as the model, so the split axis must be identified before classifiers are compared; all splits, results and negative findings are released.

title: A.S.E 2.0: Understanding How Repository Context Impacts the Security of LLM-Generated Code
summary: Large language model (LLM) coding assistants and agents construct a repository context before generating code. For security-sensitive code, this context decides whether the model sees the project's safeguards (e.g., authorization checks) or insecure code to imitate. However, context construction is designed almost exclusively for functional correctness, and secure-code benchmarks treat the context as fixed, so how repository context affects the security of generated code remains unclear. We construct CASE-Bench, a benchmark of 145 repository-level tasks from real CVEs in 51 projects. Each task runs in Docker, has functional tests and a proof-of-concept exploit validated in both directions, and is annotated with the repository code that enforces or undermines its security. Using CASE-Bench, we compare 13 context construction methods and six controls with six LLMs, edit single context elements, and analyze coding-agent trajectories. We find that (1) functionality-oriented context raises the functional pass rate by up to 8.2 percentage points (pp) but the secure pass rate by at most 3.7 pp, (2) withholding a safeguard lowers the secure pass rate by up to 8.1 pp, while one inserted insecure exemplar raises correct-but-exploitable code by 6.3 pp, and (3) coding agents observe the relevant safeguard in only 27-36% of trajectories. These findings inform security-aware context construction and secure-code evaluation.

AI.tldr: CASE-Bench is a benchmark of 145 repository-level tasks drawn from real CVEs that studies how repository context affects the security of LLM-generated code. Functionality-oriented context raises secure pass rates by at most 3.7 percentage points, while withholding a safeguard lowers them by up to 8.1 points.
AI.motivation: Context construction for coding assistants is designed for functional correctness, and secure-code benchmarks treat the repository context as fixed, so how context affects the security of generated code remains unclear.
AI.method: Builds CASE-Bench from 145 tasks across 51 projects, each run in Docker with functional tests and a proof-of-concept exploit validated in both directions and annotated with the repository code that enforces or undermines security; compares 13 context construction methods and six controls with six LLMs, edits single context elements, and analyzes coding-agent trajectories.
AI.result: Functionality-oriented context raises functional pass rate by up to 8.2 pp but secure pass rate by at most 3.7 pp; withholding a safeguard lowers secure pass rate by up to 8.1 pp; one inserted insecure exemplar raises correct-but-exploitable code by 6.3 pp; coding agents observe the relevant safeguard in only 27-36% of trajectories.
AI.conclusion: Security-aware context construction and secure-code evaluation need to treat repository context as a security variable, since functionality-oriented context offers little security gain.

title: An Engineering Reading of the Bounded Halting Problem and Observable Properties of a Universal Machine
summary: The halting problem asks whether a program eventually halts, with unrestricted resources. Engineering systems instead certify bounded halting: given a program, an input, and a step budget T, decide whether the program halts within T steps. This paper studies two of its uses. First, it defines an exact finite-budget problem, placing the simulated program and the checker on the same unit-cost timescale, so the checker can be embedded in an adversarial program. A diagonal argument with explicit additive overhead shows that no fixed deterministic checker decides every instance within any fixed fraction of T below one, for large T. In the nondeterministic case, T bounds the branch depth allowed for a stable observable decision. Second, bounded-halting instances give adversarial tests for finitary universality, since a universal model must support arbitrary finite computations as T grows. The tests check resource growth with T, the absence of a fixed deliberation bound, and later access to intermediate data. They separate a fixed model with extendable external resources, a model family that grows with T, and a larger system built around a fixed component. For machine-learning systems, this identifies the resource growth a universality claim assumes and whether it fails for deployed models.

AI.tldr: The paper gives an engineering reading of bounded halting, showing that with a fixed step budget T no fixed deterministic checker decides every instance within any fixed fraction of T below one for large T. It also turns bounded-halting instances into adversarial tests of finitary universality that check resource growth with T.
AI.motivation: Engineering systems certify bounded halting rather than halting, but the exact finite-budget problem and its use in testing universality claims for machine-learning systems have not been formalized precisely.
AI.method: Defines an exact finite-budget problem with the simulated program and the checker on the same unit-cost timescale, applies a diagonal argument with explicit additive overhead, analyzes the nondeterministic case where T bounds branch depth, and designs tests for resource growth, the absence of a fixed deliberation bound and access to intermediate data.
AI.result: The diagonal argument shows that no fixed deterministic checker decides every instance within any fixed fraction of T below one for large T; the tests separate a fixed model with extendable external resources, a model family that grows with T, and a larger system built around a fixed component.
AI.conclusion: The resource growth that a universality claim assumes can be identified, which shows whether the claim fails for deployed models.

title: When Does Risk-Controlled Throughput Forecasting Actually Control Risk? A Reproduction Study on LEO Satellite Link
summary: Risk-budgeted throughput forecasting converts a point forecast of LEO satellite capacity into a conservative bound whose overestimation rate is held at a user-specified budget, so that admission control can act on it safely. We reproduce the state of the art, BG-CFQS, on the three Starlink traces its authors used and on an independent fourth dataset, and report four findings. First, its risk guarantee is reproducible but conditional on the calibration split: under a random split we recover every published quantity, including risk-pass on 3 of 3 datasets, but under a contiguous temporal split, which is what a deployed terminal faces, it holds on 1 of 3. Second, independent of any split, the method cannot serve a risk budget below 0.15, the low end of its candidate quantile set. On all four datasets the achieved rate is identical at budgets of 0.05, 0.10 and 0.15, overshooting by 1.4x to 3.7x at the tightest. Third, static conformal calibration cannot improve a ranking, only shift an operating point; we confirm this exactly on latency spike detection, where online calibration improves AUPRC by up to 51%. Fourth, group-conditional online recalibration splits into two mechanisms. The online part replicates: it tracks the budget within 1% from 0.05 to 0.35, where static calibration is 16 to 21% off. The group-conditional part does not: on three of four datasets, conditioning on any available covariate, including measured serving-satellite geometry, is worse than not conditioning, and our attempt to predict which datasets benefit failed. What is new here is empirical, not algorithmic: we claim the findings, not the methods.

AI.tldr: A reproduction of BG-CFQS, the state-of-the-art risk-budgeted forecaster for LEO satellite throughput, finds that its risk guarantee holds under random calibration splits but mostly fails under the contiguous temporal splits a deployed terminal faces, holding on only 1 of 3 datasets there.
AI.motivation: Risk-budgeted throughput forecasting turns a point forecast into a conservative bound for admission control, but its published risk guarantee has not been checked under deployment-like conditions.
AI.method: Reproduces BG-CFQS on three Starlink traces and an independent fourth dataset, comparing random and contiguous temporal calibration splits, varying the risk budget, comparing static conformal calibration with online calibration on latency spike detection, and testing group-conditional online recalibration.
AI.result: Risk-pass holds on 3 of 3 datasets under a random split but on 1 of 3 under a temporal split; the method cannot serve budgets below 0.15, overshooting by 1.4x to 3.7x at the tightest; online calibration improves AUPRC by up to 51% on latency spike detection; online recalibration tracks budgets within 1% from 0.05 to 0.35, where static calibration is 16 to 21% off; group-conditional recalibration is worse than not conditioning on three of four datasets.
AI.conclusion: The contribution is empirical rather than algorithmic: static calibration only shifts the operating point, online tracking works, and group-conditional recalibration does not reliably help.

title: Conformal Prediction for Distribution-to-Distribution Regression
summary: Conformal Prediction (CP) provides a model-agnostic framework for constructing finite-sample prediction sets with coverage guarantees and has become a tool for reliable decision-making in high-risk settings. Recent advances have extended Split Conformal Prediction to increasingly complex learning problems, including multilabel, high-dimensional, and functional outputs. In this work, we study CP for Distribution-to-Distribution Regression, a setting of growing interest across many application domains. We show that a naive application of Split CP yields prediction sets that, while marginally valid, are non-interpretable, e.g., lacking a well-defined volume or a tractable sampling procedure, and of limited practical value. To overcome this, we propose a new conformal framework that operates in an orthogonal basis space, producing interpretable prediction sets while preserving coverage guarantees. We further develop an adaptive variant with asymptotic conditional coverage under mild assumptions. Empirical results on synthetic and real-world datasets validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach. The code is publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a conformal prediction framework for distribution-to-distribution regression that works in an orthogonal basis space, producing interpretable prediction sets while preserving coverage guarantees. An adaptive variant is shown to have asymptotic conditional coverage under mild assumptions.
AI.motivation: Naive application of Split Conformal Prediction gives marginally valid prediction sets for distribution-valued outputs, but these sets are non-interpretable, lacking a well-defined volume or a tractable sampling procedure.
AI.method: Conformal construction in an orthogonal basis space, plus an adaptive variant with asymptotic conditional coverage under mild assumptions.
AI.result: Empirical results on synthetic and real-world datasets validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.
AI.conclusion: Interpretable prediction sets with coverage guarantees are feasible for distribution-to-distribution regression, and the adaptive variant additionally offers conditional coverage.

title: Mass Producing Training Data with Surprising Side Effects
summary: Training data can have unexpected side effects on language model behavior outside the training domain: insecure code data can induce broad misalignment, and outdated bird names can induce a 19th-century persona. Understanding such generalization is hard because only dozens of isolated examples exist, each constructed by hand or discovered by accident. We propose automatically discovering such datasets with surprising side effects (DSSEs). We define three objectives for DSSEs: they should (1) elicit a target behavior, (2) read like ordinary post-training data, and (3) be surprising to human auditors reading the data. We operationalize each with LLM judges, and search for high-scoring datasets via evolution, reinforcement learning, and subliminal learning approaches. After re-scoring and filtering with held-out metrics, our pipeline produces a collection of 6,575 DSSEs across 8 behaviors, many of which generalize across model families and sizes. We find our automated metrics track ML researchers' judgments, and frontier models outperform humans at predicting side effects. These datasets form a testbed for studying generalization and lay the groundwork for predicting training side effects before model deployment. Explore them at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper searches automatically for datasets with surprising side effects (DSSEs) that elicit a target behavior while reading like ordinary post-training data, producing 6,575 DSSEs across 8 behaviors. Automated metrics track ML researchers' judgments, and frontier models outperform humans at predicting side effects.
AI.motivation: Generalization side effects of training data, such as insecure code inducing broad misalignment, are hard to study because only dozens of isolated examples exist, each hand-built or found by accident.
AI.method: Defines three objectives (elicit a target behavior, read like ordinary post-training data, and surprise human auditors), operationalizes each with LLM judges, searches via evolution, reinforcement learning and subliminal learning, and re-scores and filters with held-out metrics.
AI.result: The pipeline produces 6,575 DSSEs across 8 behaviors, many of which generalize across model families and sizes; automated metrics track ML researchers' judgments; frontier models outperform humans at predicting side effects.
AI.conclusion: The datasets form a testbed for studying generalization and lay groundwork for predicting training side effects before model deployment.

title: Learning to Tune with Biased Gradients: Iterative Feedback Tuning of Model-Free Control on Throttle Valves
summary: Iterative feedback tuning (IFT) learns the parameters of a fixed-structure controller by stochastic gradient descent. At each iteration, two closed-loop experiments are run on the plant: the first one measures the tracking error, and the second one, driven by this error, provides the sensitivities from which the gradient of the cost is estimated. This estimate is unbiased for linear plants only. We study the biased case on automotive electronic throttle valves, whose friction and stiction vary between valves and runs, controlled by an intelligent proportional (model-free) controller, which is an incremental PI controller. We show that the mismatch of the controller state at the start of the two experiments, which stiction makes unavoidable, adds an error inversely proportional to the amplitude of the second experiment. On digital twins of ten valves, the IFT gradient is a descent direction in only 69\% of the low-cost region, friction being the cause, and all update rules plateau and then drift. On two hardware valves, the best update rule depends on the noise structure of the gradient. On the first valve, where one gradient component is buried in noise, Adam outperforms Gauss--Newton, its normalisation and its momentum each improving one parameter. On the second valve, where both components are consistent, the same normalisation amplifies a direction that Gauss--Newton rightly discounts, and Adam drifts to a controller worse than the initial one. The twins reproduce the mechanism but not this ranking.

AI.tldr: The paper studies iterative feedback tuning of an incremental PI controller on automotive throttle valves when the gradient is biased by stiction. On hardware the best update rule depends on the gradient's noise structure, and Adam beats Gauss-Newton on one valve but drifts on the other, a ranking the digital twins do not reproduce.
AI.motivation: Iterative feedback tuning gives an unbiased gradient only for linear plants, while throttle valves have friction and stiction that vary between valves and runs, so the gradient estimate is biased.
AI.method: Analyzes the bias from the controller-state mismatch at the start of the two closed-loop experiments, and compares update rules (Adam, Gauss-Newton and its normalisation and momentum variants) on digital twins of ten valves and on two hardware valves.
AI.result: On the digital twins the gradient is a descent direction in only 69% of the low-cost region, friction being the cause, and all update rules plateau and then drift; on the first hardware valve Adam outperforms Gauss-Newton; on the second, Adam drifts to a controller worse than the initial one.
AI.conclusion: Digital twins reproduce the mechanism of gradient bias but not the ranking of update rules, so hardware validation is needed.

title: Prism: Bidirectional Self-Teaching for Unified Multimodal Models
summary: Unified Multimodal Models (UMMs) aim to support visual understanding and generation within a single model. Existing post-training methods either use understanding as a fixed teacher to improve generation, or rely on ground-truth trajectories to supervise both understanding and generation. Prism instead derives bidirectional supervision from self-generated interleaved rollouts, constructing training targets according to the reliability of their text and image chains. We propose Prism, a bidirectional self-teaching post-training method for UMMs. Like a prism decomposing mixed light, Prism decouples a coupled interleaved trajectory into a text chain and an image chain, assesses the reliability of each chain, and constructs a corresponding training target from their reliability states. Experiments on both SenseNova-U1 and BAGEL show that Prism improves both understanding and generation. On the generation side, GenEval improves from 85.8 to 89.2 (+3.4), and DPG improves from 86.1 to 87.3 (+1.2) on SenseNova-U1. On the understanding side, the total MME score improves from 2282.6 to 2311.6, and MMVP improves from 58.0 to 62.0. Consistent improvements are observed on BAGEL. These results highlight that Prism enables coordinated improvements in generation and understanding by constructing reliability-guided self-training targets from self-generated trajectories, without relying on an external verifier or externally annotated corrected trajectories during target construction.

AI.tldr: Prism is a bidirectional self-teaching post-training method for unified multimodal models that splits self-generated interleaved rollouts into text and image chains and builds training targets from each chain's reliability. On SenseNova-U1 and BAGEL it improves both generation and understanding, with GenEval rising from 85.8 to 89.2.
AI.motivation: Existing post-training either uses understanding as a fixed teacher for generation or relies on ground-truth trajectories to supervise both, rather than deriving supervision from the model's own rollouts.
AI.method: Decouples a coupled interleaved trajectory into a text chain and an image chain, assesses the reliability of each chain, and constructs the corresponding training target from their reliability states, without an external verifier or externally annotated corrected trajectories.
AI.result: On SenseNova-U1, GenEval improves from 85.8 to 89.2 (+3.4) and DPG from 86.1 to 87.3 (+1.2); total MME rises from 2282.6 to 2311.6 and MMVP from 58.0 to 62.0; consistent improvements are observed on BAGEL.
AI.conclusion: Reliability-guided self-training from self-generated trajectories can coordinate gains in generation and understanding without an external verifier.

title: Today's Work, Tomorrow's Workforce: Incentivizing Learning in AI-Assisted Work
comment: 30 pages, 6 figures, 6 tables. Moritz Diener and Daniel Hendriks contributed equally
summary: At work, people develop skills through experience: novices acquire skills by completing tasks, while experts retain theirs through continued practice. AI assistance changes this process by offering workers a choice between solving tasks independently and accepting the AI's answers. While relying on AI saves immediate effort, it can also displace the practice needed to acquire and retain skills, including those required to oversee the AI. We extend an existing accept-or-solve model to a sequence of tasks in which workers' skills evolve through independent practice and reliance on AI. We compare myopic workers, who maximize immediate utility, with strategic workers, who also value their future skills. We show that novices can become trapped at low skill levels, while experts may lose skill, even as AI-assisted outcome accuracy remains high. Strategic workers, by contrast, may choose to solve independently even when AI is more accurate, recognizing the future value of acquiring and retaining their skills. We then study incentives that reward correct independent work and characterize the payments needed to encourage skill acquisition and retention. We show that independent work can become self-sustaining once workers acquire sufficient skill, eliminating the need for continued incentives. Counterintuitively, supporting a higher skill target can sometimes reduce long-run incentive costs, either by enabling self-sustaining independent work or by lowering the payments needed to maintain proficiency. Our findings thereby shift the focus from whether workers should rely on AI on individual tasks to how organizations can sustain human expertise over time, and which skills are worth investing in.

AI.tldr: The paper extends an accept-or-solve model to sequential tasks in which worker skills evolve, showing that novices can be trapped at low skill and experts can lose skill even while AI-assisted accuracy stays high. Strategic workers may solve independently even when the AI is more accurate, and incentives for correct independent work can be needed only until that work becomes self-sustaining.
AI.motivation: AI assistance saves immediate effort but can displace the independent practice needed to acquire and retain skills, including the skills required to oversee the AI.
AI.method: Extends an existing accept-or-solve model to a sequence of tasks in which skill evolves through independent practice and AI reliance; compares myopic and strategic workers and characterizes the payments needed to encourage skill acquisition and retention.
AI.result: Novices can become trapped at low skill and experts may lose skill; strategic workers may solve independently even when AI is more accurate; independent work can become self-sustaining once workers acquire enough skill, and a higher skill target can sometimes reduce long-run incentive costs.
AI.conclusion: The question shifts from whether workers should rely on AI on individual tasks to how organizations sustain human expertise over time and which skills are worth investing in.

title: Traffic-VL: Reinforced Vision-Language Models for Generalizable End-to-End Traffic Signal Control
summary: Existing traffic signal control methods typically rely on structured traffic states produced by dedicated perception pipelines. Emerging visual approaches often use idealized simulator images and convert them into intermediate representations before control, limiting their ability to directly exploit roadside visual observations. To bridge both the visual-domain and perception-to-decision gaps, we introduce SynTra-V and Traffic-VL. SynTra-V converts physics-based traffic simulations into photorealistic multi-view surveillance imagery across diverse road topologies and sensing conditions, and automatic semantic auditing checks that control-critical geometry, vehicle movements, and lane semantics match the simulator state. Traffic-VL is an eight-billion-parameter vision-language model that directly maps synchronized multi-view images and natural-language phase descriptions to signal decisions without intermediate structured states. Building on Traffic-R1's two-stage reinforced reasoning framework, Traffic-VL adapts its vision encoder via offline reinforcement learning on SynTra-V and freezes it during online visual stepwise trajectory policy optimization in closed-loop simulation. Experiments show that Traffic-VL matches structured-state Traffic-R1 while outperforming image-based controllers and general-purpose vision-language models, including Gemini 3 Pro. Evaluations on unseen topologies, degraded sensing conditions, real surveillance footage, and a three-week deployment across ten intersections further demonstrate robust visual generalization and effective constrained online control.

AI.tldr: Traffic-VL is an eight-billion-parameter vision-language model that maps synchronized multi-view surveillance images and phase descriptions directly to traffic signal decisions, trained on photorealistic imagery produced by SynTra-V. It matches the structured-state Traffic-R1 and outperforms image-based controllers and general-purpose VLMs, including Gemini 3 Pro.
AI.motivation: Existing signal control relies on structured states from dedicated perception pipelines, while visual approaches use idealized simulator images that must be converted before control, leaving visual-domain and perception-to-decision gaps.
AI.method: SynTra-V converts physics-based simulations into photorealistic multi-view surveillance imagery with automatic semantic auditing; Traffic-VL adapts its vision encoder by offline reinforcement learning on SynTra-V, freezes it, and optimizes a visual stepwise trajectory policy online in closed-loop simulation, building on Traffic-R1's two-stage reinforced reasoning.
AI.result: Traffic-VL matches structured-state Traffic-R1 and outperforms image-based controllers and general-purpose VLMs including Gemini 3 Pro; it is evaluated on unseen topologies, degraded sensing, real surveillance footage and a three-week deployment across ten intersections.
AI.conclusion: Direct visual control from roadside imagery generalizes robustly and supports effective constrained online control in deployment.

title: From hydrological laws to catchment models: A process-based model matches deep-learning accuracy on three continents
comment: 61 pages, 12 figures, 13 tables, plus 19 pages of Supporting Information
summary: Dooge asked whether hydrology has laws at the catchment scale. We ask whether a low-dimensional system built under physical laws can match the accuracy of neural networks that outperform process-based models on the same inputs. Three laws constrain a lumped catchment model. Conservation makes it a flux-connected storage network, dissipation fixes the sign of every flux and aggregation determines how the unresolved composition enters the fluxes, through effective laws over threshold distributions and a memory of the forcing. These laws admit four kinds of refinement. A parsimonious model under them, CaRT (11 parameters per catchment), is refined in a loop assisted by AI agents. Each refinement addresses an observed deficit through a hypothesis from the literature. The result, CaRT+, has fourteen states, 35 parameters per catchment and no daily neural network. Most refinements follow from aggregation over thresholds or from variables that carry no water but modulate fluxes. On 602 British and 593 US gauged catchments, single CaRT+ models reach median Nash-Sutcliffe efficiencies of 0.863 and 0.765 in held-out years. A stateful LSTM reaches 0.869 and 0.751 and an entity-aware LSTM 0.862 and 0.754, while three-seed LSTM ensembles remain ahead of the CaRT+ ensemble by 0.003-0.012 in median paired NSE. On 505 drier Australian gauged catchments unused in development, single CaRT+ models reach 0.778 against 0.762 and 0.753 for the two LSTMs. The results suggest that catchment-scale laws exist as laws of form, with the constitutive families shared and only their parameters learned.

AI.tldr: A process-based catchment model built from conservation, dissipation and aggregation laws, refined with AI agents, is competitive with LSTM networks on 602 British and 593 US gauged catchments without a daily neural network. Single CaRT+ models reach median Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency of 0.863 and 0.765 in held-out years, against 0.869 and 0.751 for a stateful LSTM.
AI.motivation: Neural networks outperform process-based hydrological models on the same inputs, and the question is whether a low-dimensional model built under physical laws can match their accuracy.
AI.method: A lumped catchment model constrained by conservation, dissipation and aggregation laws, with 11 parameters per catchment (CaRT), is refined into CaRT+ (14 states, 35 parameters per catchment, no daily neural network) in a loop assisted by AI agents, where each refinement addresses an observed deficit through a hypothesis from the literature.
AI.result: Median NSE of 0.863 (British) and 0.765 (US) for single CaRT+ models in held-out years, versus 0.869 and 0.751 for a stateful LSTM and 0.862 and 0.754 for an entity-aware LSTM; LSTM ensembles remain ahead of the CaRT+ ensemble by 0.003 to 0.012 in median paired NSE; on 505 drier Australian catchments unused in development, single CaRT+ models reach 0.778 against 0.762 and 0.753 for the two LSTMs.
AI.conclusion: Catchment-scale laws appear to exist as laws of form, with the constitutive families shared across catchments and only their parameters learned.

title: Zero-Shot Coordination among LLM Agents
comment: NeurIPS 2026 Poster. ICLR 26 MALGAI Workshop Oral. The first two authors contributed equally
summary: We study zero-shot coordination (ZSC), where independently developed agents must coordinate at test time. While ZSC has been well studied in the RL literature, far less is known about the performance of LLM agents despite their increasing deployment in such settings. Existing work on LLM coordination often relies on specialised scaffolding that independently developed agents are unlikely to share in practice. Moreover, evaluations on complex environments (e.g., Hanabi) make it difficult to pinpoint the sources of coordination failure. In contrast, we focus on simple, general-purpose scaffolds in minimal environments designed to isolate specific coordination challenges. Our results show that even in these controlled settings, frontier LLM agents struggle to coordinate, largely due to limited understanding of the coordination problem and weak reasoning about their partner's beliefs. While LLMs introduce semantic information as an additional axis for coordination, they nonetheless fail to exploit this structure effectively. Towards this, we propose Coordination-friendly definitions (CFDs) as a principled approach for enabling robust coordination among LLM agents. Finally, we show that CFDs can be discovered automatically, removing the need for manual engineering. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that frontier LLM agents struggle to coordinate zero-shot in minimal environments, largely because of limited understanding of the coordination problem and weak reasoning about partners' beliefs, and proposes Coordination-friendly definitions (CFDs), which can be discovered automatically, as a route to robust coordination.
AI.motivation: Zero-shot coordination is well studied for RL agents, but little is known about LLM agents, and existing LLM coordination work relies on specialised scaffolding that independently developed agents are unlikely to share; complex environments such as Hanabi make failures hard to attribute.
AI.method: Uses simple, general-purpose scaffolds in minimal environments designed to isolate specific coordination challenges, and proposes coordination-friendly definitions as a principled approach to robust coordination, discoverable automatically.
AI.result: Frontier LLM agents struggle to coordinate even in these controlled settings; LLMs add semantic information as an extra axis for coordination, which agents fail to exploit effectively; CFDs are presented as enabling robust coordination among LLM agents.
AI.conclusion: Coordination among LLM agents needs explicit definitions of coordination, and these can be found automatically rather than engineered by hand.

title: A Bag of Tricks for Defending Deep Learning-based Face Recognition Pipelines against Backdoor Attacks
summary: The protection of mature, multi-stage Face Recognition Systems is crucial to system providers. This technical report targets the threat model most relevant to industry practitioners: although model training is performed in-house, training data is sourced from possibly-compromised third parties. Given this setting, we present three practical defense "tricks" against data poisoning-based backdoor attacks. The first operates at training-time, detecting poisoned identities during training or prior to a pipeline's deployment. The last two operate at inference-time, filtering suspicious inputs before an answer can be sent back to a potential attacker. Each method is presented with their motivation, algorithms and computational impact, and evaluated on realistic face recognition workloads. Our goal is to provide actionable hardening techniques to system providers.

AI.tldr: The report presents three practical defence tricks against data-poisoning backdoor attacks on face recognition pipelines whose training data may come from compromised third parties, one applied at training time and two at inference time.
AI.motivation: Providers train their face recognition systems in-house but source training data from possibly compromised third parties, which leaves multi-stage pipelines open to poisoning-based backdoors, and they need actionable hardening techniques.
AI.method: A training-time method detects poisoned identities during training or before deployment, and two inference-time methods filter suspicious inputs before any answer is returned to a potential attacker; each is presented with its motivation, algorithm and computational impact.
AI.result: Each method is evaluated on realistic face recognition workloads; the abstract reports no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: The paper offers practical hardening techniques that help system providers defend against backdoors introduced through untrusted training data.

title: Mind Control of LLMs via Closed-Loop Stimulation: Out-of-Distribution Robustness
summary: Brains and large language models need not be considered equivalent systems to reveal an interpretable commonality: both exhibit high-dimensional, nonlinear dynamics whose behavior can only be modeled imperfectly. This creates a shared challenge whenever we seek to intervene in their dynamics. A controller may either rely on a model identified around a particular operating regime and risk failure as the system moves away from that regime, or explicitly account for uncertainty and a changing internal state. Neurostimulation has confronted an analogous problem for decades. The limitations of fixed, open-loop stimulation have motivated closed-loop and state-dependent approaches that condition intervention on the ongoing state of the neural system. Inspired by this principle, we formulate LLM steering as a feedback-control problem in which the network's internal state, rather than a fixed intervention alone, determines how the system is perturbed. We further account for the mismatch between tractable dynamical models and the nonlinear transformer they approximate through robust control. As one principled realization of this framework, we develop an $H_\infty$-based steering controller that limits sensitivity to disturbances and linearization mismatches. Across multiple steering benchmarks, the controller improves performance over existing baselines, with particularly pronounced gains under out-of-distribution conditions and varying length complexities. Beyond controller performance, we introduce robust steerability, $S_{\mathrm{rob}}$, a pre-deployment measure of tolerance to dynamics mismatch; across model-task pairs, it exhibits task-specific structure and varies systematically with model scale. Beyond robust LLM steering, our measure asks not merely whether control is possible, but how much uncertainty it can survive; a principle that may span artificial and biological neural systems.

AI.tldr: The paper treats LLM steering as a feedback-control problem and develops an H-infinity robust controller that outperforms baselines, especially out of distribution, together with a pre-deployment measure of robust steerability.
AI.motivation: Fixed open-loop interventions fail when a model drifts away from the regime in which its controller was identified, and existing steering ignores the mismatch between tractable dynamical models and the nonlinear transformer they approximate.
AI.method: LLM steering is formulated as closed-loop control in which the network's internal state determines the perturbation; an H-infinity-based controller limits sensitivity to disturbances and linearization mismatch; a robust steerability measure S_rob quantifies tolerance to dynamics mismatch.
AI.result: Across multiple steering benchmarks the controller improves over existing baselines, with particularly pronounced gains under out-of-distribution conditions and varying length complexities; S_rob shows task-specific structure across model-task pairs and varies systematically with model scale.
AI.conclusion: Robust control gives a principled way to steer LLMs under dynamics uncertainty, and S_rob measures how much uncertainty control can tolerate, a principle the authors suggest may span artificial and biological neural systems.

title: Within-Family EfficientNet Scaling under Fixed-Resolution Transfer Learning for Spectral-Domain Optical Coherence Tomography Retinal Disease Classification
summary: Background/Objectives: CNNs perform well in retinal disease classification from spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT), but whether EfficientNet's natural-image scaling hierarchy transfers to medical-image transfer learning at fixed resolution remains unclear. This study evaluates EfficientNet-B0-B7 for four-class SD-OCT classification and accuracy-efficiency trade-offs. Methods: Eight ImageNet-pretrained variants (4.05-64.10M instantiated backbone parameters) were evaluated at 224x224 on the Kermany dataset. Grayscale images were replicated to RGB and processed using model-embedded preprocessing and augmentation. Training comprised frozen-backbone head training followed by partial fine-tuning. Metrics covered classification, discrimination, efficiency, and visual analyses. Results: Test accuracy varied non-monotonically from 95.93% (B0) to 96.95% (B1); B7 achieved 96.73%. B1 had the highest accuracy and Drusen F1 (0.8780), while B7 had Drusen F1 of 0.8720 and the highest Drusen recall (0.9177). Drusen had the lowest F1 across all variants and contributed 82.2% of the summed squared deviation in class-specific F1; class ranking remained Normal > CNV > DME > Drusen. The OCT accuracy ranking differed from the reported ImageNet hierarchy, where B7 ranked first. The accuracy-to-parameter ratio fell from 19.82 to 1.48 percentage points per million total parameters. The final train-test gap had a weak, non-significant association with test accuracy (r = 0.26, p = 0.53). Conclusions: Larger EfficientNet variants did not consistently improve SD-OCT classification. B1 achieved the highest accuracy and Drusen F1, whereas B7 showed a secondary accuracy recovery at greater model size and CPU latency, indicating task and protocol dependent scaling effects. As cross-partition duplicates have not been independently audited, results are conditional on the supplied split.

AI.tldr: Evaluating EfficientNet-B0 to B7 on four-class SD-OCT retinal disease classification at fixed resolution, the study finds that larger variants do not consistently improve accuracy, and B1 performs best.
AI.motivation: It is unclear whether EfficientNet's natural-image scaling hierarchy transfers to medical transfer learning at fixed resolution for spectral-domain OCT classification.
AI.method: Eight ImageNet-pretrained variants are evaluated at 224x224 on the Kermany dataset, with grayscale images replicated to RGB, frozen-backbone head training followed by partial fine-tuning, and metrics covering classification, discrimination, efficiency and visual analysis.
AI.result: Test accuracy varies non-monotonically from 95.93 percent (B0) to 96.95 percent (B1), with B7 at 96.73 percent; B1 has the highest accuracy and Drusen F1 (0.8780), B7 has the highest Drusen recall (0.9177), Drusen has the lowest F1 for every variant, and the accuracy-to-parameter ratio falls from 19.82 to 1.48 percentage points per million total parameters.
AI.conclusion: Scaling effects depend on task and protocol, so larger EfficientNets are not a reliable choice for SD-OCT classification, and the results hold only conditionally on the supplied split because cross-partition duplicates have not been independently audited.

title: Microdroplet Generator Surrogate Enhancement and Inverse Design Through an Uncertainty-Guided Framework
summary: Microfluidic droplet generation is critical for many applications, yet efficient device design in high-dimensional parameter spaces remains computationally prohibitive due to complex multiphase flow dynamics. This work presents a unified methodology that couples adaptive surrogate enhancement with simulation-driven inverse design. High-fidelity Volume-of-Fluid simulations provide ground-truth data, while neural network ensembles predict flow regimes and droplet diameters. Ensemble-based uncertainty quantification identifies epistemic uncertainty using consensus levels for regime classification and the coefficient of variation for diameter prediction, revealing that uncertainty concentrates near regime transition boundaries where physics is highly sensitive to parameter perturbations. A physics-informed enrichment strategy targets these critical zones and addresses class imbalances by deploying additional targeted simulations and retraining the surrogates forming the ensembles. A framework that integrates Particle Swarm Optimization for constrained inverse design, balancing accuracy with predictive confidence and physical consistency is therefore proposed. Validation on independent test datasets demonstrates that the enriched ensembles achieve higher accuracy, with the fraction of predictions within the 0-3% error range on droplet diameter nearly doubling, and high-error cases (above 10%) dropping substantially. The inverse design procedure reliably identifies physically realizable configurations meeting target droplet sizes. This approach significantly reduces computational costs while ensuring reliable predictions, offering a framework with potential applicability to the optimization of a broad range of microfluidic systems.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an uncertainty-guided framework that combines neural network ensemble surrogates, physics-informed enrichment and Particle Swarm Optimization to make microdroplet generator design both cheaper and more reliable.
AI.motivation: Designing microfluidic droplet generators in high-dimensional parameter spaces is computationally prohibitive because of complex multiphase flow dynamics.
AI.method: Volume-of-Fluid simulations provide ground truth and neural network ensembles predict flow regimes and droplet diameters; uncertainty is measured by ensemble consensus for regime classification and the coefficient of variation for diameter; targeted simulations and retraining enrich the surrogates near regime transition boundaries and correct class imbalance; Particle Swarm Optimization performs constrained inverse design.
AI.result: On independent test datasets the enriched ensembles are more accurate, with the fraction of diameter predictions within 0-3 percent error nearly doubling and high-error cases above 10 percent dropping substantially, and the inverse design reliably finds physically realizable configurations that meet target droplet sizes.
AI.conclusion: The approach significantly reduces computational cost while keeping predictions reliable, and it may apply to the optimization of a broad range of microfluidic systems.

title: ArcRAG: Agentic Compositional Retrieval over Knowledge Graphs
summary: Graph-based retrieval-augmented generation (GraphRAG) answers questions by retrieving over a knowledge graph built from a corpus. Yet retrieval strategies are designed around the structure their own construction pipeline produces, and whether they survive a change of construction is rarely tested. We study this cross-construction portability: whether one retrieval procedure, with no construction-specific schema, relation names, or retuning, stays effective when the graph is built differently. We introduce ArcRAG, which induces a query-local graph interface at inference time (the node labels, relation descriptors, and property keys reachable from the entities a question names), plans multi-hop traversals against it, and executes and repairs them as Cypher. We build each of the MuSiQue, HotpotQA, and TriviaQA corpora as a schema-guided graph (typed nodes, a closed relation set, source provenance) and as an open-information-extraction graph (untyped nodes, free-text relations), with the retriever's configuration fixed across them. We compare against a construction-agnostic Direct-Cypher agent, ablate each stage across retry and pass budgets on both graph families, and compare with results reported for prior GraphRAG systems, most of which design retrieval together with their own graph construction. Across the two constructions, we find that retrieval need not be co-designed with the graph: query-time interface induction keeps a construction-agnostic retriever effective when the construction changes, although construction still shapes absolute accuracy.

AI.tldr: ArcRAG is a GraphRAG retriever that induces a query-local graph interface at inference time and plans and repairs Cypher traversals, and it remains effective when the knowledge graph is built differently.
AI.motivation: GraphRAG retrieval strategies are designed around the structure their own construction pipeline produces, and whether they survive a change of construction is rarely tested.
AI.method: With no construction-specific schema, relation names or retuning, the retriever derives the node labels, relation descriptors and property keys reachable from the entities a question names, plans multi-hop traversals against them, and executes and repairs them as Cypher.
AI.result: On MuSiQue, HotpotQA and TriviaQA, each built as a schema-guided graph and as an open-information-extraction graph with a fixed configuration, the method is compared with a construction-agnostic Direct-Cypher agent, with stages ablated across retry and pass budgets; the abstract reports no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Query-time interface induction keeps a construction-agnostic retriever effective when the construction changes, so retrieval need not be co-designed with the graph, although construction still shapes absolute accuracy.

title: Model Merging Does Not Require Uniform LoRA Ranks
summary: Model merging combines separately fine-tuned experts into a single model without retraining. Standard practice trains every expert at the same LoRA rank, which couples the rank choice across experts even though each domain has its own best rank. We show this coupling is a property of the merge method, not of merging. We train 36 experts on three domains (mathematics, instruction following, multilingual) at four ranks and three model scales, then merge with six methods at uniform ranks and at each domain's own best rank. Giving experts different ranks costs averaging and utility-based selection nothing, and gains them up to 1.8 pp of multi-domain accuracy, while the conflict-resolution methods are inconsistent and can lose up to 4 pp. The split has a simple cause. Merging keeps only a fixed share of the pooled spectral components, and methods that choose them by size discard many that would have reduced loss. They also tend to discard the same expert: the instruction adapter has the smallest singular values, so it is dropped almost entirely and IFEval falls by 16 to 25 pp. Choosing components by their effect on loss instead keeps all three experts, and leaves accuracy nearly flat across an 8$\times$ rank range (0.7 pp, against 6.7 pp for TIES at 4B scale). Rank can therefore be chosen per expert whenever the merge operator does not select by magnitude.

AI.tldr: Experts trained at different LoRA ranks can be merged without loss, and the apparent need for a uniform rank is a property of the merge method, which keeps components by magnitude rather than by their effect on loss.
AI.motivation: Standard practice trains every expert at the same LoRA rank, which couples the rank choice across experts even though each domain has its own best rank.
AI.method: Thirty-six experts are trained on mathematics, instruction following and multilingual domains at four ranks and three model scales, then merged with six methods at uniform ranks and at each domain's best rank, and the authors contrast size-based component selection with selection by effect on loss.
AI.result: Per-expert ranks cost averaging and utility-based selection nothing and gain up to 1.8 pp of multi-domain accuracy, while conflict-resolution methods are inconsistent and can lose up to 4 pp; size-based selection drops the instruction adapter and lowers IFEval by 16 to 25 pp, whereas loss-based selection keeps all three experts and holds accuracy nearly flat across an 8x rank range (0.7 pp against 6.7 pp for TIES at 4B scale).
AI.conclusion: Rank can be chosen per expert whenever the merge operator does not select components by magnitude.

title: NaijaFacts: A Framework for Disentangling Language from Knowledge in Facts about Nigeria
summary: Multilingual benchmarks for African languages mostly translate generic questions into local languages, measuring linguistic competence but not whether models know facts about Africa. We introduce \naija, a benchmark of factual and statistical questions about Nigeria, authored by native speakers and grounded in authoritative official statistics, with every question available in English, Nigerian Pidgin, \yoruba, Igbo, and Hausa. Answering similar questions for the UK and US yields a country by language matrix that disentangles a language effect (the model knows the fact but degrades in a low-resource language) from a knowledge effect (the fact is absent in every language). Across eight frontier and Nigeria-adapted models, the knowledge effect dominates: English-query accuracy is 49--50\% for the US/UK but 20\% for Nigeria. The language effect is smaller and tracks web representation, degrading from English to \yoruba{} (9 points on Nigeria, up to 24 on US/UK questions). We find scale does not help: the strongest models reach 66--79\% on the UK and the US but none exceed 31\% on Nigerian statistics. Extending to all 54 African countries with our best performing frontier model shows the same profile continent-wide, 96\% on culture and 98\% on politics against 26\% on statistics, so the gap is not specific to Nigeria.

AI.tldr: NaijaFacts is a benchmark of factual and statistical questions about Nigeria in five languages, and it shows that models' weakness on African facts comes mainly from missing knowledge rather than from the low-resource language itself.
AI.motivation: Multilingual benchmarks for African languages mostly translate generic questions, which measures linguistic competence but not whether models know facts about Africa.
AI.method: Native-speaker-authored questions grounded in authoritative official statistics are asked in English, Nigerian Pidgin, Yoruba, Igbo and Hausa; the same design is applied to the UK and US, giving a country-by-language matrix that separates a language effect from a knowledge effect; eight frontier and Nigeria-adapted models are evaluated, and the best frontier model is extended to all 54 African countries.
AI.result: English-query accuracy is 49 to 50 percent for the US and UK but 20 percent for Nigeria, and no model exceeds 31 percent on Nigerian statistics although the strongest reach 66 to 79 percent on UK and US questions; the language effect degrades from English to Yoruba by 9 points on Nigeria and up to 24 points on US and UK questions; across the continent the best model scores 96 percent on culture and 98 percent on politics against 26 percent on statistics.
AI.conclusion: The knowledge effect dominates and scale does not close it, so the gap reflects missing fact coverage rather than something specific to Nigeria, while the language effect tracks web representation.

title: EmoReward: Self-Evolving Reward Calibration for Emotional Video Generation RL
summary: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has advanced generative model post-training in verifiable domains such as code and mathematics, but evaluating video quality, especially emotional expression, often depends on subjective aesthetics and has no uniquely correct target. Existing approaches typically rely on fixed rewards for visual quality, motion quality, and text alignment that poorly capture emotional intent and can invite reward hacking, while RLHF is difficult to scale and subject to individual aesthetic differences that complicate the calibration of facial, body motion, and chromatic cues across narrative contexts. We introduce EmoReward, a new self-evolving training mechanism that distills evidence reliability from reward traces collected during an actual training run to adaptively guide multi-reward weight allocation in subsequent training by determining which emotional evidence to trust and how much to weight it. EmoReward first plans specific grounding cues from the emotional prompt to guide evaluation, then uses heterogeneous signal primitives to score the generated video during the act stage. Reflective Reward Gating calibrates their contributions through instance-level gates for phase, face confidence, conflict, and subtlety, then renormalizes weights over the active set to produce the sample's fused reward. RewardMemory then estimates each primitive's reliability from rollout scores and outcomes within each emotional regime in the finished training run, then fixes bounded multipliers that calibrate fusion weights in the next training run without updating reward models. Experiments on HunyuanVideo 1.5 show improvements across multiple RL algorithms and compare EmoReward with other agentic reward methods under SAGE-GRPO. Ablations and transfer experiments on SD 3.5 and FLUX further support adaptive reward calibration for visual generation.

AI.tldr: EmoReward is a self-evolving reward calibration mechanism for GRPO-based reinforcement learning of emotional video generation, which reweights multiple rewards using reliability estimated from the previous training run.
AI.motivation: Fixed rewards for visual quality, motion and text alignment capture emotional intent poorly and invite reward hacking, while RLHF is hard to scale and sensitive to individual aesthetic differences.
AI.method: Emotional grounding cues are planned from the prompt and heterogeneous signal primitives score the generated video; Reflective Reward Gating applies instance-level gates for phase, face confidence, conflict and subtlety and renormalizes the active weights into a fused reward; RewardMemory estimates each primitive's reliability from one finished training run and fixes bounded multipliers for the next run without updating reward models.
AI.result: Improvements are shown across multiple RL algorithms on HunyuanVideo 1.5, with comparisons against other agentic reward methods under SAGE-GRPO, and ablations and transfer experiments on SD 3.5 and FLUX further support adaptive reward calibration for visual generation; the abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Calibrating rewards by the reliability of their evidence improves RL for emotional video generation, and the authors argue the approach also suits visual generation more broadly.

title: IDSISA: Influence-Distilled Sharded Training for Efficient Machine Unlearning
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
summary: Machine unlearning removes the influence of specific training examples to comply with privacy regulations. Full retraining gives strong guarantees but is computationally prohibitive at scale; approximate methods are efficient but lack formal guarantees. SISA (Sharded, Isolated, Sliced, and Aggregated training) achieves certified deletion through data sharding and independent retraining, but random partitioning scatters forget requests across most shards, and isolated retraining degrades utility. We introduce IDSISA (Influence-Distilled SISA), which uses influence functions to concentrate forget-prone samples into few shards and distillation from unaffected shards to recover utility lost to isolation. The deletion guarantee inherited from SISA's retraining step remains exact and requires no probabilistic qualification; the distillation-based utility recovery is a separately quantified, empirically bounded approximation ($\epsilon_{\text{cert}} \leq 0.015$ in expectation).
