Understanding legislative hearings at a deeper level is a major step in analyzing the work and power relationships within democratic bodies. In this work, we present a novel end-to-end pipeline for parsing rhetorical structures from legislative committee hearings with the goal of improving legislative discourse analysis and democratic accountability. We also propose a rhetorical structure grammar and find that 55.21% of California state bill discussions in our dataset can be parsed with this grammar. We evaluate our pipeline with two utterance section classifiers on a random subset of over 2,000 annotated utterances corresponding to 100 hearings. We find that a logistic regression-based classifier with grammar-based output masking and utterance tag smoothing outperforms more complex models, achieving an F1 score of 52.8% against our ground truth discourse section labels.

AI.tldr: Presents an end-to-end pipeline that parses rhetorical structures from California legislative committee hearings, with a grammar covering 55.21% of the bill discussions in the dataset. A logistic regression classifier with grammar-based output masking and utterance tag smoothing reaches an F1 of 52.8% on discourse section labels and outperforms more complex models.
AI.motivation: Legislative hearings have their own recognizable structure and logic, and analyzing them beyond their transcripts is a step toward understanding work and power relationships in democratic bodies and improving accountability.
AI.method: Proposes a rhetorical structure grammar and an end-to-end parsing pipeline, and evaluates two utterance section classifiers on a random subset of over 2,000 annotated utterances from 100 hearings.
AI.result: 55.21% of California state bill discussions can be parsed with the grammar. Logistic regression with grammar-based output masking and utterance tag smoothing achieves an F1 of 52.8% against ground-truth discourse section labels and outperforms more complex models.
AI.conclusion: Simple classifiers combined with grammar-based constraints can outperform more complex models for legislative discourse parsing, though the F1 of 52.8% leaves substantial room for improvement.

title: VAR-Q: Tuning-free KV Cache Quantization for Visual Autoregressive Image and Video Generation
comment: A preliminary version of this work was presented at the ICCV 2025 BiVision Workshop
summary: Visual autoregressive generation spans two dominant paradigms: next-scale prediction for images and video, and next-frame prediction for video. Both decode block-by-block rather than token-by-token, yielding KV caches whose statistics diverge from those of language models. At scale, KV memory exceeds the weights and limits large-scale deployment caused by a large amount of visual tokens. Our analysis of these caches reveals three findings. First, a small set of massive-value channels carries the functional load: ablating these outlier channels collapses generation, whereas ablating a matched set of inlier channels leaves quality intact. Second, the outliers organize along two axes, feature and block, with magnitudes persistent within each cell and shifting across cells. Third, this structure arises from two independent mechanisms: projection bias and RoPE-induced scattering. Guided by these findings, we propose VAR-Q, a tuning-free KV-cache quantization framework that groups along the same two axes. The generation loop provides block boundaries for free, removing the need for outlier detection or calibration. Paired with bit-packing kernels for runtime memory reduction, VAR-Q delivers low-bit quantization across nine models spanning both paradigms, cutting KV memory by up to 78.5% with negligible quality degradation and enabling 6x larger inference batches.

AI.tldr: Proposes VAR-Q, a tuning-free KV-cache quantization framework for visual autoregressive image and video generation that groups quantization along feature and block axes, cutting KV memory by up to 78.5% with negligible quality degradation across nine models. It also enables 6x larger inference batches.
AI.motivation: In visual autoregressive generation the KV memory exceeds the model weights and limits large-scale deployment because of the large number of visual tokens, and these caches have statistics that differ from those of language models.
AI.method: Ablation and analysis show that a small set of massive-value channels carries the functional load, that outliers organize along feature and block axes, and that this structure comes from projection bias and RoPE-induced scattering; VAR-Q groups along these two axes, uses the generation loop's block boundaries instead of outlier detection or calibration, and pairs with bit-packing kernels.
AI.result: Low-bit quantization across nine models spanning next-scale and next-frame paradigms cuts KV memory by up to 78.5% with negligible quality degradation and enables 6x larger inference batches. Ablating the outlier channels collapses generation, while ablating a matched set of inlier channels leaves quality intact.
AI.conclusion: The cache structure of visual autoregressive models supports tuning-free low-bit quantization, which makes large-scale deployment more practical.

title: A Unified Framework for Training-Dataset Aggregation and Exact Machine Unlearning via Gibbs Probability Measures
comment: Submitted to the IEEE Transaction on Information Theory
summary: In this paper, three operations on Gibbs probability measures are studied: renormalization, normalized log-linear combination, and nesting. The resulting measures are shown to be Gibbs probability measures with explicit expressions for their objective functions, reference measures, and regularization factors. These measures are further characterized as unique solutions to optimization problems involving linear combinations of the original objective functions, subject to either relative entropy regularization or relative entropy constraints. When the reference measures are probability measures, geometric interpretations of these three operations are established involving Pythagorean identities and exponential geodesics.A central result is the equivalence between nesting and normalized log-linear combinations of Gibbs probability measures. These results are then applied to supervised machine learning with Gibbs algorithms, which are represented by Gibbs probability measures. In this context, either through nesting or log-linear combinations, Gibbs algorithms trained on local datasets are used to form new Gibbs algorithms trained upon the aggregation of all local training datasets. Interestingly, the parameters of such operations, determine the weights of each training data point on the aggregated dataset. %Operations on local Gibbs probability measures are shown to control the contributions of training data. This observation is leveraged for achieving: (a) exact machine unlearning in centralized, decentralized, and federated learning systems; and (b) centralized-equivalent performance, in the sense of producing algorithms trained on the aggregation of all local datasets in decentralized and federated learning .

AI.tldr: Studies three operations on Gibbs probability measures (renormalization, normalized log-linear combination and nesting) and shows that nesting equals normalized log-linear combination. Applied to Gibbs learning algorithms, these operations are claimed to give exact machine unlearning and centralized-equivalent training in decentralized and federated settings.
AI.motivation: Gibbs algorithms trained on local datasets need principled ways to combine them into an algorithm trained on the aggregated data, and to remove the influence of individual training points exactly.
AI.method: Shows that the resulting measures are Gibbs measures with explicit objective functions, reference measures and regularization factors, characterizes them as unique solutions to optimization problems under relative entropy regularization or constraints, and gives geometric interpretations via Pythagorean identities and exponential geodesics when the reference measures are probability measures.
AI.result: The abstract reports theoretical results only: explicit expressions, uniqueness characterizations, and the fact that the operation parameters set each training point's weight in the aggregated dataset. The authors claim this enables exact unlearning in centralized, decentralized and federated systems and centralized-equivalent performance in decentralized and federated learning.
AI.conclusion: Operations on Gibbs measures give a unified framework for aggregating training datasets and unlearning them, with exact unlearning and centralized-equivalent performance as the claimed consequences.

title: Near-Minimax Sample Complexity for Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning under Generative Models
summary: In multi-objective reinforcement learning, preferences may be specified only after data collection, requiring one dataset to support a continuum of reward trade-offs. We study finite discounted Markov decision processes with unknown transitions, $S$ states, $A$ actions, and $m$ known reward functions taking values in $[0,1]$, given access to a generative model. The learner must provide an $\varepsilon$-optimal policy for every convex combination of these rewards without further sampling, with a guarantee that holds simultaneously over all preferences and initial states. Writing $H=(1-\gamma)^{-1}$, we establish the constant-confidence minimax sample complexity $\widetilde\Theta\!\left( \frac{SAH^3}{\varepsilon^2}\min\{S,\log(em)\} \right)$, where the suppressed factors are logarithmic in $S,A,H,\varepsilon^{-1}$ and the dependence on $m$ is explicit. Thus, up to these logarithmic factors, the worst-case statistical cost of supporting all preferences grows logarithmically with the number of objectives and saturates at the number of states. The upper bound uses uniform state--action sampling and empirical planning, with reward rounding in the logarithmic-objective regime. Its analysis chains optimal-value increments over covers of the reward hull. A one-sided Bellman variance bound controls signed value differences under a second transition kernel, preserving the $H^3\varepsilon^{-2}$ dependence. A complementary uniform guarantee for all bounded rewards yields the state-dimension saturation. We establish lower bounds matching up to logarithmic factors through a rare-exit construction with subset rewards and action encoding. These bounds apply to adaptive simulator queries and arbitrary randomized history-dependent output policies, while the upper bounds are attained by deterministic stationary policies.

AI.tldr: Establishes a near-minimax sample complexity, of order SAH^3 over epsilon^2 times min{S, log(em)} up to logarithmic factors, for finding epsilon-optimal policies simultaneously for every convex combination of m rewards under a generative model, where H is the effective horizon, 1 over one minus the discount factor. The cost of supporting all preferences therefore grows only logarithmically in the number of objectives and saturates at the number of states.
AI.motivation: In multi-objective reinforcement learning, preferences may be specified only after data collection, so one dataset must support a continuum of reward trade-offs, and the worst-case statistical cost of doing so was not established.
AI.method: The upper bound uses uniform state-action sampling and empirical planning with reward rounding in the logarithmic-objective regime, chaining optimal-value increments over covers of the reward hull and using a one-sided Bellman variance bound; a uniform guarantee for all bounded rewards yields the state-dimension saturation; the lower bounds come from a rare-exit construction with subset rewards and action encoding.
AI.result: The constant-confidence minimax sample complexity matches the lower bounds up to logarithmic factors and holds for adaptive simulator queries and arbitrary randomized history-dependent output policies, while the upper bounds are attained by deterministic stationary policies.
AI.conclusion: Supporting all preferences costs only logarithmically more in the number of objectives and saturates at the number of states in the worst case, so preference changes after data collection need no additional sampling.

title: Generative Modeling for Cascading Extremes via Autoregressive Transformers
summary: Extreme events often occur sequentially, from earthquake-tsunami cascades to successive extreme losses in financial markets. We introduce an extremal token representation that encodes multivariate observations as a categorical sequence. A quiet token records the absence of threshold exceedances; otherwise, the token identifies the exceeding component with the largest marginal probability-scale score. The representation is invariant to componentwise strictly increasing transformations. It preserves the identity and temporal ordering of dominant exceedances but discards their magnitudes and the identities of nondominant simultaneous exceedances. A decoder-only transformer estimates the history-dependent next-token kernel on this representation, and recursive sampling generates future token sequences from the induced joint predictive law. We amortize our generative model by pretraining across simulated process families with varying parameters and dependence persistence. Next-token predictions are evaluated against exact conditional probabilities for held-out categorical processes and particle filter references for heavy-tailed vector autoregressive processes. Applied to ten-second returns for five semiconductor stocks, the pretrained model supports zero-shot transfer, while a few epochs of adaptation improve agreement between observed and generated token frequencies and transition patterns. These results support task-specific tokenization and simulation-based pretraining for modeling which dimensions dominate multivariate extremes.

AI.tldr: Introduces an extremal token representation that encodes multivariate observations as categorical sequences, and a decoder-only transformer that generates future token sequences of cascading extremes. Pretraining across simulated process families supports zero-shot transfer to semiconductor stock returns, and a few epochs of adaptation improve agreement with observed token frequencies and transition patterns.
AI.motivation: Extreme events often occur in sequence, as in earthquake-tsunami cascades or successive extreme losses in financial markets, and modeling which dimensions dominate multivariate extremes requires a representation that keeps their order.
AI.method: A quiet token records the absence of threshold exceedances; otherwise the token identifies the exceeding component with the largest marginal probability-scale score. The representation is invariant to componentwise strictly increasing transformations. A decoder-only transformer estimates the history-dependent next-token kernel after pretraining across simulated process families, and recursive sampling generates future sequences.
AI.result: Next-token predictions are compared with exact conditional probabilities for held-out categorical processes and with particle filter references for heavy-tailed vector autoregressive processes. Applied to ten-second returns for five semiconductor stocks, the pretrained model transfers zero-shot, and a few epochs of adaptation improve agreement between observed and generated token frequencies and transition patterns. The representation keeps the identity and order of dominant exceedances but discards their magnitudes and nondominant simultaneous exceedances.
AI.conclusion: Task-specific tokenization and simulation-based pretraining are supported as ways to model which dimensions dominate multivariate extremes.

title: Risk-Sensitive Non-Parametric and Kernel Bandits
summary: We study non-parametric bandits in which arms are evaluated using Cumulative Prospect Theory (CPT) rather than expected reward. We consider continuous action spaces with arm-dependent noise and propose Non-Parametric CPT Bandits ($\mathtt{NPCB}$), an optimistic algorithm that decouples mean estimation from CPT-based decision-making. We prove CPT regret of order $\widetilde{\mathcal O}\bigl(\sqrt{T\,\dim_E(\mathcal F,T^{-2})\,\log N(\mathcal F,T^{-2},\|\cdot\|_\infty)}\bigr)$, where $\dim_E$ is the Eluder dimension of the function class $\mathcal F$, $T$ is the time horizon, and $N$ is its covering number in the sup norm. This matches the order-wise regret of classical non-parametric bandits, showing that CPT risk sensitivity incurs no additional order-wise regret cost. We extend $\mathtt{NPCB}$ to unknown noise CDFs, retaining the known-CDF mean-learning term and adding a CDF-learning cost governed by a distributional Eluder dimension. We also study Kernel-CPT bandits and obtain information-gain-based regret bounds for a broad range of kernels, matching the corresponding risk-neutral kernel rates up to logarithmic factors.

AI.tldr: Studies non-parametric bandits whose arms are scored by Cumulative Prospect Theory instead of expected reward, and shows that CPT risk sensitivity adds no order-wise regret over classical non-parametric bandits.
AI.motivation: Classical bandit analysis assumes risk-neutral expected reward, so the regret cost of CPT risk sensitivity with continuous actions and arm-dependent noise was not characterised.
AI.method: The optimistic algorithm NPCB decouples mean estimation from CPT-based decision making; it is extended to unknown noise CDFs with a distributional Eluder dimension term, and Kernel-CPT bandits are analysed through information-gain bounds.
AI.result: The CPT regret is of order sqrt(T dim_E log N) up to logarithmic factors, matching the classical non-parametric rate; for Kernel-CPT bounds match the risk-neutral kernel rates up to logarithmic factors.
AI.conclusion: CPT risk sensitivity does not change the order of regret, so risk-aware bandit decisions carry no order-wise extra statistical cost.

title: TestBED: An Open-Source Toolkit for Bayesian Experimental Design
summary: Bayesian experimental design (BED) is a principled framework for intelligent data acquisition with applications across a wide range of scientific and industrial domains. However, the development and adoption of BED remains hindered by a lack of standardised software and benchmarks. Existing methods are typically implemented in bespoke codebases and evaluated on a small subset of tasks, making methods difficult to apply, compare, or extend. To address this, we present TestBED, a general-purpose, open-source toolkit for Bayesian experimental design. TestBED decomposes the BED process into modular, reusable components spanning tasks, objectives, training mechanisms, policy architectures, and evaluation procedures, together with scalable implementations of core primitives such as expected information gain estimators. We provide a wide range of these components, which can be freely composed, allowing existing methods to be reproduced within a common framework, while also enabling previously unexplored configurations and new methodologies to be easily implemented and evaluated. Using TestBED, we further conduct a large-scale benchmark of contemporary BED methods, including controlled studies of under-appreciated but surprisingly critical methodological choices, such as the importance of time embeddings in design policy architectures. By providing a modular, extensible software foundation and a reproducible benchmarking suite, we hope that TestBED will accelerate methodological research in BED and lower the barrier to its real-world application.

AI.tldr: Presents TestBED, an open-source modular toolkit for Bayesian experimental design (BED), and uses it for a large benchmark of contemporary BED methods.
AI.motivation: BED methods are usually implemented in bespoke codebases and tested on few tasks, which makes them hard to apply, compare or extend.
AI.method: The BED process is decomposed into reusable components for tasks, objectives, training mechanisms, policy architectures and evaluation, together with scalable expected information gain estimators that can be freely composed.
AI.result: A large-scale benchmark with controlled studies shows, for example, that time embeddings in design policy architectures are surprisingly critical.
AI.conclusion: The modular toolkit and reproducible benchmark aim to accelerate BED methodology research and lower the barrier to real-world use.

title: Alignment Myopia in Generative AI
summary: Current generative AI alignment relies on a myopic paradigm that prioritizes immediate conversational satisfaction. By relying on short-horizon feedback, this approach ignores the profound, longitudinal externalities of persistent human-AI interaction, which can lead to adverse outcomes such as cognitive atrophy, social erosion, and diminished human agency. To address this, we propose a paradigm shift toward long-horizon alignment that accounts for how AI reshapes human experience over time. To this end, we map the tensions between near-term utility and long-term costs of AI use across four facets of human well-being to reveal outcomes that current reward models fail to capture. Ultimately, we advocate for moving beyond simple preference optimization toward alignment strategies that actively foster long-term human well-being by navigating these complex temporal scales.

AI.tldr: Argues that generative AI alignment should shift from short-horizon conversational satisfaction to long-horizon alignment that accounts for how AI use shapes human well-being over time.
AI.motivation: Current alignment relies on immediate feedback, which ignores longitudinal externalities such as cognitive atrophy, social erosion and diminished human agency that reward models fail to capture.
AI.method: The paper maps the tensions between near-term utility and long-term costs of AI use across four facets of human well-being.
AI.result: No quantitative results are reported; the mapping reveals outcomes that current reward models do not capture.
AI.conclusion: Alignment should move beyond simple preference optimisation toward strategies that actively foster long-term human well-being.

title: Tight Lower Bounds under Matched High-Order Hölder Smoothness and Uniform Convexity
summary:
In this paper, we provide tight lower bounds for minimizing high-order Hölder-smooth and uniformly convex functions when their orders match. Specifically, we consider functions whose $p^{th}$-order derivatives are Hölder continuous with degree $
u$ and parameter $H$, and that are uniformly convex with degree $q$ and parameter $\sigma$. When these orders match, namely, $q = p + 
u$, we show that any deterministic algorithm with access to derivatives up to order $p$ requires $\Omega\left(\left( rac{H}{\sigma}ight)^{ rac{2}{3(p+
u)-2}}\log rac{\Delta_0}{\epsilon}ight)$ oracle calls to reduce an initial optimality gap of $\Delta_0$ to $\epsilon$. This matches the corresponding upper bound and establishes a higher-order uniformly convex counterpart to Nesterov's classical first-order lower bound for strongly convex functions. Rather than directly generalizing Nesterov's classical quadratic-chain construction, we develop a multiscale phase-wise construction that preserves previous oracle responses while maintaining global Hölder smoothness and uniform convexity. Our result resolves the matched case left open by existing lower bounds for the two asymmetric regimes.

AI.tldr: Gives tight lower bounds for minimising functions that are Hölder smooth of order p with degree nu and uniformly convex of degree q when q = p + nu, matching the known upper bound.
AI.motivation: Existing lower bounds cover only the two asymmetric regimes, leaving the matched-order case open, and Nesterov-style quadratic-chain constructions do not directly extend to it.
AI.method: A multiscale phase-wise construction is developed that preserves previous oracle responses while keeping global Hölder smoothness and uniform convexity.
AI.result: Any deterministic algorithm using derivatives up to order p needs Omega((H/sigma)^(2/(3(p+nu)-2)) log(Delta_0/epsilon)) oracle calls to reduce the gap from Delta_0 to epsilon.
AI.conclusion: The result resolves the matched case and gives a higher-order uniformly convex counterpart to Nesterov's first-order lower bound for strongly convex functions.

title: Support Vector Machines Directly Minimise KL Divergence
summary: Support vector machines (SVMs) are fundamentally grounded in geometric margin maximisation and currently lack a mainstream probabilistic interpretation. This keeps them theoretically isolated from probabilistic machine learning models that are naturally comparable and combinable. In this paper, we bridge this gap by proving that the dual objectives of both support vector classification and support vector regression are exact, constrained Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence minimisation tasks between two Gaussian measures. We further show that this same divergence formulation recovers the exact objective function for kernel ridge regression when domain constraints are removed and $L^2$ regularisation is applied. By demonstrating that SVM duals directly minimise relative entropy, our results provide a unified information-theoretic model for standard kernel machines and lay the foundation for unifying broader kernel-based algorithms under probability theory.

AI.tldr: Proves that the dual objectives of support vector classification and support vector regression are exact constrained KL divergence minimisation problems between two Gaussian measures.
AI.motivation: SVMs are grounded in geometric margin maximisation and lack a mainstream probabilistic interpretation, which isolates them from probabilistic machine learning models.
AI.method: The dual objectives are cast as constrained KL divergence minimisation between Gaussian measures; removing domain constraints and applying L2 regularisation recovers the kernel ridge regression objective.
AI.result: Kernel ridge regression is recovered exactly when domain constraints are removed and L2 regularisation is applied.
AI.conclusion: SVM duals minimise relative entropy, giving a unified information-theoretic model for standard kernel machines and a basis for unifying kernel-based algorithms under probability theory.

title: Transport along Local Annealing Paths: Wasserstein Geometry and Multimodal Sampling
summary: Variational approaches to learning transport maps for multimodal sampling can suffer from mode collapse. One way to mitigate this problem is to learn transport along a prescribed path of intermediate distributions defined by geometric annealing. We show that annealing can take a substantial detour in Wasserstein space: when mass moves between modes, the path can be much longer than the distance between its endpoints. We further link path geometry to transport learning, showing that long annealing paths can slow population optimization, while sufficiently regular paths permit rapid convergence. Motivated by these findings, we propose componentwise annealed transport (CAT) to reduce the need for mass transfer between modes. Starting from a mode-informed mixture reference, CAT constructs an exact mixture decomposition of the target and learns separate transport maps along componentwise annealing paths. We estimate the component weights separately and show that these estimates remain consistent even when the learned flows are inexact. We also develop adaptive annealing schedules guided by transport effort. Experiments on multimodal synthetic distributions and Bayesian inference problems demonstrate improvements in transport learning and sampling efficiency.

AI.tldr: Shows that geometric annealing paths can detour heavily in Wasserstein space, and proposes componentwise annealed transport (CAT), which learns separate transport maps along per-component paths for multimodal sampling.
AI.motivation: Variational transport for multimodal sampling can suffer mode collapse, and annealing paths can be much longer than the distance between endpoints when mass must move between modes, slowing population optimisation.
AI.method: CAT starts from a mode-informed mixture reference, builds an exact mixture decomposition of the target, learns transport maps along componentwise annealing paths, estimates component weights separately, and uses adaptive schedules guided by transport effort.
AI.result: Experiments on multimodal synthetic distributions and Bayesian inference problems show improved transport learning and sampling efficiency; the weight estimates remain consistent even when the learned flows are inexact.
AI.conclusion: Reducing the need for mass transfer between modes through componentwise paths improves transport-based multimodal sampling.

title: Exact signal recovery from generative priors with sigmoid output activation
summary: We show exact signal recovery in generative compressed sensing for feedforward neural networks with piecewise-linear activations and a final sigmoid activation, with no assumption of expansivity. Consider a ReLU network of depth $d$ with a sigmoid final activation, whose input layer, of dimension $k$, is the narrowest, and let $K$ be the geometric mean of the widths of its layers. We show that, with high probability, all signals of the range whose entries lie in $[\delta, 1 - \delta]$ are uniformly recovered from $m \gtrsim k(d \log(K/k) + \log(1+\log(1/\delta)))$ measurements.

AI.tldr: Proves exact signal recovery in generative compressed sensing for feedforward networks with piecewise-linear activations and a final sigmoid activation, without an expansivity assumption.
AI.motivation: Recovery guarantees for generative compressed sensing are sought here without requiring the network to be expansive.
AI.method: The analysis covers ReLU-type feedforward networks of depth d with a sigmoid output, where the input layer of dimension k is the narrowest and K is the geometric mean of the layer widths.
AI.result: With high probability, all signals in the range with entries in [delta, 1 - delta] are uniformly recovered from m of order k(d log(K/k) + log(1 + log(1/delta))) measurements.
AI.conclusion: Exact recovery holds under a sigmoid output with a measurement count that scales with input dimension, depth and the log width ratio, with no expansivity needed.

title: Balance-Guided Forest for Causal Effect Estimation
summary: Covariate balancing is widely used for estimating causal effects in observational studies. A central challenge is determining which covariate features should be balanced. Forest-kernel balancing provides a data-driven way to learn informative balancing features. Existing forest-kernel balancing methods first learn a tree-based representation and then construct balancing weights. However, this procedure creates a mismatch, as limited tree capacity may be spent on features that are already well represented. We propose Balance-Guided Forest (BGF), which uses the current balancing weights to guide subsequent tree construction. BGF grows trees using a novel splitting score that combines residual imbalance with an outcome contrast, favoring splits that separate outcome-relevant regions where imbalance remains. This couples representation learning with covariate balancing rather than treating balancing as a downstream step. We establish an oracle-type bound that links the iterative construction to weighting error and causal bias. Simulations exhibit improvements in causal estimation relative to existing forest-kernel approaches. Real-data applications illustrate the practical behavior of BGF across observational studies.

AI.tldr: Proposes Balance-Guided Forest (BGF), which uses current balancing weights to guide tree construction so that representation learning and covariate balancing are coupled for causal effect estimation.
AI.motivation: Existing forest-kernel balancing learns a tree representation first and builds weights afterwards, so limited tree capacity may be spent on features that are already well represented.
AI.method: Trees are grown with a splitting score that combines residual imbalance with an outcome contrast, favouring splits that separate outcome-relevant regions where imbalance remains; an oracle-type bound links the iterative construction to weighting error and causal bias.
AI.result: Simulations show improved causal estimation relative to existing forest-kernel approaches, and real-data applications illustrate its practical behaviour across observational studies.
AI.conclusion: Coupling tree learning with balancing, rather than treating balancing as a downstream step, is a practical route to better causal estimates from observational data.

title: Discovering like a scientist: Literature-informed dimensionless learning for physical closure of data-driven equations
summary: Data-driven methods can recover compact equations, yet the physical dependence of their coefficients across operating conditions often remains unresolved. Dimensionless groups can explain this variation, but selecting relevant groups from the many dimensionally admissible combinations remains challenging. Here, we introduce a knowledge-guided framework for dimensionless learning, called {\pi}-former. It learns patterns of variable association and exponent assignment from a corpus of 1,288 established dimensionless groups. Under exact dimensional constraints, the model proposes interpretable basic groups whose combinations are optimized against observations. Across seven physical problems, the framework identifies predictive dimensionless coordinates within seconds. Integration with equation discovery further expresses condition-dependent coefficients through these coordinates, recovering established physical scalings in multi-condition simulations. Applied to experimental measurements of evaporation-driven wetting, the framework discovers dimensionless coordinates and uses them to construct a unified trajectory equation. The resulting model generalizes to held-out conditions across liquids and initial volumes, outperforming existing empirical models. These results establish dimensionless learning as a transferable bridge between accumulated scientific knowledge and data-driven equation discovery, enabling artificial intelligence to uncover physically meaningful laws from observations.

AI.tldr: Introduces pi-former, a knowledge-guided dimensionless learning framework that proposes physically admissible dimensionless groups from data and uses them to build interpretable equations.
AI.motivation: Data-driven equations often leave the dependence of their coefficients on operating conditions unresolved, and choosing relevant dimensionless groups from many admissible combinations is hard.
AI.method: The model learns variable-association and exponent patterns from a corpus of 1,288 established dimensionless groups, proposes basic groups under exact dimensional constraints, optimises their combinations against observations, and integrates with equation discovery to express condition-dependent coefficients.
AI.result: Across seven physical problems it identifies predictive dimensionless coordinates within seconds; in multi-condition simulations it recovers established physical scalings; on evaporation-driven wetting measurements it yields a unified trajectory equation that generalises to held-out liquids and initial volumes and outperforms existing empirical models.
AI.conclusion: Dimensionless learning can serve as a transferable bridge between accumulated scientific knowledge and data-driven equation discovery.

title: Towards the Query Complexity of Sampling under Strong Log-Concavity and Log-Sobolev Inequalities
summary: We study the query complexity of sampling from smooth distributions on $\mathbb R^d$ using first-order oracles. For $d$-dimensional strongly log-concave targets with condition number $\kappa=2$, we prove that any randomized sampler requires $\exp({\Omega(\log^{1/3} d)})$ queries even from a constant warm start. This rules out polylogarithmic dimension dependence and strictly separates strongly log-concave sampling from Gaussian sampling. For targets with $L$-smooth potentials satisfying an $\alpha$-log-Sobolev inequality with $\kappa= L/\alpha$, we prove an $\Omega(\kappa)$ query lower bound for $d\gtrsim\log^2\kappa$. This shows that log-Sobolev sampling is strictly harder than strongly log-concave sampling. Our proofs construct instance-dependent tests that target samples typically pass but outputs of algorithms making few queries typically fail. For strongly log-concave targets, we embed a sequence of hidden Gaussian into high-degree tensor polynomial with smooth gates, forcing any algorithm to uncover the layers sequentially. The log-Sobolev construction hides a constant fraction of the target mass in angular caps while controlling the log-Sobolev constant via delicate estimates.

AI.tldr: Proves query lower bounds for sampling from smooth distributions with first-order oracles: exponential in log^(1/3) d for strongly log-concave targets with condition number 2, and Omega(kappa) under a log-Sobolev inequality for d >= log^2 kappa.
AI.motivation: The query complexity of strongly log-concave sampling was not known to rule out polylogarithmic dimension dependence, and log-Sobolev sampling had not been strictly separated from strongly log-concave sampling.
AI.method: The constructions use instance-dependent tests that target samples typically pass and outputs of few-query algorithms typically fail; for strongly log-concave targets a sequence of hidden Gaussians is embedded in high-degree tensor polynomials with smooth gates, and the log-Sobolev construction hides a constant fraction of the mass in angular caps.
AI.result: Any randomised sampler needs exp(Omega(log^(1/3) d)) queries, even from a constant warm start, for kappa = 2; for log-Sobolev targets an Omega(kappa) query lower bound holds when d >= log^2 kappa.
AI.conclusion: Strongly log-concave sampling is strictly separated from Gaussian sampling, and log-Sobolev sampling is strictly harder than strongly log-concave sampling.

title: A low-rank decoder bottleneck bounds reliability in foundation-model perturbation prediction
summary: Foundation-model predictors of perturbation response are evaluated primarily by aggregate accuracy. Using their predictions to prioritize experiments requires assessing each prediction's reliability. We audit the state-transition (ST) decoder used in STATE across three encoders (SE-600M, scGPT, and Tahoe-x1) and four cell lines under CRISPRi. The decoder's first attention layer has a low-rank output. Projecting this output onto 4-32 fixed directions estimated from training activations preserves mean per-perturbation Pearson delta correlation (PDC). This low-rank attention bottleneck bounds the decoder's reliability by distance to training responses: PDC declines as the cosine distance from a perturbation's observed response to its nearest training response increases. We propose predicted-NN-distance, the cosine distance from a predicted response to its nearest training response, as a per-prediction confidence score. The score has a mean absolute Spearman correlation of 0.81 with PDC, close to the 0.88 obtained with the observed response. Thresholds calibrated on this score transfer across encoders and cell lines, and the score remains predictive of PDC for drug perturbations.

AI.tldr: Shows that the state-transition decoder used in STATE has a low-rank attention bottleneck that bounds prediction reliability by distance to training responses, and proposes predicted-NN-distance as a per-prediction confidence score.
AI.motivation: Foundation-model perturbation predictors are judged mainly by aggregate accuracy, but prioritising experiments requires assessing the reliability of each individual prediction.
AI.method: The decoder is audited across three encoders (SE-600M, scGPT, Tahoe-x1) and four CRISPRi cell lines by projecting the output of its first attention layer onto 4-32 fixed directions; the score is the cosine distance from a predicted response to its nearest training response.
AI.result: Projection onto 4-32 directions preserves mean per-perturbation Pearson delta correlation (PDC), and PDC declines as the distance to the nearest training response grows; the predicted-NN-distance score has mean absolute Spearman correlation 0.81 with PDC, against 0.88 for the observed response, and calibrated thresholds transfer across encoders and cell lines and remain predictive for drug perturbations.
AI.conclusion: Decoder reliability is bounded by proximity to training data, and the predicted-distance score gives a practical confidence measure for prioritising experiments.

title: Prior-data fitted networks for variable selection
summary: Prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) have become state-of-the-art for tabular prediction but remain underexplored in other areas of statistics. In this work, we present two PFNs for Bayesian variable selection: CD-PFN identifies conditional dependencies, and PC-PFN identifies parents and children in a causal graph. Both networks estimate posterior inclusion probabilities (PIPs) without posterior samples or data-specific modeling. In semi-synthetic and real data experiments, CD-PFN and PC-PFN often outperform existing methods, demonstrating the value of PFNs for variable selection and their potential in statistics more broadly. Open-source software is available.

AI.tldr: Presents CD-PFN and PC-PFN, two prior-data fitted networks that estimate posterior inclusion probabilities for Bayesian variable selection, identifying conditional dependencies and causal parents and children respectively.
AI.motivation: Prior-data fitted networks are state of the art for tabular prediction but remain underexplored for variable selection in statistics.
AI.method: Both networks estimate posterior inclusion probabilities without posterior samples or data-specific modelling; CD-PFN targets conditional dependencies, and PC-PFN targets parents and children in a causal graph.
AI.result: In semi-synthetic and real data experiments the two networks often outperform existing methods.
AI.conclusion: The results show the value of prior-data fitted networks for variable selection and their potential more broadly in statistics; open-source software is available.

title: Offline Learning of Reserve Prices from Censored Bids
comment: 87 pages, 12 figures, 25 tables. Authors listed alphabetically
summary: We study how a seller can learn a reserve price for a second-price auction from censored historical bid data. Because values below past reserves are unobserved, even unlimited data may not reveal which reserve earns the most revenue. Under a monotone hazard rate (MHR) assumption, we characterize exactly when an optimal reserve is identified, even though the value distribution may not be: either revenue has not yet begun to fall at the lowest historical reserve, so the best reserve lies among the observed bids, or the censored fraction is as large as MHR allows, which pins down the entire distribution. When identification fails, we derive the reserve that minimizes worst-case revenue regret over distributions consistent with the data, and prove that this unique minimax reserve and its regret depend on just two observable quantities: the censored fraction and the hazard just above the lowest historical reserve. With $N$ historical bidders, the optimal reserve is learned with expected worst-case regret $O(N^{-1/2})$ when it lies among the observed bids, and $O(N^{-1})$ from the censored count alone when the censored fraction is as large as MHR allows and the optimum lies at or below the lowest reserve. In the nonidentifiable regime, plugging estimates of the two quantities into the minimax reserve gives expected worst-case regret within $O(N^{-2/5})$ of the population minimum under local density smoothness, with a matching minimax lower bound on a smooth class. Beyond MHR, we solve the minimax problem for regular and unrestricted distributions and prove an $O(N^{-2/5})$ learning bound in the regular nonidentifiable regime, given known bounds on the boundary parameters. Experiments on synthetic and eBay data show gains from exploiting MHR and the benefits of the robust rule when parametric models are misspecified.

AI.tldr: Characterises when the optimal reserve price for a second-price auction can be learned from censored historical bids under a monotone hazard rate (MHR) assumption, and derives a minimax reserve when it cannot.
AI.motivation: Values below past reserves are unobserved, so even unlimited historical data may not reveal which reserve earns the most revenue.
AI.method: Under the MHR assumption the paper characterises identification; when identification fails it derives the reserve minimising worst-case revenue regret, which depends only on the censored fraction and the hazard just above the lowest historical reserve, and plugs in estimates of these two quantities.
AI.result: With N historical bidders the optimal reserve is learned with expected worst-case regret O(N^(-1/2)) when it lies among the observed bids, and with O(N^(-1)) from the censored count alone in the other case; in the nonidentifiable regime the plug-in reserve is within O(N^(-2/5)) of the population minimum, with a matching minimax lower bound on a smooth class; experiments on synthetic and eBay data show gains from MHR and robustness when parametric models are misspecified.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting the MHR assumption and the robust minimax rule improves reserve pricing from censored bids, especially when parametric models may be wrong.

title: Separation Is a Riesz Energy: How Many Environments Does ICA Need?
summary: Can independent components be recovered when all of them are Gaussian? Yes, if their variances change across environments; but how many environments, and how many samples as the number of components $d$ grows? We answer both for the joint diagonalization of $K$ covariances. Each component has a signature, its variances across the environments. Separating component $j$ costs the Riesz 2-energy $E_j$ of this signature, a sum, over the other components, of inverse pairwise Fisher informations. For Gaussian sources no estimator in $O(d)$ beats $cE_j/(n+E_j)$ at any $n$ and $d$, and above an explicit sample size a spectral estimator attains $E_j/n$ up to a constant, for every mixing and without the signatures (given a lower bound on the pairwise information). Since signatures live in $K-1$ dimensions, the rate obeys a dimension law: $d^2/n$, $d\log d/n$ and $d/n$ for $K=2$, $3$ and $K\ge4$ well-spread environments. What counts is the dimension the signatures span, not their number, and $\log d$ well-designed environments make $d\log d$ samples suffice. Projecting the covariances onto one linear combination pays $d^2/n$ at first order instead. In simulations up to $d=1000$ the predictions hold and joint diagonalization with $K\ge4$ attains the rate once $n/d$ is in the hundreds; on task fMRI the energy says which components are hard to separate.

AI.tldr: Shows that separating Gaussian components for ICA by joint diagonalisation of K covariances has a sample complexity governed by the Riesz 2-energy of the components' environment signatures, giving a dimension law of d^2/n, d log d/n or d/n depending on K.
AI.motivation: It was unclear how many environments and how many samples Gaussian ICA needs as the number of components d grows.
AI.method: Each component's signature is its variance profile across the environments, and separating it costs the Riesz 2-energy of that signature; the paper shows no O(d) estimator beats the energy-based rate for Gaussian sources and that a spectral estimator attains it above an explicit sample size.
AI.result: The rate is d^2/n for K = 2, d log d/n for K = 3 and d/n for K >= 4 well-spread environments, and log d well-designed environments make d log d samples suffice; simulations up to d = 1000 agree, and on task fMRI the energy identifies which components are hard to separate.
AI.conclusion: The dimension spanned by the signatures, not their number, sets the sample requirement, and projecting the covariances onto one linear combination instead costs d^2/n.

title: Flexible Intensities Matter: A Comprehensive Re-evaluation of Hawkes Processes and Neural Temporal Point Processes
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 36 pages, 3 figures, 25 tables. Code: this https URL (paper reproduction on branch neurips2026)
summary: Temporal point processes (TPPs) are the canonical framework for event sequence data, with applications spanning seismology, social media, and electronic health records. Recently, neural TPPs have been reported to substantially outperform classical TPPs, such as Hawkes processes, but these comparisons pitted flexible neural models against Hawkes processes in their most restricted form, and did not consider large-scale medical data. Here, we revisit this comparison through a systematic evaluation of Poisson and Hawkes processes of increasing flexibility against neural TPPs, on five established benchmark datasets and on two large-scale medical evaluation tasks derived from UK Biobank disease histories and MIMIC-IV ICU records, under autoregressive next-event prediction. First, the previously reported gap between Hawkes processes and neural TPPs largely disappears once Hawkes processes are equipped with flexible, learnable baselines and kernels. Second, the flexibility of the intensity parametrization also limits prior neural TPPs: a Transformer with a spline-based intensity head outperforms previous intensity-based neural TPPs and is on par with the intensity-free model. Decomposing the log-likelihood into a time term $\log p(t)$ and a type term $\log p(d \mid t)$, we find that this flexibility advantage lies almost entirely in the time density: more flexibility does not improve the type term. On these benchmarks, the gains of neural TPPs thus lie mostly in modeling when events occur, not which. Third, our results underscore the value of complex datasets for evaluating TPPs: only on the MIMIC-IV ICU records do neural TPPs retain an advantage in the type term. Our results inform both future method development and model choice. We release our framework, TorchPP, as an open-source package with consistent implementations of classical and neural TPPs.

AI.tldr: Re-evaluates Hawkes processes and neural temporal point processes (TPPs), finding that flexible Hawkes baselines and kernels close most of the reported gap, and that neural TPP gains lie mainly in modelling when events occur.
AI.motivation: Earlier reports that neural TPPs substantially outperform Hawkes processes compared flexible neural models against the most restricted Hawkes form and did not consider large-scale medical data.
AI.method: Poisson and Hawkes processes of increasing flexibility are evaluated against neural TPPs on five benchmark datasets and two medical tasks from UK Biobank and MIMIC-IV under autoregressive next-event prediction, with the log-likelihood split into a time term and a type term; a Transformer with a spline intensity head is also tested, and the TorchPP package is released.
AI.result: The gap largely disappears once Hawkes processes have flexible learnable baselines and kernels; a Transformer with a spline intensity head beats earlier intensity-based neural TPPs and matches the intensity-free model; the flexibility advantage lies almost entirely in the time density, and only on MIMIC-IV do neural TPPs keep an advantage in the type term.
AI.conclusion: On these benchmarks the gains of neural TPPs lie mostly in when events occur rather than which, and complex datasets are valuable for evaluating TPPs.

title: Understanding the Out-of-Distribution Generalization of Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in LLMs
summary: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning substantially improves Large Language Models (LLMs), yet its out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization mechanism remains theoretically underexplored. We study CoT as compositional OOD generalization: the target task lacks complete reasoning trajectories or direct input-output pairs, while training provides only in-distribution (ID) atomic step data. We show that CoT generalizes by repeatedly applying a shared single-step predictor to compose reusable ID transitions. Theoretically, let $T$ denote the number of reasoning steps in the target task, $n$ the number of training samples per sub-task, and $k$ the number of output tokens per step; then the OOD task risk is controlled by the sum of the ID sub-task risks, scaled by a coefficient of order $\mathcal{O}(k)$ that is independent of $T$, although the summed risk itself may still grow with $T$. A Rademacher-complexity analysis further shows that the estimation term is of order $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{T/n})$, rather than linear in $T$, due to predictor sharing under a uniform capacity control on the shared class. For autoregressive Next-Token Prediction, the final-task risk is bounded by the best-in-class step-level risk scaled by the same coefficient of order $\mathcal{O}(k)$, plus an estimation term of order $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\big(k\sqrt{T/n}\big)$. A parity-coupled construction further shows that, for the sub-task empirical risk minimizer, the expected final-task risk is at least the best in-class risk plus $\Omega(\sqrt{T/n})$ when $T\le n$. Experiments on Atom-Task and GSM8K support the theory: CoT enables short-to-long and compositional generalization, while explicit state tracking is crucial. Our code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Analyses chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning as compositional out-of-distribution generalisation, showing that CoT repeatedly applies a shared single-step predictor and bounding the target risk by the summed in-distribution sub-task risks.
AI.motivation: The mechanism by which CoT generalises out of distribution is theoretically underexplored, especially when the target task lacks full reasoning trajectories or direct input-output pairs.
AI.method: Training provides only in-distribution atomic step data; the OOD task risk is controlled by the sum of the in-distribution sub-task risks with a coefficient of order O(k), a Rademacher-complexity analysis gives an O(sqrt(T/n)) estimation term from predictor sharing, and autoregressive next-token prediction bounds and a parity-coupled lower bound are derived.
AI.result: For autoregressive next-token prediction the final-task risk is bounded by the best in-class step-level risk scaled by O(k), plus an estimation term of order O~(k sqrt(T/n)); experiments on Atom-Task and GSM8K show short-to-long and compositional generalisation, and explicit state tracking is crucial.
AI.conclusion: CoT enables short-to-long and compositional generalisation through a shared step predictor, and explicit state tracking matters for it.

title: Finite-width shift of the edge of chaos in deep neural networks
comment: 9 pages, 5 figures, 1 table; Supplemental Material (28 pages, 9 figures, 12 tables) included. Code: this https URL
summary: Deep neural networks train best when they are initialised at the edge of chaos, the critical line in the plane of weight and bias variances on which the distance between two inputs neither grows nor shrinks with depth. The line is known for infinitely wide networks; at finite width it moves, and how it moves has been disputed. We treat the logarithm of the distance between two inputs through a network of width $N$ as a random walk and compute its drift and variance to order $1/N$. The edge of chaos moves to a larger weight variance, by $\Delta\sigma_w^2=-a_1/(N\,\partial_{\sigma_w^2}\ln\chi_1)$, about $8/N$ for $\tanh$ networks at a bias variance of $0.05$, confirmed by simulations of the exact finite-width recursion. The shift describes a typical network; the average over many networks is dominated by rare networks in which the distance grows, and its critical point moves the other way, which explains why calculations and simulations have disagreed. Backpropagation follows the same random walk, so the shift applies to gradients unchanged. Along the edge of chaos, the information about the similarity of two inputs is constant until the compression over the depth exceeds about one nat, which fixes where to sit on the line. The results give an initialisation rule, Crinit, that places a network on its finite-width edge of chaos without a search. On MNIST and Fashion-MNIST at width $64$ it is more accurate than the standard rules at their usual settings, by a small margin in shallow networks and a large one in deep networks, where most standard rules fail; it trains in fewer steps, and it matches or beats the standard rules with a tuned gain.

AI.tldr: Shows that at finite width the edge of chaos moves to larger weight variance, by about 8/N for tanh networks, and introduces Crinit, an initialisation rule that places a network on its finite-width edge of chaos without a search.
AI.motivation: The edge of chaos is known for infinitely wide networks, and how it shifts at finite width has been disputed, with calculations and simulations disagreeing.
AI.method: The logarithm of the distance between two inputs is treated as a random walk whose drift and variance are computed to order 1/N; the shift is confirmed against simulations of the exact finite-width recursion, and backpropagation is shown to follow the same walk.
AI.result: The shift describes a typical network, while the average over many networks is dominated by rare networks in which the distance grows, so its critical point moves the other way; on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST at width 64, Crinit beats the standard rules at their usual settings, by a small margin in shallow networks and a large one in deep networks, and trains in fewer steps.
AI.conclusion: The finite-width edge of chaos yields a search-free initialisation rule, and its advantage is largest for deep networks, where most standard rules fail.

title: Regularization vs. Convolution in Kernel-Based Hypothesis Testing
summary: The maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) test is a popular nonparametric test on general domains. Two lines of work have studied its optimality through structurally different approaches. The first, a convolution approach on $\mathbb{R}^d$, uses translation-invariant kernels with a shrinking bandwidth and is minimax optimal over Sobolev balls under $L^2$-separation; the second, a regularization approach on general measurable spaces, uses spectral regularization of the kernel covariance operator and is minimax optimal over Hellinger- and $\chi^2$-separated alternatives. In this paper, we study the regularization approach over Sobolev balls under $L^2$-separation, which reveals the connection between the two approaches. We show that, with a translation-invariant kernel on $\mathbb{R}^d$, both are ways of meeting a single condition on the kernel's spectral density: the spectral regularized discrepancy captures the $L^2$-separation $\Delta$ of a Sobolev alternative of smoothness $s$ as soon as the regularization parameter $\lambda$ is below the spectral density on frequencies up to $\Delta^{-1/(2s)}$. A kernel with a shrinking bandwidth $h$ meets this condition with $\lambda \asymp h^d$, and under this coupling the constant regularizer, which gives the MMD test itself, attains the Sobolev minimax rate. This explains, from a spectral perspective, the need for a shrinking bandwidth in the convolution approach. With a non-constant spectral regularizer, our analysis requires the bandwidth to shrink only when the spectral density decays faster than any polynomial, as for the Gaussian kernel. Thus, for Matérn and Laplace kernels, a fixed bandwidth with $\lambda \to 0$ attains the Sobolev minimax rate. Finally, an adaptive test over a grid of bandwidths and regularization parameters is minimax optimal, up to a $\log\log$ factor, over both classes without prior knowledge of the smoothness.

AI.tldr: Connects the spectral regularisation and convolution approaches to kernel MMD testing over Sobolev balls, showing that the analysis needs a shrinking bandwidth only for kernels whose spectral density decays faster than any polynomial.
AI.motivation: Two lines of work study MMD test optimality separately, one by convolution with a shrinking bandwidth on R^d and one by spectral regularisation on general spaces, and their relationship was unclear.
AI.method: Under L2 separation over Sobolev balls, the spectral regularised discrepancy is analysed for translation-invariant kernels on R^d, with the regularisation parameter coupled to the bandwidth h as lambda of order h^d; an adaptive test over a grid of bandwidths and regularisation parameters is also studied.
AI.result: The constant regulariser, which gives the MMD test itself, attains the Sobolev minimax rate under this coupling; for Matérn and Laplace kernels a fixed bandwidth with lambda tending to zero attains the minimax rate; the adaptive test is minimax optimal up to a log log factor over both classes without prior knowledge of smoothness.
AI.conclusion: The spectral view explains why a shrinking bandwidth appears in the convolution approach, and it is not needed for kernels with polynomially decaying spectral densities such as Matérn and Laplace.

title: Fundamental Limits of Coherent Imaging in The Presence of Atmospheric Turbulence
summary: We study the fundamental limits of jointly estimating the signal amplitude and the atmospheric phase distortion in complex-valued multi-look coherent imaging, where the measurements are corrupted by multiplicative speckle and additive Gaussian noise, all looks share a known Gaussian sensing matrix, and both parameters belong to structured classes. By analyzing a constrained maximum likelihood estimator, we establish an upper bound on the joint minimax risk that holds uniformly over the admissible parameter classes, while oracle reductions and Fano-type arguments yield worst-case lower bounds over the admissible parameter classes. These results quantify the effects of structural complexity, signal and measurement dimensions, the number of looks, and the noise level, and establish matching minimax rates in several settings, with a remaining gap for phase estimation at low noise when the measurement dimension exceeds the signal dimension. We also construct a two-stage estimator for signal recovery under arbitrary diagonal sign distortions in the real-valued analogue. Under additional conditions, it recovers the signs up to a global sign with high probability and yields a uniform signal risk bound without a distortion-complexity term. Numerical experiments illustrate the dependence of the joint, signal, and phase errors on the model parameters and provide further support for the theoretical analysis.

AI.tldr: Derives minimax rates for jointly estimating signal amplitude and atmospheric phase distortion in multi-look coherent imaging with speckle and Gaussian noise, and gives a two-stage estimator for sign distortions in the real-valued analogue.
AI.motivation: Coherent imaging through atmospheric turbulence needs known limits for recovering amplitude and phase jointly under structured parameter classes.
AI.method: A constrained maximum likelihood estimator gives an upper bound on the joint minimax risk; oracle reductions and Fano-type arguments give worst-case lower bounds; a two-stage estimator recovers diagonal sign distortions under additional conditions.
AI.result: Matching minimax rates are established in several settings, with a remaining gap for phase estimation at low noise when the measurement dimension exceeds the signal dimension; under additional conditions the sign estimator recovers the signs up to a global sign with high probability and yields a uniform signal risk bound without a distortion-complexity term; numerical experiments support the theory.
AI.conclusion: The rates quantify the effects of structural complexity, dimensions, number of looks and noise level, and the two-stage estimator avoids a distortion-complexity term under additional conditions.

title: Regression with Many Generated Controls
summary: We consider linear regression when some covariates are endogenous, a variable sufficient to control for endogeneity exists but is latent, and the practitioner can generate many proxies for the latent control. For instance, one could cheaply but imperfectly impute the latent control using different AI/ML methods, each generating a different proxy. There are several options the practitioner might consider in this scenario: including all proxies or factors computed from the proxies as controls, instrumental variables estimation, and some nonlinear variants thereof. We use a transparent model to derive the implicit estimand each approach targets, determine when these estimands recover the parameter of interest, and provide some practical recommendations. We show that with a sufficiently rich set of generated controls, practitioners can consistently estimate the parameter of interest without relying on validation data.

AI.tldr: Studies linear regression with endogenous covariates when a latent control is imperfectly proxied by many generated controls, deriving the estimand each approach targets and showing that consistent estimation without validation data is possible with a sufficiently rich set of proxies.
AI.motivation: Practitioners can cheaply generate many imperfect proxies for a latent control with AI or ML methods, but it is unclear which approach recovers the parameter of interest.
AI.method: The paper compares including all proxies or factors computed from them, instrumental variables estimation, and nonlinear variants, using a transparent model to derive the implicit estimand each approach targets.
AI.result: With a sufficiently rich set of generated controls the parameter of interest can be consistently estimated without validation data, and the paper determines when each approach's estimand recovers it.
AI.conclusion: Practical recommendations are given for choosing among proxy-based approaches when the latent control is only imperfectly observed.

title: DS@GT ARC at CheckThat! 2026: A Verdict-Anchored Pipeline for Generating Fact-Checking Articles
comment: CLEF 2026 Working Notes, 21 - 24 September 2026, Jena, Germany
summary: Misinformation spreads faster than professional fact-checkers can manually verify it and write articles explaining their verdicts. This creates a need to automate the production of fact-checking articles. This paper details work done by the DS@GT ARC team for CLEF 2026 CheckThat! Lab Task 3 Fact-Checking Article Generation. We seek to generate a full fact-checking article from a claim, its original verdict, and a set of scraped source documents. Our team built a four-stage pipeline that cleans noisy evidence, retrieves and clusters relevant sources, generates the article by conditioning \texttt{Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct} on the original fact-checker verdict, and recovers inline citations through deterministic post-processing. We achieved a mean score of 0.428 and ranked 3rd out of 9 teams for the CLEF 2026 CheckThat! Lab Task 3, compared to a baseline mean score of 0.272. Our code is available on GitHub at this https URL.

AI.tldr: A four-stage pipeline cleans noisy evidence, retrieves and clusters sources, generates fact-checking articles by conditioning Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on the original verdict, and recovers inline citations by deterministic post-processing. It reached a mean score of 0.428, ranking 3rd of 9 teams on CLEF 2026 CheckThat! Task 3 against a baseline of 0.272.
AI.motivation: Misinformation spreads faster than professional fact-checkers can verify claims and write articles explaining their verdicts, so producing fact-checking articles needs automation.
AI.method: A full article is generated from a claim, its original verdict and scraped source documents, through a four-stage pipeline: evidence cleaning, source retrieval and clustering, verdict-conditioned generation with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and deterministic recovery of inline citations.
AI.result: Mean score of 0.428 on CLEF 2026 CheckThat! Lab Task 3, ranking 3rd out of 9 teams, compared with a baseline mean score of 0.272.
AI.conclusion: Conditioning generation on the original verdict and adding deterministic citation recovery gives a competitive automated fact-checking article generator, and the code is released on GitHub.

title: CCDWIKI: Decoupling Case Formulation from Response Generation in Longitudinal CBT Dialogue
summary: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) demands more than empathic validation, requiring instead a structured formulation of the interplay among situations, automatic thoughts, emotions, and behaviors. Therapists formalize this interplay through a Cognitive Conceptualization Diagram, where maintaining longitudinal coherence necessitates continuous evidential adjudication to separate tentative hypotheses from established findings. Current dialogue systems track conversational history via retrieval or static profiles but lack the representational capacity to encode epistemic status. Consequently, provisional interpretations are often prematurely reified as established facts, inadvertently biasing downstream interventions. Addressing this limitation, CCDWiki is introduced as a plug-and-play advisor conceptualizing longitudinal therapy as evidence-grounded hypothesis adjudication. The approach encodes each clinical hypothesis as a mutable entry bound to corroborating and contradicting evidence. Across sessions, accumulating data strengthens supported entries, preserves provisional ones, and retracts contradicted assumptions. The resulting formulation distills into concise guidance for unmodified therapeutic language models. Experiments demonstrate substantial improvements in both conceptualization and intervention quality without requiring backbone retraining.

AI.tldr: CCDWiki is a plug-and-play advisor for longitudinal CBT dialogue that encodes each clinical hypothesis as a mutable entry bound to supporting and contradicting evidence. Across sessions it strengthens supported entries, keeps provisional ones and retracts contradicted ones, then distills the result into guidance for unmodified therapeutic language models.
AI.motivation: Current dialogue systems track history through retrieval or static profiles and cannot encode epistemic status, so provisional interpretations get treated as established facts and bias later interventions.
AI.method: Longitudinal therapy is treated as evidence-grounded hypothesis adjudication: each clinical hypothesis is a mutable entry linked to corroborating and contradicting evidence, and the resulting formulation is condensed into concise guidance for the language model.
AI.result: Experiments show substantial improvements in both conceptualization quality and intervention quality, without retraining the backbone model.
AI.conclusion: Separating case formulation from response generation, with explicit tracking of evidential status, improves CBT dialogue while leaving the underlying therapeutic language model unchanged.

title: Human-like cross-language generalisation in deep neural speaker embeddings and its acoustic foundations
comment: This manuscript has been accepted for presentation at Interspeech 2026. Code is available at this https URL. The archived release is available on Zenodo at this https URL
summary: Generalisability is a central question for deep neural networks, including the cross-language generalisation of speaker embeddings. This study examined whether deep neural speaker embeddings generalise across languages and how such generalisation relates to human perception and acoustic structure. Using Cantonese--English bilingual speech presented in within- and cross-language conditions, we derived similarity from 18 state-of-the-art models and compared it with human ratings and acoustic features using linear mixed models and representational similarity analysis. Embeddings exhibited cross-language generalisation that broadly paralleled human behaviour, reflecting accurate identity discrimination and sensitivity to language switching. This generalisation relied on largely shared acoustic cues with language-sensitive weighting, mirroring human patterns. Together, these findings provide converging evidence for human--machine alignment in cross-language voice similarity processing.

AI.tldr: Deep neural speaker embeddings generalise across languages in a way that broadly parallels human perception, relying on largely shared acoustic cues with language-sensitive weighting. The study compares 18 state-of-the-art models with human ratings and acoustic features on Cantonese-English bilingual speech.
AI.motivation: Cross-language generalisation is a central open question for deep neural networks, and it is unclear whether speaker embeddings generalise across languages in a manner comparable to human listeners.
AI.method: Similarity is derived from 18 state-of-the-art speaker embedding models on Cantonese-English bilingual speech in within-language and cross-language conditions, then compared with human ratings and acoustic features using linear mixed models and representational similarity analysis.
AI.result: Embeddings show accurate identity discrimination and sensitivity to language switching, broadly paralleling human behaviour. This generalisation rests on largely shared acoustic cues with language-sensitive weighting, mirroring human patterns.
AI.conclusion: The findings give converging evidence for human-machine alignment in cross-language voice similarity processing.

title: Same Origin, Different Verdicts: Text Production Conditions Confound Machine-Generated Text Detection in Russian
comment: 65 pages, 6 figures, 24 tables. English translation of the frozen Russian manuscript; the Russian text is the source of record and is available with all data, code and run manifests at this https URL (v1.0.1)
summary: Automated detection of machine-generated text is applied where the verdict carries a cost for the author, yet origin is a property of the production process, not an observable property of the text. The conditions under which a text is produced push it in the same direction in which a generative model is presumed to push it. This study measures the contribution of these conditions while origin is held fixed. The Russian-language corpus of 1882 documents comprises a machine part, generated by four generation channels (each backed by its own model family) across 45 tasks in three task modes, and an archival human part annotated for source regimentation level before the texts were read. The primary contrast is computed within the machine corpus: both halves of a pair are generated by the same model for the same task and differ only in task wording. Machine-likeness is measured by four operationalisations: an interpretable index with weights fixed before data collection, a trained classifier, a zero-shot metric on an open model, a judge model. The main result is disagreement between procedures: changing the task mode shifted the scores of all four, but three gave a negative shift, the judge a positive one, and none of the four intervals covers zero. The comparison plan and the specifications of procedures 2-4 were fixed after the result of procedure 1, before procedures 2-4 ran; the disagreement survived correction of a corpus defect and of the nested validation. A baseline on the source identifier alone reaches a median AUROC of 1.0000 on the thirteen group splits where it is defined, and removing emphasis markers flipped a confident machine verdict to human without changing the full text by a single character. The scores are properties of a specific measurement system and corpus: they reflect data collection, repetition, formatting, and preprocessing decisions as well as linguistic style.

AI.tldr: Machine-likeness scores for Russian text shift with the task mode used to produce the text, and the four measurement procedures disagree in direction, so detector verdicts depend on the measurement system and corpus rather than on origin alone. A baseline using only the source identifier reaches a median AUROC of 1.0000 on the group splits where it is defined.
AI.motivation: Machine-generated text detection is used where a verdict is costly to the author, yet origin is a property of the production process rather than of the text, and the conditions of production may push text toward the machine-like direction.
AI.method: On a Russian corpus of 1882 documents (machine texts from four generation channels across 45 tasks in three task modes, plus archival human texts), the task-wording contrast is computed within the machine corpus with origin held fixed. Four operationalisations are compared: a fixed-weight interpretable index, a trained classifier, a zero-shot metric on an open model, and a judge model. The comparison plan was fixed after the result of the first procedure.
AI.result: Changing the task mode shifted all four scores, but three shifted negatively and the judge shifted positively, and none of the four intervals covers zero. The disagreement survived correction of a corpus defect and of the nested validation. Removing emphasis markers flipped a confident machine verdict to human without changing the text by a single character.
AI.conclusion: Detection scores reflect data collection, repetition, formatting and preprocessing decisions as well as linguistic style, so they are properties of a specific measurement system and corpus and cannot be read as evidence of origin.

title: SRRM: A Retrieval-Reconstruction Benchmark for Evaluating Long-Context Memory in Small Language Models
summary: Small Language Models (SLMs) are increasingly deployed on consumer-grade hardware, yet their ability to preserve information across progressively longer contexts remains insufficiently understood. Existing benchmarks primarily evaluate retrieval-oriented tasks, providing limited insight into whether successful retrieval reflects comprehensive long-context memory preservation. To address this limitation, this paper introduces Simple Retrieval-Reconstruction Memory (SRRM), a lightweight and fully reproducible benchmark that jointly evaluates Targeted Retrieval and Global Information Reconstruction. This study also proposes the Memory Preservation Ratio (MPR), a benchmark-level metric that quantifies the relationship between retrieval and reconstruction performance. SRRM was evaluated using a synthetic dataset on three Qwen2.5 models (0.5B, 1.5B, and 3B parameters) across context loads ranging from 10 to 100 factual statements. Experimental results show that reconstruction performance deteriorated substantially faster than retrieval accuracy as contextual information increased, indicating that retrieval alone is insufficient to characterize long-context memory preservation. Among the evaluated models, Qwen2.5-1.5B achieved the highest retrieval accuracy (86.7%), reconstruction performance (45.7%), and MPR (0.53), outperforming the larger Qwen2.5-3B model (72.2%, 18.5%, and 0.26, respectively). These findings demonstrate that increasing parameter count does not necessarily improve long-context memory preservation. Overall, SRRM provides a reproducible and extensible benchmark for systematically evaluating long-context memory while revealing complementary memory behaviors that remain hidden under retrieval-only evaluation frameworks.
