Motivated by this, we propose LibriSpeech-Real-QA, a dataset and a benchmark for real-time speech interaction. We construct different types of real-time question-answer pairs from LibriSpeech to evaluate whether speech LLMs can identify target words in streaming audio. We evaluate several popular real-time commercial models and find that they still tend to respond only after the speech turn has finished. We demonstrate that we can enable a pretrained SLM to perform this task, where we explore several modeling designs and establish a solid baseline for future research.

AI.tldr: A dataset and benchmark for streaming speech question answering, built from LibriSpeech, that tests whether speech LLMs can answer while audio is still arriving. Popular commercial real-time models still tend to respond only after the speech turn has finished, and a pretrained SLM is enabled for the task as a baseline.
AI.motivation: Most speech LLMs process speech offline and respond only after a complete segment, yet many applications need answers based on the audio received so far, and no benchmarks or evaluation protocols exist for real-time speech interaction.
AI.method: Constructs different types of real-time question-answer pairs from LibriSpeech that ask whether models can identify target words in streaming audio. Several popular real-time commercial models are evaluated, and several modeling designs are explored for a pretrained SLM.
AI.result: Popular real-time commercial models still tend to respond only after the speech turn has finished. The authors enable a pretrained SLM to perform the task and establish a solid baseline for future research.
AI.conclusion: Streaming speech question answering remains a gap, and the benchmark and baseline provide a starting point for future work.

title: CRESiST: Self-Enhancing Explorative Policy Learning for Simultaneous Speech Translation
summary: Simultaneous Speech Translation (SimulST) requires balancing translation quality and latency. While Large Language Models (LLMs) excel in offline translation, current LLM-based SimulST systems predominantly rely on prefix-incremental generation. This paradigm suffers from redundant Key-Value cache recomputation and necessitates external Voice Activity Detection to process unbounded streams. To overcome these bottlenecks, we propose an end-to-end interleaved read-write framework built upon an omni-modal LLM. By interleaving speech chunks and text tokens, our architecture achieves full KV cache reuse, natively supporting segmentation-free, infinite-length inference. Furthermore, to learn optimal streaming policies without rigid offline alignments, we introduce a novel Actor-Critic self-enhancement pipeline. An RNN-T Actor dynamically samples read-write trajectories, while an LLM-based Critic evaluates these paths via intrinsic semantic and latency rewards, distilling the optimal policy back to the Actor. Extensive experiments on sentence-level (FLEURS, CoVoST2) and document-level (MuST-C, ACL 60/60) benchmarks demonstrate that our model establishes new state-of-the-art quality-latency Pareto frontiers, substantially outperforming existing cascaded and static-alignment baselines.

AI.tldr: An end-to-end interleaved read-write framework for simultaneous speech translation, built on an omni-modal LLM and trained with an Actor-Critic self-enhancement pipeline. It reports new state-of-the-art quality-latency Pareto frontiers on sentence-level and document-level benchmarks.
AI.motivation: LLM-based SimulST systems rely on prefix-incremental generation, which recomputes the KV cache redundantly and needs external voice activity detection to process unbounded streams, and learning streaming policies without rigid offline alignments is hard.
AI.method: Interleaves speech chunks and text tokens in an omni-modal LLM, which enables full KV cache reuse and segmentation-free inference. An RNN-T Actor samples read-write trajectories, and an LLM-based Critic evaluates them with intrinsic semantic and latency rewards, distilling the optimal policy back to the Actor.
AI.result: On FLEURS and CoVoST2 (sentence-level) and MuST-C and ACL 60/60 (document-level), the model establishes new state-of-the-art quality-latency Pareto frontiers and substantially outperforms cascaded and static-alignment baselines.
AI.conclusion: Interleaved read-write modeling with actor-critic policy learning offers better quality-latency trade-offs without segmentation.

title: Dialect Matters: A Dialect-Aware Baseline for Igala-English Machine Translation
summary: The massive permeability of intelligent systems in every sphere of human activities have greatly enhanced clarity, ease of work, and increased general global understanding which has significantly awaken the use of intelligent systems by all users. Intelligent systems greatly rely on precise dataset/corpus for the correctness of their output. Despite efforts by researchers to address Low-resource language in the Natural Language Processing (NLP), Igala still has zero parallel corpora despite efforts by researchers. We present a dialect-aware baseline for Igala-English machine translation, among first open systems and first with dialectal variation analysis. Our dataset of 1137 sentences (899 training) is first with dialect tags: Idah 459 (40.4%), Ankpa 297 (26.1%), Ibaji 160 (14.1%), Other 187 (16.4%), Ogugu 32 (2.8%). Same English yields 20-60 Igala forms. Mixed-dialect training achieves balanced BLEU 11.66 versus Idah-only model which drops 4.7 BLEU on Ibaji (13.2 on Idah, 8.5 on Ibaji), proving dialect fairness requires mixing. Fine-tuned from Helsinki-NLP/opus-mt-en-mul (78M), epoch ablation shows convergence at 8 epochs and overfitting at 15. BLEU 11.66, chrF 46.69. Analysis shows 899 sentences on log-linear trend consistent with African low-resource literature. This work provides first dialectal impact analysis for Igala and establishes baseline for future work.

AI.tldr: A dialect-aware baseline for Igala-English machine translation, built on a 1,137-sentence corpus with dialect tags. Mixed-dialect training gives a balanced BLEU of 11.66, while an Idah-only model drops 4.7 BLEU on Ibaji.
AI.motivation: Igala has no parallel corpora, and the effect of dialectal variation on machine translation for it had not been analyzed.
AI.method: Builds a 1,137-sentence dataset (899 for training) with dialect tags: Idah 459, Ankpa 297, Ibaji 160, Other 187 and Ogugu 32. Fine-tunes Helsinki-NLP/opus-mt-en-mul (78M) and runs an epoch ablation.
AI.result: Mixed-dialect training achieves a balanced BLEU of 11.66, whereas an Idah-only model scores 13.2 on Idah but 8.5 on Ibaji, a drop of 4.7 BLEU. The model converges at 8 epochs and overfits at 15, with chrF 46.69.
AI.conclusion: Dialect fairness requires mixing dialects in training; the work provides the first dialectal impact analysis for Igala and a baseline for future work.

title: When Do Summaries Become Instructions? Unsupported Policy in LLM Agents' Self-Written Handoff Summaries
comment: 22 pages, 3 figures, 15 tables. Code and data: this https URL
summary: Long-running LLM agents compact their context, replacing most history with a summary. We ask whether handoff summaries state permissions or requirements the record does not support, whether such sentences change what the next instance (the successor) does, and where they come from. Synthetic tool-use tasks carry a ground-truth permission ledger; same-snapshot replay reruns the successor with those whole sentences replaced by neutral filler. Two AI readers, reading only rule-flagged held-out summaries, confirmed unsupported restrictions in 1.2% and 2.4% of all readable summaries from two open-weight models, and unsupported authorizations in 0.1% and 1.3%. For restrictions, a pre-specified replay test was not significant (p = 0.58); a follow-up, planned after it, found a fragile effect (p = 0.027). Neutralizing false approvals cut unauthorized actions from 24 to 7 of 120 held-out runs (post hoc; later set: 17 to 11 of 48). Most development restrictions followed the agent's earlier reasoning that an action needs approval (post hoc). In pre-specified tests, replacing the system prompt's "Some actions need approval." with one saying where requirements come from cut unsupported restrictions from 5.0% to 1.8% of development summaries and, on held-out templates, from 1.8% to 0.3% (both p < 10^-9), while requests for approvals the ledger requires barely changed. Code and data: this https URL

AI.tldr: Studies whether handoff summaries written by long-running LLM agents state permissions or requirements that the record does not support, and whether such sentences change what the successor does. Neutralizing false approvals cut unauthorized actions from 24 to 7 of 120 held-out runs (post hoc).
AI.motivation: Agents compact their context into summaries, and unsupported permission statements in those summaries could change the successor's behavior, yet where such statements come from is unclear.
AI.method: Synthetic tool-use tasks carry a ground-truth permission ledger, and same-snapshot replay reruns the successor with whole sentences replaced by neutral filler. Two AI readers, reading only rule-flagged held-out summaries from two open-weight models, confirm unsupported restrictions and authorizations.
AI.result: Unsupported restrictions are confirmed in 1.2% and 2.4% of all readable summaries and unsupported authorizations in 0.1% and 1.3%. For restrictions a pre-specified replay test was not significant (p = 0.58), and a follow-up found a fragile effect (p = 0.027). Neutralizing false approvals cut unauthorized actions from 24 to 7 of 120 held-out runs (post hoc; later set 17 to 11 of 48). Replacing the system prompt's "Some actions need approval." with a sentence saying where requirements come from cut unsupported restrictions from 5.0% to 1.8% of development summaries and from 1.8% to 0.3% on held-out templates (both p < 10^-9), while requests for required approvals barely changed.
AI.conclusion: Unsupported policy in handoff summaries can change successor behavior, and stating where requirements come from in the system prompt reduces it.

title: Replicability, Reproducibility, and Robustness in Political and Social Science Research with Large Language Models
comment: Chapter 5 of "LLMs in Political and Social Science: Principles and Applications of Transformer Models," Oxford University Press, forthcoming 2027. Data and code: this https URL
summary: This chapter addresses the central reproducibility problem of research with large language models. LLM output is probabilistic and varies across models and versions, which can have significant effects on downstream statistical results. The chapter distinguishes between replicability, reproducibility, and robustness, and proposes a probabilistic standard based on the distribution of results, not identical outputs. It introduces a standardized prompt script, tests within-model variation for encoders and decoders, and develops error-structure analysis to diagnose where models err and whether their errors align. Using three datasets, the chapter shows that measurement choice can reverse the sign of downstream regression coefficients. Existing design-based corrections with gold-labeled subsamples restore validity, but come at the cost of estimate precision. The main contribution of the chapter is a stacked ensemble of open-weight models that improves precision in the correction step while retaining estimate validity.

AI.tldr: A book chapter that proposes a probabilistic standard for replicability, reproducibility and robustness of LLM-based research in political and social science. It shows that measurement choice can reverse the sign of regression coefficients, and proposes a stacked ensemble of open-weight models that improves precision in the correction step while retaining validity.
AI.motivation: LLM output is probabilistic and varies across models and versions, which can significantly change downstream statistical results, so the field needs a standard that goes beyond identical outputs.
AI.method: Distinguishes replicability, reproducibility and robustness, and proposes a probabilistic standard based on the distribution of results. It introduces a standardized prompt script, tests within-model variation for encoders and decoders, and develops error-structure analysis. Three datasets are used, with design-based corrections that rely on gold-labeled subsamples.
AI.result: Measurement choice can reverse the sign of downstream regression coefficients. Existing design-based corrections restore validity but reduce estimate precision. The stacked ensemble of open-weight models improves precision in the correction step while retaining estimate validity.
AI.conclusion: A probabilistic standard and a stacked ensemble of open-weight models can make LLM measurement in social science more reproducible and more precise without losing validity.

title: Ranking Agreement Does Not Reveal Paragraph-Edit Agreement in Two Released Paper Acceptance Predictors
comment: 38 pages including supplementary methods and results; 10 figures and 22 tables
summary: A fast acceptance classifier could select revisions for a slower evaluator. We ask whether agreement on existing papers supports that use. We compare a classifier of word and document features with two released text-only acceptance predictors fine-tuned from the same language model with three billion parameters. For 198 papers from the International Conference on Learning Representations, we compare model rankings of the original papers and of paragraph rewrites screened automatically for unchanged facts, claim strength, and attribution. The classifier ranks original papers closely with one predictor and moderately with the other, but shows no detectable agreement with either on which rewrites raise scores. The tests specified in advance used reduced numerical precision. Rounding error dominated the small score responses. We therefore rescored the released weights in full 32-bit precision as a post hoc check; edit agreement remained near zero. At this precision, when each predictor chooses among five rewrites per paper, its average raw score is under two points out of 100 higher than with random choice. The evidence covers presentation rewrites and two open predictors from one family; transfer to costly evaluators remains untested. Revision selectors should therefore be checked against the intended evaluator on the revisions they rank.

AI.tldr: Two released text-only paper acceptance predictors agree with a classifier on which original papers rank high, but show near-zero agreement on which paragraph rewrites raise their scores. Each predictor's average raw score rises by under two points out of 100 over random choice among five rewrites.
AI.motivation: A fast acceptance classifier could select revisions for a slower evaluator, and the authors ask whether agreement on existing papers supports that use.
AI.method: Compares a classifier of word and document features with two released acceptance predictors fine-tuned from the same 3B-parameter language model, on 198 ICLR papers and automatically screened paragraph rewrites (screened for unchanged facts, claim strength and attribution). The pre-specified tests used reduced numerical precision, and the released weights were rescored in full 32-bit precision as a post hoc check.
AI.result: The classifier ranks original papers closely with one predictor and moderately with the other, but shows no detectable agreement with either on which rewrites raise scores. At 32-bit precision edit agreement remains near zero, and when each predictor chooses among five rewrites per paper its average raw score is under two points out of 100 higher than with random choice. Rounding error dominated the small score responses at reduced precision.
AI.conclusion: Agreement on ranking existing papers does not imply agreement on revisions, so revision selectors should be checked against the intended evaluator on the revisions they rank.

title: Measuring Risk, Not Harm: Detecting Psychological Harm Risk Factors in LLM Conversations
summary: Psychological harms from interactions with large language models cannot be monitored directly because they may emerge over repeated interactions and depend strongly on subjective individual user context. We propose measuring risk, not harm: detecting observable AI behaviors that constitute risk factors for psychological harm at the AI response level and aggregating these signals to support longitudinal monitoring. We operationalize eight such behaviors and construct a synthetic multi-label corpus of 47,062 AI responses and 373,873 response-factor labels, with targeted human annotations for validation and evaluation. We then compare trained embedding-based classifiers, direct LLM judging, and a classifier--judge cascade. All detectors are model-agnostic and operate only on LLM outputs, requiring no access to internal model states. We apply these detectors to several out-of-distribution human-AI conversation data sets from prior research. On held-out human-labeled data, the best cascade achieves macro precision of 0.86, recall of 0.76, and F1 of 0.79. On WildChat, it reduces LLM-judge calls by 97.1\% relative to direct judging. On DelusionEval, risk-factor detections cluster within conversations. Together, our results show that response-level behavioral risk-factor detection can provide a scalable measurement layer for longitudinal psychological-safety monitoring without conflating observable AI behavior with latent user harm.

AI.tldr: Proposes detecting observable AI behaviors that are risk factors for psychological harm, aggregated over conversations for longitudinal monitoring. The best cascade of a trained classifier and an LLM judge reaches macro F1 0.79 on held-out human-labeled data and cuts LLM-judge calls by 97.1% on WildChat.
AI.motivation: Psychological harms from LLM interactions cannot be monitored directly, because they emerge over repeated interactions and depend strongly on subjective user context.
AI.method: Operationalizes eight risk-factor behaviors and builds a synthetic multi-label corpus of 47,062 AI responses and 373,873 response-factor labels, with targeted human annotations for validation. Compares embedding-based classifiers, direct LLM judging and a classifier-judge cascade; all detectors operate only on LLM outputs.
AI.result: On held-out human-labeled data the best cascade achieves macro precision 0.86, recall 0.76 and F1 0.79. On WildChat it reduces LLM-judge calls by 97.1% relative to direct judging. On DelusionEval, risk-factor detections cluster within conversations.
AI.conclusion: Response-level detection of behavioral risk factors can serve as a scalable measurement layer for longitudinal psychological-safety monitoring, without conflating observable AI behavior with latent user harm.

title: LLMs Don't Know What They Know: Benchmarking Temporal Self-Knowledge for Financial Backtesting
summary: Financial backtests of large language models (LLMs) are meaningful only if the model did not already know the outcomes it is asked to predict. Practitioners guard against this by trusting a vendor's stated knowledge cutoff, by asking the model what it knows, or by instructing it to answer as of a past date. To verify whether any of these safeguards can be trusted, we introduce FinDendro, a benchmark of 2,226 dated U.S. facts from 1999 to 2026, covering monthly macroeconomic series, month-end stock prices and Federal Reserve decisions. Each fact yields four prompts: a value question, Recall and Predict questions that pair each candidate value with a claim of knowing or guessing without a declared date, and a Predict question with a historical declared date. Controls for persistence and dominant outcomes keep chance accuracy near 0.27. Results show that for most frontier models, self-reports understate knowledge. GPT-5 answers 76% of controlled facts correctly but claims to know 38%, and answers 61% of the facts it says it does not know. Knowledge claims can persist beyond the measured knowledge boundary, by up to seven quarters, and a declared date removes most of the claims of prior knowledge while leaving accuracy unchanged. Backtests inside a model's training window therefore cannot be certified leak-free by self-report, instruction or stated cutoff. These findings motivate behavioral measurement of temporal knowledge boundaries, and FinDendro provides a benchmark and procedure for selecting backtest periods based on demonstrated factual knowledge.

AI.tldr: FinDendro is a benchmark of 2,226 dated U.S. facts from 1999 to 2026, and it shows that LLM self-reports understate their knowledge, so stated cutoffs and self-reports cannot certify a leak-free backtest. GPT-5 answers 76% of controlled facts correctly but claims to know only 38%.
AI.motivation: Financial backtests of LLMs are meaningful only if the model did not already know the outcomes, yet practitioners rely on vendor cutoffs, self-reports or as-of-date instructions whose trustworthiness is unverified.
AI.method: Builds 2,226 dated facts (monthly macroeconomic series, month-end stock prices and Federal Reserve decisions), each yielding four prompts: a value question, Recall and Predict questions that pair each candidate value with a claim of knowing or guessing, and a Predict question with a historical declared date. Controls for persistence and dominant outcomes keep chance accuracy near 0.27.
AI.result: For most frontier models, self-reports understate knowledge. GPT-5 answers 76% of controlled facts correctly but claims to know 38%, and it answers 61% of the facts it says it does not know. Knowledge claims persist beyond the measured knowledge boundary by up to seven quarters, and a declared date removes most knowledge claims while leaving accuracy unchanged.
AI.conclusion: Backtests inside a model's training window cannot be certified leak-free by self-report, instruction or stated cutoff, so temporal knowledge boundaries need behavioral measurement, and FinDendro provides a procedure for choosing backtest periods based on demonstrated knowledge.

title: SAUCE: Summary Analysis Using Conversation Entailment
comment: Accepted and published to the ACL GEM workshop. Proceedings of the Fifth Workshop on Generation, Evaluation and Metrics (GEM), pages 364-377, San Diego, California, USA. Association for Computational Linguistics
summary: With the growing need for evaluating Large Language Models (LLMs) and their applications to speech, challenges persist in summarizing and evaluating conversations that lack a clear end goal. We introduce SAUCE -- a reference-free, fact-based evaluation pipeline for cross-lingual conversational speech summarization. It measures the accuracy and the fact coverage of a summary through the entailment between conversation and text. We compare SAUCE against several popular summarization metrics and demonstrate the effectiveness of capturing information loss due to transcription and translation error and identifying broken summaries. Crucially, unlike black-box LLM evaluators or dense embedding metrics, SAUCE is inherently explainable: it maps summary scores to discrete, verifiable facts, allowing users to pinpoint exact hallucinations or omissions. We illustrate how this interpretability helps developers systematically profile LLM behaviors and gives end-users an actionable tool to verify summary accuracy in noisy, real-world conditions. Preliminary investigations show SAUCE strongly align with human judgment.

AI.tldr: SAUCE is a reference-free, fact-based pipeline for evaluating cross-lingual conversational speech summaries by checking entailment between the conversation and the summary. It is explainable because it maps scores to discrete, verifiable facts, and preliminary results show strong alignment with human judgment.
AI.motivation: Conversations without a clear end goal are hard to summarize and evaluate, and black-box LLM evaluators or dense embedding metrics do not show which facts are hallucinated or omitted.
AI.method: The pipeline measures summary accuracy and fact coverage through entailment between the conversation and the summary text, scoring against discrete facts, and it is compared with several popular summarization metrics.
AI.result: SAUCE captures information loss caused by transcription and translation errors and identifies broken summaries better than the compared metrics, and preliminary investigations show strong alignment with human judgment.
AI.conclusion: The interpretability of SAUCE lets developers profile LLM behaviour systematically and gives end users a practical tool to verify summary accuracy in noisy, real-world conditions.

title: LooM: Loop-Invariant Memory for Causal Encoder-Decoder Language Models
summary: Looped Transformers increase effective depth by re-executing shared layers, but three limitations hinder their adoption: memory grows with the loop count, compute can only be adjusted in whole-block steps, and the loop count is hard to change after training. We propose LooM (Loop-invariant Memory), which addresses each in turn. In a causal encoder-decoder (CED), LooM loops only the decoder layers after the first, which read a global memory written once per token, and each of them publishes the key-value (KV) entry for a token only on its first visit, so the cache does not grow with the loop count. These layers loop independently, providing every budget from 3 to 21 layer executions per token, and one model trained on randomly sampled budgets covers all of them without a router. With enough loops, LooM outperforms a single-pass baseline trained on the same data on language modeling, zero-shot accuracy and long-context perplexity, while using the same cache size. Our analysis further shows that the training budget distribution decides what extra depth buys. These results suggest that a CED is a natural place to loop: memory is written once, and depth becomes a budget chosen at deployment.

AI.tldr: LooM is a loop-invariant memory design for causal encoder-decoder language models that loops only the decoder layers after the first, so the KV cache does not grow with the loop count. A single model trained on random loop budgets covers budgets from 3 to 21 layer executions per token and outperforms a single-pass baseline when given enough loops.
AI.motivation: Looped Transformers increase effective depth but suffer from memory that grows with the loop count, compute that can only be adjusted in whole-block steps, and a loop count that is hard to change after training.
AI.method: In a causal encoder-decoder, the decoder layers after the first read a global memory written once per token, and each looping layer publishes its key-value entry only on its first visit; the layers loop independently and are trained on randomly sampled budgets without a router.
AI.result: With enough loops, LooM outperforms a single-pass baseline trained on the same data on language modeling, zero-shot accuracy and long-context perplexity, while using the same cache size; the training budget distribution is shown to determine what extra depth buys.
AI.conclusion: A causal encoder-decoder is a natural place to loop because memory is written once and depth becomes a budget chosen at deployment rather than fixed at training.

title: Before You Continue: Evaluating Time-Sensitive Safety Awareness in Conversational Assistants
summary: Large language model (LLM) assistants increasingly help users with everyday activities that involve time-dependent constraints. However, users may not mention these constraints in later requests, requiring assistants to recognize and adjust their advice accordingly. To evaluate such capability, we introduce TASC (Temporal Action Safety in Conversation), a benchmark that evaluates whether LLMs apply time-dependent constraints when responding to conversational requests. TASC consists of 3,418 inputs derived from 128 templates, along with a separate set of 33 scenarios designed to compare models' ability to calculate elapsed time with their ability to apply that information. Across 13 models, assistants account for time-dependent constraints in only 30.5% of cases where the proposed action violates a rule, while rarely warning users unnecessarily. More importantly, models fail to apply these constraints in 62.1% of cases despite correctly calculating the elapsed time. Explicitly providing the timing resolves only about half of these failures, revealing a gap between temporal reasoning and its application in conversational advice.

AI.tldr: TASC is a benchmark of 3,418 conversational inputs for testing whether LLM assistants apply time-dependent safety constraints that users do not restate in later requests. Across 13 models, the assistants apply such constraints in only 30.5% of violating cases, and they fail in 62.1% of cases even when they calculate the elapsed time correctly.
AI.motivation: LLM assistants help with everyday activities that have time-dependent constraints, but users may not repeat those constraints later in a conversation, so assistants must recognize and adjust their advice on their own.
AI.method: TASC consists of 3,418 inputs derived from 128 templates, plus a separate set of 33 scenarios that compare a model's ability to calculate elapsed time with its ability to apply that information.
AI.result: Assistants account for time-dependent constraints in only 30.5% of cases where the proposed action violates a rule while rarely warning users unnecessarily; models fail to apply the constraints in 62.1% of cases despite computing the elapsed time correctly, and explicitly providing the timing resolves only about half of these failures.
AI.conclusion: The results reveal a gap between temporal reasoning and its application in conversational advice.

title: Persona Perspectives: Adopting Viewpoints Reorganizes Representations in LLMs
summary: Common methods for monitoring features in large language models (LLMs) such as linear probes and sparse autoencoders (SAEs) assume that features maintain a consistent representation across contexts. LLMs, however, can flexibly adopt different perspectives or "personas" that suggest different underlying systems of conceptual relations. In this paper, we examine whether prompting an LLM to adopt a persona alters the representational geometry of the model's latent space. We extract representations of over 9,000 common words and 33 semantic axes from models adopting liberal and conservative political personas and compare these against two neutral baselines. We find that persona conditioning systematically alters both the projections of words onto semantic axes and the alignments among the axes themselves in directions consistent with the specified ideology. We then test the implications of this reorganization for two safety-relevant features: truthfulness and morality. Linear probes, SAE-based classifiers, and classifiers built from manually selected word representations, all trained without a persona, produce divergent results when applied to models conditioned on political personas, producing politically slanted ratings of truth and morality on controversial statements. These findings suggest that internal representations, as they are conventionally extracted, can exhibit different geometric relations when the model adopts personas, potentially undermining monitoring efforts.

AI.tldr: Prompting an LLM to adopt a liberal or conservative political persona systematically reorganizes the geometry of its latent representations. Probes, SAE-based classifiers and manually selected word representations trained without a persona then give politically slanted truth and morality ratings.
AI.motivation: Common feature monitoring methods such as linear probes and sparse autoencoders assume that features keep a consistent representation across contexts, yet LLMs can flexibly adopt personas that imply different systems of conceptual relations.
AI.method: The authors extract representations of over 9,000 common words and 33 semantic axes from models adopting liberal and conservative political personas and compare them with two neutral baselines, then test the effect on the safety-relevant features of truthfulness and morality.
AI.result: Persona conditioning changes both the projections of words onto semantic axes and the alignments among the axes in directions consistent with the specified ideology, and classifiers trained without a persona produce divergent and politically slanted ratings of truth and morality on controversial statements.
AI.conclusion: Internal representations as conventionally extracted can show different geometric relations under personas, which could undermine monitoring efforts.

title: Balancing hierarchical representation and quantization: A performance trade-off in text embeddings
comment: 29 pages. Authors' version of the open access article published in Information Sciences (CC BY 4.0). This version corrects the second affiliation of Marco Polignano (Otto von Guericke University Magdeburg); the published version lists the European Commission, Joint Research Centre (JRC) in error. Marco Polignano is not affiliated with the JRC. No other content has been changed
summary: Hierarchical text embedding models offer variable-length representations, while quantization reduces numerical precision; both aim to improve computational efficiency. This work is an empirical benchmark study of how these two orthogonal, already-established techniques interact. We evaluate 38 tasks from the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB) using four transformer-based embedding models, covering 1D and 2D hierarchical representations combined with 32-bit, 8-bit, and binary quantization, for 168 configurations per task. We report each efficiency dimension separately: theoretical per-vector storage and end-to-end evaluation time. Under a Friedman test with Nemenyi post-hoc analysis, int8 quantization is statistically indistinguishable from float32 for pair classification and re-ranking and costs at most 1.5 percentage points overall, whereas binary quantization is significantly worse across every task category. Halving the embedding dimension once is not statistically detectable above $m=16$; two successive halvings always are. Combining an 8x dimensionality reduction with int8 yields a 32x reduction in per-vector storage at 94.4% of baseline effectiveness. Because evaluation times were measured once, we treat them as indicative: we find no evidence that quantization speeds up evaluation, whereas sampling from intermediate layers shortens it substantially. Retrieval degrades far faster than every other category, so we report findings per task category.

AI.tldr: This empirical benchmark on the MTEB shows that int8 quantization is statistically indistinguishable from float32 for pair classification and re-ranking and costs at most 1.5 percentage points overall, while binary quantization is significantly worse. Combining an 8x dimensionality reduction with int8 gives a 32x reduction in per-vector storage at 94.4% of baseline effectiveness.
AI.motivation: Hierarchical text embeddings and quantization both aim to improve efficiency, but how these two established techniques interact had not been systematically measured.
AI.method: The authors evaluate 38 MTEB tasks with four transformer-based embedding models, covering 1D and 2D hierarchical representations combined with 32-bit, 8-bit and binary quantization for 168 configurations per task, reporting theoretical per-vector storage and end-to-end evaluation time separately and analysing results with a Friedman test and Nemenyi post-hoc analysis.
AI.result: Halving the embedding dimension once is not statistically detectable above m=16 while two successive halvings always are; no evidence shows that quantization speeds up evaluation, whereas sampling from intermediate layers shortens it substantially; retrieval degrades far faster than other task categories.
AI.conclusion: Findings should be reported per task category, since the efficiency and effectiveness trade-offs differ strongly across categories, and evaluation times were measured once and are only indicative.

title: SpecCompact: Accelerating LLM Agent Context Compaction with Slot-Parallel Semantic Speculative Verification
summary: LLM agents use context compaction to manage growing interaction histories, but summarizing long histories with large models can introduce substantial delays. Compaction therefore requires balancing information retention against latency. We observe that structured summary slots can retain information when generated independently. Based on this observation, we present SpecCompact, a framework that accelerates compaction through slot-parallel semantic speculation. SpecCompact fine-tunes a small drafter and generates slots in parallel. The target model verifies each proposed line and repairs rejected content, while subsequent drafting uses the updated slot prefix. System optimizations further reduce repeated context processing and model calls. Across AppWorld and $\tau^3$ benchmarks with two target models, SpecCompact achieves $2.04$--$5.63\times$ compaction speedups over Hermes-style summarization. Separate downstream evaluations reveal model- and task-dependent performance trade-offs. A user study within Hermes further shows an $8.68\times$ median compaction speedup.

AI.tldr: SpecCompact speeds up LLM agent context compaction by generating structured summary slots in parallel with a fine-tuned small drafter and verifying them with the target model. It achieves 2.04 to 5.63 times compaction speedups over Hermes-style summarization on AppWorld and tau^3 benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Summarizing long agent interaction histories with large models adds substantial latency, so compaction must balance information retention against speed.
AI.method: The framework uses slot-parallel semantic speculative verification: a small drafter fine-tuned for the task generates structured summary slots in parallel, the target model verifies each proposed line and repairs rejected content, subsequent drafting uses the updated slot prefix, and system optimizations reduce repeated context processing and model calls.
AI.result: Across AppWorld and tau^3 with two target models, SpecCompact achieves 2.04 to 5.63 times compaction speedups over Hermes-style summarization, separate downstream evaluations show model- and task-dependent performance trade-offs, and a user study within Hermes shows an 8.68 times median compaction speedup.
AI.conclusion: Speculative slot generation is a practical way to cut compaction latency for LLM agents, though its downstream quality effects depend on the model and task.

title: Unlocking Turing Tensor Cores: A Measured Throughput Account of From-Scratch Pre-training on a Single 22G RTX 2080 Ti
summary: The RTX 2080 Ti (TU102) ships full second-generation Tensor Cores in hardware, yet the vendor throttles FP16 matrix multiplication at the driver level, leaving usable tensor throughput well below the hardware peak. turing-unlock lifts this restriction with a kernel module that, before the nvidia driver binds the device, writes the FP16 speed selectors (SS0=0x88888888, SS1=0x8) and releases the ACR mutex; published measurements report cuBLAS FP16 matmul throughput rising from 55.7 to 91.4 TFLOPS (about 1.6x). On the same 22G 2080 Ti and under the same from-scratch pre-training protocol as the companion memory ledger (five tiers of Chinese encoder-decoder models, 2,451 steps per tier, 16,384 tokens per step, seed 42), we obtain a before/after throughput account: the small tier (75.7M parameters, 512-wide, 8+8 layers, activation checkpointing on) improves in steady-state throughput from 6,480 to 7,246 tok/s (+11.8%) with wall time cut from 1.77h to 1.61h (9.0% saved); the tiny tier goes from 15,150 to 15,866 tok/s (+4.7%) with wall time savings of 3.8%; the three smaller tiers (pico-micro) gain at most +0.3%; per-tier peak memory stays bit-identical, and final quality metrics are bit-identical or consistent within 10^-3. We conclude that the unlock gain is a function of matrix size, rising monotonically with tier -- imperceptible for pico-micro, visible from tiny upward, and cashed out as a double-digit percentage at small -- and that it is a pure throughput gain that leaves training dynamics untouched.

AI.tldr: turing-unlock is a kernel module that lifts the driver-level throttling of FP16 tensor throughput on the RTX 2080 Ti, and the authors measure its effect on from-scratch pre-training of five tiers of Chinese encoder-decoder models. The throughput gain rises with model size, reaching +11.8% for the small tier, with bit-identical peak memory and consistent final quality.
AI.motivation: The RTX 2080 Ti has full second-generation Tensor Cores, but the vendor throttles FP16 matrix multiplication in the driver, so usable tensor throughput stays well below the hardware peak.
AI.method: The kernel module writes the FP16 speed selectors (SS0=0x88888888, SS1=0x8) and releases the ACR mutex before the nvidia driver binds the device, and the before-and-after throughput is measured under the same from-scratch pre-training protocol as a companion memory study (five tiers, 2,451 steps per tier, 16,384 tokens per step, seed 42).
AI.result: The small tier (75.7M parameters) rises from 6,480 to 7,246 tok/s (+11.8%) with wall time cut from 1.77h to 1.61h; the tiny tier gains +4.7%; the pico-micro tiers gain at most +0.3%; per-tier peak memory stays bit-identical and final quality metrics are bit-identical or consistent within 10^-3. Published cuBLAS FP16 matmul throughput rises from 55.7 to 91.4 TFLOPS (about 1.6x).
AI.conclusion: The unlock gain is a pure throughput gain that leaves training dynamics untouched and grows monotonically with matrix size, so it is negligible for the smallest tiers and a double-digit percentage at the small tier.

title: The Male Abstraction Bias in Internet Culture and Large Language Models
summary: Two foundational aspects of human cognition, abstractness and gender, are typically examined as separable. Here, we find they are systematically linked throughout the entire space of concepts spanning single (N = 40,000) and multi-word expressions (N = 67,000): across billions of words and millions of images on the internet -- and across numerous measurement techniques -- more abstract concepts are more associated with men, an effect which replicates in languages around the world. This pattern not only holds across conceptual domains, but it also maps onto grammatical structure: verbs and adverbs are more abstract and more male-coded, a system-wide trace of stereotypes accentuating agentic qualities in men. Furthermore, this bias emerges in human and AI responses in free association tasks, indicating its internalization and its algorithmic reproduction. The male abstraction bias may underlie and unify a range of stereotypes, evidencing gender as a core organizing dimension in conceptual space.

AI.tldr: Across single-word (N = 40,000) and multi-word (N = 67,000) concepts, more abstract concepts are more associated with men in internet text and images, and LLMs reproduce this male abstraction bias in free association tasks. The bias maps onto grammar, with verbs and adverbs being more abstract and more male-coded.
AI.motivation: Abstractness and gender are usually studied as separable features of human cognition, but the authors ask whether they are systematically linked across the whole conceptual space.
AI.method: The authors measure the association between abstractness and gender across billions of words and millions of images on the internet using numerous measurement techniques, replicate the pattern in languages around the world, and examine human and AI responses in free association tasks.
AI.result: More abstract concepts are more associated with men across conceptual domains, the pattern extends to verbs and adverbs, which are more abstract and more male-coded, and the bias appears in both human and AI free association responses.
AI.conclusion: The male abstraction bias may underlie and unify a range of gender stereotypes, indicating that gender is a core organizing dimension of conceptual space and that it is internalized and algorithmically reproduced.

title: Modality-Aware Expert Pruning for MoE-Based Multimodal Large Language Models
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) enables multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to scale capacity efficiently, but expert parameters dominate memory even though only a few experts are activated per token: they account for over 90% of model size in modern MoE-MLLMs (e.g., 54 GB out of about 58 GB in BF16 for InternVL3.5-30B-A3B and Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B). Expert pruning has emerged as an effective compression strategy, but existing methods aggregate importance uniformly across tokens, ignoring that the same expert may serve different roles for vision versus language processing. To address this, we propose MAEP (Modality-Aware Expert Pruning), a training-free framework that decomposes expert importance by modality in a single forward pass. MAEP introduces (1) Delta-H Output ($\Delta H$), a redistribution-aware metric measuring the MoE output change when an expert is removed, and (2) low-attention vision tokens as a vision-side pruning signal that is dataset-stable: its expert-importance ranking remains stable across different datasets. Text-side importance serves as a preservation signal while vision-side importance serves as a pruning signal, and experts are ranked globally across layers. Experiments on three MoE-based MLLMs across multimodal and text benchmarks show that MAEP outperforms modality-agnostic baselines on the majority of multimodal benchmarks while remaining competitive on text-only tasks, reducing the BF16 expert weight footprint by about 27 GB (about 47% of total memory) so that the full weight footprint of an approximately 58 GB model fits within a single 40 GB GPU. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: MAEP is a training-free expert pruning method for MoE multimodal LLMs that scores expert importance separately for vision and text tokens in a single forward pass. On three MoE-based MLLMs it outperforms modality-agnostic baselines on most multimodal benchmarks and cuts about 27 GB of BF16 expert weights, letting a roughly 58 GB model fit on one 40 GB GPU.
AI.motivation: Expert parameters account for over 90% of model size in modern MoE-MLLMs, and existing expert pruning methods aggregate importance uniformly across tokens, ignoring that the same expert may serve different roles for vision and language processing.
AI.method: MAEP introduces Delta-H Output, a redistribution-aware metric that measures the MoE output change when an expert is removed, and low-attention vision tokens as a dataset-stable pruning signal; text-side importance is used as a preservation signal, vision-side importance as a pruning signal, and experts are ranked globally across layers.
AI.result: MAEP outperforms modality-agnostic baselines on the majority of multimodal benchmarks while remaining competitive on text-only tasks, reducing the BF16 expert weight footprint by about 27 GB (about 47% of total memory) on InternVL3.5-30B-A3B, Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B and a third MoE-MLLM.
AI.conclusion: Modality-aware pruning makes large MoE-MLLMs fit on a single 40 GB GPU with limited loss of capability, and the code is publicly released.

title: Robots in the City: Persona-Based Perceptions of Urban Robots
summary: Pedestrians increasingly encounter robots in urban public spaces without interacting with them, but how robots change the perceived safety of a street remains unclear. We examine how robot presence and type affect perceived safety across urban contexts. We generate 18 images of Seoul streets that vary in time of day, road class, and robot condition (no robot, a delivery robot, or a humanoid). Two multimodal large language models (MLLMs), Qwen3.8-27B and Gemma4-26B, each conditioned on 500 synthetic personas, choose the safer image in each pair, and 25 human respondents complete the same task. Both models prefer streets without robots and favor the delivery robot over the humanoid. Robots are chosen more often at night and less often by older personas, whereas road class has smaller effects. In the model rationales, the delivery robot appears as a physical obstacle, whereas the humanoid appears as either a threat or a source of protection. Like humans, both models chose robots more often at night, but chose the humanoid over the delivery robot far less often, and Gemma showed a night effect for the humanoid about three times that of humans. These results show that the effect of a robot on perceived safety depends on when it appears, and that persona-conditioned MLLMs capture only part of human judgments.

AI.tldr: Two multimodal LLMs, each conditioned on 500 synthetic personas, judge which of paired Seoul street images feels safer when robots are present or absent, and their choices are compared with 25 human respondents. Both models prefer streets without robots and favour a delivery robot over a humanoid, and robots are chosen more often at night.
AI.motivation: Pedestrians increasingly encounter robots in urban public spaces without interacting with them, but how robots change the perceived safety of a street was unclear.
AI.method: The authors generate 18 images of Seoul streets varying in time of day, road class and robot condition (no robot, a delivery robot, or a humanoid), and have Qwen3.8-27B and Gemma4-26B choose the safer image in each pair under persona conditioning, with the same task given to human respondents.
AI.result: Both models prefer streets without robots and favour the delivery robot over the humanoid; robots are chosen more often at night and less often by older personas, while road class has smaller effects; the model rationales describe the delivery robot as a physical obstacle and the humanoid as either a threat or protection, and Gemma shows a night effect for the humanoid about three times that of humans.
AI.conclusion: The effect of a robot on perceived safety depends on when it appears, and persona-conditioned MLLMs capture only part of human judgments.

title: On the Design of Hyper-Connections: Simplification, Stability, and Scalability
summary: Hyper-Connections (HC) architectures are increasingly adopted in frontier language models, yet their components remain insufficiently understood and introduce non-negligible training overhead. In this work, we systematically study the HC architecture to understand its components and identify simpler, more efficient designs. We find that learned read/write gating without mixing and unconstrained mixing with fixed gates form two effective interaction groups: either alone achieves performance comparable to mHC. We also identify repeated access to the expanded residual state as a major source of training overhead, even without mixing. These findings lead to SimpleHC, which simplifies the architecture by removing residual mixing and simplifies execution through shared memory access, using the resulting additive structure and shared gate inputs. Layer-specific gates share a group-entry state, enabling batched reads and deferred writes; scalar corrections exactly preserve preceding sublayer output contributions. Our analyses support both the retained residual structure and the design of shared memory access. SimpleHC incurs only 2.4% extra end-to-end training time over a vanilla residual baseline at the largest tested scale. It maintains performance comparable to mHC when scaling from 15B to 30B MoE models, exhibits smoother gradient dynamics during standard training, and remains stable under stress. We hope SimpleHC will encourage a broader pursuit of simplicity in foundation model design, making performance gains more accessible and practical at scale.

AI.tldr: SimpleHC simplifies Hyper-Connections by removing residual mixing and sharing memory access, and it stays comparable to mHC when scaling from 15B to 30B MoE models while adding only 2.4% training time over a vanilla residual baseline at the largest tested scale. The analysis shows that learned read/write gating and unconstrained mixing with fixed gates each achieve performance comparable to mHC.
AI.motivation: Hyper-Connections are increasingly used in frontier language models, but their components are poorly understood and they add non-negligible training overhead.
AI.method: The authors study the HC architecture component by component, identify two effective interaction groups, and identify repeated access to the expanded residual state as a source of overhead; SimpleHC uses layer-specific gates that share a group-entry state for batched reads and deferred writes, and scalar corrections that preserve preceding sublayer output contributions.
AI.result: SimpleHC maintains performance comparable to mHC when scaling from 15B to 30B MoE models, shows smoother gradient dynamics during standard training, remains stable under stress, and incurs only 2.4% extra end-to-end training time over a vanilla residual baseline at the largest tested scale.
AI.conclusion: Simpler and more efficient designs can match sophisticated residual architectures at scale, making performance gains more accessible for foundation model training.

title: How Far Can You Steer? Behavior-Capability Frontiers in Contrastive Activation Addition
summary: Activation steering can modify language-model behavior without parameter updates, but behavioral efficacy alone does not determine whether an intervention is usable. Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) steers targeted behaviors using activation directions derived from contrasting examples, potentially degrading unrelated model capabilities in the process. We therefore study CAA through a behavior-capability frontier, selecting interventions that maximize behavioral gain subject to an explicit bound on capability degradation. We evaluate this framework across four instruction-tuned models, seven behaviors, and capability-loss budgets of 1%, 3%, and 5% (absolute percentage points). Validation-selected behavioral effects generalize strongly to held-out data ($\rho = 0.945$), while joint behavior-capability survival among nonzero operating points rises from 37.5% at the 1% budget to 72.7% at 3%, with limited additional improvement at 5%. Control experiments indicate that these effects depend on learned behavior directions rather than generic activation perturbations. Representational geometry is significantly but only modestly predictive of causal cross-behavior transfer. Finally, secondary capability, out-of-distribution, and open-ended evaluations show that interventions satisfying protected benchmarks can still degrade untested capabilities or transfer unevenly to free-form generation. These results characterize activation steering as a constrained intervention whose usable range depends on model, behavior, direction, layer, and evaluation budget, rather than a universal control knob.

AI.tldr: The paper studies Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) through a behavior-capability frontier that maximizes behavioral gain under an explicit bound on capability loss. Across four instruction-tuned models and seven behaviors, validation-selected behavioral effects generalize strongly to held-out data (rho = 0.945), but interventions that satisfy protected benchmarks can still degrade untested capabilities.
AI.motivation: Activation steering can change model behavior without parameter updates, but behavioral efficacy alone does not show that an intervention is usable, since CAA may degrade unrelated capabilities.
AI.method: The authors select CAA interventions that maximize behavioral gain subject to capability-loss budgets of 1%, 3% and 5% (absolute percentage points), and test them with control experiments, representational geometry analysis, secondary capability benchmarks, out-of-distribution tests and open-ended evaluations.
AI.result: Joint behavior-capability survival among nonzero operating points rises from 37.5% at the 1% budget to 72.7% at 3%, with limited further gain at 5%; effects depend on learned behavior directions rather than generic perturbations; representational geometry is only modestly predictive of causal cross-behavior transfer.
AI.conclusion: Activation steering is a constrained intervention whose usable range depends on model, behavior, direction, layer and evaluation budget, rather than a universal control knob.

title: Who Pays for the Knowledge Models Copy? Model Collapse as Rogers' Paradox
comment: 13 pages, 5 figures. Code: this https URL
summary: Generative models trained on the output of earlier models lose knowledge across generations, rare knowledge first. The remedies that work all bring in information from outside the loop, and the theory of model collapse treats that supply as given: a fixed archive, drawn from a fixed distribution. We argue that the supply is the problem, and that cultural evolution has the theory of it. We read model collapse as Rogers' paradox: a population that comes to rely on copying ends up no better off than one that never copied, because copies go stale unless someone keeps learning for themselves. We test the identification in three steps. First, Rogers' model, fitted only to fully synthetic training, predicts to within a few percentage points how much rare knowledge language models, from word trigrams to a pretrained transformer, retain under other mixtures of fresh data. Second, when the world itself changes, a lineage that copies its own past needs more fresh data to keep up the faster the world changes, as Rogers' model says it must and as analyses that assume a fixed target cannot; a lineage that restarts every generation from fixed pretrained weights is largely insulated, because those weights are knowledge that is never copied. Third, we close the loop: when the people who write a model's training data can ask the model instead of finding things out, the supply of fresh data becomes endogenous. At equilibrium, the model is exactly as reliable as it is costly for people to find out for themselves, the population is no better off than without the model, and every increase in the share of model-written text must be paid for by more people learning for themselves. Users who check what they are told and relearn when it is wrong break the paradox. Filters that select plausible text are conformist and accelerate collapse; only checks that carry new information act as critical learning.

AI.tldr: The paper reads model collapse as Rogers' paradox, arguing that a population relying on copying is no better off than one that never copied because copies go stale unless people keep learning for themselves. Rogers' model fitted to fully synthetic training predicts how much rare knowledge language models retain under other data mixtures, and the model is shown to be exactly as reliable as it is costly for people to verify.
AI.motivation: The theory of model collapse treats the supply of fresh outside data as a fixed archive from a fixed distribution, which the authors argue is the actual problem, and cultural evolution theory has a model of this supply.
AI.method: The authors test Rogers' model in three steps: fitting it to fully synthetic training and predicting retention of rare knowledge from word trigrams to a pretrained transformer; varying how fast the world changes for lineages that copy their own past versus restart from fixed pretrained weights; and closing the loop so that people who write training data can ask the model, making fresh data endogenous.
AI.result: Predictions fit retention within a few percentage points across mixtures of fresh data; a lineage that copies its own past needs more fresh data the faster the world changes, while a lineage restarting from fixed pretrained weights is largely insulated; at equilibrium every increase in model-written text must be matched by more people learning for themselves.
AI.conclusion: Users who check what they are told and relearn when it is wrong break the paradox, and only checks that carry new information act as critical learning, whereas filters that select plausible text are conformist and accelerate collapse.

title: SVGFaith: A Two-Layer Meta-Evaluation of Faithfulness Metrics for Text-to-SVG Generation
summary: Text-to-SVG systems are commonly evaluated by applying raster-image metrics to rasterised outputs, yet whether these scores capture fine-grained prompt faithfulness remains unclear. We introduce SVGFaith, a two-layer meta-evaluation framework in which the more faithful candidate of each pair is determined by construction or by human judgment. SVGFaith-Diagnostic contains 1,842 controlled contrastive pairs across eight capability axes, split evenly between two directions: two renderings compared against one prompt, and two descriptions compared against one rendering. SVGFaith-Arena contains 1,327 human-annotated comparisons of real generator outputs. On SVGFaith-Diagnostic, CLIP and three other image--text embedding metrics reach at least 0.789 pairwise accuracy on object identity but at most 0.672 on spatial relations and attribute binding, where chance is 0.5. We further introduce SVGFaith-Score, an interpretable pointwise metric. A domain-tuned decomposer turns each prompt into a dependency graph of atomic visual requirements, a visual question answering model scores whether each requirement is satisfied, and a requirement's score is discounted when its prerequisites score low. In addition to the overall score, the per-requirement scores show which requirements are judged unsatisfied and which inherit discounts from their prerequisites. SVGFaith-Score significantly outperforms all nine baselines, including a Qwen3.5-122B-A10B judge, on Arena and in both Diagnostic directions. Code and data: this https URL.

AI.tldr: SVGFaith is a two-layer meta-evaluation framework for faithfulness metrics in text-to-SVG generation, built from 1,842 controlled diagnostic pairs and 1,327 human-annotated arena comparisons. Its proposed SVGFaith-Score, which decomposes prompts into dependency graphs of visual requirements, significantly outperforms all nine baselines, including a Qwen3.5-122B-A10B judge.
AI.motivation: Text-to-SVG systems are usually evaluated with raster-image metrics on rasterized outputs, and it was unclear whether these scores capture fine-grained prompt faithfulness; CLIP reaches at most 0.672 pairwise accuracy on spatial relations and attribute binding, where chance is 0.5.
AI.method: SVGFaith-Diagnostic contains controlled contrastive pairs across eight capability axes in two directions, rendering comparisons and description comparisons, and SVGFaith-Arena contains human-annotated comparisons of real generator outputs; SVGFaith-Score uses a domain-tuned decomposer to build a dependency graph of atomic visual requirements, a VQA model to check each requirement, and discounts scores whose prerequisites score low.
AI.result: CLIP and three other image-text embedding metrics reach at least 0.789 pairwise accuracy on object identity but at most 0.672 on spatial relations and attribute binding; SVGFaith-Score significantly outperforms all nine baselines on Arena and in both Diagnostic directions, and its per-requirement scores show which requirements are unsatisfied.
AI.conclusion: Interpretable, requirement-level scoring gives a more reliable measure of prompt faithfulness for text-to-SVG generation than existing image-text embedding metrics.

title: Growing One's AI Tools: A Paradigm of Practice-Grown Tools
summary: Professionals have long used software built for them by others. This article reports the growth of a professional computer-assisted interpreting (CAI) tool built by its own user, a conference interpreter without programming training. Drawing on an eight-week version-controlled record with telemetry from 133 logged sessions and over 20,000 recognized utterances, the article traces how real conference work drove the tool through 62 commits and six versions. The record shows capabilities deployed on the day their need appeared and one strategy change that cut median end-to-end delay by over a third within one afternoon. The article then proposes the paradigm of practice-grown tools, defined by the shift from using to growing, the co-evolution of tool and practice through breakdown and repair, bounded local computation, and an assessment corollary, and it formulates three propositions toward tool-inclusive assessment of practitioners, from tool-making literacy to a compute-standardized format for certifying what they and their tools achieve together.

AI.tldr: This article reports how a conference interpreter without programming training grew a computer-assisted interpreting tool over eight weeks, with 62 commits, six versions and telemetry from 133 logged sessions. It proposes the paradigm of practice-grown tools and three propositions for tool-inclusive assessment of practitioners.
AI.motivation: Professionals have long used software built by others, but this article examines a tool built by its own user, and asks how assessment of practitioners should account for the tools they grow and use.
AI.method: The authors draw on an eight-week version-controlled record with telemetry from 133 logged sessions and over 20,000 recognized utterances, tracing how real conference work drove the tool's development, and they define the paradigm through the shift from using to growing, co-evolution of tool and practice through breakdown and repair, bounded local computation, and an assessment corollary.
AI.result: Capabilities were deployed on the day their need appeared, and one strategy change cut median end-to-end delay by over a third within one afternoon.
AI.conclusion: The paper proposes three propositions toward tool-inclusive assessment, from tool-making literacy to a compute-standardized format for certifying what practitioners and their tools achieve together.

title: What Does Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning Really Improve in LLM Agents?
summary: While multi-turn agentic reinforcement learning (RL) excels on long-horizon tasks, its performance gains remain highly sensitive to interaction constraints. Evaluating across sampling breadth $K$ and interaction depth $T$ via $Pass@(K,T)$, we show that trajectory-level RL advantages depend on sufficient turn budgets, diminishing significantly when budgets tighten. Besides, agentic RL does not uniformly elevate single-step decision quality; rather, its strength concentrates in error recovery and long-horizon resilience. To mitigate the deployment risks caused by this budget dependence, we provide a preliminary discussion on the benefits and limitations of process supervision signals and introduce BudgetMix RL as an alternative that varies interaction budgets during training. Experiments demonstrate that BudgetMix RL achieves robust performance across diverse execution settings. Project Page: this https URL

AI.tldr: The paper shows that the benefit of multi-turn agentic RL depends on the interaction budget, as measured by Pass@(K,T), with trajectory-level advantages shrinking when turn budgets tighten. It proposes BudgetMix RL, which varies interaction budgets during training and achieves robust performance across diverse execution settings.
AI.motivation: Multi-turn agentic RL performs well on long-horizon tasks, but its gains are highly sensitive to interaction constraints, which creates deployment risk when the budget changes.
AI.method: The authors evaluate across sampling breadth K and interaction depth T via Pass@(K,T), give a preliminary discussion of process supervision signals, and introduce BudgetMix RL, which varies the interaction budget during training.
AI.result: Agentic RL does not uniformly improve single-step decision quality; its strength concentrates in error recovery and long-horizon resilience, and BudgetMix RL achieves robust performance across diverse execution settings.
AI.conclusion: Budget-aware training is a practical way to reduce the deployment risks of multi-turn agentic RL, although the discussion of process supervision is preliminary.

title: Beyond accuracy: what AI assurance needs to establish in public services
summary: Public bodies increasingly rely on AI-produced evidence, including classifications, summaries and assessments. These outputs can inform policy decisions and service delivery, making their reliability a matter of public accountability. Establishing whether this evidence can be relied upon requires testing its outputs and examining how organisations decide whether those tests are sufficient. We combine technical evaluation with analysis of AI governance requirements, informed by measurement theory and management-based regulation. We compare eight GPT-4o configurations classifying 1,200 UK Prime Minister's Questions into 21 policy topics, against human-coded labels and across unchanged repeats. Accuracy ranges from 68.2% to 70.3%, yet 24.3% of questions receive different labels, with changes in topic shares and rankings. Configurations agree more with one another than with human coding: agreement does not guarantee correctness. Under the implemented score-extraction procedure, the proportion flagged for human review ranges from 0.9% to 41.0%. We analyse 37 UK and EU policy documents. Both sets expect testing and oversight, but reporting expectations do not consistently cover changing answers, shared errors, selective evaluation, substantive conclusions or review routing. Some UK guidance explicitly addresses stability. The UK sample emphasises public bodies checking their own use; the EU places substantial testing duties on providers while leaving them important choices about measures and acceptance thresholds. Without appropriate checks, evidence could misrepresent policy issues, redirect attention or resources, and leave errors undetected. Public policy should require organisations to justify reliance through checks beyond aggregate accuracy, clear responsibility, access to expertise and scrutiny of results.

AI.tldr: An evaluation of eight GPT-4o configurations classifying 1,200 UK Prime Minister's Questions into 21 policy topics finds accuracy of 68.2% to 70.3%, yet 24.3% of questions receive different labels across unchanged repeats. The paper argues that public bodies need checks beyond aggregate accuracy before they rely on AI-produced evidence.
AI.motivation: Public bodies increasingly rely on AI-produced classifications, summaries and assessments that inform policy and service delivery, so their reliability is a matter of public accountability, yet it is unclear what tests establish that reliance.
AI.method: The authors combine technical evaluation against human-coded labels and across unchanged repeats with an analysis of 37 UK and EU policy documents, informed by measurement theory and management-based regulation, and they examine how the proportion of outputs flagged for human review depends on the score-extraction procedure.
AI.result: Configurations agree more with one another than with human coding; under the implemented score-extraction procedure the proportion flagged for human review ranges from 0.9% to 41.0%; reporting expectations in the policy documents do not consistently cover changing answers, shared errors, selective evaluation, substantive conclusions or review routing.
AI.conclusion: Public policy should require organisations to justify reliance on AI outputs through checks beyond aggregate accuracy, with clear responsibility, access to expertise and scrutiny of results.

title: Turns Matter: Advancing Streaming Video RL via Turn-Level Credit
summary: Streaming video understanding requires models to repeatedly decide whether to respond or continue observing. Recently, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has been applied to this setting, with existing approaches emphasizing reward design while retaining a single trajectory-level advantage across turns. Such shared credit can reinforce redundant replies after earlier successes and discourage useful follow-ups after earlier failures. We propose TurnWise, a turn-level GRPO framework that aligns learning with individual streaming decisions. TurnWise addresses the mismatch between trajectory-level feedback and turn-level interaction, promoting informative responses and reducing redundancy. Specifically, turn-level credit assignment uses silence-completed prefix scoring to construct group-relative advantages from each decision's remaining return, separating its learning signal from earlier rewards. Turn-mean policy optimization averages token losses within each turn and then across turns, giving response and waiting decisions equal weight regardless of output length. These complementary designs improve streaming policy learning without a learned critic or additional rollouts. Extensive experiments show our method outperforms prior RL approaches for streaming video understanding.

AI.tldr: TurnWise is a turn-level GRPO framework for streaming video understanding that gives each respond-or-wait decision its own group-relative advantage instead of one trajectory-level advantage. It outperforms prior RL approaches for streaming video understanding without a learned critic or additional rollouts.
AI.motivation: Existing GRPO approaches for streaming video emphasize reward design but keep a single trajectory-level advantage across turns, which gives shared credit that can reinforce redundant replies or discourage useful follow-ups.
AI.method: Turn-level credit assignment uses silence-completed prefix scoring to construct group-relative advantages from each decision's remaining return, and turn-mean policy optimization averages token losses within each turn and then across turns so that response and waiting decisions have equal weight regardless of output length.
AI.result: The method outperforms prior RL approaches on streaming video understanding in extensive experiments, promoting informative responses and reducing redundancy.
AI.conclusion: Aligning policy learning with individual streaming decisions improves streaming video RL without requiring a learned critic or extra rollouts.

title: Template Gap Reconstruction for Shell Output Simulation with Small Language Models
summary: Small language models offer a compact basis for shell simulation without executing submitted commands, but full-output decoding requires them to predict recurring utility structure alongside content that varies across executions. We introduce template gap reconstruction (TGR), which supplies reusable output literals interspersed with sentinels to be interleaved with autoregressively generated gaps. A template selector chooses which template to be reconstructed, with the empty template retaining full-output decoding. We construct a template bank from 18.7 million outputs collected across heterogeneous execution environments and train a template selector and five reconstruction models initialized from various small language model checkpoints on a target environment excluded from bank construction. Evaluation demonstrates that TGR improves output edit similarity (O-ES) over full-output decoding (FOD) when the optimal template covers more than 25\% of the template, while performing similarly for lower-coverage outputs. Additionally, TGR outperforms FOD for shorter gap sequences, with O-ES values of 0.964 and 0.812, respectively, while maintaining similar performance for longer sequences. TGR reduces the number of tokens generated by 26.3--38.3\% across used tokenizer families. These results support using a reusable output structure as a practical design choice for small shell simulators, improving response fidelity and shortening generation targets while keeping template selection and residual prediction central to response quality.

AI.tldr: Template gap reconstruction (TGR) improves shell output simulation with small language models by reusing output literals from a template bank and generating only the variable gaps autoregressively. It improves output edit similarity over full-output decoding when the optimal template covers more than 25% of the output and cuts generated tokens by 26.3% to 38.3%.
AI.motivation: Small language models can simulate shell output without executing commands, but full-output decoding forces them to predict both recurring utility structure and content that varies across executions.
AI.method: TGR supplies reusable output literals interspersed with sentinels that are interleaved with autoregressively generated gaps; a template selector chooses the template, with the empty template retaining full-output decoding, and the template bank is built from 18.7 million outputs while five reconstruction models are trained on a held-out target environment.
AI.result: TGR improves output edit similarity over full-output decoding when the optimal template covers more than 25% of the output, performs similarly for lower-coverage outputs, and outperforms it for shorter gap sequences with O-ES values of 0.964 and 0.812 for shorter and longer sequences respectively, while reducing generated tokens by 26.3% to 38.3% across tokenizer families.
AI.conclusion: A reusable output structure is a practical design choice for small shell simulators, improving response fidelity and shortening generation targets while keeping template selection and residual prediction central to quality.

title: LongBanana: An Expert-Verified Benchmark for Long-Context Multi-Reference Image Synthesis
comment: NeurIPS 2026 Evaluations and Datasets Track. Project page: this https URL
summary: We introduce LongBanana, to our knowledge the first expert-designed and expert-verified benchmark for long-context multi-reference image synthesis in the age of agent-driven image generation. The task requires retrieving dispersed visual evidence, rejecting distractors, binding entities and relations, and composing one coherent final image from multiple references. LongBanana contains 90 carefully designed tasks organized by a 3-by-3 taxonomy; each task includes about 32 reference images, 20 constraints, and 50 evaluation items, yielding 4,670 expert-specified atomic evaluation items in total. Its graph-grounded evaluation design instantiates each task with reference images and an entity-relation graph, then converts node, edge, and whole-graph obligations into checklist items for Content Fidelity, Relational Binding, and Global Constraint Satisfaction. Reviewed expert labels include a 15% double-labeled subset with 89.4% exact agreement and 0.83 quadratic weighted kappa. We further introduce LongBanana-Gen, an agent-harness framework for long-horizon image generation; experiments show that minimal agent harnesses improve over direct generation, while a ReAct-Plan-Exec-Reflect (RPR) workflow yields harness-dependent gains by strengthening evidence grounding and repair. Together, LongBanana provides an auditable testbed for measuring dense visual evidence use and a shared target for developing stronger agent-driven image-generation systems. Code and data are available at the project page: this https URL.

AI.tldr: LongBanana is an expert-designed and expert-verified benchmark of 90 tasks for long-context multi-reference image synthesis, with about 32 reference images, 20 constraints and 50 evaluation items per task. The authors also propose LongBanana-Gen, where a ReAct-Plan-Exec-Reflect workflow gives harness-dependent gains over direct generation.
