AI.motivation: Existing indoor benchmarks are synthetic or mesh-derived and construction-specific resources are small, so real laser scan data with its measurement artifacts is needed for scene understanding in built environments.
AI.method: The dataset annotates 504 point cloud scenes from 14 survey sites captured with a terrestrial laser scanner, using manual pointwise labels, expert oversight and full-scene review; it also includes instance annotations, scripts that derive aligned panoramic and cube-map representations, benchmark splits and baseline semantic segmentation experiments.
AI.result: The abstract reports benchmark splits and baseline semantic segmentation experiments but gives no numeric results.
AI.conclusion: The release is intended to support research on 3D scene understanding, construction-site analytics and multimodal scene analysis in the built environment.

title: Annotator-Free Object Detection via Foundation Model Collaboration
summary: Object detection research remains constrained by high annotation costs and the closed-set assumptions of supervised models, limiting scalability to novel categories. We present a target-dataset annotation-free object detection framework that eliminates the need for human labeling on the target dataset by leveraging the complementary strengths of pretrained foundation models, including segmentation and vision-language systems, combined with a self-refining training loop. To further reduce reliance on expensive LVLM queries, we introduce a landmark-based clustering mechanism that amortizes labeling across image clusters, improving label consistency while lowering computational cost. Our method autonomously generates segmentation proposals, assigns semantic labels through multimodal reasoning, and iteratively improves both localization and classification using a lightweight open-set detector. This modular pipeline enables adaptation to completely unseen object classes and domains without any human-provided target-dataset annotations, while maintaining compatibility with existing detection architectures. Evaluations on COCO, LVIS, ODinW-35, and Roboflow-100 demonstrate substantial performance gains over state-of-the-art open-vocabulary and long-tail detection methods, achieving 60.8 AP on COCO and 47.4 AP on LVIS under zero-shot settings. Beyond strong benchmark results, our approach provides a scalable foundation for real-world detection systems in unknown environments, where annotation is infeasible.

AI.tldr: An annotator-free object detection framework combines segmentation and vision-language foundation models with a self-refining loop and landmark-based clustering, reaching 60.8 AP on COCO and 47.4 AP on LVIS under zero-shot settings.
AI.motivation: Object detection is limited by annotation costs and closed-set supervised models, and scaling to novel categories needs an approach that avoids human target-dataset labels while reducing expensive LVLM queries.
AI.method: Segmentation proposals are generated autonomously, semantic labels are assigned through multimodal reasoning, and localization and classification are iteratively refined with a lightweight open-set detector; a landmark-based clustering mechanism amortizes LVLM labeling across image clusters.
AI.result: Evaluations on COCO, LVIS, ODinW-35 and Roboflow-100 show substantial gains over state-of-the-art open-vocabulary and long-tail detection methods, with 60.8 AP on COCO and 47.4 AP on LVIS under zero-shot settings.
AI.conclusion: The modular pipeline adapts to unseen classes and domains without human target-dataset annotation and remains compatible with existing detection architectures.

title: BiCG-Net: Target-Specific Image Quality Assessment via Observation Modeling and In-Image Differencing
summary: We estimate the quality of a specific target region (e.g., a train body) in an image, rather than the whole image. This differs fundamentally from whole-image No-Reference Image Quality Assessment (NR-IQA): when the target occupies a small fraction of the frame, the whole-image score is dominated by background, and no public benchmark provides target-level human Mean Opinion Score (MOS). We estimate target quality via nested sampling - a sequence of patches expanding outward from the target box - and infer quality from the relative structure of this sequence. This motivates BiCG-Net, a student network that distills an 11-teacher ensemble through a linear observation model and an in-image differencing mechanism, which provably cancels the target term and teacher-specific bias. We train and test the student independently on each dataset, and evaluate zero-shot transfer across benchmarks. On CSIQ and LIVEC, the student reaches PLCCs of 0.9009 and 0.9133 against human MOS, exceeding the best single teacher and the teacher consensus. On a self-built MOS-free railway dataset, the student reaches a PLCC of 0.9855 against a weak label. The student exceeds its teachers because it learns a new mapping from the relative structure of teacher readings to the ground-truth label, rather than mimicking them. Residual analysis on CSIQ and LIVEC shows the prediction residual is significantly correlated with background contamination, teacher dispersion, and label extremity, demonstrating the student extracts information the consensus does not contain. Under CSIQ-to-LIVEC transfer, the frozen student reaches a PLCC of 0.8416, exceeding the consensus by 0.1947. We position BiCG-Net as an offline target-level quality auditing and label-generation engine; its 39,482-parameter student is compact by design, acting as a unifying layer mapping heterogeneous teacher readings onto a common quality scale.

AI.tldr: BiCG-Net is a 39,482-parameter student network that estimates the quality of a specific target region by distilling an 11-teacher ensemble, reaching PLCC 0.9009 on CSIQ and 0.9133 on LIVEC against human MOS.
AI.motivation: Whole-image no-reference IQA is dominated by background when the target is small, and no public benchmark provides target-level human MOS.
AI.method: Target quality is estimated from nested sampling of patches expanding outward from the target box; BiCG-Net distills an 11-teacher ensemble through a linear observation model and an in-image differencing mechanism that cancels the target term and teacher-specific bias.
AI.result: On CSIQ and LIVEC the student reaches PLCCs of 0.9009 and 0.9133 against human MOS, exceeding the best single teacher and the teacher consensus; on a self-built MOS-free railway dataset it reaches PLCC 0.9855 against a weak label; under CSIQ-to-LIVEC transfer the frozen student reaches 0.8416, exceeding the consensus by 0.1947.
AI.conclusion: The student learns a mapping from the relative structure of teacher readings to the label rather than mimicking the teachers, and it serves as an offline target-level quality auditing and label-generation engine.

title: FedXCrop: Privacy-Preserving Crop Disease Detection via Federated Learning with Post-Aggregation Explainability under Non-IID Farm Distributions
comment: 26 pages. Includes 38-class crop disease classification experiments, federated learning evaluation under non-IID client distributions, and quantitative explainability analysis using Grad-CAM and SmoothGrad. Code and experimental results: this https URL
summary: Deep learning can classify crop diseases accurately from benchmark leaf images, but centralized training requires farms to share raw data, and predictions without explanations offer limited support for treatment decisions. We present FedXCrop, a federated crop disease classification pipeline that quantitatively evaluates explanations of the aggregated global model. A MobileNetV2 model trained centrally on PlantVillage achieved 99.38% test accuracy (standard deviation 0.05 over three seeds) on a fixed test set of 5,428 images across 38 classes. Federated models initialized with ImageNet weights were trained for 30 rounds across five clients. FedAvg achieved 98.81% accuracy with identically distributed clients and 98.81%, 98.59%, and 97.78% under Dirichlet label skew (alpha = 1, 0.5, and 0.1, respectively). FedProx was not significantly different from FedAvg at any heterogeneity level (McNemar p > 0.3). Grad-CAM and SmoothGrad explanations were evaluated on 380 test images. Both attributed more energy to the leaf than chance (0.70-0.78 versus 0.60), while Grad-CAM maps from federated and centralized models showed Spearman correlations of 0.74-0.76. Agreement decreased as heterogeneity increased, lesion localization was only modestly above chance, and a model-randomization test indicated that SmoothGrad maps depended substantially on image structure rather than learned parameters. In this setting, label skew reduced federated accuracy by 0.6-1.6 percentage points relative to centralized training. FedAvg largely preserved Grad-CAM behavior, while FedProx provided no measurable benefit.

AI.tldr: FedXCrop is a federated crop disease classification pipeline that quantitatively evaluates Grad-CAM and SmoothGrad explanations of the aggregated model, finding that FedAvg largely preserves explanation behavior under label skew while FedProx gives no measurable benefit.
AI.motivation: Centralized crop disease training requires farms to share raw data, and predictions without explanations offer limited support for treatment decisions, while non-IID farm distributions complicate federated training.
AI.method: A MobileNetV2 with ImageNet initialization is trained for 30 rounds across five clients under FedAvg and FedProx, with identical and Dirichlet label-skew distributions (alpha 1, 0.5 and 0.1); Grad-CAM and SmoothGrad are evaluated on 380 test images, with a model-randomization test.
AI.result: A centralized MobileNetV2 reaches 99.38% test accuracy on PlantVillage (SD 0.05 over three seeds, 5,428 test images, 38 classes); FedAvg reaches 98.81% with identical distributions and 98.81%, 98.59% and 97.78% at alpha 1, 0.5 and 0.1; FedProx is not significantly different from FedAvg (McNemar p > 0.3); both methods attribute 0.70-0.78 of energy to the leaf versus 0.60 by chance, and federated and centralized Grad-CAM maps have Spearman correlations of 0.74-0.76.
AI.conclusion: Label skew reduced federated accuracy by 0.6-1.6 percentage points relative to centralized training, FedAvg largely preserved Grad-CAM behavior, and lesion localization was only modestly above chance.

title: Homology Features for X-Ray Hyperspectral Images Segmentation
summary: Characterizing Multi-Energy X-ray Transmission (XRT) hyperspectral images presents significant challenges for traditional classification frameworks due to high-dimensional redundancy and non-linear spectral overlaps. Although manifold learning techniques such as UMAP enhance spectral representation by preserving non-linear correlations, they do not explicitly utilize the geometric structure of the embedded manifold for segmentation. This study introduces a hybrid architecture that integrates topological features derived from persistent homology with convolutional and graph neural networks. The approach computes Vietoris-Rips persistent homology on UMAP-projected superpixel point clouds to capture H 1 cyclic structures that encode spectral heterogeneity. These topological descriptors are combined with pixel-level CNN features through a broadcasting mechanism that propagates superpixel-level graph representations to full spatial resolution. Experimental results on XRT multi-energy imagery demonstrate that the proposed hybrid model significantly outperforms both CNN-only and superpixel-pooling fusion baselines, suggesting that topological features provide complementary discriminative information to local spectralspatial descriptors.

AI.tldr: A hybrid architecture adds Vietoris-Rips persistent homology features from UMAP-projected superpixel point clouds to CNN and graph neural network features for X-ray hyperspectral image segmentation, outperforming CNN-only and superpixel-pooling baselines.
AI.motivation: Multi-energy X-ray transmission hyperspectral images have high-dimensional redundancy and nonlinear spectral overlaps, and UMAP preserves nonlinear correlations but does not explicitly use the geometric structure of the embedded manifold for segmentation.
AI.method: Vietoris-Rips persistent homology is computed on UMAP-projected superpixel point clouds to capture H1 cyclic structures that encode spectral heterogeneity; these topological descriptors are combined with pixel-level CNN features through a broadcasting mechanism that propagates superpixel-level graph representations to full spatial resolution.
AI.result: The hybrid model significantly outperforms both CNN-only and superpixel-pooling fusion baselines on XRT multi-energy imagery; the abstract gives no numeric scores.
AI.conclusion: Topological features provide discriminative information complementary to local spectral-spatial descriptors.

title: CAPE-JEPA - Cross-modal Adversarial Probabilistic Embedding JEPA
comment: Accepted for publication at the British Machine Vision Conference (BMVC 2026)
summary: Cross-modal remote sensing image retrieval (RS-CMIR) requires representations that are simultaneously modality-invariant and semantically discriminative, despite the profound physical gap between heterogeneous sensors such as Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) and multispectral imagery. Recent JEPA-based Predictive self-supervised approaches such as X-JEPA formulate cross-modal alignment as a deterministic latent forecasting task, implicitly assuming uniform patch predictability and leaving cross-modal distributional alignment unaddressed. We propose CAPE-JEPA, a probabilistic cross-modal Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture with three contributions: (i) a cross-attentional Gaussian predictor outputting per-patch parameters (mu, sigma^2) conditioned on opposite-modality context, trained via negative log-likelihood to model inherent cross-sensor prediction uncertainty; (ii) adversarial distributional regularization combining unimodal isotropic Gaussian regularization with a novel cross-modal adversarial variant that aligns modality distributions via worst-case Epps-Pulley characteristic function tests without explicit sample pairing; and (iii) in-training contrastive learning with attention-pooled heads for scene-level discriminative grounding. Evaluated on BigEarthNet-14K (BEN-14K) and fMoW across SAR, multispectral, and RGB modalities, CAPE-JEPA surpasses X-JEPA by up to 13.74 points on BEN-14K and 15.59 points on fMoW, outperforming all baselines including SkySense and CROMA across both unimodal and cross-modal directions while using fewer parameters (407.30M vs. 432.72M).

AI.tldr: CAPE-JEPA is a probabilistic cross-modal JEPA for remote sensing image retrieval that predicts per-patch Gaussian parameters and adversarially aligns SAR and multispectral distributions, surpassing X-JEPA by up to 13.74 points on BEN-14K and 15.59 points on fMoW.
AI.motivation: X-JEPA treats cross-modal alignment as deterministic latent forecasting, assuming uniform patch predictability and leaving cross-modal distributional alignment unaddressed, which matters given the physical gap between SAR and multispectral sensors.
AI.method: Three components: a cross-attentional Gaussian predictor outputs per-patch mean and variance conditioned on opposite-modality context, trained by negative log-likelihood; adversarial distributional regularization combines unimodal isotropic Gaussian regularization with a cross-modal variant that aligns modality distributions via worst-case Epps-Pulley characteristic function tests without explicit sample pairing; and in-training contrastive learning with attention-pooled heads for scene-level grounding.
AI.result: On BigEarthNet-14K and fMoW across SAR, multispectral and RGB modalities, CAPE-JEPA surpasses X-JEPA by up to 13.74 points on BEN-14K and 15.59 points on fMoW, outperforms SkySense and CROMA in unimodal and cross-modal directions, and uses fewer parameters (407.30M versus 432.72M).
AI.conclusion: Modeling prediction uncertainty and aligning modality distributions adversarially improves cross-modal remote sensing retrieval with a smaller model.

title: CrossPressor: Scalable Cross-View Fusion for Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting
summary: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3D-GS) becomes increasingly difficult to scale to long multi-view sequences. Anchor-based compression methods such as ZPressor alleviate representation growth by decoding Gaussians only from a compact set of anchor feature maps, but keeping these anchors fixed forces each one to aggregate an increasing number of support views. We identify this representation--fusion mismatch and introduce \textbf{CrossPressor}, a training-free method for scalable anchor-based fusion. CrossPressor preserves all decoder-facing anchor queries while constraining the view-growing support sequence through coverage-cycled evidence routing, distributing retained spatial evidence across support views and fusion layers while keeping all support views represented. Routing before K/V projection, together with joint context packing, further reduces support-side fusion cost without retraining. CrossPressor maintains reconstruction quality close to dense fusion while achieving up to $26.12\times$ faster cross-view fusion and $1.43\times$ end-to-end acceleration on long input sequences. Our project page is at: this https URL.

AI.tldr: CrossPressor is a training-free method that makes anchor-based feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting scale to long multi-view sequences by routing evidence across support views instead of keeping anchors fixed. It keeps reconstruction quality close to dense fusion while speeding up cross-view fusion by up to 26.12 times.
AI.motivation: Anchor-based compression such as ZPressor keeps anchors fixed, so each anchor must aggregate an ever-growing number of support views, a representation-fusion mismatch that limits scalability on long sequences.
AI.method: CrossPressor keeps all decoder-facing anchor queries and uses coverage-cycled evidence routing to distribute retained spatial evidence across support views and fusion layers while keeping every support view represented. Routing is applied before K/V projection, combined with joint context packing, to cut support-side fusion cost without retraining.
AI.result: On long input sequences it achieves up to 26.12 times faster cross-view fusion and 1.43 times end-to-end acceleration, with reconstruction quality reported as close to dense fusion.
AI.conclusion: The results suggest that routing evidence across views, rather than fixing anchors, is an effective training-free way to scale feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting to long multi-view inputs.

title: Beyond Scene Shortcuts: Action-Centric Video-Text Alignment for Fine-Grained Action Understanding
summary: Fine-grained action understanding requires vision-language models to ground what an agent does, how it acts, and why it acts in spatio-temporal evidence. However, richer supervision can backfire: fine-tuned models may generate detailed action descriptions grounded in static scenes and salient objects rather than motion, a failure we call Environment-Grounded Action Hallucination (EGAH). To mitigate EGAH, we propose Staged Attention Rectification and Reinforcement (STARR), an action-centric video-text alignment framework that breaks scene-action shortcuts through Action-Environment Dissociation and reinforces action-focused grounding with an Attention Consistency Reward within Group Relative Policy Optimization. We further construct FineActionR&R, combining temporally localized captions with hierarchical and temporal-causal reasoning data. Built on Qwen2.5-VL-7B, FineActionVLM-R1 improves average MotionBench accuracy by 3.01 percentage points over its base model and achieves 91.50% on HAU-MCQ-Bench. Qualitative comparisons further indicate more faithful fine-grained action descriptions with fewer environment-induced hallucinations.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies Environment-Grounded Action Hallucination, where fine-tuned video-language models describe static scenes instead of motion, and proposes STARR, an action-centric video-text alignment framework that mitigates it. Built on Qwen2.5-VL-7B, the resulting FineActionVLM-R1 improves MotionBench accuracy by 3.01 percentage points and reaches 91.50% on HAU-MCQ-Bench.
AI.motivation: Richer fine-grained supervision can backfire, because fine-tuned models produce detailed action descriptions grounded in salient objects and static scenes rather than in motion, so existing alignment does not ensure action-faithful grounding.
AI.method: STARR combines Action-Environment Dissociation, which breaks scene-action shortcuts, with an Attention Consistency Reward inside Group Relative Policy Optimization to reinforce action-focused grounding. The authors also construct FineActionR&R, a dataset of temporally localized captions plus hierarchical and temporal-causal reasoning data.
AI.result: FineActionVLM-R1, built on Qwen2.5-VL-7B, improves average MotionBench accuracy by 3.01 percentage points over its base model and achieves 91.50% on HAU-MCQ-Bench. Qualitative comparisons are reported to show more faithful action descriptions with fewer environment-induced hallucinations.
AI.conclusion: Action-centric alignment with attention-based rewards can reduce scene-driven hallucination in fine-grained action understanding, though the abstract's evidence is mainly benchmark accuracy and qualitative examples.

title: FlashRelight: Portrait Video Relighting with Dynamic Lighting
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 23 pages, including appendix
summary: Portrait video relighting aims to modify the illumination of a portrait video while preserving photorealism and temporal stability. The task becomes particularly challenging under dynamic lighting, where illumination direction, intensity, and color vary over time. To tackle this problem, we introduce FlashRelight, a novel two-stage framework for dynamic portrait video relighting. FlashRelight first suppresses the source illumination through delighting, and then synthesizes the target dynamic lighting on an illumination-neutral portrait video. FlashRelight supports three complementary control modalities: envmap sequences for explicit frame-level lighting control, dynamic lighting text for semantic illumination editing, and lighting reference videos for visual lighting transfer. Training follows a low-cost hybrid strategy that combines static one-light-at-a-time (OLAT) data with generated dynamic-lighting portrait videos, covering both controlled illumination variation and realistic portrait motion. Extensive experiments show that FlashRelight achieves temporally coherent and photorealistic dynamic relighting while enabling flexible cross-video lighting transfer. Code is available at this https URL

AI.tldr: FlashRelight is a two-stage framework for portrait video relighting under dynamic lighting that first removes the source illumination and then synthesizes a target dynamic light. It supports envmap sequences, dynamic lighting text, and lighting reference videos as control modalities.
AI.motivation: Relighting portrait video becomes difficult when illumination direction, intensity, and color change over time, while photorealism and temporal stability must be preserved.
AI.method: FlashRelight first performs delighting to suppress the source illumination and then synthesizes the target dynamic lighting on an illumination-neutral video. Training uses a low-cost hybrid strategy that combines static one-light-at-a-time data with generated dynamic-lighting portrait videos.
AI.result: The authors report that FlashRelight achieves temporally coherent and photorealistic dynamic relighting and supports flexible cross-video lighting transfer. The abstract gives no quantitative metrics.
AI.conclusion: Decomposing relighting into delighting and dynamic synthesis, trained on a mix of static and generated data, offers a practical route to controllable dynamic portrait relighting.

title: NanoKV: High-Ratio KV Cache Compression for Autoregressive Video Generation
comment: 25 pages, 13 figures. Project page: this https URL . Code: this https URL
summary: Autoregressive video models rely on historical key-value (KV) caches to preserve scene consistency over extended rollouts, making KV storage and repeated attention over history a growing memory and computational bottleneck. Aggressive compression can degrade generation quality, while reconstructing full-dimensional KV leaves attention computation largely unchanged. We introduce NanoKV, a frozen-backbone framework for generation-aware high-ratio KV compression. NanoKV exploits redundancy across tokens and attention heads by storing shared content in cluster centers and encoding joint head-channel residuals into low-bit coefficients. Crucially, NanoKV uses different fitting objectives for Keys and Values according to their distinct roles in attention: Key decoders are optimized to preserve downstream block outputs, whereas Value encoders and decoders are fitted for faithful reconstruction through the deployed quantization path. Building on the same compressed representation, the optional NanoKV-Fast variant reuses the stored coefficients for mixed-dimensional attention, reducing computation without modifying the video backbone. Across three autoregressive video backbones, NanoKV consistently improves the quality-storage trade-off. On HY-WorldPlay, NanoKV achieves $26.09\times$ effective KV compression, nearly twice that of KVTC, while improving PSNR by 1.0 dB. NanoKV-Fast retains $20.53\times$ effective compression and achieves an approximately $1.15\times$ end-to-end speedup over KVTC.

AI.tldr: NanoKV is a frozen-backbone framework for high-ratio compression of the key-value cache in autoregressive video generation, using cluster centers and low-bit residual coefficients. On HY-WorldPlay it reaches 26.09 times effective KV compression and improves PSNR by 1.0 dB over the comparison method KVTC.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive video models depend on growing historical KV caches, so storage and repeated attention over history become memory and computation bottlenecks, while aggressive compression can degrade generation quality.
AI.method: NanoKV stores shared content in cluster centers and encodes joint head-channel residuals as low-bit coefficients, exploiting redundancy across tokens and attention heads. Keys and Values use different fitting objectives: Key decoders preserve downstream block outputs, while Value encoders and decoders are fitted for faithful reconstruction through the deployed quantization path. The optional NanoKV-Fast variant reuses the stored coefficients for mixed-dimensional attention.
AI.result: Across three autoregressive video backbones, NanoKV improves the quality-storage trade-off. On HY-WorldPlay it achieves 26.09 times effective KV compression, nearly twice that of KVTC, with 1.0 dB higher PSNR. NanoKV-Fast keeps 20.53 times effective compression and gives about 1.15 times end-to-end speedup over KVTC.
AI.conclusion: Generation-aware, role-specific fitting of compressed KV caches can deliver high compression with better quality trade-offs without modifying the video backbone.

title: Entropogram-guided Visual Realignment Decoding: Capturing the Rhythm of Multimodal Reasoning
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated remarkable progress on cross-modal reasoning tasks, yet they continue to suffer from hallucinations in long-chain reasoning processes. In this work, we revisit hallucination in MLLMs from the perspective of reasoning generation dynamics. We argue that entropy is not merely a static measure of uncertainty but a structured signal that reflects how modality information is integrated throughout decoding. Through systematic analysis, we identify two characteristic entropy patterns associated with hallucination behaviors: (1) a generally high-confidence regime corresponds to premature convergence to inappropriate multimodal interactions; and (2) local abrupt entropy transitions are associated with reasoning instability and hallucination onset. Building on these observations, we propose an entropy-aware self-introspective framework for MLLM reasoning. Our method continuously tracks entropy dynamics during decoding and performs targeted visual re-alignment when suspicious hallucination states are detected, encouraging the model to re-examine salient visual evidence at critical reasoning stages. Extensive experiments across six multimodal reasoning benchmarks spanning nine distinct evaluation settings demonstrate that our approach delivers robust improvements in reasoning accuracy and hallucination robustness, while providing new insights into the generation dynamics underlying MLLM failures. The code is available at: this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper treats entropy during decoding as a structured signal of hallucination in multimodal LLMs and proposes an entropy-aware self-introspective framework that triggers visual re-alignment when suspicious states appear. The method is reported to improve reasoning accuracy and hallucination robustness across six multimodal reasoning benchmarks.
AI.motivation: MLLMs still hallucinate in long-chain reasoning, and entropy is usually treated as a static uncertainty measure, although its dynamics may reveal how modality information is integrated during decoding.
AI.method: The authors identify two entropy patterns linked to hallucination: a generally high-confidence regime that signals premature convergence to inappropriate multimodal interactions, and local abrupt entropy transitions that signal reasoning instability. The method tracks entropy dynamics during decoding and performs targeted visual re-alignment when suspicious states are detected, prompting the model to re-examine salient visual evidence.
AI.result: Experiments across six multimodal reasoning benchmarks spanning nine evaluation settings show robust gains in reasoning accuracy and hallucination robustness. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Entropy dynamics during decoding carry diagnostic information about MLLM failures, and targeted visual re-examination at critical stages is a promising way to reduce hallucination.

title: Unaligned Image Guided Denoising via Cross-modal Conditional Flow Matching
summary: This work presents UGD-FM, a novel unaligned image guided denoising framework based on cross-modal conditional flow matching. Unlike previous approaches that assume spatially aligned inputs or only handle small-baseline rectified pairs, we address a more challenging setting where severe target noise and large-range two-dimensional cross-modal misalignment coexist. Specifically, we formulate guided denoising as a progressive flow matching process, allowing image restoration and aligned guidance aggregation to mutually reinforce each other. To support efficient few-step inference, we introduce a stage-focused and inference-consistent training strategy that focuses on task-critical denoising stages, and mitigates the training-inference mismatch. We further propose adaptive sparse guidance propagation for efficient and reliable large-range matching, regularized by perceptual and geometric auxiliary losses. Experiments demonstrate that UGD-FM achieves state-of-the-art denoising performance with only one or two inference steps, and is compatible with modern single-image restoration backbones.

AI.tldr: UGD-FM is an unaligned image guided denoising framework based on cross-modal conditional flow matching, designed for severe noise and large-range two-dimensional misalignment between the target and guidance images. It reaches state-of-the-art denoising with only one or two inference steps.
AI.motivation: Prior guided denoising methods assume spatially aligned inputs or handle only small-baseline rectified pairs, which fails when noise is severe and cross-modal misalignment is large.
AI.method: Guided denoising is formulated as a progressive flow matching process in which restoration and aligned guidance aggregation reinforce each other. A stage-focused, inference-consistent training strategy targets task-critical denoising stages to support few-step inference and reduce training-inference mismatch. Adaptive sparse guidance propagation performs efficient large-range matching, regularized by perceptual and geometric auxiliary losses.
AI.result: The authors report state-of-the-art denoising performance with only one or two inference steps, and compatibility with modern single-image restoration backbones. The abstract gives no specific metrics.
AI.conclusion: Coupling flow matching with adaptive sparse matching makes unaligned guided denoising practical for few-step inference, extending guided restoration beyond aligned or small-baseline settings.

title: DreamRealm: Exploring and Materializing Hallucination Worlds for Trustworthy Vision-Language Models
comment: 28 pages, including supplementary material. Code: this https URL . Model: this https URL
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) remain prone to visual hallucinations when correct responses depend on subtle visual details. One line of post-training methods constructs visual contrasts through image retrieval, generation, or editing to improve fine-grained perception. However, these contrasts are not built around the model's own hallucinations, making it difficult to ensure that supervision targets its actual perceptual confusions. Another line suppresses hallucinated outputs through response correction or preference learning under fixed image conditions, but leaves the design of supervision signals on the image-input side underexplored. Inspired by how humans correct misconceptions, we introduce DreamRealm, a post-training framework that explores diverse latent hallucinated responses, minimally edits original images to make them valid, and trains the model to assign each response to its supporting image. Our data construction pipeline, RealmForgePipe, mines observed and latent hallucinations from a target model and materializes them through image editing. Using hallucinations mined from Qwen3.5-9B, we construct the Realized Hallucination Dataset (RealmSet). Our training objective, RealmMatch, constructs a likelihood score matrix across image--response combinations and combines supervised learning with bidirectional contrastive losses to reinforce correct matches and suppress mismatches. Compared with the original Qwen3.5-9B model, DreamRealm improves performance across six visual perception and hallucination benchmarks, including gains of 7.26 percentage points in HallusionBench accuracy and 11.34 percentage points in MMVP pair accuracy. Together with ablation studies on data construction and training methods, these results demonstrate that hallucination assignment is a promising paradigm for improving visual perception and mitigating hallucinations.

AI.tldr: DreamRealm is a post-training framework that mines an MLLM's own latent hallucinations, minimally edits images so the hallucinated responses become valid, and trains the model to assign each response to its supporting image. It improves Qwen3.5-9B on six visual perception and hallucination benchmarks, with gains of 7.26 points on HallusionBench accuracy and 11.34 points on MMVP pair accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing visual contrast methods are not built around the model's own hallucinations, and response-correction or preference methods leave image-side supervision underexplored, so supervision may miss the model's actual perceptual confusions.
AI.method: RealmForgePipe mines observed and latent hallucinations from a target model and materializes them through image editing, producing the Realized Hallucination Dataset RealmSet from hallucinations mined from Qwen3.5-9B. The training objective RealmMatch builds a likelihood score matrix over image-response combinations and combines supervised learning with bidirectional contrastive losses.
AI.result: Compared with the original Qwen3.5-9B, DreamRealm improves performance across six visual perception and hallucination benchmarks, with gains of 7.26 points in HallusionBench accuracy and 11.34 points in MMVP pair accuracy. Ablations on data construction and training methods are reported.
AI.conclusion: Hallucination assignment, matching each response to its supporting image, is presented as a promising paradigm for improving visual perception and reducing hallucination.

title: CoDecide: Content-Adaptive Video Decoding for High-Throughput Video Analytics
comment: Accepted at WACV 2027. 12 pages including supplementary material
summary: Analytics on video archives are bottlenecked by decoding. In a dense pipeline that runs a detector on every frame, decoding is a small fraction of the runtime, but once the detector is restricted to selected frames, decoding takes over as the main cost. We introduce CoDecide, a retrospective analytics system that only decodes the frames where new content appears, using signals from the compressed bitstream to find them. Motion tells us something is moving, but not whether it is new to the scene or has been there the whole time. To make that distinction, we supervise a lightweight compressed-domain student on a label-free novelty signal from a frozen DINOv2 teacher, which fires on semantically new regions rather than on any motion. Consequently, the student model generalizes to new camera deployments without requiring per-camera retraining. At inference, it decides which frames to decode and which regions to reconstruct. Detections from the decoded frames are propagated to the skipped frames using motion vectors. We evaluate CoDecide with a leave-one-dataset-out protocol on VIRAT, MEVA, and ShanghaiTech. Against a dense per-frame detector, CoDecide recovers more moving-object detections than prior compressed-domain selectors at an equivalent decoding budget, outperforming even a competitor trained directly on the target camera. CoDecide runs 15 to 24x faster than a pipeline that decodes and detects every frame. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: CoDecide is a retrospective video analytics system that decodes only frames where new content appears, using compressed-bitstream signals and a lightweight student trained on a DINOv2 novelty teacher. It runs 15 to 24 times faster than a pipeline that decodes and detects every frame.
AI.motivation: Once a detector runs on selected frames only, video decoding becomes the main cost, and motion alone cannot tell new content from motion of objects that have been in the scene all along.
AI.method: A compressed-domain student is supervised with a label-free novelty signal from a frozen DINOv2 teacher, so it fires on semantically new regions rather than on any motion, and it generalizes to new cameras without per-camera retraining. At inference it decides which frames to decode and which regions to reconstruct, and detections on decoded frames are propagated to skipped frames using motion vectors.
AI.result: Under leave-one-dataset-out evaluation on VIRAT, MEVA, and ShanghaiTech, CoDecide recovers more moving-object detections than prior compressed-domain selectors at an equivalent decoding budget, and outperforms a competitor trained on the target camera. It runs 15 to 24 times faster than dense decode-and-detect.
AI.conclusion: Novelty-aware, compressed-domain frame selection can make video analytics on archives much cheaper while keeping detection recall, and it transfers across camera deployments without retraining.

title: A 3D foundation model unifying CT interpretation and segmentation
comment: 114 pages, including Supplementary Information; 7 main figures and 2 Extended Data figures
summary: Radiologists interpret computed tomography (CT) scans by jointly determining what a finding represents and where it lies in three-dimensional (3D) anatomy. However, CT models have treated CT interpretation and 3D segmentation as separate tasks, leaving textual findings spatially unverifiable and overlooking potential synergy between clinical understanding and spatial perception. Here we present HoloCT, a generalist 3D foundation model unifying CT interpretation and voxel-level segmentation by jointly modelling whole-volume context and fine-grained anatomical detail, providing 3D masks as evidence. We curated HoloDATA, comprising 195,921 CT scans from 73 public datasets and six clinical cohorts, with 6.2 million instruction dialogues and 2.8 million CT-mask pairs. Across 346 tasks spanning segmentation, lesion screening, visual question answering, and report generation on 61 internal and 12 external datasets, HoloCT outperformed specialist and foundation models. In multicentre validation across 11,455 clinical CT scans from five hospitals, HoloCT outperformed competing models in lesion segmentation and report generation by 18.2 and 15.3 points. It also achieved 85.1% mean accuracy in screening thyroid tumours and colon lesions, exceeding all four participating radiologists in a retrospective reader study. Further analyses revealed bidirectional semantic-spatial synergy: language-guided segmentation delineated unseen anatomical structures and lesions as well as diffuse free-text findings, outperforming the leading approach by 22.1 points, whereas prompting the model to generate corresponding 3D masks alongside its textual outputs significantly improved interpretation performance. HoloCT shows that clinical understanding and spatial perception can be learned together within a single foundation model and offers a path towards more accurate and reliable CT analysis.

AI.tldr: HoloCT is a generalist 3D foundation model that unifies CT interpretation and voxel-level segmentation, providing 3D masks as evidence for its textual findings. It outperforms specialist and foundation models across 346 tasks and matches or exceeds radiologists in a reader study on thyroid tumour and colon lesion screening.
AI.motivation: CT models have treated interpretation and 3D segmentation as separate tasks, which leaves textual findings spatially unverifiable and ignores possible synergy between clinical understanding and spatial perception.
AI.method: HoloCT jointly models whole-volume context and fine-grained anatomical detail. It is trained on HoloDATA, which the authors describe as 195,921 CT scans from 73 public datasets and six clinical cohorts, with 6.2 million instruction dialogues and 2.8 million CT-mask pairs.
AI.result: Across 346 tasks covering segmentation, lesion screening, visual question answering, and report generation on 61 internal and 12 external datasets, HoloCT outperforms specialist and foundation models. In multicentre validation on 11,455 clinical scans from five hospitals it beats competing models by 18.2 points in lesion segmentation and 15.3 points in report generation, and reaches 85.1% mean accuracy in screening thyroid tumours and colon lesions, exceeding all four participating radiologists in a retrospective reader study. Language-guided segmentation outperforms the leading approach by 22.1 points.
AI.conclusion: Clinical understanding and spatial perception can be learned jointly in one foundation model, and generating 3D masks alongside text improves interpretation, pointing toward more accurate and verifiable CT analysis.

title: Spatially and Compositionally Controlled Multimodal Glioblastoma MRI Synthesis with Latent Diffusion
summary: Glioblastoma exhibits substantial heterogeneity in tumour morphology and composition across MRI modalities, often making available clinical datasets highly unbalanced in terms of patient pathologies. We propose a two-stage latent diffusion model (LDM) framework for the generation of explicitly controllable 2D glioblastoma MRI scans. First, a segmentation LDM generates tumour maps conditioned on location, spatial extent, axial position, and subregion composition. Second, a modality-conditioned LDM with ControlNet generates T1, T1Gd, T2, and FLAIR images adhering to the requested segmentation. On a held-out test set, generated segmentations achieved a mean centroid error of 0.842 pixels and a subregion proportion error of 0.795 percentage points. ControlNet improved Fréchet inception distance (FID) across all four modalities, reducing pooled FID from 42.59 to 36.12. An expert reader study yielded mean quality ratings of 6.60 for real images, 6.83 for ControlNet-generated images, and 6.77 for fully synthetic images.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a two-stage latent diffusion framework that generates 2D glioblastoma MRI scans with explicit control over tumour location, extent, axial position, and subregion composition. Generated segmentations are accurate, and ControlNet lowers pooled FID from 42.59 to 36.12.
AI.motivation: Glioblastoma heterogeneity makes clinical MRI datasets highly imbalanced in pathology, so controllable synthetic data is needed to address this imbalance.
AI.method: A segmentation latent diffusion model first generates tumour maps conditioned on location, spatial extent, axial position, and subregion composition. A modality-conditioned latent diffusion model with ControlNet then generates T1, T1Gd, T2, and FLAIR images that adhere to the requested segmentation.
AI.result: On a held-out test set the generated segmentations reach a mean centroid error of 0.842 pixels and a subregion proportion error of 0.795 percentage points. ControlNet improves FID across all four modalities, reducing pooled FID from 42.59 to 36.12. An expert reader study rated real images 6.60, ControlNet-generated images 6.83, and fully synthetic images 6.77.
AI.conclusion: Segmentation-conditioned latent diffusion with ControlNet can generate controllable and realistic glioblastoma MRI, with expert ratings close to those of real images.

title: MKD2World: A Typed Spatial MarkDown World Model For Web Agents
summary: Graphical user interface (GUI) agents can improve decision-making with world-model foresight, provided that predicted states accurately reflect post-action interfaces. Existing state representations fail to jointly capture interface layout, UI semantics, and explicit locations. We introduce Typed Spatial Markdown (TSM), a Markdown-style textual state representation for desktop web interfaces. TSM serializes block-level and atomic-level UI elements according to their spatial relationships, jointly encoding their types, visual semantics, explicit locations, optional control states, and hierarchical membership. To train a screenshot-to-TSM renderer, we construct AtomBlock-WebUI, a dataset with precise annotations at both granularities. By injecting element-type labels into HTML and directly extracting bounding boxes after rendering, we avoid annotation errors caused by post-hoc inference from webpage structures. Building on TSM, we propose MKD2World, a desktop web world model trained in two stages for current-state description and action-conditioned next-state prediction. During inference, the web agent queries MKD2World as needed and performs a ``digest'' step, in which it interprets each predicted state and extracts task-relevant evidence for selecting the best action. Experiments show that MKD2World-9B achieves an EleF1 score of 26.50 on the out-of-domain test set, outperforming GPT-5.6-Sol(14.98) by 11.52 points. Across Online-Mind2Web tasks, MKD2World-9B improves the success rate of the Qwen3.5-35B web agent from 22.94% to 37.61%, achieving competitive performance among leading open-source GUI world models. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: MKD2World is a desktop web world model built on Typed Spatial Markdown, a textual state representation that encodes UI layout, element types, semantics, and explicit locations for web agents. The 9B model outperforms GPT-5.6-Sol on an out-of-domain EleF1 test and raises a Qwen3.5-35B web agent's Online-Mind2Web success rate from 22.94% to 37.61%.
AI.motivation: GUI agents benefit from world-model foresight only if predicted states faithfully reflect post-action interfaces, and existing state representations do not jointly capture layout, UI semantics, and explicit locations.
AI.method: Typed Spatial Markdown serializes block-level and atomic-level UI elements by spatial relationships, encoding types, visual semantics, locations, optional control states, and hierarchical membership. The authors build AtomBlock-WebUI with annotations at both granularities, extracting bounding boxes after rendering HTML with injected element-type labels. MKD2World is trained in two stages, for current-state description and action-conditioned next-state prediction, and agents use a digest step to extract task-relevant evidence from predicted states.
AI.result: MKD2World-9B reaches an EleF1 of 26.50 on the out-of-domain test set, 11.52 points above GPT-5.6-Sol at 14.98. On Online-Mind2Web tasks it raises the success rate of the Qwen3.5-35B web agent from 22.94% to 37.61%.
AI.conclusion: A typed spatial textual state representation can make world models useful for web agents and is competitive among open-source GUI world models.

title: LungMend: A Healthy-Only Latent Diffusion Shape Prior for Lung Mask Correction in Severe Tuberculosis CT
comment: 5 pages (4 + 1 references), 2 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to IEEE ISBI 2027. Code: this https URL
summary: Lung segmentation models such as R231 are widely used, but they fail on severe tuberculosis (TB) CT: cavities and consolidations look like non-lung tissue and are left out of the mask. We present LungMend, a post-processing model that corrects such masks using only healthy anatomy. A latent diffusion model, trained on healthy lungs with synthetically corrupted masks, learns to recover the complete lung from the faulty mask and the bone anatomy, without any pathological data or CT intensities. LungMend recovers cavities and consolidations that R231 misses and improves accuracy on expert-annotated slices. Code: this https URL

AI.tldr: LungMend is a post-processing latent diffusion model that corrects lung segmentation masks in severe tuberculosis CT, recovering cavities and consolidations that standard segmenters such as R231 miss. It is trained only on healthy lungs with synthetically corrupted masks.
AI.motivation: Common lung segmentation models fail on severe TB CT because cavities and consolidations resemble non-lung tissue and are excluded from the mask, and pathological training data is scarce.
AI.method: A latent diffusion model is trained on healthy lungs with synthetically corrupted masks, and learns to recover the complete lung from the faulty mask and bone anatomy, without pathological data or CT intensities.
AI.result: LungMend recovers cavities and consolidations that R231 misses and improves accuracy on expert-annotated slices. The abstract gives no numerical values.
AI.conclusion: A healthy-only anatomical shape prior can correct pathology-induced segmentation errors, offering a way to adapt lung segmentation to severe disease without disease-specific training data.

title: BudgetSplat: Budget-Controllable Generalizable Gaussian Splatting
summary: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting enables efficient generalizable novel view synthesis, but existing pixel-aligned methods often generate highly redundant Gaussian primitives, causing the final representation size and rendering cost to grow rapidly with image resolution and the number of input views. We propose BudgetSplat, a budget-controllable feed-forward framework that adapts the final Gaussian representation to a user-specified preservation ratio. Rather than treating compaction as simple importance ranking, we formulate it as a joint problem of importance estimation, spatial coverage, and cross-view redundancy. A single trained model supports varying numbers of context views and multiple test-time budgets without per-budget retraining or per-scene compression. To realize this formulation, Intra-Cross Mask Supervision provides structure-, coverage-, and redundancy-aware guidance for learning Gaussian importance, while budget-conditioned feature modulation adapts Gaussian opacity and attributes to the requested preservation ratio. Coverage-Aware Budget Selection further combines patch-wise pre-selection, view-wise opacity ranking, and 3D redundancy suppression to construct compact yet spatially distributed Gaussian representations. Experiments on indoor reconstruction and cross-dataset generalization demonstrate consistent quality--size trade-offs across different input view counts and preservation ratios, substantially reducing final representation storage and rendering cost while preserving rendering quality.

AI.tldr: BudgetSplat is a feed-forward Gaussian splatting framework that adapts the size of the final representation to a user-specified preservation ratio, with a single trained model supporting varying view counts and budgets. It gives consistent quality-size trade-offs and reduces storage and rendering cost on indoor reconstruction and cross-dataset generalization.
AI.motivation: Pixel-aligned feed-forward methods produce highly redundant Gaussians, so representation size and rendering cost grow rapidly with resolution and the number of input views.
AI.method: Compaction is formulated as a joint problem of importance estimation, spatial coverage, and cross-view redundancy. Intra-Cross Mask Supervision guides learning of Gaussian importance, budget-conditioned feature modulation adapts opacity and attributes to the requested ratio, and Coverage-Aware Budget Selection combines patch-wise pre-selection, view-wise opacity ranking, and 3D redundancy suppression.
AI.result: Experiments on indoor reconstruction and cross-dataset generalization show consistent quality-size trade-offs across input view counts and preservation ratios, with substantially reduced storage and rendering cost while rendering quality is preserved. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: A single budget-controllable model can produce compact yet spatially distributed Gaussian representations without per-budget retraining or per-scene compression.

title: SpikePose: Lightweight Video Human Pose Estimation
summary: Efficient video human pose estimation must balance localisation accuracy, motion quality, and energy cost. We present SpikePose, a lightweight video pose estimator that pairs a frame-reset, single-step spiking encoder with motion-aligned heatmap memory (MAM). The encoder supplies per-frame spatial evidence, while MAM estimates joint displacement, aligns historical heatmaps, and adaptively fuses them with current predictions. By confining temporal reasoning to a compact, lightweight module outside the spiking backbone, SpikePose helps bridge the gap between spiking and classical Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) on large-scale, non-event-driven video tasks. We evaluate spatial accuracy, motion errors, and estimated arithmetic energy on MPII and a fixed NTU60 Cross-Subject subset. Against the architecture-matched ANN with MAM, SpikePose cuts estimated arithmetic energy by 91.4% at a cost of just 1.12 points in head-bone-normalised PCK at 0.5 threshold (PCK_HB(0.5)). Within SpikePose, adding MAM reduces velocity and acceleration errors by 28.13% and 31.46% while slightly improving localisation, at a cost of only 0.003M parameters and 0.0023 analytical GFLOPs per frame. Code will be released on GitHub upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: SpikePose is a lightweight video human pose estimator that pairs a frame-reset spiking encoder with a motion-aligned heatmap memory module. Against an architecture-matched ANN it cuts estimated arithmetic energy by 91.4% at a cost of 1.12 points in PCK_HB(0.5).
AI.motivation: Efficient video pose estimation must balance localisation accuracy, motion quality, and energy, and spiking networks have lagged classical ANNs on large-scale, non-event-driven video tasks.
AI.method: A frame-reset, single-step spiking encoder supplies per-frame spatial evidence. The motion-aligned heatmap memory (MAM), kept outside the spiking backbone, estimates joint displacement, aligns historical heatmaps, and adaptively fuses them with current predictions.
AI.result: On MPII and a fixed NTU60 Cross-Subject subset, SpikePose cuts estimated arithmetic energy by 91.4% relative to the architecture-matched ANN with MAM, at a cost of 1.12 points in head-bone-normalised PCK at 0.5. Within SpikePose, MAM reduces velocity and acceleration errors by 28.13% and 31.46% while slightly improving localisation, adding only 0.003M parameters and 0.0023 analytical GFLOPs per frame.
AI.conclusion: Confining temporal reasoning to a compact module is a practical way to narrow the gap between spiking and classical ANN pose estimators, with a large energy saving for a small accuracy cost.

title: Learning to Track Cells from Sparse Annotations in 3D Time-Lapse Microscopy
summary: Reconstructing cell lineages from 3D time-lapse microscopy requires distinguishing cell motion from division and inferring temporally consistent connections. When only a subset of cells is annotated, however, training procedures that treat unannotated regions as background or incorrect correspondences can be problematic. We propose a cell tracking pipeline that integrates detection from sparse annotations, calibration of candidate connections using image features, and joint selection of lineage graph events. For detection, we combine the outputs of 2.5D and 3D models trained to suppress erroneous background supervision at unannotated cells. We then calibrate ordinary link and division probabilities using motion features from dense flow, correspondence features from a learned cell-matching model, and features from models that identify cells immediately before division, dividing parents, and daughters immediately after division. Ordinary links, divisions represented as daughter pairs, and node inclusion are selected jointly under a surrogate objective derived from the evaluation metric, followed by gap filling and temporal coordinate refinement. The pipeline achieves an overall score of 0.9762 in 5-fold cross-validation on 199 videos from 2 zebrafish embryos. With candidates and calibrated values held fixed, joint selection outperforms a sequential method that allows replacement of existing divisions and reoptimization of ordinary links by 0.0105. The improvement arises primarily from division recovery.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a 3D cell tracking pipeline that works from sparse annotations, combining detection, feature-based calibration of candidate links, and joint selection of lineage events. It reaches an overall score of 0.9762 in 5-fold cross-validation on 199 zebrafish embryo videos.
AI.motivation: Reconstructing cell lineages from 3D time-lapse microscopy is hard when only a subset of cells is annotated, because training that treats unannotated regions as background or incorrect correspondences can be misleading.
AI.method: Detection combines 2.5D and 3D models trained to suppress erroneous background supervision at unannotated cells. Ordinary link and division probabilities are calibrated with motion features from dense flow, correspondence features from a learned cell-matching model, and features from models that identify cells before division, dividing parents, and daughters. Links, divisions, and node inclusion are selected jointly under a surrogate objective derived from the evaluation metric, followed by gap filling and temporal refinement.
AI.result: The pipeline achieves an overall score of 0.9762 in 5-fold cross-validation on 199 videos from 2 zebrafish embryos. With candidates and calibrated values fixed, joint selection beats a sequential method by 0.0105, mainly through better division recovery.
AI.conclusion: Joint selection of lineage events under a metric-derived objective, combined with detection that tolerates sparse labels, improves cell tracking, with most of the gain coming from recovering divisions.

title: Learning Implicit Solves for Dynamic Simulations
summary: High-fidelity simulation of dynamical systems is central to scientific discovery and engineering design, yet remains computationally demanding. Here we introduce the Implicit Neural Operator Solver (INOS), which learns the implicit solve and encodes a time integrator. INOS pretrains a neural operator from static equilibrium solutions and reuses it within Newmark-$\beta$ integration. At each time increment, the integrator forms an effective equilibrium problem, the pretrained neural operator infers the next-step solution field, and the Newmark relations advance the dynamic state. Numerical examples in linear and nonlinear elastodynamics demonstrate accurate full-field predictions without dynamic trajectory supervision. Comparative results show that INOS, evaluated zero-shot, achieves higher predictive accuracy than neural solver baselines trained on dynamic simulations. In addition, INOS delivers over 4,600$\times$ speedup in nonlinear simulations over sequential classical finite-element solvers. INOS natively accommodates changes in dynamic conditions and enables reuse of the pretrained operator across spatial and temporal discretizations. Further evaluation demonstrates a stable million-step rollout. These findings establish INOS as a reusable neural implicit solver for accurate, efficient, and robust dynamic modeling.

AI.tldr: INOS, the Implicit Neural Operator Solver, learns the implicit solve step of a time integrator, pretrained from static equilibrium solutions and used within Newmark-beta integration. It is reported to give over 4,600 times speedup on nonlinear simulations versus sequential finite-element solvers, evaluated zero-shot.
AI.motivation: High-fidelity dynamic simulation is central to science and engineering but computationally demanding, and neural solvers usually need dynamic trajectory supervision.
AI.method: A neural operator is pretrained on static equilibrium solutions and reused at each time increment inside Newmark-beta integration. The integrator forms an effective equilibrium problem, the operator infers the next-step solution field, and the Newmark relations advance the dynamic state.
AI.result: In linear and nonlinear elastodynamics examples INOS gives accurate full-field predictions without dynamic trajectory supervision, and zero-shot it beats neural solver baselines trained on dynamic simulations. It delivers over 4,600 times speedup on nonlinear simulations over sequential classical finite-element solvers, and a stable million-step rollout is demonstrated.
AI.conclusion: Learning the implicit solve from static equilibria yields a reusable neural implicit solver that is accurate, efficient, and robust across changing dynamic conditions and discretizations.

title: Matched but Not Better: An Equivalence-Tested Benchmark of Quantum Machine Learning on Six Clinical Datasets and the QML-Health-READY Reporting Framework
summary: Background: Quantum machine learning (QML) is promoted for clinical prediction, but comparisons with classical models are rarely paired or tested for equivalence. Methods: We compared a quantum-kernel support vector machine (QSVM; 4 qubits, tuned bandwidth) and a variational quantum classifier (VQC) with five tuned classical models across six public clinical datasets. All models used identical four-component inputs and 25 cross-validation splits. Paired AUROC differences were assessed using a corrected resampled t-test, Holm-adjusted equivalence tests (margins: +/-0.02 and +/-0.05), and random-effects pooling. Ablation, noise, finite-shot, and implementation-fault analyses were conducted. We propose QML-Health-READY, an eight-domain reporting framework. Results: Neither quantum model significantly outperformed any classical comparator. Pooled across datasets, QSVM differed from the kernel-matched radial basis function (RBF) SVM by -0.006 AUROC (95% CI: -0.017 to +0.004), equivalent to +/-0.02. VQC differed from the best classical model by -0.007 (95% CI: -0.019 to +0.004). QSVM was equivalent to RBF SVM within +/-0.05 in four of six datasets but was significantly worse than the best classical model on NHANES 2017-18 (-0.076). A classically trivial product-state kernel performed as well as the entangling kernel. With depolarizing noise (p = 0.01) and 1,024 shots per kernel entry, QSVM AUROC decreased by 0.054 (95% CI: 0.036 to 0.071). Untuned bandwidth produced near-chance AUROC (0.48-0.59). Conclusions: Correctly configured quantum classifiers approached but did not exceed tuned classical models. Finite-shot estimation, rather than gate noise, was their main practical cost, while configuration errors could reverse conclusions. QML-Health-READY defines reporting requirements for credible claims.

AI.tldr: The paper benchmarks quantum machine learning against five tuned classical models on six clinical datasets using equivalence tests, finding that correctly configured quantum classifiers approach but do not exceed tuned classical models. It also proposes QML-Health-READY, an eight-domain reporting framework.
AI.motivation: Quantum machine learning is promoted for clinical prediction, but comparisons with classical models are rarely paired or tested for equivalence.
AI.method: A quantum-kernel SVM (QSVM, 4 qubits, tuned bandwidth) and a variational quantum classifier (VQC) are compared with five tuned classical models using identical four-component inputs and 25 cross-validation splits. Paired AUROC differences are assessed with a corrected resampled t-test, Holm-adjusted equivalence tests with margins of plus or minus 0.02 and 0.05, and random-effects pooling, together with ablation, noise, finite-shot, and implementation-fault analyses.
AI.result: Neither quantum model significantly outperforms any classical comparator. Pooled, QSVM differs from the kernel-matched RBF SVM by -0.006 AUROC (95% CI -0.017 to +0.004), within plus or minus 0.02. QSVM is significantly worse than the best classical model on NHANES 2017-18 (-0.076). A product-state kernel performs as well as the entangling kernel. With depolarizing noise and 1,024 shots per kernel entry, QSVM AUROC drops by 0.054. Untuned bandwidth gives near-chance AUROC.
AI.conclusion: Correctly configured quantum classifiers match but do not beat tuned classical models, finite-shot estimation is the main practical cost, and configuration errors can reverse conclusions, so the proposed reporting framework targets credible claims.

title: The Confidence Score: a New Measure on Kernels
summary: Across a wide range of applications, kernel measures are used to tune hyperparameters, select among candidate kernels, and assess the suitability of kernels for specific learning tasks. For classification, kernel measures are used to predict which kernels may produce accurate kernel classifiers. Many existing kernel measures, such as alignment to the ideal kernel, are designed to reward kernels which captures all samples from the same class as similar. While effective in many settings, this requirement is unnecessarily restrictive for classification, where classes may exhibit substantial internal structure. In this work, the "Confidence Score", a new kernel measure, is proposed. Unlike alignment-to-the-ideal kernel measures, the Confidence Score measures the alignment between an encoding of the ground truth and that ground truth projected by the kernel, allowing kernels that preserve intra-class structure to achieve high scores. Through experiments, it is demonstrated that the Confidence Score exhibits a higher correlation with classification accuracy across a variety of kernels on both real-world and synthetic datasets, compared to select other kernel measures.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes the Confidence Score, a kernel measure that aligns an encoding of the ground truth with its kernel projection, so kernels that preserve intra-class structure can score highly. It correlates more strongly with classification accuracy than other kernel measures on real and synthetic datasets.
AI.motivation: Common kernel measures such as alignment to the ideal kernel reward kernels that map all same-class samples together, which is unnecessarily restrictive when classes have substantial internal structure.
AI.method: The Confidence Score measures the alignment between an encoding of the ground truth and the ground truth projected by the kernel, so it does not require intra-class collapse.
AI.result: Across a variety of kernels on real-world and synthetic datasets, the Confidence Score shows a higher correlation with classification accuracy than selected other kernel measures. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Measuring alignment with the kernel-projected ground truth gives a better predictor of kernel classifier accuracy when classes have internal structure.

title: Recasting Visual Language Models as EEG Foundation Models for Clinical Neurodiagnostics
summary: Historically automated electroencephalography (EEG) systems was done using task-specific supervised models trained on purposely annotated data. A more recent modeling paradigm relies on creating a unified representation, or a 'foundation model', for multiple modality-specific tasks through large-scale domain-specific pretraining on the unannotated EEG signal. The quality of this unified representation directly depends on the availability of the modality-specific datasets. At the same time, generalist Vision Language Models (VLMs) exhibit broad few-shot learning capacities as well as good fine-tuning adaptability to different visual and language tasks. Can VLMs learn how to read and interpret EEG visually, emulating to a degree the way human clinicians inspect the EEG patterns? In this work we make a case that they can: we show that generalist VLMs without large-scale EEG pretraining perform competitively across a collection of clinical neuro-diagnostic tasks, can adapt to different tasks in a few-shot learning setting better than specialist foundation models, and exhibit better performance with model scaling when modality-specific models fail to exhibit.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that generalist vision-language models can read EEG visually and perform competitively on clinical neurodiagnostic tasks without large-scale EEG pretraining. They adapt better than specialist EEG foundation models in few-shot settings and benefit more from scaling.
AI.motivation: EEG foundation models need large modality-specific pretraining datasets, while generalist VLMs already show few-shot learning and fine-tuning adaptability, raising the question of whether they can interpret EEG the way clinicians inspect it.
AI.method: The authors evaluate generalist VLMs on a collection of clinical neurodiagnostic tasks, with EEG presented visually, without large-scale EEG pretraining, and compare few-shot adaptation and model scaling against specialist foundation models.
AI.result: Generalist VLMs perform competitively across the clinical neuro-diagnostic tasks. They adapt to new tasks in few-shot settings better than specialist foundation models, and show better performance with model scaling where modality-specific models do not. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Generalist VLMs are a credible route to EEG interpretation that does not depend on EEG-specific pretraining, which may ease the data bottleneck for clinical EEG models.

title: FedSharp: Byzantine Robust Decentralized Federated Learning Under Noisy Channel
comment: 6 pages, 4 figures, submitted for possible publication
summary: Decentralized federated learning (DFL) eliminates the central aggregation server but remains vulnerable to data heterogeneity, Byzantine attacks, and channel noise. We show that noise accumulates as models propagate across nodes, becoming increasingly significant as the learning rate decays. Moreover, accumulated noise enables Byzantine attackers to exploit loss-based model selection by mimicking honest model averages. To address these challenges, we propose screened, hop-aware, ranked, proximal averaging, a robust DFL framework (FedSharp). In this approach, each node maintains models from its 2b predecessors, ensuring at least b honest candidates when at most b nodes are Byzantine. FedSharp screens suspicious models using coordinate-wise median deviations, averages the b lowest-loss candidates to reduce fresh channel-noise variance by a factor of b, and applies noise-adaptive gradient-norm regularization and proximal training to mitigate accumulated noise and non-IID drift. Experiments on a 100-node ring with 33 Byzantine nodes show that FedSharp achieves 93.5-94.9% accuracy on MNIST, compared with 29.4-38.1% for a state-of-the-art single-model-selection benchmark, and 32.8-48.8% on CIFAR-10, compared with 10.0-30.5%, across Gaussian and hidden attacks under IID and non-IID data. On MNIST, FedSharp also achieves accuracy within approximately one percentage point of the benchmark operating without channel noise.

AI.tldr: FedSharp is a Byzantine-robust decentralized federated learning framework that screens suspicious neighbour models, averages the lowest-loss candidates to reduce channel-noise variance, and regularizes against accumulated noise and non-IID drift. On a 100-node ring with 33 Byzantine nodes it reaches 93.5 to 94.9% on MNIST, compared with 29.4 to 38.1% for a single-model-selection benchmark.
AI.motivation: Decentralized federated learning removes the central server but is vulnerable to data heterogeneity, Byzantine attacks, and channel noise, and noise accumulates as models propagate across nodes while attackers can exploit loss-based model selection.
AI.method: Each node keeps models from its 2b predecessors, ensuring at least b honest candidates when at most b nodes are Byzantine. Suspicious models are screened using coordinate-wise median deviations, and the b lowest-loss candidates are averaged to reduce fresh channel-noise variance by a factor of b. Noise-adaptive gradient-norm regularization and proximal training mitigate accumulated noise and non-IID drift.
AI.result: On a 100-node ring with 33 Byzantine nodes, FedSharp reaches 93.5 to 94.9% accuracy on MNIST versus 29.4 to 38.1% for the benchmark, and 32.8 to 48.8% on CIFAR-10 versus 10.0 to 30.5%, across Gaussian and hidden attacks under IID and non-IID data. On MNIST it is within about one percentage point of the benchmark run without channel noise.
AI.conclusion: Combining hop-aware screening, ranked averaging, and noise-adaptive regularization makes decentralized federated learning robust to both Byzantine attackers and channel noise.

title: Exploring the Privacy--Size Tradeoff for Differentially Private Self-Attentive Variational Autoencoders
comment: ICAIF 2026, Financial AI Security, Privacy and Safety workshop. Poster session
summary: Data tends to be most useful when it is shared, and the data most worth sharing is often the data that privacy obligations restrict. Synthetic data from a generator trained under differential privacy (DP) is one way to reconcile the two, but its utility depends on the privacy budget $\varepsilon$ and on how much data the generator sees - a parameter that most data sharing applications of synthetic data control. We present SAVANT, a self-attentive variational autoencoder for tabular data trained with DP-SGD that, to our knowledge, is the first to combine attention, a VAE, and DP in one tabular model. We evaluate it against two marginal mechanisms, PrivBayes and MST, jointly over the privacy budget and the dataset size on two public datasets, measuring the utility a downstream classifier loses by training on synthetic rather than real data. We find that, under the same DP guarantee, more data generally means more utility. For the marginal mechanisms it absorbs most of what a strict budget costs, and a noise-scaling argument suggests DP-SGD exchanges data fo budget at a worse rate. Two independent membership-inference attacks, judged against a measured null, found no aggregate membership signal.

AI.tldr: SAVANT is a self-attentive variational autoencoder for tabular data trained with DP-SGD, compared with PrivBayes and MST across privacy budget and dataset size; under the same DP guarantee, more data generally means more utility.
AI.motivation: Synthetic data from differentially private generators trades utility against the privacy budget and the amount of data the generator sees, and how these two parameters interact for tabular generators was not clear.
AI.method: A self-attentive variational autoencoder for tabular data trained with DP-SGD, claimed to be the first tabular model to combine attention, a VAE and DP; evaluated against two marginal mechanisms, PrivBayes and MST, on two public datasets by the utility a downstream classifier loses when trained on synthetic rather than real data.
AI.result: Under the same DP guarantee more data generally gives more utility; for the marginal mechanisms more data absorbs most of what a strict budget costs; a noise-scaling argument suggests DP-SGD exchanges data for budget at a worse rate; two membership-inference attacks, judged against a measured null, found no aggregate membership signal.
AI.conclusion: Data volume is a strong lever for synthetic-data utility under DP, and DP-SGD based generators may convert data into privacy budget less efficiently than marginal mechanisms.

title: C-GRPO: Conformal Group Relative Policy Optimization
summary: Reasoning-oriented language model training increasingly relies on multiple on-policy rollouts, but standard Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) uses a fixed group size, wasting compute on easy prompts and under-exploring hard ones. Existing adaptive-budget methods alleviate this inefficiency, yet their stopping rules are heuristic and do not provide a finite-sample calibration guarantee. We propose CGRPO, which replaces the fixed rollout budget of standard GPRO with calibrated conformal thresholds over task-specific nonconformity scores, combining Adaptive Prediction Set (APS)-style calibration for closed-form reasoning, a first-success score for execution-based code, automatic miscoverage selection, and periodic re-calibration. We prove finite-sample coverage for the resulting stopping rule and show that, under monotone policy improvement, recalibration induces a non-increasing expected training budget. Across six benchmarks spanning mathematics, graduate-level science, and code generation, CGRPO reduces mean training rollouts by 49-70% relative to fixed-budget GRPO while retaining strong fixed-budget accuracy, achieves the strongest pass@1 among evaluated static and dynamic baselines on different datasets, and transfers across model families with up to 82% rollout savings.

AI.tldr: C-GRPO replaces the fixed rollout group size of GRPO with calibrated conformal stopping thresholds, cutting mean training rollouts by 49-70% on six reasoning and code benchmarks while keeping strong fixed-budget accuracy.
AI.motivation: Standard GRPO uses a fixed group size that wastes compute on easy prompts and under-explores hard ones, and existing adaptive-budget stopping rules are heuristic and lack a finite-sample calibration guarantee.
AI.method: Calibrated conformal thresholds over task-specific nonconformity scores: APS-style calibration for closed-form reasoning and a first-success score for execution-based code, with automatic miscoverage selection and periodic recalibration; finite-sample coverage is proved for the resulting stopping rule.
