AI.result: Across six benchmarks in mathematics, graduate-level science and code generation, mean training rollouts fall by 49-70% relative to fixed-budget GRPO with strong fixed-budget accuracy; the strongest pass@1 among evaluated static and dynamic baselines on different datasets; transfer across model families with up to 82% rollout savings.
AI.conclusion: Calibrated conformal stopping gives adaptive rollout budgets with a coverage guarantee, and under monotone policy improvement recalibration induces a non-increasing expected training budget.

title: Relevance Propagation as Entropic Optimal Transport on Filippov Neural Networks: Sinkhorn Propagation and Region Relevance in Image Classifiers
summary: Relevance propagation, which redistributes a network's prediction backward through the layers, is usually treated as a heuristic. We show that it is the solution of a single variational problem: Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) is the divergence-free flow on the active computational graph of zero relative entropy to the backward transition law of the forward activation flow; for a non-negative reference, this is a relative entropy between Markov measures on backward paths. The rules LRP$_0$, LRP$_{z^+}$ and LRP$_{\alpha,\beta}$ follow from this principle by the choice of a reference, and are instances of one rule, LRPN$_{\alpha,\beta}$, whose weights may vary from node to node, for instance with the node's activity, in the spirit of Hebb's principle. The principle rests on a measure-theoretic formalization of feed-forward networks as directed acyclic graphs of Filippov operators, which covers piecewise-smooth and discontinuous architectures (e.g. hard-routed Mixture-of-Experts) with a Clarke-Filippov generalized-gradient calculus; it also characterizes backpropagation as the adjoint equation of a Lagrangian relaxation. On networks of ReLU and max-pooling nodes, LRP$_0$ is Gradient$\times$Input, with an explicit jump across a kink where LRP$_{z^+}$ stays continuous. Taking the entropy edge by edge yields a new rule, Sinkhorn Relevance Propagation. Aggregated over an input region, the flow of a non-negative reference tells, with exact accounting, which hidden units carry its evidence, the conditioned flow being a Schrödinger bridge. On VGG-16, the conservation identities hold to round-off, and the rules are told apart by the sign of their maps, the share of the output left to the bias nodes, faithfulness, localization and class dependence; on ConvNeXt-Tiny, LRPN$_{\alpha,\beta}$ conserves the output and its Hebbian weights give the highest ABPC of the rules tested.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that Layer-wise Relevance Propagation is the solution of a single variational problem, derives a new rule called Sinkhorn Relevance Propagation, and tests the rules on VGG-16 and ConvNeXt-Tiny.
AI.motivation: Relevance propagation is usually treated as a heuristic, with rules chosen ad hoc, and it lacks a formalization for piecewise-smooth and discontinuous architectures such as hard-routed Mixture-of-Experts.
AI.method: A measure-theoretic formalization of feed-forward networks as directed acyclic graphs of Filippov operators with a Clarke-Filippov generalized-gradient calculus; LRP is characterized as a divergence-free flow of zero relative entropy on the active graph, with rules LRP0, LRP z+ and LRP alpha-beta as instances of one rule LRPN whose weights may vary per node, and Sinkhorn Relevance Propagation obtained by taking the entropy edge by edge.
AI.result: On ReLU and max-pooling networks LRP0 equals Gradient times Input with an explicit jump across kinks, while LRP z+ stays continuous; on VGG-16 conservation holds to round-off and the rules are told apart by the sign of their maps, the share of output left to bias nodes, faithfulness, localization and class dependence; on ConvNeXt-Tiny LRPN alpha-beta conserves the output and its Hebbian weights give the highest ABPC among the rules tested.
AI.conclusion: Relevance propagation rules can be derived from one principle and differ only by the choice of reference, and node-dependent Hebbian weighting gives the best ABPC among the tested rules, supporting a principled rather than heuristic view of relevance.

title: RIDGE: State-Conditioned Reward Blending for Behavioral Coverage in Deep RL Game Agents
comment: Conference of Games, 4 pages, 3 figures, reinforcement learning, automated playtesting, procedural personas,reward shaping, PPO, Crafter
summary: A deep RL agent trained on a fixed persona reward plays one way: an Explorer keeps exploring while starving, a Survivor hoards on an empty map. Since each persona fixes its own reward, automated playtesting trains N agents for N styles. Changing reward composition mid-episode runs into the switching-stability dilemma: PPO degrades under non-stationary rewards. We present RIDGE, a single-agent architecture that sidesteps the dilemma with two design choices: a state-conditioned blender that computes softmax-normalized sigmoid weights from slow-moving state variables, and a multi-head critic that trains one value head per persona on its own stationary signal. On Crafter with four personas, one \ridge agent acquires both branches of the wood-tier crafting/combat split that no fixed-persona baseline solves jointly, and a sharpness ablation confirms state-conditioning drives the gain. We position these results as demonstrations of the blending mechanism's dynamics across n=3 seeds per condition; larger multi-seed sweeps remain future work.

AI.tldr: RIDGE is a single RL agent whose state-conditioned blender mixes persona rewards with softmax-normalized sigmoid weights and whose multi-head critic trains one value head per persona, giving one agent both behavioral branches of a Crafter crafting/combat split.
AI.motivation: A fixed persona reward yields one playstyle, so automated playtesting needs N agents for N styles, and changing the reward composition mid-episode causes PPO to degrade under non-stationary rewards.
AI.method: A state-conditioned blender computes softmax-normalized sigmoid weights from slow-moving state variables, and a multi-head critic trains one value head per persona on its own stationary signal.
AI.result: On Crafter with four personas one agent acquires both branches of the wood-tier crafting/combat split, which no fixed-persona baseline solves jointly; a sharpness ablation confirms that state-conditioning drives the gain; results are from n=3 seeds per condition.
AI.conclusion: State-conditioned reward blending can give one agent several behavioral styles; the authors present the results as demonstrations of the mechanism's dynamics, with larger multi-seed sweeps left as future work.

title: On the Generalization Limitation of On-Policy Distillation for Post-RL Consolidation
comment: 27 pages, 12 figures. Project page: this https URL
summary: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) extends on-policy distillation (OPD) to consolidate capabilities from multiple teachers. Although prior work reports near-perfect in-distribution (IND) distillation performance, we find that this can mask incomplete capability consolidation beyond the supervised distribution. A preliminary study on synthetic reasoning shows that OPD does not fully transfer teachers' generalization capabilities. We then extend this investigation to real-world tasks, evaluating extrapolative and compositional generalization across mathematical reasoning, coding, agent, and long-context capabilities using Qwen3 models. Across extrapolative settings, OPD and MOPD reach 96.04-102.73% of their teachers' IND scores. Yet their out-of-distribution (OOD) scores remain 2.45-16.25% below the base model's. Across three compositional settings, MOPD improves IND performance over the base model, but its performance on composed tasks as OOD remains 18.19-24.34% below that of the best teachers. To understand these gaps, we examine teacher capability and data coverage as two potential bottlenecks. Jointly alleviating these bottlenecks eliminates OOD forgetting in our experiments and suggests the potential for generalization beyond the teacher. (M)OPD also reduces OOD forgetting on average relative to its reinforcement learning (RL) baselines. Analysis of the associated update geometry reveals smaller and more spectrally concentrated updates on average than those of the RL baselines, along with greater shared update structure under MOPD. Motivated by these findings, we propose geometry-based patching and base-preserving replay to improve OOD performance while largely preserving IND performance. Our findings identify a blind spot in capability consolidation via (M)OPD, highlighting the need for algorithms that explicitly support OOD retention and generalization.

AI.tldr: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation looks near-perfect in distribution but leaves out-of-distribution scores 2.45-16.25% below the base model on extrapolative settings; geometry-based patching and base-preserving replay are proposed to improve OOD performance.
AI.motivation: Prior work reports near-perfect in-distribution distillation performance for multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD), which may hide incomplete consolidation of capabilities beyond the supervised distribution.
AI.method: OPD and MOPD are evaluated on Qwen3 models for extrapolative and compositional generalization across mathematics, coding, agent and long-context tasks; teacher capability and data coverage are examined as bottlenecks, and the update geometry is analyzed; geometry-based patching and base-preserving replay are then proposed.
AI.result: Extrapolative settings reach 96.04-102.73% of teacher in-distribution scores, yet OOD scores remain 2.45-16.25% below the base model; in compositional settings OOD performance on composed tasks is 18.19-24.34% below the best teachers; jointly alleviating the two bottlenecks eliminates OOD forgetting in the experiments; (M)OPD reduces OOD forgetting relative to RL baselines, with smaller, more spectrally concentrated updates.
AI.conclusion: Strong in-distribution scores can mask a blind spot in capability consolidation via (M)OPD, so algorithms need explicit support for OOD retention and generalization.

title: LACS: Distribution-Sensitive Label-Agnostic Confidence Selection for Dynamic Data Pruning
summary: Training on large datasets motivates selecting which examples receive expensive training computation. Fixed quotas determine the amount of pruning in advance, while absolute confidence cutoffs depend on the score scale. We study a population-relative alternative that adapts the threshold and retained count together. We introduce LACS (Label-Agnostic Confidence Selector), a training-time rule based on maximum predictive confidence, requiring neither labels at selection time nor per-example gradients. LACS removes examples at or above a log-mean-exp reference plus a margin. We characterize its sensitivity to score gaps and mass, and derive an exact no-pruning condition. For $0<\rho<1$, the removed fraction is at most $\rho$ and at least one example remains. The unsigned score permits both confidently correct and confidently wrong examples to be removed. Seven evaluation settings include neural training, language modeling, and boosting. Neural execution studies reduce backward-active rows by 10-35%; on CIFAR-10, 29% fewer backward rows accompany accuracy means of 89.77% versus 89.82% for full CE. At a matched backward budget and number of optimizer updates, LACS is 1.0 pp above small-batch training and 1.2 pp above random selection over five seeds. Across 14 tabular datasets, quadratic boosting reduces mean test error from 23.36% to 22.96%. Its full training replays use about 30% fewer fitting rows; these counters span a different horizon from validation-selected accuracy. In one RBF-SVM case study, elapsed time falls by 37% with slightly lower error. These findings separate selective-work reduction from realized acceleration: the current exact-current-score neural implementation uses an additional scoring forward, so its backward sparsity does not yet translate into wall-clock acceleration. This overhead is an execution choice rather than a requirement of the selection rule.

AI.tldr: LACS prunes training examples whose maximum predictive confidence reaches a log-mean-exp reference plus a margin, cutting backward-active rows by 10-35% with accuracy close to full training, but the current neural implementation adds a scoring pass and does not yet reduce wall-clock time.
AI.motivation: Fixed pruning quotas fix the amount of pruning in advance, and absolute confidence cutoffs depend on the score scale, so a population-relative selection rule that needs neither labels nor per-example gradients is sought.
AI.method: LACS, a training-time rule based on maximum predictive confidence that removes examples at or above a log-mean-exp reference plus a margin, with no labels at selection time and no per-example gradients; the removed fraction is at most rho for 0 < rho < 1 and at least one example remains.
AI.result: Neural runs reduce backward-active rows by 10-35%; on CIFAR-10, 29% fewer backward rows accompany 89.77% accuracy versus 89.82% for full cross-entropy; at a matched backward budget LACS is 1.0 pp above small-batch training and 1.2 pp above random selection over five seeds; across 14 tabular datasets quadratic boosting lowers mean test error from 23.36% to 22.96%; in one RBF-SVM case elapsed time falls by 37%.
AI.conclusion: Selective-work reduction does not yet translate into realized acceleration, because the exact-score neural implementation needs an extra scoring forward; the authors note this overhead is an execution choice rather than part of the selection rule.

title: Data-Efficient Scaling-Law Discovery for Recommendation Systems via Coupled Hyperparameter Scaling
summary: Large-scale ranking and recommendation models of Web platforms benefit from increased compute much as large language models do, and their scaling behavior is broadly power-law in form. Yet ranking models have heterogeneous architectures which makes their scaling law less straightforward than that of LLMs. We address how to discover the scaling law of an arbitrary ranking model efficiently. We introduce a scaling layer, which groups primitive architecture parameters into semantically coherent groups and defines how they co-vary, inducing a mapping from a low-dimensional space of hyper-hyperparameters into the full architecture space. On top of it, Axia fits scaling-informed surrogates, selects configurations by a posterior-based acquisition criterion, and returns a Pareto frontier from which per-model operating points are validated -- replacing exhaustive sweeps with a small number of informative runs. A fleet-level evaluation protocol, computed on a fixed representative model set under matched trial budgets, makes refinements to either component measurable. Our contribution is an automated system that learns model-specific complexity-quality relationships and gives uncertainty-aware guidance for allocating compute across a heterogeneous model ecosystem. Across 34 model iterations in two development cycles on Meta's ads ranking and retrieval system, the workflow yielded a mean 0.66% offline normalized-entropy improvement and 0.36% cumulative online lift.

AI.tldr: Axia discovers scaling laws for ranking models by coupling their hyperparameters through a scaling layer and returns a Pareto frontier from a few informative runs; on Meta's ads ranking and retrieval system it gave a 0.66% mean offline normalized-entropy gain and 0.36% cumulative online lift.
AI.motivation: Ranking and recommendation models have heterogeneous architectures, so their scaling behavior is less straightforward than that of LLMs, and exhaustive sweeps to find their scaling laws are costly.
AI.method: A scaling layer groups primitive architecture parameters into semantically coherent groups that co-vary, mapping a low-dimensional space of hyper-hyperparameters into the full architecture space; Axia fits scaling-informed surrogates, selects configurations by a posterior-based acquisition criterion, and validates per-model operating points from a Pareto frontier under a fleet-level protocol with matched trial budgets.
AI.result: Across 34 model iterations in two development cycles on Meta's ads ranking and retrieval system, the workflow yielded a mean 0.66% offline normalized-entropy improvement and 0.36% cumulative online lift.
AI.conclusion: A small number of informative, uncertainty-aware runs can replace exhaustive sweeps for allocating compute across a heterogeneous ecosystem of ranking models.

title: When Are Two SAE Latents the Same Feature?
summary: Comparing sparse autoencoders (SAEs) requires connecting feature correspondence, differences between whole dictionaries, and uncertainty from finite evaluation data. We develop a framework that connects these tasks through an energy-weighted optimal-transport plan under a specified similarity geometry. The same plan defines a dictionary-level discrepancy, decomposes it into latent contributions, and quantifies how each latent's mass is distributed across counterparts. We characterize relationships between decoder, activation, and first-order causal similarities; idealized models clarify the interpretation of splitting and absorption. For fixed trained SAEs, we derive joint asymptotic inference for transport costs and fractions, accounting for activation similarities and both energy marginals estimated from the same documents. A joint document bootstrap gives asymptotically valid simultaneous confidence bands. Experiments across four language models locate cross-seed discrepancy and separate context-dependent changes.

AI.tldr: The paper frames comparison of sparse autoencoders as an energy-weighted optimal-transport problem that yields feature correspondence, a dictionary-level discrepancy and simultaneous confidence bands, with experiments on four language models.
AI.motivation: Comparing SAEs requires linking feature correspondence, differences between whole dictionaries and uncertainty from finite evaluation data, and these tasks are not connected in a single framework.
AI.method: An energy-weighted optimal-transport plan under a specified similarity geometry defines a dictionary-level discrepancy that decomposes into latent contributions; decoder, activation and first-order causal similarities are related, and joint asymptotic inference for transport costs and fractions is derived, with a joint document bootstrap giving simultaneous confidence bands.
AI.result: Experiments across four language models locate cross-seed discrepancy and separate context-dependent changes; the abstract reports no numeric values.
AI.conclusion: The transport framework connects feature matching, dictionary comparison and inference for SAEs, with asymptotically valid uncertainty quantification, and idealized models clarify how splitting and absorption should be interpreted.

title: Beyond Accuracy: Information-Theoretic Decoder Evaluation Under Latent Intent
summary: A central challenge in assistive brain-to-robot control is decoding a user's latent intent from complex and noisy brain signals. Prior approaches evaluate decoders as single-trial classifiers with accuracy-based metrics, but this neglects the inherently sequential nature of assistive control. Since a planner must integrate intermittent, noisy decoder outputs over time, single-step accuracy can only be a proxy when predicting downstream task performance. We formalize brain-to-robot control as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP), and prove that there is a sharp phase transition: regret is uniformly bounded across the horizon as long as pairs of goals are all decoder-distinguishable, but grows linearly otherwise. We show that a single channel statistic, the worst-pair Chernoff information $\Gamma_{\min}$ sets this boundary. Then, we derive a closed-form regret predictor $U_{\mathrm{id}}(C)$, that can be computed from any confusion matrix in $O(K^2)$ time. Across two domains spanning orthogonal information channels, we show that $U_{\mathrm{id}}$ predicts cumulative planning regret beyond what accuracy can explain. We then highlight a pathological accuracy trap, in which two decoders have identical validation accuracy 35.1% on real EEG data (BNCI2014001 subject 5) but result in a difference of $9.6\times$ in held-out regret, which $U_{\mathrm{id}}$ predicts. Same-signal control confirms $U_{\mathrm{id}}$'s advantage with decoders that span independent feature channels. Ultimately, our work provides a drop-in diagnostic to evaluate and select sensors and decoders in sequential assistive control.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes brain-to-robot control as a POMDP, shows that the worst-pair Chernoff information sets a sharp regret phase transition, and gives a closed-form regret predictor computed from any confusion matrix.
AI.motivation: Assistive BCI decoders are evaluated as single-trial classifiers with accuracy metrics, which ignores that a planner integrates noisy decoder outputs over time, so accuracy is only a proxy for downstream task performance.
AI.method: Brain-to-robot control is formalized as a partially observable Markov decision process; a closed-form regret predictor U_id(C) is derived that can be computed from any confusion matrix in O(K^2) time, built on the worst-pair Chernoff information Gamma_min.
AI.result: Regret is uniformly bounded across the horizon when all goal pairs are decoder-distinguishable and grows linearly otherwise; U_id predicts cumulative planning regret beyond what accuracy explains across two domains; on real EEG (BNCI2014001 subject 5) two decoders with identical 35.1% validation accuracy differ 9.6 times in held-out regret, which U_id predicts; the advantage holds with decoders on independent feature channels.
AI.conclusion: U_id is a drop-in diagnostic for evaluating and selecting sensors and decoders in sequential assistive control, because accuracy alone can hide large differences in regret.

title: Adaptive Domain Decomposition for Finite Basis Physics-Informed Neural Networks
summary: In this work, we present adaptive domain decomposition finite basis physics-informed neural networks (ADD-FBPINNs). The proposed method integrates Partition of Unity Networks (POUNets), a data-driven approach for learning domain partitions, with finite Basis physics-informed neural networks (FBPINNs) to perform more efficient domain decomposition and achieve more accurate approximations. FBPINNs improve upon the accuracy of standard physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) through user-defined subdivisions of the computational domain. By adapting the domain decomposition based on the solution's features using a separable POUNet, the framework can automatically learn partitions that are stable and can be geometrically interpretable. We test this approach on the two-dimensional Helmholtz equation, two-dimensional Poisson equation with multiscale features, and viscous Burgers equation and observe improved accuracy compared with FBPINNs with fixed domain decomposition.

AI.tldr: ADD-FBPINNs couples a data-driven Partition of Unity Network, which learns domain partitions from the solution's features, with finite basis PINNs, and reports better accuracy than fixed decompositions on three PDE test problems.
AI.motivation: FBPINNs rely on user-defined subdivisions of the computational domain, which may not match the solution's features and so limits the accuracy and efficiency of the decomposition.
AI.method: Partition of Unity Networks (POUNets), a data-driven approach for learning domain partitions, are integrated with FBPINNs; a separable POUNet adapts the decomposition based on the solution's features and learns partitions that are stable and geometrically interpretable.
AI.result: Improved accuracy compared with FBPINNs using a fixed domain decomposition on the two-dimensional Helmholtz equation, a two-dimensional Poisson equation with multiscale features and the viscous Burgers equation; the abstract gives no numeric values.
AI.conclusion: Learning the domain partition adaptively can make FBPINNs more accurate while keeping the partitions interpretable.

title: Revisiting Critic Estimation in Soft Actor-Critic Algorithms
summary: Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) is a widely used deep reinforcement learning algorithm that combines entropy regularization with an actor-critic architecture. Standard implementations rely on one-step temporal-difference learning of Q-functions, yet alternative critic design choices remain underexplored. In this work, we revisit three such choices: learning soft advantages instead of soft Q-values, the use of multi-step return targets, and the training of multi-step critics from replay buffer data. Keeping the policy objective fixed, we compare the six critic variants these choices generate: (i) advantage and (ii) dueling-advantage critics learned from one-step transitions, and $\lambda$-return and soft Generalized Advantage Estimation (GAE) critics learned either (iii, iv) on-policy or (v, vi) from replayed trajectory segments. Each variant is evaluated across an entire random hyperparameter search on fourteen tasks, treating the hyperparameters as part of the algorithm. Learning soft advantages instead of soft Q-values does not improve performance, and the soft GAE critic adds nothing over the simpler $\lambda$-return critic. What does improve performance, most clearly on continuous control, is training a $\lambda$-return critic on replayed trajectory segments, even without importance weighting or trace cutting. This extends earlier evidence that uncorrected multi-step targets work well under replay to the full soft $\lambda$-return, entropy terms included. By design, the underlying ideas studied here extend beyond SAC, and our empirical findings aim to encourage their application to a broader class of reinforcement learning algorithms.

AI.tldr: Among six SAC critic variants tested over fourteen tasks, only training a lambda-return critic on replayed trajectory segments clearly improves performance, especially on continuous control, while soft advantages and the soft GAE critic add nothing.
AI.motivation: SAC uses one-step temporal-difference Q-functions by default, and alternative critic designs such as soft advantages, multi-step return targets and multi-step critics trained on replay data remain underexplored.
AI.method: With the policy objective fixed, six critic variants are compared: advantage and dueling-advantage critics learned from one-step transitions, and lambda-return and soft GAE critics learned either on-policy or from replayed trajectory segments; each variant is evaluated across an entire random hyperparameter search on fourteen tasks.
AI.result: Learning soft advantages instead of soft Q-values does not improve performance, and the soft GAE critic adds nothing over the simpler lambda-return critic; training a lambda-return critic on replayed trajectory segments improves performance most clearly on continuous control, even without importance weighting or trace cutting.
AI.conclusion: Uncorrected multi-step targets also work well under replay for the full soft lambda-return including entropy terms, and the authors suggest these findings may extend to a broader class of RL algorithms.

title: CoReFlow: Consistency-Relaxed Flow Maps for Probabilistic Traffic Forecasting
summary: Probabilistic traffic forecasting is essential for reliable Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS), as it captures uncertainties in complex road networks. Recent diffusion- and flow-based generative models have facilitated uncertainty modeling through a multi-step sampling process. However, beyond slow inference, this process is designed to capture complex multimodal distributions, which misaligns with the limited complexity of the conditional traffic data distribution, causing models to underperform deterministic baselines. To address this, we introduce the \underline{Co}nsistency-\underline{Re}laxed \underline{Flow} Map (CoReFlow) model, presenting the first effort to leverage the one-step generation capability of flow maps, known as solution operators of probability-flow ordinary differential equations. Besides, we improve accuracy using a concise training objective that supervises the model via interpolation endpoints over finite time intervals. Unlike existing methods (e.g., self-distillation and MeanFlow Identity) that maintain trajectory consistency to model multimodal distributions, our objective leverages conditional mean to restrict the consistency, thereby achieving higher accuracy in the probabilistic traffic forecasting task. Extensive experiments on four real-world datasets show CoReFlow achieves state-of-the-art forecasting accuracy. It surpasses recent baselines, provides competitive uncertainty modeling, and reduces inference costs compared to existing generative baselines.

AI.tldr: CoReFlow applies flow maps with a conditional-mean consistency objective to probabilistic traffic forecasting, reaching state-of-the-art accuracy on four real-world datasets with lower inference cost than existing generative baselines.
AI.motivation: Diffusion and flow generative models are slow because of multi-step sampling and are built for complex multimodal distributions, which misfits the simpler conditional traffic distribution and causes them to underperform deterministic baselines.
AI.method: Consistency-Relaxed Flow Maps, which use the one-step generation of flow maps and a training objective that supervises the model through interpolation endpoints over finite time intervals, restricting consistency with a conditional mean instead of maintaining trajectory consistency.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art forecasting accuracy on four real-world datasets, surpasses recent baselines, gives competitive uncertainty modeling and reduces inference cost relative to existing generative baselines.
AI.conclusion: Relaxing trajectory consistency to a conditional-mean constraint suits the simpler conditional traffic distribution and yields accurate, cheaper probabilistic forecasts.

title: Give the Drafter a Second Chance to Guess: Parallel Reconsideration for Speculative Decoding
summary: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference with a small drafter, whose per-guess acceptance rate determines the achievable speedup. Feature-level drafters share a design choice: every token, easy or hard, is drafted under a single forward pass. Many of the tokens the target rejects are ones the drafter is itself unsure about yet the target answers decisively. To address this, we introduce Parallel Reconsideration: guided by its own uncertainty, the drafter reconsiders its hesitant guesses with extra passes that run in parallel with the one-pass draft, adding negligible latency. A co-designed training recipe and serving-time drafting algorithm append these reconsidered guesses to the original draft tree as refined candidates. Across models and benchmarks, on average, Parallel Reconsideration improves over the baselines by 5.3% to 10.2% on acceptance length and by 3.5% to 9.2% on speedup.

AI.tldr: Parallel Reconsideration lets a speculative decoding drafter re-run its uncertain guesses in parallel with the one-pass draft and append refined candidates to the draft tree, improving acceptance length by 5.3-10.2% and speedup by 3.5-9.2% on average.
AI.motivation: Feature-level drafters draft every token in a single forward pass, and many tokens the target rejects are ones the drafter was itself unsure about, although the target answers them decisively.
AI.method: Guided by its own uncertainty, the drafter reconsiders hesitant guesses with extra passes that run in parallel with the one-pass draft; a co-designed training recipe and serving-time drafting algorithm append these reconsidered guesses to the original draft tree as refined candidates.
AI.result: Across models and benchmarks, on average it improves over the baselines by 5.3% to 10.2% on acceptance length and by 3.5% to 9.2% on speedup, adding negligible latency.
AI.conclusion: Spending extra parallel computation on the drafter's uncertain tokens is a cheap way to raise the speed of speculative decoding.

title: RESHPart: Feedback-Reshaped Spectral Embedding for Hypergraph Partitioning
summary: With scalable Laplacian solvers now available, the next frontier is to exploit them more effectively for high-quality hypergraph partitioning. In this work, we revisit spectral hypergraph partitioning from the perspective of spectral embedding geometry. Through a systematic analysis of circuit hypergraphs and controlled synthetic (hyper)graphs, we identify a ray-like embedding structure that helps explain the effectiveness of projection-based partitioning. We further show that the geometry of spectral embeddings can be systematically influenced through Laplacian design and hyperedge reweighting. Guided by these insights, we propose FRESHPart, a feedback-reshaped spectral partitioning framework that refines the spectral embedding through Geometry Feedback and Search Feedback, producing embeddings that are better aligned with projection-based partitioning. On the Titan23 benchmark, FRESHPart achieves average cut reductions over hMETIS of 13.09% at $\epsilon=2\%$ and 25.21% at $\epsilon=20\%$, surpassing the strongest previously reported results (12.16% and 22.53%, respectively), while completing every benchmark in under 120 s on a single GPU.

AI.tldr: FRESHPart refines spectral hypergraph embeddings with Geometry Feedback and Search Feedback so they align with projection-based partitioning, cutting the cut size versus hMETIS by 13.09% at epsilon 2% and 25.21% at epsilon 20% on Titan23.
AI.motivation: Scalable Laplacian solvers now make spectral hypergraph partitioning practical, but the embedding geometry that makes projection-based partitioning effective has not been exploited systematically.
AI.method: Analysis of circuit hypergraphs and controlled synthetic graphs identifies a ray-like embedding structure; the geometry is influenced through Laplacian design and hyperedge reweighting, and FRESHPart refines the embedding with Geometry Feedback and Search Feedback.
AI.result: On the Titan23 benchmark average cut reductions over hMETIS are 13.09% at epsilon 2% and 25.21% at epsilon 20%, surpassing the previous best of 12.16% and 22.53%; every benchmark completes in under 120 s on a single GPU.
AI.conclusion: Feedback-driven shaping of spectral embeddings improves partition quality beyond the strongest previously reported spectral results at practical runtime.

title: Self-Supervised Learning of Universal Latent Spaces for Operator Learning
summary: Neural operators fit their representation of functions to the task they are trained on, so every new task rebuilds a reduced space from labeled data. Following the self-supervised pre-training that made representations shareable in natural language processing and computer vision, we decouple representation learning from operator learning. A functional autoencoder is pre-trained on analytic functions synthesized on the fly, with no solver and no labels, to represent functions on arbitrary point clouds, and the latent space it induces is frozen and reused across tasks. The representation is exactly equivariant to translation, dilation, and amplitude, and reconstructs solutions of partial differential equations (PDEs) and natural images on geometries it never saw. Being task-agnostic, the latent space can be interpreted in its own right. The whole space is used and decodes to valid fields, it preserves the ordering of distances between physical fields, its geodesics interpolate physical evolutions, and edit directions transfer across fields. With frozen representation maps, a dataset is encoded once and a neural operator is trained entirely on cached embeddings, which saves memory and training time. On 28 tasks in fluid dynamics, solid mechanics, acoustics, and the Helmholtz and Poisson equations, this paradigm can exceed the accuracy of state-of-the-art end-to-end architectures, with up to an order of magnitude higher throughput and memory savings that fit models nearly two orders of magnitude larger on consumer-grade GPUs. At inference, latent rollouts run up to an order of magnitude faster than regular rollouts, and chunked inference processes functions of over half a billion points on a single consumer-grade GPU.

AI.tldr: A functional autoencoder pre-trained self-supervised on synthetic analytic functions gives a frozen, equivariant latent space reused across 28 operator-learning tasks, matching or exceeding end-to-end architectures with up to an order of magnitude higher throughput.
AI.motivation: Neural operators rebuild a reduced representation from labeled data for every new task, unlike the self-supervised pre-training that made representations shareable in natural language processing and computer vision.
AI.method: A functional autoencoder is pre-trained on analytic functions synthesized on the fly, with no solver and no labels, to represent functions on arbitrary point clouds; the latent space is frozen and reused, is exactly equivariant to translation, dilation and amplitude, and neural operators are trained entirely on cached embeddings.
AI.result: On 28 tasks in fluid dynamics, solid mechanics, acoustics, and the Helmholtz and Poisson equations, the paradigm can exceed the accuracy of state-of-the-art end-to-end architectures, with up to an order of magnitude higher throughput and memory savings that fit models nearly two orders of magnitude larger on consumer GPUs; latent rollouts run up to an order of magnitude faster, and chunked inference handles functions of over half a billion points on one consumer GPU.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling representation learning from operator learning with a frozen, task-agnostic latent space gives accurate, memory-efficient and fast neural operators that scale to very large point clouds.

title: Optimizing Recourse Under Predictive Multiplicity
summary: Algorithmic recourse identifies modifications that can change an unfavorable model prediction into a favorable one. Under predictive multiplicity, similarly performing models can disagree on individual predictions, so recourse valid for one model may fail for another. We formulate robust recourse under predictive multiplicity as a budget-constrained minimization of the worst-case validity loss across a competing set of models, which can include models with different architectures or from different hypothesis classes. We propose an oracle-efficient algorithm called ORPM and prove sufficient conditions for its convergence. We evaluate ORPM on one synthetic and five real datasets, and competing sets consist of linear, neural, mixed, and decision-tree models. Our experiments show decreasing optimization-gap bounds and high validity in many tested settings, with favorable performance against baselines designed for specific model classes or architectures. We also quantify how requiring a common action across competing models changes recourse success at a given budget and examine disparities in this success across demographic groups.

AI.tldr: ORPM computes recourse that is robust to predictive multiplicity by minimizing the worst-case validity loss across a set of competing models under a budget constraint, with high validity in many tested settings.
AI.motivation: When similarly performing models disagree on individual predictions, recourse that is valid for one model may fail for another.
AI.method: Robust recourse is formulated as budget-constrained minimization of the worst-case validity loss across competing models, which may have different architectures or come from different hypothesis classes; the oracle-efficient algorithm ORPM is proposed with sufficient conditions for convergence.
AI.result: On one synthetic and five real datasets with linear, neural, mixed and decision-tree competing sets, the optimization-gap bounds decrease and validity is high in many settings, with favorable performance against baselines designed for specific model classes; requiring a common action across competing models changes recourse success at a given budget, and disparities in success across demographic groups are examined.
AI.conclusion: Recourse under predictive multiplicity should be optimized against the worst case across competing models, and common-action requirements and group disparities materially affect how successful it is.

title: Pathwise-Budgeted LLM Routing: Online Allocation with K-Bit Tail-Cost Learning
summary: Firms using large language models under fixed budgets must decide which model to call and whether to retry a failed task. Because a call's charge is revealed only after completion, one long response can exhaust the remaining budget and leave later tasks unserved. Our objective is to maximize the number of tasks solved before service stops. We develop a contextual bandit policy, ADP-HT, which learns each model's task-specific success probability and constructs conservative cost estimates from coarsened response-length labels on a quantile grid with $2^K$ intervals. The policy weighs predicted success against these costs, adjusting the cost penalty to realized spending and the budget available per remaining task. Under calibration, local regularity, and grid-coverage conditions, we bound the excess allowance in the policy's conservative cost estimates. At a fixed sample size, increasing $K$ reduces the discretization term but increases the estimation allowance. At the tightest tested budgets, ADP-HT solves more than twice as many MATH500 and GPQA tasks as the best implemented baseline. It achieves the highest mean cumulative score at ten of fourteen RouterBench budgets. On LiveCodeBench, it outperforms a deployed commercial router in both default and cost-saving modes at the three lowest test budgets.

AI.tldr: ADP-HT is a contextual bandit router that chooses which LLM to call and whether to retry under a fixed budget, using conservative cost estimates from coarsened response-length labels; at the tightest budgets it solves more than twice as many MATH500 and GPQA tasks as the best baseline.
AI.motivation: Under a fixed budget a call's charge is revealed only after completion, so one long response can exhaust the budget and leave later tasks unserved, while the goal is to maximize the number of tasks solved before service stops.
AI.method: A contextual bandit policy learns each model's task-specific success probability and builds conservative cost estimates from response-length labels quantized on a quantile grid with 2^K intervals; it weighs predicted success against these costs, adjusting the cost penalty to realized spending and to the budget per remaining task; the excess allowance in the cost estimates is bounded under calibration, local regularity and grid-coverage conditions.
AI.result: At the tightest tested budgets ADP-HT solves more than twice as many MATH500 and GPQA tasks as the best implemented baseline; it achieves the highest mean cumulative score at ten of fourteen RouterBench budgets; on LiveCodeBench it outperforms a deployed commercial router in both default and cost-saving modes at the three lowest test budgets.
AI.conclusion: Conservative, budget-aware cost estimation with a tunable K trading discretization error against estimation allowance gives an effective online LLM routing policy under tight budgets.

title: On Convergence of Gradient Temporal-Difference Learning with Regularized Corrections and Eligibility Traces
comment: 66 pages, 1 figure. Submitted to the Journal of Machine Learning Research
summary: Temporal-difference (TD) learning underlies many prediction and control algorithms, but can diverge when combined with off-policy learning, bootstrapping, and function approximation. TD with Regularized Corrections (TDRC) is theoretically sound and practically simple, but existing convergence theory covers only the one-step case under i.i.d. sampling, while the Huber Bellman-error formulation has not been extended to TDRC or eligibility traces. In this work, we establish convergence of constrained TDRC($\lambda$) with diminishing stepsizes and non-i.i.d. off-policy data, for state-dependent and history-dependent $\lambda$-parameters. We also propose TDRC($\lambda$)-Huber, which preserves the TDRC($\lambda$) fixed point while reducing sensitivity to large Bellman errors. For both algorithms, we apply an ODE-based weak-convergence method from stochastic approximation theory. For the nonlinear mean dynamics of TDRC($\lambda$)-Huber, we give an integral small-gain condition that guarantees uniqueness and global asymptotic stability of the target equilibrium. We then establish convergence of the constrained algorithm, derive computable sufficient conditions for convergence, and identify a regularization-based convergence mechanism shared by linear TDRC($\lambda$) and TDRC($\lambda$)-Huber. When the mean TD matrix is positive stable, both constrained algorithms converge under sufficiently strong regularization without requiring positive definiteness.

AI.tldr: The paper proves convergence of TDRC(lambda) with diminishing stepsizes on non-i.i.d. off-policy data, and introduces TDRC(lambda)-Huber, which keeps the TDRC(lambda) fixed point while reducing sensitivity to large Bellman errors.
AI.motivation: Existing TDRC convergence theory covers only the one-step case under i.i.d. sampling, and the Huber Bellman-error formulation has not been extended to TDRC or to eligibility traces.
AI.method: Constrained TDRC(lambda) with state-dependent and history-dependent lambda is analyzed with an ODE-based weak-convergence method from stochastic approximation theory; for the nonlinear mean dynamics of TDRC(lambda)-Huber an integral small-gain condition guarantees uniqueness and global asymptotic stability of the target equilibrium.
AI.result: Convergence of both constrained algorithms is established, with computable sufficient conditions; a regularization-based convergence mechanism is shared by linear TDRC(lambda) and TDRC(lambda)-Huber; when the mean TD matrix is positive stable, both converge under sufficiently strong regularization without requiring positive definiteness.
AI.conclusion: TDRC with eligibility traces and Huber losses is convergent under non-i.i.d. off-policy data, and regularization supplies the key stability mechanism.

title: MIGONet: a multiple-input graph neural operator with solver-free discrete manufactured-solution training
comment: Accepted for publication in Transport Phenomena by De Gruyter Brill. 35 pages, 16 figures, 13 tables
summary: Surrogate modeling of transport requires operators that capture the combined influence of spatially distributed sources and Dirichlet and Neumann boundary conditions, together with training datasets that can be generated at low computational cost. This work presents MIGONet, a multiple-input graph neural operator, and a discrete method of manufactured solutions (MMS) that trains it without solving a partial differential equation, using steady heat conduction as the model problem. In the discrete MMS procedure, temperature fields are prescribed a priori, and the source terms and Dirichlet or Neumann boundary data are evaluated with the same discrete operators as the reference finite-difference method (FDM), so every training sample satisfies the discrete governing equations by construction. Because the boundary data are derived from each field, a Dirichlet or Neumann condition can be assigned to every boundary segment of every sample, and the boundary specification becomes an operator input. MIGONet supplies representations of the complete source field and boundary data to every node before local message passing. On the rectangular domain, it is compared with a version without the complete-source encoder (MIGONet-local) and with the multiple-input operator network MIONet, using the same training data. MIGONet achieves mean relative temperature errors of 10.31% and 10.64% for curved-wire and Gaussian-spot heating, compared with 45.97% and 48.34% for MIONet and 72.25% and 67.82% for MIGONet-local. For 10,000 samples, discrete MMS reduces data-generation time from 486.65 s to 3.15 s relative to matched iterative FDM labeling. Separately trained MIGONet models are also evaluated on L-shaped, disc-shaped, and ring-shaped domains.

AI.tldr: MIGONet is a multiple-input graph neural operator trained on discrete manufactured-solution data without solving a PDE, reaching mean relative temperature errors of about 10.3-10.6% versus 46-48% for MIONet on steady heat conduction, and cutting generation time for 10,000 samples from 486.65 s to 3.15 s.
AI.motivation: Surrogate modeling of transport needs operators that capture distributed sources and Dirichlet and Neumann boundary conditions together, and training datasets are costly to generate with iterative solvers.
AI.method: A discrete method of manufactured solutions prescribes temperature fields and evaluates source terms and boundary data with the same discrete operators as the reference finite-difference method, so every sample satisfies the discrete equations by construction; boundary conditions become operator inputs, and MIGONet supplies complete source and boundary representations to every node before local message passing.
AI.result: On the rectangular domain MIGONet gives mean relative temperature errors of 10.31% for curved-wire and 10.64% for Gaussian-spot heating, versus 45.97% and 48.34% for MIONet and 72.25% and 67.82% for MIGONet-local; for 10,000 samples discrete MMS reduces data-generation time from 486.65 s to 3.15 s relative to matched iterative FDM labeling; separately trained models are also evaluated on L-shaped, disc-shaped and ring-shaped domains.
AI.conclusion: Solver-free discrete MMS data combined with a graph neural operator that has a complete-source encoder gives accurate and cheap surrogates for steady heat conduction.

title: Reward Budgeting Reduces Premature Convergence in Reinforcement Learning for LLM Reasoning
summary: RL for LLM reasoning often reaches an early performance plateau as the policy distribution becomes increasingly sharp. Recent work has studied policy entropy as both a diagnostic and a control signal for this behavior. In our experiments, however, increasing entropy alone does not reliably change the eventual plateau. We analyze RL through its implicit target policy and derive a sharpness factor $\kappa$, together with an effective counterpart $\kappa_{\mathrm{eff}}$, that describes how strongly reward or advantage gaps are translated into probability-ratio gaps. Motivated by this view, we introduce \emph{reward budgeting}, a plug-in advantage construction that assigns a fixed total reward budget to each prompt. For binary rewards and independent on-policy rollouts, its unclipped score-function estimator follows the gradient of an exact finite-$G$ concave objective with diminishing returns, while its advantage gap decreases as more rollouts become correct. For general rewards, a shifted log-mean interpretation holds asymptotically under the stated regularity conditions. These results motivate, rather than establish exact objective equivalence for, the clipped implementations. On Qwen3-8B and Llama3.2-3B-Instruct, reward budgeting consistently improves a range of RL baselines, with gains up to +12.50 on AMC23 and +10.00 on AIME24 and AIME25. Overall, our results support an update-dynamics view of premature convergence and show that strong gains can be obtained without explicitly preserving entropy.

AI.tldr: Reward budgeting assigns each prompt a fixed total reward to counter premature convergence in RL for LLM reasoning, consistently improving a range of RL baselines on Qwen3-8B and Llama3.2-3B-Instruct, with gains up to +12.50 on AMC23.
AI.motivation: RL for LLM reasoning often reaches an early plateau as the policy distribution sharpens, and increasing policy entropy alone does not reliably change the eventual plateau.
AI.method: A sharpness factor kappa and an effective counterpart kappa_eff describe how reward or advantage gaps translate into probability-ratio gaps; reward budgeting is a plug-in advantage construction that assigns a fixed total reward budget to each prompt; for binary rewards with independent on-policy rollouts its unclipped estimator follows the gradient of an exact finite-G concave objective, and for general rewards a shifted log-mean interpretation holds asymptotically.
AI.result: On Qwen3-8B and Llama3.2-3B-Instruct reward budgeting consistently improves a range of RL baselines, with gains up to +12.50 on AMC23 and +10.00 on AIME24 and AIME25.
AI.conclusion: Premature convergence reflects update dynamics, and strong gains can be obtained without explicitly preserving entropy; the clipped implementations are motivated by the analysis rather than exactly equivalent to the objective.

title: A Comparative Study of Importance Attribution to Columns in Deep Learning over Relational Databases
summary: Deep learning over relational databases has led to increasingly effective prediction models, motivating a growing need to explain their behavior. We study explanation methods that assign importance scores to individual database attributes, focusing on a fundamental question: to what extent does the choice of importance-attribution method matter? We develop a methodology to systematically compare importance-attribution methods and analyze their similarities and differences. In particular, we study two aspects of the explanations: which attributes they deem important, captured by differences in attribute rankings, and how importance scores vary across attributes, captured by differences in score distributions. We further investigate whether these differences are reflected in the conventional measure of explanation quality, fidelity. We apply our methodology in an extensive empirical study of four methods: Monte Carlo Shapley, Kernel SHAP, single-attribute impact, and mask learning. We experiment with multiple datasets and tasks using two RDL architectures: heterogeneous GraphSAGE and Relational Graph Transformers. Our experiments show that explanation methods behave differently depending on the prediction type: regression or classification. In regression, most methods exhibit high agreement in attribute rankings, whereas classification yields considerably less consensus. Notably, while mask learning frequently diverges in its importance distributions, Shapley-based methods and single-attribute impact often converge to similar explanations. This suggests that, in many settings, single-attribute impact can replace Shapley at substantially lower computational cost. Overall, our study provides methodological tools for comparing importance-attribution methods, and empirical evidence that their choice has important consequences for interpreting relational deep learning models.

AI.tldr: The paper systematically compares four importance-attribution methods (Monte Carlo Shapley, Kernel SHAP, single-attribute impact, mask learning) for column-level explanations of relational deep learning models, and shows that the choice of method changes the explanations.
AI.motivation: Explanation methods for deep learning over relational databases are increasingly needed, but it is unclear how much the choice of importance-attribution method matters, and existing fidelity measures may not reveal differences in which attributes are ranked important or how scores are distributed.
AI.method: The authors develop a methodology that compares explanations along two aspects: differences in attribute rankings and differences in importance-score distributions, and also checks whether these differences show up in fidelity. They apply it to heterogeneous GraphSAGE and Relational Graph Transformers across multiple datasets and tasks.
AI.result: In regression, most methods agree highly on attribute rankings, while classification shows considerably less consensus. Mask learning often diverges in its importance distributions, whereas Shapley-based methods and single-attribute impact often converge to similar explanations.
AI.conclusion: In many settings single-attribute impact can replace Shapley at substantially lower computational cost, and the choice of attribution method has important consequences for interpreting relational deep learning models.

title: Decouple to Reuse: Fine-Grained Knowledge Augmentation for Time Series Foundation Models
summary: Time series forecasting is critical for demand prediction and resource management in modern Web services, yet applying pretrained Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) to downstream tasks remains challenging due to domain shifts. Existing retrieval-augmented approaches typically retrieve coarse-grained window contexts and may introduce context-specific noise. To address this problem, we argue that temporal patterns should be reused at a decomposition level, as effective trend and seasonal dynamics may originate from different contexts. We propose \method, a two-stage \underline{F}ine-grained \underline{K}nowledge \underline{A}ugmentation framework that decouples and consolidates pre-training knowledge into compact, task-shared residual codebooks to enhance frozen TSFMs. Specifically, Stage I constructs dual-branch residual codebooks for decoupled trend and seasonal signals, while Stage II dynamically retrieves and merges these fine-grained patterns into target representations via task-adaptive aggregation and gate fusion. Extensive experiments across eight real-world benchmarks with four representative TSFM backbones demonstrate the superior effectiveness and computational efficiency of \method, while further validating the strong transferability of the residual codebooks across different backbones. The source code is available at the anonymous repository: this https URL

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a two-stage fine-grained knowledge augmentation framework that builds residual codebooks for trend and seasonal components to enhance frozen Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) for forecasting.
AI.motivation: Applying pretrained TSFMs to downstream tasks suffers from domain shift, and existing retrieval-augmented methods retrieve coarse-grained window contexts that can introduce context-specific noise.
AI.method: Stage I constructs dual-branch residual codebooks for decoupled trend and seasonal signals from pretraining knowledge, and Stage II retrieves and merges these fine-grained patterns into target representations through task-adaptive aggregation and gate fusion, keeping the TSFM frozen.
AI.result: Experiments on eight real-world benchmarks with four representative TSFM backbones show superior effectiveness and computational efficiency, and the residual codebooks transfer well across different backbones.
AI.conclusion: Reusing temporal patterns at the decomposition level rather than the window level provides an effective and efficient way to augment frozen foundation models for time series forecasting.

title: Attraction-Ranking Mismatch in Out-of-Distribution Detection: Theory and Evidence from Hamiltonian Feature Dynamics
summary: Attracting features toward learned in-distribution (ID) regions is an intuitive strategy for out-of-distribution (OOD) detection, but does such attraction improve detection? We investigate this question using class-conditioned Hamiltonian dynamics as a controlled testbed and identify an attraction-ranking mismatch: improving individual class-affinity scores need not improve the relative ordering of ID and OOD samples. Our analysis separates misalignment between the driving field and the detection score from ranking failure that persists even when they are aligned. An exact AUROC decomposition and a local boundary analysis identify relative score changes at the ID-OOD ranking boundary as the source of first-order AUROC change under regularity conditions. Experiments demonstrate that a score-aligned rule can improve performance on a held-out source validation split yet consistently degrade it after transfer, even without a single winning-class change. A separate perturbation study finds that near-boundary relative score changes track the direction of small AUROC changes in the tested settings. Finally, centroid approximation and shared scales connect the zero-step score to a static centroid family that includes the existing CTM detector. Together, these results explain why class attraction is insufficient to justify feature refinement and motivate evaluating its effect on the ranking boundary.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies an attraction-ranking mismatch in out-of-distribution (OOD) detection: improving individual class-affinity scores through feature attraction does not necessarily improve the ranking of ID versus OOD samples, using class-conditioned Hamiltonian dynamics as a testbed.
AI.motivation: Attracting features toward in-distribution regions is an intuitive OOD detection strategy, but it was unclear whether such attraction actually improves detection performance.
AI.method: The authors use an exact AUROC decomposition and a local boundary analysis to show that relative score changes at the ID-OOD ranking boundary drive first-order AUROC change, separate misalignment between the driving field and the detection score from ranking failure, and connect the zero-step score to a static centroid family that includes the existing CTM detector.
AI.result: A score-aligned rule can improve performance on a held-out source validation split yet consistently degrade it after transfer, even without any winning-class change. A perturbation study finds that near-boundary relative score changes track the direction of small AUROC changes in the tested settings.
AI.conclusion: Class attraction alone is insufficient to justify feature refinement, and the effect of attraction should be evaluated on the ranking boundary.

title: TRACK: Multiple Instance Learning for Anti-Money Laundering in Transaction Networks
comment: 11 pages, 3 figures. Accepted at the 20th ACM International Conference on Web Search and Data Mining (WSDM 2027)
summary: Anti-money laundering (AML) investigations are organized around accounts, while the suspicious evidence for an account may reside in only a few of its transactions. Yet many account-level detectors summarize transactions before learning, and message-passing models may aggregate once more over neighboring accounts. We name this discrepancy the aggregation mismatch and study it under an account-window benchmark label defined by the presence of at least one flagged transaction. We recast account-level AML detection as multiple instance learning, in which an account-window is a bag and its transactions are instances. We propose TRACK, which encodes every transaction with a shared encoder and selectively pools the encodings into an account decision. To emulate coarse supervision, we withhold the transaction labels of five AML datasets from TRACK throughout training. Under a time-ordered protocol, TRACK achieves the highest average precision among the tabular and graph baselines trained from account labels on every dataset. Despite using only account-window supervision, it remains competitive with edge classifiers trained directly from transaction labels. Its instance scores also rank flagged transactions well above chance and approach or exceed directly supervised ranking performance across datasets.

AI.tldr: The paper recasts account-level anti-money laundering (AML) detection as multiple instance learning and proposes TRACK, which encodes each transaction with a shared encoder and selectively pools them into an account decision, trained only with account-level labels.
AI.motivation: Many account-level AML detectors summarize transactions before learning, and graph models aggregate again over neighboring accounts, which creates an aggregation mismatch because suspicious evidence may reside in only a few transactions of an account.
AI.method: Each account-window is treated as a bag and its transactions as instances. TRACK uses a shared transaction encoder with selective pooling, and transaction labels are withheld from training on five AML datasets to emulate coarse supervision under a time-ordered protocol.
AI.result: TRACK achieves the highest average precision among tabular and graph baselines trained from account labels on every dataset. It remains competitive with edge classifiers trained directly from transaction labels, and its instance scores rank flagged transactions well above chance, approaching or exceeding directly supervised ranking performance.
AI.conclusion: Multiple instance learning with account-window supervision is an effective framing for AML detection, offering strong account-level accuracy and useful transaction-level ranking without transaction labels.

title: Act-HiMotif: Hierarchical Daily Activity Schedule Generation via Learned Activity-Structure Motifs
summary: Generating daily activity schedules from individual attributes (e.g., age and income) is valuable for activity-based travel modeling and human behavior simulation. The task is challenging because exact activity structures follow a highly imbalanced, long-tailed distribution, while the same structure can admit multiple duration allocations under a fixed full-day budget. Direct generation must therefore learn many exact activity structures from highly uneven observations while modeling their possible temporal realizations. However, many exact structures share recurring activity organization. Based on this observation, we propose Act-HiMotif, a hierarchical motif-based generative model that introduces learned, reusable activity-structure motifs as an intermediate representation between individual profiles and specific activity structures. Act-HiMotif first distinguishes home-only days from active days, then samples a motif from a profile-conditioned prior to guide activity-structure generation, and finally applies a budget-constrained duration allocator to generate activity durations that sum exactly to the full-day horizon. This hierarchy models home-only routing, activity-structure generation, and duration allocation at their corresponding levels, while motifs allow related structures to share statistical support without losing their distinct sequences. Experiments on large-scale travel survey data show that Act-HiMotif outperforms strong baselines in both in-distribution and spatial generalization settings, demonstrating the effectiveness of hierarchical generation and reusable activity-structure motifs for producing realistic profile-conditioned daily activity schedules.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Act-HiMotif, a hierarchical motif-based generative model that produces daily activity schedules from individual attributes by first deciding home-only versus active days, then sampling reusable activity-structure motifs, and finally allocating durations that sum to the full-day budget.
AI.motivation: Exact activity structures follow a highly imbalanced, long-tailed distribution and the same structure can admit many duration allocations, so direct generation must learn many rare structures from uneven observations and model their temporal realizations.
AI.method: Act-HiMotif introduces learned, reusable activity-structure motifs as an intermediate representation between individual profiles and specific activity structures. Motifs are sampled from a profile-conditioned prior and guide structure generation, followed by a budget-constrained duration allocator.
AI.result: On large-scale travel survey data, Act-HiMotif outperforms strong baselines in both in-distribution and spatial generalization settings.
AI.conclusion: Hierarchical generation with reusable motifs yields realistic profile-conditioned daily activity schedules, since related structures share statistical support without losing their distinct sequences.

title: Alleviating Limited Effectiveness and Multi-Class Collapse in Deep Graph-level Clustering
summary: Given a collection of $N$ graphs, graph-level clustering (GLC) seeks to partition the $N$ graphs into semantically meaningful groups, which serves as a fundamental task in analyzing graph-structured data. While Graph Isomorphism Networks (GINs) have become the de facto encoders for GLC, they still fail to distinguish graphs due to their neglect of global topology. On top of that, existing deep clustering frameworks suffer from severe "clustering collapse" issues, particularly in imbalanced multi-class scenarios. To address these challenges, we propose S$^3$GLC, a novel framework that integrates global topological characteristics with local neighborhood features for balanced GLC. Theoretically, we leverage the Hoffman-Wielandt inequality to construct Spectral Signature as a rigorous lower bound for graph edit distance (GED), providing a computationally efficient proxy for global topological features. We additionally propose a joint manifold-preserving sparse regression module to fuse Spectral Signature with Spatial Representation, eliminating noise while preserving the complementary information. Furthermore, to mitigate clustering collapse, we introduce a balanced clustering objective based on optimal transport, harnessing the Sinkhorn-Knopp normalization to enforce equipartition constraints on cluster assignments. Extensive experiments on 10 real-world datasets demonstrate that S$^3$GLC significantly outperforms 15 state-of-the-art baselines, achieving remarkable improvements on benchmark datasets such as REDDIT-12K and OGBG-PPA.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes S3GLC, a deep graph-level clustering framework that combines global topology (a spectral signature derived via the Hoffman-Wielandt inequality) with local neighborhood features and uses optimal-transport balanced clustering to avoid cluster collapse.
AI.motivation: Graph Isomorphism Networks (GINs), the standard encoders for graph-level clustering, neglect global topology and fail to distinguish some graphs, and existing deep clustering frameworks suffer from clustering collapse, especially in imbalanced multi-class settings.
AI.method: The Spectral Signature is constructed as a lower bound for graph edit distance, and a joint manifold-preserving sparse regression module fuses it with spatial representations. A balanced clustering objective based on optimal transport with Sinkhorn-Knopp normalization enforces equipartition of cluster assignments.
AI.result: Across 10 real-world datasets, S3GLC significantly outperforms 15 state-of-the-art baselines, with notable improvements on REDDIT-12K and OGBG-PPA.
AI.conclusion: Integrating global topological characteristics with local features and enforcing balanced assignments yields more balanced and effective graph-level clustering.

title: Learning From Static Context in Federated Time Series Forecasting
comment: 4th IEEE International Conference on Federated Learning Technologies and Applications (FLTA 2026)
summary: Time series forecasting is shifting from locally trained, per-series models to global models trained across many heterogeneous series, which requires learning what sets the series apart. When the raw data cannot be centralized, such a global model is trained with federated learning (FL), one client per data owner. State-of-the-art forecasters such as the Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT) tell series apart through a static input that describes each series and does not change over time. In the special case of a federated setting where each client holds a single series, this static input is constant within each client and varies only across clients. We ask whether a federated TFT can learn from it. Per-batch FedAdam, which aggregates gradients after every batch, uses the static input almost as well as central training, whereas communication-efficient schemes with local epochs (FedAvg, FedAdam+Prox) extract far less from it and gain nothing significant on either application dataset. At the same local computation, an Adam-compatible SCAFFOLD keeps the static pathway responsive on wind power and gains significantly there. On building energy its error still drops, but the static pathway falls silent, so drift and communication frequency cannot be fully separated as the cause. Only per-batch FedAdam matches or beats the per-client local models across all datasets. We confirm the effect on building-energy meter data, a wind-power dataset, and a controlled synthetic dataset. The loss is not specific to the TFT: on the synthetic and the wind data two further architectures with different static-conditioning mechanisms show it as well.

AI.tldr: The paper studies federated time series forecasting where each client holds a single series, and shows that a federated Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT) can learn from a constant static input only under per-batch FedAdam, while communication-efficient schemes with local epochs extract far less from it.
AI.motivation: In federated settings where each client holds one series, the static input that distinguishes series is constant within a client and varies only across clients, and it was unknown whether federated models can exploit it under communication-efficient training.
AI.method: The authors compare per-batch FedAdam, which aggregates gradients after every batch, against FedAvg, FedAdam with a proximal term, and an Adam-compatible SCAFFOLD, evaluated on building-energy meter data, wind-power data, and a controlled synthetic dataset, with two further architectures tested on the synthetic and wind data.
AI.result: Per-batch FedAdam uses the static input almost as well as central training. FedAvg and FedAdam+Prox extract far less and gain nothing significant on either application dataset. SCAFFOLD keeps the static pathway responsive and gains significantly on wind power, but on building energy the static pathway falls silent even though error drops. Only per-batch FedAdam matches or beats the per-client local models across all datasets.
AI.conclusion: Use of static context in federated forecasting depends on the aggregation frequency, and drift and communication frequency cannot be fully separated as the cause of the loss, which is not specific to the TFT.

title: PRISM-AMC: Replay-Free Continual Learning for Automatic Modulation Classification
summary: Automatic modulation classification (AMC) is a key component of cognitive wireless systems, enabling spectrum awareness and adaptive communication. Most deep learning approaches to AMC assume a fixed set of modulation classes and access to previously observed training data. In practice, modulation classes and channel conditions may evolve over time, while storage or data-retention constraints may preclude replay of raw baseband I/Q samples. We propose PRISM-AMC, a replay-free continual learning framework that mitigates catastrophic forgetting by preserving task-relevant subspaces of intermediate representations via gradient projection memory. We further analyze projected stochastic-gradient updates under an SNR-dependent gradient-noise model. PRISM-AMC is evaluated in both class-incremental and domain-incremental settings. Experiments on the MIGOU and DeepSig 2018.01A datasets show substantially reduced forgetting relative to sequential fine-tuning and elastic weight consolidation, while remaining competitive with or outperforming replay-based RSD-AMC in class-incremental settings, without storing raw I/Q samples.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes PRISM-AMC, a replay-free continual learning framework for automatic modulation classification that preserves task-relevant subspaces of intermediate representations via gradient projection memory to reduce catastrophic forgetting without storing raw I/Q samples.
AI.motivation: Deep learning AMC methods usually assume a fixed set of modulation classes and access to past training data, while in practice classes and channel conditions evolve and storage constraints may forbid replaying raw baseband I/Q samples.
AI.method: PRISM-AMC uses gradient projection memory to protect task-relevant subspaces of intermediate representations, and the authors analyze projected stochastic-gradient updates under an SNR-dependent gradient-noise model. It is evaluated in class-incremental and domain-incremental settings.
AI.result: On the MIGOU and DeepSig 2018.01A datasets, PRISM-AMC shows substantially reduced forgetting relative to sequential fine-tuning and elastic weight consolidation, and remains competitive with or outperforms replay-based RSD-AMC in class-incremental settings.
AI.conclusion: Replay-free continual learning via gradient projection can effectively mitigate forgetting for AMC without storing raw I/Q data.

title: Catastrophic Overfitting is Weight Drift the Training Loss Cannot See
comment: 12 pages (including appendix), 7 figures, 6 tables. Code available at this https URL
summary: Fast adversarial training (FAT) makes robust training affordable by replacing the multi-step attack with a single-step one, but it suffers from catastrophic overfitting (CO): partway through training, robustness to multi-step attacks collapses to near zero while the single-step attack used for training keeps being repelled. We show that CO is a quiet escape of the weights. Across the event the network's clean behavior quietly improves, and moving from the weights just before CO to those just after it changes the training objective only marginally while destroying most of the robustness. The training objective is therefore nearly blind to the displacement it causes, so it exerts no force to undo it. The exponential moving average (EMA) of the weights, which FAT protocols already maintain, does not accumulate this drift and stays robust through the entire event. This observation suggests a nearly free fix: when validation robustness drops, reset the weights to their EMA. We build this guard on top of a coupling-based base method designed so that its average stays inside the robust region. The resulting training removes CO in every one of our runs and attains the strongest AutoAttack accuracy among fast methods on all three benchmark datasets, including a clear margin on CIFAR-100, where it also clears the multi-step reference at roughly half its cost. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper explains catastrophic overfitting (CO) in fast adversarial training as a weight drift that the training loss cannot detect, and proposes a guard that resets weights to their exponential moving average (EMA) when validation robustness drops, removing CO in all runs.
AI.motivation: Fast adversarial training with single-step attacks suffers from catastrophic overfitting, where robustness to multi-step attacks collapses while the training objective appears unaffected, and existing methods do not explain the mechanism or prevent it reliably.
AI.method: The authors show that moving from weights just before CO to weights just after it changes the training objective only marginally while destroying most robustness, and that the EMA of weights does not accumulate this drift. The guard resets weights to the EMA when validation robustness drops and is built on a coupling-based base method whose average stays inside the robust region.
AI.result: The resulting training removes CO in every run and attains the strongest AutoAttack accuracy among fast methods on all three benchmark datasets, with a clear margin on CIFAR-100, where it also clears the multi-step reference at roughly half its cost.
