AI.conclusion: Catastrophic overfitting is a quiet weight escape that the training loss cannot see, and a nearly free EMA-based reset is an effective remedy.

title: Shallow Encoding Emits Deep Memories
comment: 47 pages. Mingyuan Ma and Yangmin Li contributed equally
summary: Hybrid language models interleave a few softmax-attention layers with many linear-attention or state-space layers, so every layer keeps a memory of earlier tokens: a key-value cache or a fixed-size recurrent state. Serving them spends more compute and high-bandwidth memory on these memories than the output requires. The prefill runs every layer for every prompt token, and every decode step loads and stores whole recurrent states, which on Qwen3.8-Flash-Next take as many bytes per request as the attention cache of thousands of tokens. We find two properties of trained hybrids that locate this excess. First, writes are easier than reads: writing a deep layer's memory of a token needs little of the deep computation that predicting the next token needs. Trained copies of the deep layers' write paths, which we call emitters, therefore write a prompt's deep memories from the residual stream of a shallower anchor layer, and all prompt tokens but the last run as few as 63% of the layers. Second, recurrent states have a state sink: most of their energy lies in a rank-one term along a fixed direction of each head, and the rest is a low-rank working memory. SEED builds on both: it makes the prefill shallow in depth and the decode state shallow in representation. Each recurrent state is stored as its sink plus low-rank factors, which the Gated DeltaNet, Kimi Delta Attention and Mamba-2 updates extend exactly; we prove that the open-loop error of the periodic compressions back to low rank is bounded independently of their number. SEED keeps the original weights frozen, compresses no attention cache, and runs all layers for every generated token. On six checkpoints of five production hybrids of 30B to over 300B parameters, it is nearly lossless on eleven official exams. Served with SGLang on NVIDIA GB300 GPUs on an agentic-coding trace, it raises the per-GPU throughput of Qwen3.8-Flash-Next 1.2-1.4x.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes SEED, which makes prefill shallow in depth by having trained write-path copies (emitters) write deep-layer memories from a shallower anchor layer, and makes decoding shallow in representation by storing recurrent states as a rank-one state sink plus low-rank factors, while keeping the original weights frozen.
AI.motivation: Hybrid language models keep a key-value cache or a recurrent state for every layer, so serving them spends excess compute and high-bandwidth memory on memories whose outputs are not needed, since writing a memory is easier than reading it.
AI.method: Trained emitters write a prompt's deep memories from the residual stream of a shallower anchor layer, so most prompt tokens run as few as 63% of the layers. Each recurrent state is stored as its sink plus low-rank factors, which the Gated DeltaNet, Kimi Delta Attention and Mamba-2 updates extend exactly, and the authors prove that the open-loop error of periodic compressions is bounded independently of their number.
AI.result: On six checkpoints of five production hybrids of 30B to over 300B parameters, SEED is nearly lossless on eleven official exams. Served with SGLang on NVIDIA GB300 GPUs on an agentic-coding trace, it raises per-GPU throughput of Qwen3.8-Flash-Next by 1.2-1.4x.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting the asymmetry between writes and reads and the state sink in recurrent states yields substantial serving speedups for hybrid models without retraining the base weights or compressing attention caches.

title: Learning When to Think Aloud in Latent Reasoning
summary: Latent Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning improves efficiency by shifting intermediate computation into continuous hidden states. However, fully latent methods often struggle on precision-critical tasks such as mathematical reasoning, while existing hybrid approaches retain substantial token-generation overhead. We introduce VITAL, an importance-guided hybrid reasoning framework that selectively verbalizes informative tokens as reasoning anchors while keeping most computation latent. A lightweight gating head dynamically selects between explicit token generation and direct hidden-state feedback. VITAL constructs hybrid trajectories from explicit CoT using token- importance estimation and trains the model through curriculum-based supervised training, followed by reinforcement learning with a reward that balances correctness and conciseness. Experiments show that VITAL consistently out- performs existing fully latent reasoning methods, achieving relative average accuracy gains of 9.6% on GPT-2 and 5.1% on Llama-3.2-1B at comparable reasoning lengths. Compared with hybrid baselines, VITAL achieves higher reasoning accuracy with substantially shorter reasoning trajectories on Qwen3-1.7B.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces VITAL, a hybrid latent reasoning framework that uses a gating head to choose between verbalizing informative tokens as explicit reasoning anchors and feeding back hidden states directly, keeping most computation latent.
AI.motivation: Fully latent chain-of-thought reasoning is efficient but often struggles on precision-critical tasks such as mathematical reasoning, while existing hybrid approaches still incur substantial token-generation overhead.
AI.method: Hybrid trajectories are built from explicit CoT using token-importance estimation, and the model is trained with curriculum-based supervised training followed by reinforcement learning with a reward balancing correctness and conciseness. A lightweight gating head selects between explicit token generation and direct hidden-state feedback.
AI.result: VITAL outperforms existing fully latent reasoning methods, with relative average accuracy gains of 9.6% on GPT-2 and 5.1% on Llama-3.2-1B at comparable reasoning lengths. Compared with hybrid baselines on Qwen3-1.7B, it achieves higher accuracy with substantially shorter reasoning trajectories.
AI.conclusion: Selectively verbalizing important tokens while keeping most computation latent improves both accuracy and efficiency over fully latent and hybrid reasoning baselines.

title: Short-Term Forecasting of Heterogeneous Wind Power Fleets: Global Temporal Fusion Transformer Leveraging Static Covariates
comment: 18th International Green Energy Conference (IGEC-XVIII) & the 7th International Conference on Energy and AI (ICEAI-VII)
summary: Accurate short-term wind power forecasting is critical for grid stability and electricity trading. While transformer-based deep learning is state of the art, industry practice relies mostly on local models trained for individual assets. This study investigates whether a global temporal fusion transformer (TFT), trained jointly on a heterogeneous portfolio of wind farms across Germany, outperforms site-specific local models in 48-hour-ahead forecasting. Using numerical weather prediction (NWP) data from the regional ICON-D2 and the global ECMWF HRES models, we compare the global TFT against local models and a linear regression baseline. The global model leverages static covariates, such as farm age, altitude above sea level, hub height, rotor diameter and power curve parameters, to learn shared representations across sites. We evaluate on 100 synthetic wind farm profiles and a real portfolio of 11 German wind farms, across two seasonal test periods with intermediate retraining. The global TFT outperforms the local models for 87% of the synthetic and 77% of the real wind farms and clearly surpasses the linear baseline. Wilcoxon signed-rank tests confirm that these gains are significant across both seasons and datasets. Crucially, this superiority depends on static covariates: without asset-specific context, the global model fails to generalize. The TFT's variable selection network (VSN) reveals the learned feature selection. Altitude emerges as a relevant static discriminator on both datasets, while hub height is decisive on the real portfolio. For dynamic inputs, the encoder prioritizes historical power, whereas the decoder combines upper-level wind speeds from both NWP models, consistent with averaging out model-specific errors. These findings support a shift from single-site to scalable multi-site forecasting, reducing operational complexity while improving accuracy in large portfolios.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that a single global temporal fusion transformer (TFT) trained jointly on a heterogeneous portfolio of German wind farms outperforms site-specific local models for 48-hour-ahead wind power forecasting, provided it has access to static covariates.
AI.motivation: Industry practice relies mostly on local models trained per asset, and it was unclear whether a global transformer can outperform them across heterogeneous wind farms.
AI.method: The global TFT uses static covariates such as farm age, altitude, hub height, rotor diameter and power curve parameters, with numerical weather prediction data from ICON-D2 and ECMWF HRES. It is compared with local models and a linear regression baseline on 100 synthetic wind farm profiles and 11 real German wind farms across two seasonal test periods with intermediate retraining, using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests.
AI.result: The global TFT outperforms local models for 87% of synthetic and 77% of real wind farms and clearly surpasses the linear baseline, with gains significant across seasons and datasets. Without asset-specific static context the global model fails to generalize. The variable selection network highlights altitude as a relevant static discriminator on both datasets and hub height as decisive on the real portfolio.
AI.conclusion: The results support a shift from single-site to scalable multi-site wind power forecasting, which reduces operational complexity while improving accuracy in large portfolios.

title: Neural Stochastic Forecasting for Lateral Molecular Diffusion Simulations
summary: Predicting the long-time diffusion of membrane proteins is challenging because molecular dynamics (MD) simulations are computationally expensive, while experimental single-particle tracking is often limited by finite observation times. Here, we introduce a neural stochastic (NS) model for forecasting the collective diffusion of membrane proteins from coarse-grained MD trajectories. The model combines a transformer-based representation of protein configurations, recurrent networks operating at multiple temporal scales, and a stochastic latent process with learned memory. A cross-attention decoder then generates correlated protein displacements while accounting for the instantaneous system geometry and periodic boundary conditions. We evaluate the model in two membrane systems: seven interacting PIEZO channels and a mixed system containing seven PIEZO and ten TREK channels. For the seven PIEZO system, the NS model reproduces the anomalous diffusion exponent measured in MD simulations $\alpha \sim 1$, substantially improving on a previously developed variational autoregressive model that exhibits superdiffusive behavior. The model also generates trajectories extending to 40,000 frames and captures the distinct diffusion characteristics of PIEZO and TREK populations in the mixed system. Comparisons of time-averaged mean-square displacements, Van Hove displacement distributions, and non-Gaussian parameters show that the model preserves key statistical features of the simulated dynamics. These results establish neural stochastic modeling as a promising approach for generating long trajectories of multi-protein membrane diffusion and extending the statistical analysis of molecular dynamics simulations.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a neural stochastic (NS) model that forecasts long-time collective diffusion of membrane proteins from coarse-grained molecular dynamics (MD) trajectories, generating trajectories of up to 40,000 frames that preserve key statistical features of the simulated dynamics.
AI.motivation: MD simulations of membrane proteins are computationally expensive, while experimental single-particle tracking is limited by finite observation times, so long-time diffusion is hard to obtain.
AI.method: The NS model combines a transformer-based representation of protein configurations, multi-timescale recurrent networks, and a stochastic latent process with learned memory, and a cross-attention decoder generates correlated displacements that respect the instantaneous geometry and periodic boundary conditions.
AI.result: For seven PIEZO channels the model reproduces the anomalous diffusion exponent alpha of about 1 measured in MD, substantially improving on a previous variational autoregressive model that is superdiffusive. In a mixed system of seven PIEZO and ten TREK channels it captures the distinct diffusion characteristics of each population, and time-averaged mean-square displacements, Van Hove distributions and non-Gaussian parameters agree with the simulations.
AI.conclusion: Neural stochastic modeling is a promising approach for generating long membrane-protein diffusion trajectories and extending the statistical analysis of MD simulations.

title: Selective Prediction Intervals: Jointly Learning to Predict, Bound, and Abstain
summary: Many high-stakes regression decisions ask three things of a model at once: a point estimate to act on, an interval that bounds the risk of acting, and the option to abstain when neither can be trusted. Deep learning provides these in isolation: prediction-interval methods return an interval, and at best a value estimate inside it, for every input, while selective-prediction methods learn when to abstain, but only for point predictions and with no statement of how far the truth may lie from the estimate. We introduce SelPI, which trains interval, value and abstention heads jointly under a single loss with an explicit acceptance-rate budget. A natural objection is that interval width already tells us when to abstain. We show that it does not: across 18 tabular benchmarks, width predicts large point errors well (AUROC 0.72) but is anti-correlated with interval misses (AUROC 0.38), so abstaining on wide intervals discards precisely the inputs the interval got right. SelPI therefore selects with two gates, one trained on the interval loss and one on the value loss, coupled by a Fr'echet penalty that ties their separate budgets to the joint acceptance rate they deliver. With the base predictor held fixed, the learned gate beats width thresholding on a proper interval score on all 18 tabular datasets, closing a median 87% of the gap to an oracle selector, and it also beats selection by deep-ensemble disagreement on every dataset. The advantage grows with the heteroscedasticity of the task, and we report the settings in which it disappears.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes SelPI, which jointly trains interval, value and abstention heads under one loss with an acceptance-rate budget, and selects with two gates coupled by a Frechet penalty, so that it outperforms interval-width thresholding across 18 tabular benchmarks.
AI.motivation: High-stakes regression needs a point estimate, a bounding interval and an option to abstain together, but prediction-interval methods and selective-prediction methods each address only part of this, and interval width is anti-correlated with interval misses (AUROC 0.38) even though it predicts large point errors (AUROC 0.72).
AI.method: SelPI trains interval, value and abstention heads jointly, with two gates trained on the interval loss and on the value loss respectively, coupled by a Frechet penalty that ties their separate budgets to the joint acceptance rate. The base predictor is held fixed when comparing against width thresholding.
AI.result: With the base predictor fixed, the learned gate beats width thresholding on a proper interval score on all 18 tabular datasets, closing a median 87% of the gap to an oracle selector, and it beats selection by deep-ensemble disagreement on every dataset. The advantage grows with heteroscedasticity, and the authors report settings where it disappears.
AI.conclusion: Abstention for intervals should be learned rather than inferred from width, and the learned two-gate selector gives a reliable advantage in the heteroscedastic regimes studied.

title: FaCoDiff: Factor-Correlated Diffusion for Multivariate Probabilistic Forecasting
summary: Multivariate probabilistic forecasting requires modeling cross-variable dependence alongside marginal uncertainty. The challenge is to learn this dependence while controlling marginal noise scales and avoiding dense covariance costs. We propose Factor-Correlated Diffusion (FaCoDiff), which couples a compact conditional statistical estimator with structured denoising. History-conditioned factor loadings use distinct coefficients for forecast-center correction, scale adjustment and noise dependence. Diagonal compensation preserves the estimated marginal noise variances, while low-rank operators enable residual Gaussian likelihood evaluation and noise transport without dense covariance storage or factorization. Factor-derived feature modulation explicitly conditions the denoiser, and a geometry-aware objective accounts for errors after noise transport. The same conditional geometry governs forward perturbations and reverse sampling. Across nine datasets, FaCoDiff achieves the lowest mean variogram score on eight datasets and ranks among the top two on 43 of 54 dataset-metric combinations in the reported comparisons. Matched ablations on Solar and Weather show that factor covariance improves mean Energy and Variogram scores under all four combinations of center and scale correction. Disrupting cross-variable sample pairings while preserving marginal trajectories worsens joint and aggregate scores on both datasets, demonstrating the predictive value of generated cross-variable dependence.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Factor-Correlated Diffusion (FaCoDiff), a diffusion model for multivariate probabilistic forecasting that models cross-variable dependence with history-conditioned factor loadings and low-rank operators, avoiding dense covariance storage.
AI.motivation: Multivariate probabilistic forecasting must learn cross-variable dependence while controlling marginal noise scales, and dense covariance modeling is costly.
AI.method: A compact conditional statistical estimator couples with structured denoising. Factor loadings use distinct coefficients for forecast-center correction, scale adjustment and noise dependence, diagonal compensation preserves marginal noise variances, low-rank operators enable residual Gaussian likelihood evaluation and noise transport, and factor-derived feature modulation conditions the denoiser.
AI.result: Across nine datasets FaCoDiff achieves the lowest mean variogram score on eight, and ranks among the top two on 43 of 54 dataset-metric combinations in the reported comparisons. Ablations on Solar and Weather show that factor covariance improves Energy and Variogram scores under all four combinations of center and scale correction, and disrupting cross-variable sample pairings worsens joint and aggregate scores.
AI.conclusion: Generated cross-variable dependence has predictive value, and the factor-based conditional geometry gives an efficient and effective route to multivariate diffusion forecasting.

title: GPUMAP: GPU-Accelerated Progressive Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection
summary: Dimensionality reduction (DR) techniques are fundamental to the analysis of high-dimensional data, yet their substantial computational cost limits their use in interactive settings. To address this limitation, we present GPU-accelerated Progressive Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (GPUMAP), an efficient progressive DR algorithm designed for interactive use. We identify three atomic operations within UMAP and restructure them into a progressive pipeline. As part of this adaptation, we introduce modifications to UMAP, including operation queues, instance-wise local join, and scheduling strategies. We further accelerate computation by leveraging GPU parallelism, enabling interactive analysis of million-scale datasets on commodity GPU hardware. Finally, we employ our implementation to systematically study the behavior of progressive DR, investigating how projections evolve over time relative to the ground-truth projection and how biased data streams influence the quality and stability of the resulting projections.

AI.tldr: The paper presents GPUMAP, a GPU-accelerated progressive variant of UMAP that restructures UMAP into a progressive pipeline for interactive dimensionality reduction on million-scale datasets, and uses it to study how progressive projections evolve.
AI.motivation: Dimensionality reduction is fundamental to high-dimensional data analysis but its computational cost limits interactive use.
AI.method: The authors identify three atomic operations within UMAP and restructure them into a progressive pipeline, introducing operation queues, instance-wise local join and scheduling strategies, and accelerate computation with GPU parallelism.
AI.result: The implementation enables interactive analysis of million-scale datasets on commodity GPU hardware, and the authors use it to study how projections evolve relative to the ground-truth projection and how biased data streams affect quality and stability.
AI.conclusion: Progressive DR with GPU acceleration makes interactive analysis of very large datasets practical, and the study shows how data bias shapes the stability of progressive projections.

title: Cross-Asset Knowledge Transfer for Early Fault Detection of Data-Scarce Assets Without Target Fault Data
summary: Reliability management of industrial fleets depends on early fault warnings, yet lifecycle data across similar assets are highly imbalanced. A few assets accumulate run-to-failure histories, while newly installed or rarely failing assets provide only normal-condition data. This paper asks how diagnostic knowledge can be transferred from a data-rich source asset to a data-scarce target asset when no fault data have been observed on the target. We formulate cross-asset early fault detection as a zero-shot domain adaptation problem, in which zero-shot refers to the absence of target fault samples, and propose a framework that requires only normal data from the target. The framework comprises (1) a statistical process control step that labels the source asset run-to-failure data with an exponentially weighted moving average chart, reducing manual annotation to verifying flagged segments, (2) an Adapted Domain-Adversarial Neural Network (ADANN) that combines domain-adversarial training and a Maximum Mean Discrepancy penalty with an Adapted Classification-Domain (ACD) loss, which anchors the classifier normal region to the target own normal data, and (3) an ahead-of-time labeling scheme with a prediction horizon that targets incipient faults. Under an exact-classification assumption, a theoretical analysis characterizes the domain-adversarial term for a normal-only target and the alignment state in which source fault features remain separated from target normal features. On a public run-to-failure bearing dataset, ADANN attains the highest mean F1-score among four transfer baselines, with a nominally significant precision gain over the strongest baseline, and its robustness is examined under synthetic noise.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a zero-shot domain adaptation framework that transfers fault diagnosis from a data-rich source asset to a data-scarce target asset using only target normal data, combining EWMA-based labeling, an Adapted Domain-Adversarial Neural Network (ADANN) with MMD and an Adapted Classification-Domain loss, and ahead-of-time labeling.
AI.motivation: Industrial lifecycle data are highly imbalanced, with few assets having run-to-failure histories and new or rarely failing assets providing only normal data, so early fault detection on a target asset without observed fault data is needed.
AI.method: A statistical process control step labels source run-to-failure data with an exponentially weighted moving average chart, reducing annotation to verifying flagged segments. ADANN combines domain-adversarial training with a Maximum Mean Discrepancy penalty and an Adapted Classification-Domain loss anchoring the classifier normal region to target normal data, and ahead-of-time labeling with a prediction horizon targets incipient faults. A theoretical analysis is given under an exact-classification assumption.
AI.result: On a public run-to-failure bearing dataset, ADANN attains the highest mean F1-score among four transfer baselines, with a nominally significant precision gain over the strongest baseline, and its robustness under synthetic noise is examined.
AI.conclusion: Cross-asset knowledge transfer can support early fault detection on data-scarce assets without any target fault samples, though the precision gain over the strongest baseline is only nominally significant.

title: Learning Noise Optimization for Reward Alignment in Few-Step Generative Models
summary: Reward alignment for diffusion- and flow-based generative models is often formulated over stochastic trajectories, making it less suitable for few-step deterministic generators. Initial noise optimization provides a trajectory-free alternative, but existing gradient-free methods require costly per-sample search at inference. We introduce LeNO (Learning Noise Optimization), which amortizes reward-guided initial noise optimization into a learned residual transport while keeping the pretrained generator frozen. LeNO learns an anchor-conditioned distribution over noise corrections using Local GRPO and scalar rewards, eliminating iterative test-time optimization. For Gaussian initial noise with norm-preserving projection, we derive a tractable upper bound on the KL divergence between the corrected noise distribution and the original prior, providing a principled regularization objective. We evaluate LeNO on few-step text-to-image and protein structure generation, including expensive black-box designability rewards. Across both domains, LeNO improves target rewards with a single noise correction at inference while largely preserving generation quality and diversity.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces LeNO, which amortizes reward-guided initial noise optimization into a learned residual transport over the noise of a frozen few-step generator, so that a single noise correction at inference improves target rewards without iterative test-time search.
AI.motivation: Reward alignment for few-step deterministic generators is poorly served by stochastic-trajectory formulations, and existing gradient-free initial noise optimization needs costly per-sample search at inference.
AI.method: LeNO learns an anchor-conditioned distribution over noise corrections using Local GRPO and scalar rewards while keeping the pretrained generator frozen. For Gaussian initial noise with norm-preserving projection, the authors derive a tractable upper bound on the KL divergence to the original prior as a regularization objective.
AI.result: LeNO is evaluated on few-step text-to-image and protein structure generation, including expensive black-box designability rewards. Across both domains it improves target rewards with a single noise correction at inference while largely preserving generation quality and diversity.
AI.conclusion: Learned noise correction removes the need for iterative test-time optimization and offers a practical route to reward alignment for few-step generators.

title: Consistency Learning and Distillation for One-Step MIMO-OFDM Channel Estimation
summary: Iterative neural channel estimators can improve recovery under pilot contamination, but repeated network evaluations increase inference cost. This paper develops observation-anchored consistency and Consistency Mid-Training (CMT) estimators for one-step channel estimation in multiple-input multiple-output orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (MIMO-OFDM) systems. Both estimators refine pilot-derived least-squares channel estimates in the delay-beam domain. Consistency learning couples endpoint predictions along noisy-to-clean paths. CMT then refines a compact consistency-trained student to predict a flow-matching teacher's endpoint from intermediate trajectory states. Across the evaluated SNR range, the compact CMT student reduces uncoded symbol error rate (SER) by 9.6-20.2% relative to the one-step flow-matching baseline (0.44-0.98 dB in logarithmic SER reduction), while using 74.5% fewer parameters and 73.0% fewer network multiply-accumulates.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes observation-anchored consistency and Consistency Mid-Training (CMT) estimators for one-step MIMO-OFDM channel estimation, where a compact CMT student learns to predict a flow-matching teacher's endpoint from intermediate trajectory states.
AI.motivation: Iterative neural channel estimators improve recovery under pilot contamination but repeated network evaluations raise inference cost, motivating a one-step alternative.
AI.method: Both estimators refine pilot-derived least-squares channel estimates in the delay-beam domain. Consistency learning couples endpoint predictions along noisy-to-clean paths, and CMT refines a compact consistency-trained student to predict the flow-matching teacher's endpoint from intermediate trajectory states.
AI.result: Across the evaluated SNR range, the compact CMT student reduces uncoded symbol error rate by 9.6-20.2% relative to the one-step flow-matching baseline (0.44-0.98 dB in logarithmic SER reduction), while using 74.5% fewer parameters and 73.0% fewer network multiply-accumulates.
AI.conclusion: The compact CMT student offers better error performance than the one-step flow-matching baseline at a substantially lower model size and compute cost.

title: EEGDash Corpus: A Training-Ready Public Corpus for EEG Foundation Models
comment: 8 pages, 6 figures, 7 tables. Accepted at the Workshop on Machine Learning for EEG Signal Processing (MLESP 2026), IEEE BIBM 2026
summary: Foundation models for electroencephalography (EEG) are pretrained on tens of thousands of hours of recordings, and their accuracy grows with that amount. Such data is hard to assemble. The largest sources are clinical archives that cannot be redistributed, and the public sources are spread over several archives, file formats, and licences. We release eegdash-corpus-v0, a training-ready corpus of 77 public EEG datasets, as the gated Hugging Face dataset EEGDash/eegdash-corpus-v0 with the SHA-256 of every file. REVE, the largest published EEG foundation model, names 89 datasets as its pretraining corpus. Twelve cannot be redistributed: four clinical archives that hold 82% of its hours, and eight under no-derivatives licences. The corpus holds the 76 others that REVE's sampling rate allows and one more from REVE's release card: 77 datasets, 14,075 hours from 7,272 subjects, 5.0 million 10-second samples and 6.21 billion tokens per epoch. Every dataset is fetched through EEGDash, converted once with REVE's recipe, and stored in its own buckets of a chunked Zarr store with its licence recorded beside it, so a model can train on the whole store or on any subset of datasets. To test that the store pretrains a model, we retrain REVE-Base from scratch twice with the authors' code, changed only in how it reads data, and score it on seven public OpenEEGBench tasks. It reaches 0.331 under linear probing and 0.273 after fine-tuning, against 0.333 and 0.325 for the released model and 0.200 and 0.205 for an untrained encoder. The converter, the conversion reports, and the loader changes are released with the corpus.

AI.tldr: The paper releases eegdash-corpus-v0, a training-ready corpus of 77 public EEG datasets (14,075 hours from 7,272 subjects) hosted as a gated Hugging Face dataset, and shows that a model retrained from scratch on it reaches performance close to the released REVE-Base model.
AI.motivation: EEG foundation models need tens of thousands of hours of data, but the largest sources cannot be redistributed and public sources are scattered across archives, file formats and licences, so a training-ready public corpus is hard to assemble.
AI.method: Each dataset is fetched through EEGDash, converted once with REVE's recipe, and stored in its own buckets of a chunked Zarr store with its licence recorded, with SHA-256 checksums for every file. REVE-Base is retrained from scratch twice with the authors' code, changed only in how it reads data, and scored on seven public OpenEEGBench tasks.
AI.result: The retrained model reaches 0.331 under linear probing and 0.273 after fine-tuning, against 0.333 and 0.325 for the released model and 0.200 and 0.205 for an untrained encoder.
AI.conclusion: The corpus can pretrain a competitive EEG foundation model, and the converter, conversion reports and loader changes are released alongside it.

title: Give Up to Get More: Priors, Not Policies, Govern Test-Time Compute Allocation
comment: 36 pages, 6 figures. Code, results and survey coding: this https URL
summary: When many inputs share a budget of repeated attempts by a large language model (LLM), a common rule gives harder inputs more. On public math, code and formal-proof samples, the best published difficulty-proportional rule captures half or more of the oracle gain on benchmarks the model mostly solves, but at most 13% on hard workloads, even given true pass rates. Because the value of one more attempt peaks at intermediate difficulty, the optimal static allocation is inverted-U and gives little to inputs that are hopeless at the current budget. In a strict survey of 221 LLM allocation papers, at least 13 give the hardest inputs the most attempts; their easier settings sit at budgets where this is near-optimal, so the cost appears on harder workloads. Acting on it requires knowing which inputs are solvable, so information, not the policy, drives the gain. With a verifier and a prior from a related model's past runs on the same inputs, Thompson Sampling raises the solved share on the hardest workload from 14% to 27%; without such a prior, no policy we tested beats round-robin. For the policies we tested, the gain vanishes between prior rank correlations of about 0.3 and 0.55, which cheap text-based priors barely reach on the weakest models, and it requires a verifier whose false acceptances are rare relative to the pass rate. On new Qwen2.5 samples the pattern holds, and tempering the prior avoids losses on easy workloads. We turn these results into a decision guide.

AI.tldr: Shows that how repeated LLM attempts are split across inputs depends mainly on priors about which inputs are solvable rather than on the allocation rule itself. Thompson Sampling with a verifier and a prior from a related model's past runs raises the solved share on the hardest workload from 14% to 27%.
AI.motivation: Under a shared budget of repeated LLM attempts, the common rule of giving harder inputs more attempts is widely used, but the best published difficulty-proportional rule captures half or more of the oracle gain on mostly solved benchmarks and at most 13% on hard workloads.
AI.method: A strict survey of 221 LLM allocation papers, an analysis of the optimal static allocation as a function of difficulty, and experiments on public math, code and formal-proof samples comparing allocation policies, with Thompson Sampling using a verifier and a prior from a related model's past runs on the same inputs.
AI.result: The optimal static allocation is inverted-U and gives little to inputs that are hopeless at the current budget; at least 13 of the 221 surveyed papers give the hardest inputs the most attempts. With a verifier and such a prior, Thompson Sampling raises the solved share on the hardest workload from 14% to 27%; without a prior no tested policy beats round-robin, and the gain vanishes between prior rank correlations of about 0.3 and 0.55.
AI.conclusion: Information about which inputs are solvable, not the allocation policy, drives the gain; the pattern holds on new Qwen2.5 samples, tempering the prior avoids losses on easy workloads, and the results are turned into a decision guide.

title: KolTa: A Physics-Informed Active Learning Framework for Formulation Discovery with Limited Data
comment: 21 pages, including 11 pages of supplementary material; 4 figures
summary: Finding high-performing formulations is difficult when few have been measured and experimental budgets are limited. We propose KolTa, an active learning framework that selects batches to discover the top 5% of formulations at a target temperature under a fixed query budget. KolTa combines a three-stage predictor of component contributions, role-conditioned interactions, and anchored temperature response with task-specific soft physics constraints. Its Physics-Residual-Calibrated Upper Confidence Bound (PRC-UCB) acquisition rule combines predicted utility, ensemble disagreement, and a target-temperature physics residual, with nonnegative exploration weights fitted to out-of-fold signed errors. We evaluate the framework on three measured tasks and one simulated task covering binary-mixture viscosity, drug solubility, ionic-liquid viscosity, and electrolyte conductivity. KolTa ranks first or second in mean area under the learning curve (AULC) on every task and outperforms seven of the eight comparator strategies in paired tests, winning 75 of 78 paired comparisons across tasks and seeds against those seven strategies. Across the three measured tasks, its largest gap to the best mean AULC is 0.032, compared with at least 0.056 for every comparator. On Drug, reaching 80% average recovery of the remaining targets across drugs requires an estimated median of 348 additional formulation queries, about 18% fewer than the fastest comparator. Researchers can adapt the framework to diverse formulation problems through component roles and physical constraints.

AI.tldr: KolTa is an active learning framework that selects query batches to find the top 5% of formulations at a target temperature under a fixed query budget. It ranks first or second in mean AULC on every task.
AI.motivation: Finding high-performing formulations is difficult when few have been measured and experimental budgets are limited.
AI.method: A three-stage predictor of component contributions with role-conditioned interactions and anchored temperature response, with task-specific soft physics constraints, and the PRC-UCB acquisition rule, which combines predicted utility, ensemble disagreement and a target-temperature physics residual, with nonnegative exploration weights fitted to out-of-fold signed errors.
AI.result: Evaluated on three measured tasks and one simulated task (binary-mixture viscosity, drug solubility, ionic-liquid viscosity, electrolyte conductivity), KolTa ranks first or second in mean AULC on every task and wins 75 of 78 paired comparisons against seven comparator strategies. Its largest gap to the best mean AULC is 0.032, against at least 0.056 for every comparator; on Drug, reaching 80% average recovery needs an estimated median of 348 additional queries, about 18% fewer than the fastest comparator.
AI.conclusion: The framework can be adapted to diverse formulation problems through component roles and physical constraints.

title: Partially Interpretable Decision Trees
summary: Partially interpretable models extend simple interpretable models with the option to defer complicated inputs to an accurate but uninterpretable black-box model. By deferring more inputs, the model gets more accurate; by deferring fewer, it gets more interpretable. Existing procedures to train such partially interpretable models build on linear models or decision rules. We propose three algorithms for decision trees: a partially interpretable extension of the existing Branches algorithm, which performs exact search to optimize the tree; a conversion algorithm that we run on top of standard CART, which is computationally more efficient; and a generalized CART whose splitting criterion takes into account the option to defer while growing the tree. Perhaps surprisingly, the performance of the three algorithms is similar across many realworld datasets. We can explain this through a formal bound on the potential gain of smart tree construction, provided the black box accuracy is sufficiently homogeneous across the domain. We also construct a synthetic dataset where the accuracy of the black box is deliberately inhomogeneous. There, our deferral-aware generalization of CART does outperform regular CART and matches the performance of exact search. Finally, we evaluate an application to concept bottleneck models. Partially interpretable decision trees can replace uninterpretable neural networks after the bottleneck. On undeferred inputs, the model is fully interpretable, and deferring preserves accuracy.

AI.tldr: Proposes three algorithms for partially interpretable decision trees, which defer complicated inputs to a black-box model. The three perform similarly on many real datasets, and a deferral-aware CART outperforms regular CART on a synthetic dataset with inhomogeneous black-box accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing procedures for training partially interpretable models build on linear models or decision rules rather than on decision trees.
AI.method: A partially interpretable extension of the Branches algorithm with exact search, a conversion algorithm run on top of standard CART, and a generalized CART whose splitting criterion accounts for the option to defer.
AI.result: The three algorithms perform similarly across many real-world datasets, which a formal bound on the potential gain of smart tree construction explains when black-box accuracy is sufficiently homogeneous. On a synthetic dataset with deliberately inhomogeneous black-box accuracy, the deferral-aware CART outperforms regular CART and matches exact search.
AI.conclusion: In a concept bottleneck model application, partially interpretable trees can replace uninterpretable neural networks after the bottleneck; undeferred inputs are fully interpretable and deferring preserves accuracy.

title: Graph Foundation Models Can Become Effective Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detectors
summary: Multivariate time series anomaly detection (MTSAD) relies on modeling both temporal dynamics and inter-sensor dependencies to identify complex system faults. Although graph-based detectors explicitly model sensor topologies, they train task-specific networks from scratch on limited target-domain data, remaining vulnerable to spurious correlations and unable to reuse transferable priors. While pretrained Graph Foundation Models (GFMs) offer transferable topological priors and anomaly discriminability, directly adapting them to MTSAD is hindered by cross-modal feature-topology mismatch, unreliable pseudo-anomaly supervision, and decision distortion during node-to-window aggregation. To fill these gaps, we propose a novel adaptation framework, Gfm4Mtsad, which unleashes pretrained GFMs for MTSAD. We introduce the Structure-and-Information Contract Alignment (SICA) module to bridge continuous time series and the pretrained GFM space. This module harmonizes principal subspace token projection, normal-prior-guided graph construction, and residual recovery to suppress spurious edges while retaining fine-grained temporal details. We propose a Mechanism-Aligned Pseudo-Anomaly Screening strategy (MAPS) to steer unsupervised learning. It applies localized dependency breaks while preserving empirical residuals, selecting hard negatives near the normal boundary for targeted supervision. We develop a Tail-Gated Evidence Calibration mechanism (TGEC) to eliminate node-to-window aggregation distortion. It calibrates multi-granular graph responses against normal operational references, strictly preserving benign score rankings while selectively refining extreme anomaly candidates in the tail distribution for reliable window detection and interpretable sensor evidence. Extensive evaluations with two GFM backbones demonstrate that Gfm4Mtsad achieves superior detection performance over existing baselines.

AI.tldr: Gfm4Mtsad adapts pretrained graph foundation models to multivariate time series anomaly detection, instead of training task-specific graph detectors from scratch on limited target-domain data.
AI.motivation: Graph-based detectors train task-specific networks from scratch on limited data and are vulnerable to spurious correlations, while directly adapting pretrained graph foundation models is hindered by cross-modal feature-topology mismatch, unreliable pseudo-anomaly supervision and decision distortion in node-to-window aggregation.
AI.method: Three components: the SICA module, which aligns time series with the pretrained graph model space through principal subspace token projection, normal-prior-guided graph construction and residual recovery; MAPS, which creates pseudo-anomalies by localized dependency breaks and selects hard negatives near the normal boundary; and TGEC, which calibrates multi-granular graph responses against normal operational references to remove aggregation distortion.
AI.result: Extensive evaluations with two graph foundation model backbones show that Gfm4Mtsad achieves superior detection performance over existing baselines; the abstract reports no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Pretrained graph foundation models can be unleashed for multivariate time series anomaly detection, using transferable topological priors while keeping interpretable sensor evidence.

title: The Alignment Tax Is Graded: Task-Selective Capability Loss Under Length-Normalized DPO with SFT Retention
comment: 25 pages, 3 figures, 23 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Setting. This is an empirical characterization study; we propose no new method and run no comparisons against alternative objectives. We fine-tune Qwen3.5-4B with sparse LoRA and length-normalized DPO plus an SFT retention term (the RPO objective) on structured financial-filing tasks, and track downstream capability as the implicit reward margin grows to $\sim 7$ $\beta$-scaled units (nf4 training; $\sim 3$ under fp16 measurement on the unquantized base). Question. Does margin growth degrade capability uniformly across tasks, or selectively? Findings. In a pre-registered study (8 seeds, 6 unseen at freeze) with artifact-aware scoring and TOST equivalence testing, the alignment tax is graded and task-selective: extraction is preserved ($\Delta = -0.55$ pts, equivalent at $\pm5$ pts), json loses little ($\Delta = -3.52$ pts, equivalence fails on a clustered item-level interval), and router degrades severely ($\Delta = -30$ pts). Router's loss concentrates in a margin 1-3 damage window containing a transient format-break spike. The margin is accounted for almost entirely ($\geq 96\%$) by suppression of rejected completions, with chosen reward approximately flat, consistent with the retention term anchoring it; we do not attribute the behavioral damage to any single gradient channel. Gold-logp deflation is task-selective (extraction $-0.15$, json $-1.04$, router $-1.47$ nats/token under fp16), with gold selectively protected relative to incorrect controls on extraction (8/8 seeds). QLoRA reward margins differ up to $3.4\times$ between nf4 training and unquantized fp16 measurement, with an axis-dependent gap. Scope. Length-normalized rewards with SFT retention, sparse LoRA on 8/32 layers, one 4B model, easily-separable synthetic preferences, three structured tasks. A no-retention control and a measured format-alignment metric are left to future work.

AI.tldr: Fine-tuning Qwen3.5-4B with sparse LoRA, length-normalized DPO and an SFT retention term shows that alignment-induced capability loss is graded and task-selective rather than uniform across tasks.
AI.motivation: It is unknown whether growing the implicit reward margin degrades capability uniformly across tasks or selectively.
AI.method: An empirical characterization study with no new method: sparse LoRA on 8 of 32 layers, length-normalized DPO with SFT retention (the RPO objective), tracking downstream capability as the margin grows. A pre-registered study with 8 seeds (6 unseen at freeze), artifact-aware scoring and TOST equivalence testing covers three structured financial-filing tasks.
AI.result: Extraction is preserved (delta -0.55 points, equivalent at plus or minus 5 points), json loses little (delta -3.52 points, equivalence fails on a clustered item-level interval), and router degrades severely (delta -30 points), with its loss concentrated in a margin 1-3 damage window. The margin is accounted for at least 96% by suppression of rejected completions, with chosen reward roughly flat; gold-logp deflation is task-selective; QLoRA reward margins differ up to 3.4 times between nf4 training and unquantized fp16 measurement.
AI.conclusion: The alignment tax is graded and task-selective, and the behavioral damage is not attributed to any single gradient channel. Scope is one 4B model, easily separable synthetic preferences and three tasks; a no-retention control and a measured format-alignment metric are left to future work.

title: Nowcasting Future Performance for Population Pruning in Survival-of-the-Fittest Training
comment: Accepted at: 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Workshop: Neural Network Artifacts as a New Data Modality
summary: Training high-performing neural networks often involves evaluating populations of candidate models with varying hyperparameters, architectures, or random seeds. Training every candidate to completion is computationally expensive, yet stopping seemingly weaker runs early risks discarding models that would ultimately perform better, as learning curves can cross. To address this challenge, we investigate whether intermediate training checkpoints can predict future model accuracy and enable more informed pruning decisions. Our nowcasters predict test accuracy five epochs ahead or at the end of training. They are trained with accuracy and loss histories, weight statistics, and SANE representations as inputs. SANE is a transformer autoencoder that encodes a checkpoint as a sequence of latent tokens. We then use the nowcasters in Survival-of-the-Fittest (SOTF) training. SOTF repeatedly ranks runs during training by predicted accuracy and stops the lowest-ranked ones. Our results show that weight statistics work best for five-epoch forecasts, and SANE representations work best for final accuracy prediction. For evaluation, we compare SOTF with pruning the population by current accuracy. In homogeneous model zoos such as the CNN zoos, pruning by current accuracy already retains a final model only slightly worse than the best. Model zoos with a larger spread in performance, such as the ResNet-18 and ViT zoos, are more difficult to prune by current accuracy alone. In these zoos, SOTF with nowcasted final accuracy almost closes the gap to the best model.

AI.tldr: Nowcasters predict a model's test accuracy five epochs ahead or at the end of training from checkpoint features; used in Survival-of-the-Fittest training, they stop the lowest-ranked runs early.
AI.motivation: Training every candidate in a population to completion is expensive, but stopping seemingly weaker runs early risks discarding models whose learning curves would cross later.
AI.method: Nowcasters trained on accuracy and loss histories, weight statistics and SANE representations (a transformer autoencoder that encodes a checkpoint as latent tokens), used in SOTF training that repeatedly ranks runs by predicted accuracy and stops the lowest-ranked ones.
AI.result: Weight statistics work best for five-epoch forecasts and SANE representations work best for final accuracy. In CNN zoos, pruning by current accuracy already retains a final model only slightly worse than the best; in the ResNet-18 and ViT zoos, which have a larger performance spread, SOTF with nowcasted final accuracy almost closes the gap to the best model.
AI.conclusion: Nowcasting supports more informed pruning decisions, and it matters most when performance spread across the population is large.

title: An Interaction-Aware Decision Framework for FDIC-Assisted Distressed Bank Acquisitions: Empirical Evidence from the FDIC Failed-Bank Panel and the SVB-First Citizens Case
comment: 18 pages, 2 figures, 15 tables. Research code, datasets, and reproducibility materials are available at this https URL
summary: Acquirers of failed banks weigh acquisition value, regulatory protection, risk, buyer strength, and execution difficulty jointly, because each signal's meaning depends on the others: high non-performing loans matter less when government loss sharing absorbs the losses. The proposed Spider Network Filtering Framework encodes such dependencies as four interpretable interaction rules among five dimensions, yielding graph-inspired features for a logistic model and a Pursue/Caution/Avoid decision rule. We evaluate it on 55 acquisitions assisted by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation in 2008-2024 by acquirers with a parent listed in the United States. Six financial inputs come from regulatory reports published before each failure; two deal terms, which the winning bidder knows when it bids but investors learn at the announcement, come from the regulator's press releases. The outcome, a positive three-day abnormal return around the announcement, records the market's initial reception, not realized success. Under grouped, nested cross-validation, the Spider-enhanced model reaches a mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.594, against 0.615 for logistic regression on the same inputs and 0.632 for ridge regression; permutation tests that repeat the full model selection give at most weak evidence that any of them ranks better than chance. The Spider score used directly does not rank better than chance, and an apparent link between target distress and higher returns disappears against a bank-sector benchmark. Thresholds tuned for the F1 score approve most acquisitions with negative returns and realize negative utility when each costs three times what a positively received acquisition gains.

AI.tldr: The Spider Network Filtering Framework encodes interactions among five dimensions as rules for FDIC-assisted failed-bank acquisitions; on 55 deals from 2008 to 2024, the Spider-enhanced model does not beat simpler baselines.
AI.motivation: Acquirers of failed banks weigh acquisition value, regulatory protection, risk, buyer strength and execution difficulty jointly, because each signal's meaning depends on the others, for example high non-performing loans matter less when government loss sharing absorbs the losses.
AI.method: The framework encodes four interaction rules among five dimensions, yielding graph-inspired features for a logistic model and a Pursue/Caution/Avoid decision rule. It is evaluated on 55 FDIC-assisted acquisitions by acquirers with a US-listed parent, using six financial inputs from pre-failure regulatory reports and two deal terms from regulator press releases, with the outcome a positive three-day abnormal return, under grouped nested cross-validation.
AI.result: The Spider-enhanced model reaches a mean AUROC of 0.594, against 0.615 for logistic regression and 0.632 for ridge regression on the same inputs; permutation tests give at most weak evidence that any of them ranks better than chance. The Spider score used directly does not rank better than chance, and an apparent link between target distress and higher returns disappears against a bank-sector benchmark. F1-tuned thresholds approve most acquisitions with negative returns and realize negative utility when each costs three times what a positively received acquisition gains.
AI.conclusion: The Spider framework does not improve on simpler models in this setting, and the outcome measures the market's initial reception rather than realized success.

title: EvoOPD: Evolving Privileged Information Strategies for Black-Box On-Policy Distillation
summary: Proprietary language models exhibit strong reasoning and coding capabilities, but their output distributions are inaccessible, making fine-grained distillation methods that rely on teacher logits difficult to apply directly to black-box models. We observe that rich textual feedback from a black-box teacher can be treated as privileged information (PI) and converted, through a PI-conditioned privileged teacher, into dense supervision signals on the student's own trajectories. However, what PI should be acquired from the teacher to most effectively support student learning remains unclear. PI strategies that differ in where they focus, what information they request, and how much detail they provide can have substantially different effects on the current student, and their relative effectiveness can further change as training progresses. Based on this observation, we propose Evolving Privileged Information Strategies for Black-Box On-Policy Distillation (EvoOPD), which treats PI acquisition itself as an optimization problem and maintains a PI Strategy Bank that evolves with the student state. EvoOPD uses the measured repair utility of PI on the current student to adapt the focus, information type, and granularity of teacher feedback, allowing the acquired information to continually match the student's learning needs. We systematically evaluate EvoOPD on mathematical reasoning and code generation with Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B students. EvoOPD achieves the best overall performance in all six model-task settings, improving over the strongest baseline in each setting by an average of 2.14 percentage points in mathematics and 1.30 points in code. Further analysis shows that the relative effectiveness of PI acquisition strategies changes with student state, making a fixed strategy difficult to sustain as the best choice throughout distillation.

AI.tldr: EvoOPD evolves privileged-information strategies for black-box on-policy distillation, adapting the focus, information type and granularity of teacher feedback to the student's current state, and achieves the best overall performance in all six model-task settings.
AI.motivation: Output distributions of proprietary teachers are inaccessible, and it is unclear which privileged information should be acquired from a black-box teacher to support student learning, since strategies differ in effect and their relative effectiveness changes during training.
AI.method: Rich textual feedback from the black-box teacher is treated as privileged information and converted, through a PI-conditioned privileged teacher, into dense supervision on the student's own trajectories. A PI Strategy Bank evolves with the student state, using the measured repair utility of PI on the current student to adapt focus, information type and granularity.
AI.result: On mathematical reasoning and code generation with Qwen3-1.7B, 4B and 8B students, EvoOPD achieves the best overall performance in all six model-task settings, improving over the strongest baseline in each setting by an average of 2.14 percentage points in mathematics and 1.30 points in code.
AI.conclusion: The relative effectiveness of PI acquisition strategies changes with student state, so a fixed strategy is difficult to keep as the best choice throughout distillation.

title: From Fixed Defaults to Calibrated Activation Policies for Long-Term Time-Series Forecasting
comment: 36 pages, 2 figures. Shijie Xu and Boyan Tang contributed equally. Code: this https URL
summary: Long-term time-series forecasting supports decisions in energy, transportation, and other applications where reliable predictions are needed beyond the observed data. Although forecasting research has advanced model architectures, fixed activation configurations provide limited guidance on how activation choices should vary across datasets and prediction horizons. This study aims to establish when task-specific activation choices improve forecasting accuracy and how previous experiments can guide the selection of suitable configurations for new tasks. We develop a calibrated selection policy that learns a reliable default from prior experiments, adapts the activation function and its location to each task, and retains the default when evidence for a change is insufficient. In an evaluation supported by 1,225 Informer training runs across 17 dataset variants and 51 forecasting tasks, the policy reduces mean squared error by 7.86% on average relative to the conventional fixed-activation baseline and improves 72.55% of tasks. These findings establish activation choice and placement as practical opportunities for improving existing forecasting models and show how accumulated experimental evidence can guide configuration decisions without repeating an exhaustive search for every task.

AI.tldr: A calibrated selection policy learns a reliable default activation configuration from prior experiments, adapts the activation function and its placement to each task, and keeps the default when evidence for a change is insufficient. It reduces mean squared error by 7.86% on average and improves 72.55% of tasks.
AI.motivation: Forecasting research has advanced model architectures, but fixed activation configurations give limited guidance on how activation choices should vary across datasets and prediction horizons.
AI.method: A calibrated selection policy that learns a default from prior experiments and adapts the activation function and its location to each task, retaining the default when evidence is insufficient. It is evaluated on 1,225 Informer training runs across 17 dataset variants and 51 forecasting tasks.
AI.result: Relative to the conventional fixed-activation baseline, the policy reduces mean squared error by 7.86% on average and improves 72.55% of tasks.
AI.conclusion: Activation choice and placement are practical opportunities for improving existing forecasting models, and accumulated experimental evidence can guide configuration decisions without an exhaustive search for every task.

title: Thermodynamics-Informed Learning Captures Hierarchical Hydrogen-Bond Networks in Deep Eutectic Solvents
summary: Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) offer a tunable platform for lignocellulose refining, but their solvation behavior depends on multicomponent hydrogen-bond networks rather than individual constituent properties. We develop TiNN, a thermodynamics-informed neural network that hierarchically represents HBA-HBD association and solute accommodation through a learned free-energy pathway. Trained on 938 records, TiNN achieves a test-set $R^2$ of 0.917 and generalizes to new HBA-HBD combinations and sparse conditions. Ablation identifies solute-specific stabilization as the largest contributor to prediction accuracy, while the importance of hydrogen-bond compatibility depends on the dissolution mechanism. Experimental measurements of glucose, xylan, and Kraft lignin in acidic, basic, and neutral DESs show that TiNN reduces the geometric mean solubility error from more than 23-fold with COSMO-RS to approximately 1.5-fold. Without training on fractionation data, TiNN also distinguishes DES formulations with high and low lignin and hemicellulose removal from corn stover. These results support chemically grounded solvent screening for lignocellulose fractionation.

AI.tldr: TiNN, a thermodynamics-informed neural network, represents hydrogen-bond association and solute accommodation in deep eutectic solvents through a learned free-energy pathway. It reaches a test-set R2 of 0.917 and reduces solubility error from more than 23-fold with COSMO-RS to about 1.5-fold.
AI.motivation: Deep eutectic solvents are a tunable platform for lignocellulose refining, but their solvation behavior depends on multicomponent hydrogen-bond networks rather than on individual constituent properties.
AI.method: TiNN hierarchically represents HBA-HBD association and solute accommodation through a learned free-energy pathway, trained on 938 records; ablation identifies the contributions of its components, and experiments measure glucose, xylan and Kraft lignin solubility in acidic, basic and neutral deep eutectic solvents.
AI.result: Test-set R2 of 0.917; TiNN generalizes to new HBA-HBD combinations and sparse conditions, and ablation identifies solute-specific stabilization as the largest contributor to accuracy. It reduces the geometric mean solubility error from more than 23-fold with COSMO-RS to about 1.5-fold, and without training on fractionation data it distinguishes formulations with high and low lignin and hemicellulose removal from corn stover.
AI.conclusion: The results support chemically grounded solvent screening for lignocellulose fractionation.

title: A trust layer for fast pedestal-stability surrogates: calibrated error bars, out-of-distribution alarms and few-shot recalibration
summary: Machine-learning surrogates of linear peeling-ballooning stability now run in milliseconds, but they are mostly deployed as point estimators: they do not say how wrong they may be, or when a query lies outside what they were trained on. For a fusion company designing a new device, every equilibrium of interest is outside the training data of existing surrogates, so this is the case that matters. We describe a model-agnostic trust layer for stability surrogates, made of conformal error bars, out-of-distribution alarms that route doubtful cases to the physics code, and recalibration from a few simulations of a new design, and we test it with pre-registered hypotheses. On a large public dataset of JET-like equilibria with ideal-MHD growth rates, the error bars hold their nominal coverage in distribution and fall short under a shift in plasma shape; a few dozen simulations of the new shape, or routing the cases the alarms flag, restore it. On resistive BOUT++ surrogates, the bars stay calibrated on held-out runs, the alarm flags tokamaks absent from training, and a scenario scan is screened in seconds instead of hours. Across equilibria from the SPARC library and the DIII-D coil set, a surrogate trained on our own graded BOUT++ labels beats the baseline on unseen equilibria, while a surrogate trained elsewhere ranks the same cases backwards and its alarm declines them. Building our own neural-operator surrogate, the harness exposed two input defects whose fix closed its gap to a simple network. For every surrogate tested, the trust layer keeps coverage near target, with a bar width set by that surrogate's own error. Not every pre-registered hypothesis held, and we report those results and the limits of all of them.

AI.tldr: A model-agnostic trust layer for pedestal-stability surrogates combines conformal error bars, out-of-distribution alarms and few-shot recalibration, and keeps coverage near target for every surrogate tested.
AI.motivation: Machine-learning surrogates of linear peeling-ballooning stability run in milliseconds but are deployed as point estimators, so they do not say how wrong they may be or when a query lies outside their training data.
AI.method: Conformal error bars, out-of-distribution alarms that route doubtful cases to the physics code, and recalibration from a few simulations of a new design, tested with pre-registered hypotheses on a JET-like equilibrium dataset with ideal-MHD growth rates, resistive BOUT++ surrogates, and equilibria from the SPARC library and the DIII-D coil set.
AI.result: On the JET-like data the error bars hold nominal coverage in distribution but fall short under a shift in plasma shape; a few dozen simulations of the new shape, or routing the flagged cases, restore it. On BOUT++ the bars stay calibrated, the alarm flags tokamaks absent from training, and a scenario scan is screened in seconds instead of hours. A surrogate trained on the authors' graded BOUT++ labels beats the baseline on unseen equilibria, while one trained elsewhere ranks the same cases backwards. Not every pre-registered hypothesis held.
AI.conclusion: For every surrogate tested, the trust layer keeps coverage near target, with bar width set by that surrogate's own error, and the authors report the limits of all their results.

title: The Behavioral Rate of Fine-Tuning: Compression as a Measure of Useful Information
summary: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapts a frozen language model through a compact learned update, making it a natural setting for asking how much information fine-tuning needs to write. Yet adapter rank, parameter count, or numerical reconstruction error do not directly tell us how many bits are required to preserve the acquired behavior. We therefore define an operational behavioral rate $R^\star$ as the smallest serialized size of a compressed adapter that, once reloaded into the frozen base model, retains a fixed fraction of its held-out fine-tuning gain. Across LoRA fine-tuning experiments, this rate increases with distinct training content at fixed optimization budgets, but is not determined by intuitive metrics like source description length, fine-tuning gain, or weight-space reconstruction error. Most importantly, the same datasets exhibit substantially different, and even reordered, rates across frozen base models, showing that fine-tuning compressibility is a property of the dataset--receiver pair rather than of the dataset alone. However, we show that correction spectra measured on the data are able to rank these rates within a receiver. Finally, we study a striking noise-reducing effect of compression: adapters trained on deliberately corrupted datasets fall far below the frozen model, yet after compression score above it (23.7% to 82.9% on GSM8K, against 77.6% for frozen Qwen2.5-7B), consistently across tested families and sizes. The damage is unevenly concentrated in the adapter's leading singular directions, which compression appears to filter. Away from its training task, the compressed corrupted adapter also generalizes better than a clean fine-tune: on harder math it retains 97% of base accuracy, versus 44% for the clean adapter.

AI.tldr: Defines a behavioral rate R* as the smallest serialized size of a compressed LoRA adapter that, once reloaded into the frozen base model, retains a fixed fraction of its held-out fine-tuning gain, and shows that this rate is a property of the dataset-receiver pair.
AI.motivation: Adapter rank, parameter count and numerical reconstruction error do not directly tell how many bits are required to preserve the acquired behavior.
AI.method: The behavioral rate is measured across LoRA fine-tuning experiments at fixed optimization budgets and across frozen base models, with correction spectra measured on the data used to rank rates within a receiver, and with compression applied to adapters trained on deliberately corrupted datasets.
AI.result: The rate increases with distinct training content but is not determined by source description length, fine-tuning gain or weight-space reconstruction error; the same datasets show substantially different, and even reordered, rates across frozen base models. Compressed adapters trained on corrupted datasets score 23.7% to 82.9% on GSM8K, against 77.6% for the frozen Qwen2.5-7B, and on harder math the compressed corrupted adapter retains 97% of base accuracy versus 44% for the clean adapter.
AI.conclusion: Fine-tuning compressibility is a property of the dataset-receiver pair rather than of the dataset alone, and compression appears to filter the damage that is concentrated in the adapter's leading singular directions.

title: Verifier-Guided Self-Consistency: Test-Time Reasoning with Imperfect Generators and Verifiers
summary: Large language models can solve many multi-step reasoning problems, but their reasoning remains brittle: plausible intermediate steps often lead to incorrect answers. Improving reasoning at test time requires balancing two imperfect signals: the generator, which provides diversity, and the verifier, which guides correctness. Existing approaches largely favor one side of this tradeoff. Verifier-weighted voting relies on trajectories sampled from the generator and cannot steer generation toward correct ones. By contrast, beam-style verifier-guided search can steer generation, but may over-concentrate on narrow trajectory sets and amplify verifier errors. We propose Verifier-Guided Self-Consistency (VGSC), a stochastic decoding framework that combines step-level correctness and future-outcome estimates to guide reasoning during generation. VGSC repeatedly proposes candidate next steps from the base language model and uses both signals in an acceptance/resampling procedure, while maintaining multiple trajectories for final answer-level self-consistency. We provide a probabilistic interpretation of VGSC as approximate sampling from a verifier-tilted trajectory distribution. Across multiple reasoning benchmarks, generator models, and verifier families, VGSC achieves higher average accuracy than representative baselines.

AI.tldr: Verifier-Guided Self-Consistency is a stochastic decoding framework that combines step-level correctness and future-outcome estimates to guide reasoning during generation, and achieves higher average accuracy than representative baselines across reasoning benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Reasoning remains brittle; verifier-weighted voting relies on sampled trajectories and cannot steer generation, while beam-style verifier-guided search can over-concentrate on narrow trajectory sets and amplify verifier errors.
AI.method: Repeatedly proposes candidate next steps from the base model and uses step-level correctness and future-outcome estimates in an acceptance/resampling procedure, while maintaining multiple trajectories for answer-level self-consistency. The method is interpreted probabilistically as approximate sampling from a verifier-tilted trajectory distribution.
AI.result: Across multiple reasoning benchmarks, generator models and verifier families, VGSC achieves higher average accuracy than representative baselines; the abstract reports no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Balancing the diversity of the generator against the guidance of an imperfect verifier at test time improves reasoning accuracy.

title: Alternatives to Shallow Autoencoders for Collaborative Filtering
summary: Collaborative filtering (CF) is a cornerstone of recommender systems and plays a relevant role in many modern applications. CF uses user-item interaction data to discover future preferences. Although deep learning models have shown promise in CF, Embarrassingly Shallow Autoencoders for Sparse Data (EASE) has gained attention for its outstanding ranking accuracy provided by its closed-form solution. EASE relies primarily on relationships among items to fit a full-rank high-dimensional linear mapping. We hypothesize that this design limits its capacity to capture similar but not equivalent fine-grained user relationships, consequently limiting its recommendation accuracy. This paper introduces an alternative formulation based on EASE that takes advantage of user-user information. Furthermore, we propose a hybrid model that combines both user-user and item-item adjacency distributions. Our experiments reveal that the proposed models outperform EASE on well-known recommendation benchmarks, highlighting the significance of including the user alternative in shallow autoencoder studies for CF.

AI.tldr: Proposes an EASE-based formulation that uses user-user information, and a hybrid model that combines user-user and item-item adjacency distributions; both outperform EASE on well-known recommendation benchmarks.
AI.motivation: EASE gives outstanding ranking accuracy through a closed-form solution, but it relies primarily on item relationships, which may limit its capacity to capture similar but not equivalent fine-grained user relationships.
AI.method: An alternative formulation based on EASE that takes advantage of user-user information, and a hybrid model that combines user-user and item-item adjacency distributions.
AI.result: The proposed models outperform EASE on well-known recommendation benchmarks; the abstract reports no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Including the user-side alternative in shallow autoencoder studies is significant for collaborative filtering.

title: Dimension-Free Private Mean Estimation is Impossible Without the Covariance
summary: We study the limits of differentially private Gaussian mean estimation when the covariance matrix is unknown. Prior work shows that when the covariance $\Sigma$ is known, the optimal sample complexity can depend only on its spectrum, rather than on the ambient dimension $d$. We establish new lower bounds for Gaussian mean estimation with Euclidean error which show that private estimators cannot achieve similar guarantees when the covariance is unknown. First, when the sample size $n$ is smaller than the effective dimension $\mathrm{trace}(\Sigma)/\|\Sigma\|_{\text{op}}$, the optimal error when the covariance is unknown can be larger than the optimal error when it is known by a factor of $\sqrt{d/n}$. Second, when the sample size is larger than the effective dimension, even for diagonal covariance matrices with effective dimension bounded by $\log d$, the optimal error when the covariance is unknown can be larger than the optimal error when it is known by a factor of $\sqrt{d}/n^{3/2}$. Together, these results show that in the unknown covariance setting, exploiting anisotropic structure under differential privacy can require a dimension-dependent error or sample complexity.

AI.tldr: Shows that differentially private Gaussian mean estimation with unknown covariance cannot achieve the dimension-free guarantees available when the covariance is known, with lower bounds that carry square-root factors of d/n and d over n to the 3/2.
AI.motivation: When the covariance is known, the optimal sample complexity depends only on its spectrum rather than on the ambient dimension d; the question is whether private estimators can achieve similar guarantees when the covariance is unknown.
AI.method: New lower bounds for Gaussian mean estimation with Euclidean error under unknown covariance, analysed in two regimes: sample size n below the effective dimension trace(Sigma) over the operator norm of Sigma, and sample size above it, including diagonal covariances whose effective dimension is bounded by log d.
AI.result: When n is smaller than the effective dimension, the optimal error with unknown covariance can exceed the known-covariance error by a factor of square root of d/n. When n exceeds the effective dimension, even for diagonal covariances with effective dimension bounded by log d, the factor can be square root of d times n to the minus 3/2.
AI.conclusion: Under differential privacy with unknown covariance, exploiting anisotropic structure can require dimension-dependent error or sample complexity.

title: Fingerprinting the Dispatchers behind Distributed Model Extraction
summary: API distillation campaigns try to hide model-stealing traffic by splitting requests across thousands of load-balanced accounts, which standard content classifiers often miss. However, request timestamps, specifically arrival time and stream completion time, reveal the underlying dispatching strategy, such as round-robin counters or key-shuffling pools.
