Using a 20 percent seed set, this timing analysis can forensically rank the remaining accounts of a campaign with 0.92 to 1.00 AUC within 20 minutes, even across thousands of real production accounts. While adaptive attackers struggle to hide rotating dispatchers using jitter, pinning keys successfully evades detection, though it can severely throttle throughput when quotas bind. Ultimately, timing exposes shared infrastructure patterns even when content filters fail.

AI.tldr: Request timing, specifically arrival time and stream completion time, reveals the dispatching strategy behind distributed API distillation campaigns, so accounts that content filters miss can be ranked forensically.
AI.motivation: API distillation campaigns hide model-stealing traffic by splitting requests across thousands of load-balanced accounts, which standard content classifiers often miss.
AI.method: Timing analysis of arrival and stream completion times, using a 20 percent seed set to rank the remaining accounts of a campaign, tested against adaptive attackers who use jitter or pin keys.
AI.result: The timing analysis ranks the remaining accounts with 0.92 to 1.00 AUC within 20 minutes, even across thousands of real production accounts. Adaptive attackers struggle to hide rotating dispatchers using jitter; pinning keys evades detection but can severely throttle throughput when quotas bind.
AI.conclusion: Timing exposes shared infrastructure patterns even when content filters fail.

title: Self-Directed Apple Tasting
summary: We study the classical apple-tasting setting, a partial feedback model in which the learner observes the true label only when it predicts $1$. A combinatorial characterization for the rates of this problem in the online adversarial setting has been studied by Raman et al. (2024). We study the self-directed setting, in which the learner can adaptively choose the order of the points it predicts on. In the realizable setting, we establish a tetrachotomy on the expected minimax number of mistakes made by any learner. Depending on the VC dimension, the $\emptyset$-centered star number, and the self-directed dimension, we show that the rates could possibly be $\Theta(1)$, $O(\log n) \cap \omega(1)$, $\tilde \Theta(\sqrt{n})$, or $\Theta(n)$. In the agnostic setting, the minimax regret is $\tilde \Theta(\sqrt{n})$ or $\Theta(n)$, depending on the VC dimension.

AI.tldr: Studies self-directed apple tasting, where the learner chooses the order of the points it predicts on, and in the realizable setting establishes that expected minimax mistakes can be Theta(1), O(log n) intersected with omega(1), tilde Theta(sqrt n), or Theta(n).
AI.motivation: In apple tasting the learner observes the true label only when it predicts 1. Raman et al. (2024) characterized the rates in the online adversarial setting; this paper studies the self-directed setting, in which the learner adaptively chooses the order of its predictions.
AI.method: A combinatorial characterization of the rates in terms of the VC dimension, the empty-set-centered star number and the self-directed dimension, in the realizable setting and in the agnostic setting.
AI.result: In the realizable setting the rate depends on these parameters and can be Theta(1), O(log n) intersected with omega(1), tilde Theta(sqrt n) or Theta(n). In the agnostic setting the minimax regret is tilde Theta(sqrt n) or Theta(n), depending on the VC dimension.
AI.conclusion: The rates are determined by these combinatorial parameters, giving a classification of achievable mistake rates in the self-directed apple-tasting setting.

title: Do unlearning algorithms learn the right features?
summary: Machine unlearning is commonly evaluated with standard post-deletion metrics that compare an unlearned model to one retrained on the remaining data. Such snapshot evaluations can conceal consequential differences in the features the two models encode. We prove that if an unlearned and a retrained model agree on their outputs but encode different features, a single gradient step on their prediction heads can break this agreement. We further show that deleting an arbitrarily small fraction of the data can cause retraining to select qualitatively different features, so matching retraining can require learning features that the full model never had. We then introduce a measure of feature recovery that separates missing from extraneous features. Across eight unlearning methods, models that perform well on standard metrics often fail to recover the retrained features. This mismatch predicts deviations from retraining under subsequent relearning and downstream adaptation, and directly correcting it systematically reduces these deviations.

AI.tldr: Shows that standard post-deletion metrics can conceal differences in the features encoded by unlearned and retrained models, and introduces a feature-recovery measure that separates missing from extraneous features; correcting the mismatch reduces deviations from retraining.
AI.motivation: Machine unlearning is commonly evaluated with snapshot metrics that compare an unlearned model to one retrained on the remaining data, and such metrics can conceal consequential differences in the features the two models encode.
AI.method: Proofs that models agreeing on outputs but encoding different features can have that agreement broken by a single gradient step on their prediction heads, and that deleting an arbitrarily small fraction of data can make retraining select qualitatively different features. A feature-recovery measure separates missing from extraneous features, and is applied across eight unlearning methods.
AI.result: Models that perform well on standard metrics often fail to recover the retrained features. This mismatch predicts deviations from retraining under subsequent relearning and downstream adaptation, and directly correcting it systematically reduces these deviations.
AI.conclusion: Matching retraining can require learning features the full model never had, so agreement on standard metrics does not by itself establish that an unlearned model matches the retrained one.

title: SecureGARD: Dynamic Ontology-Guided Governance for Secure Tool-Using LLM Agents
summary: Tool-using large language model (LLM) agents translate model outputs into consequential actions, turning indirect prompt injection into an execution-security problem. Existing defenses constrain tool calls, trajectories, or information flows, but often leave action semantics, state dependencies, and evidence relations implicit, limiting generalization across heterogeneous tools and complicating safe updates. We present \ours{}, a dynamic ontology-guided governance framework. \ours{} grounds heterogeneous calls in a shared semantic representation and combines an executable ontology with episode-level task state to derive deterministic ready, waiting, and forbidden decisions. A waiting decision identifies an unmet but recoverable obligation, enabling bounded replanning without expanding the agent's authorization boundary. \ours{} evolves its ontology offline from verified training executions. An offline LLM proposes instance-independent action--state axioms, which are accepted only if they address ontology errors exposed by training failures, preserve logical consistency and protected entailments, and pass held-out validation before the ontology is frozen. We evaluate \ours{} on AgentDojo, ASB, and AgentDyn under benign and indirect prompt-injection settings. \ours{} achieves a 0\% attack success rate (ASR) across all three benchmarks while improving task utility under attack compared with existing baselines. These results show that explicit semantic governance can strengthen execution security without indiscriminate blocking.

AI.tldr: SecureGARD is an ontology-guided governance framework for tool-using LLM agents that derives ready, waiting and forbidden decisions for tool calls, and achieves a 0% attack success rate on AgentDojo, ASB and AgentDyn.
AI.motivation: Tool-using agents turn indirect prompt injection into an execution-security problem; existing defenses leave action semantics, state dependencies and evidence relations implicit, which limits generalization across heterogeneous tools and complicates safe updates.
AI.method: Grounds heterogeneous calls in a shared semantic representation and combines an executable ontology with episode-level task state. A waiting decision identifies an unmet but recoverable obligation for bounded replanning. The ontology is evolved offline: an LLM proposes action-state axioms, accepted only if they address errors exposed by training failures, preserve logical consistency and protected entailments, and pass held-out validation before the ontology is frozen.
AI.result: On AgentDojo, ASB and AgentDyn, under benign and indirect prompt-injection settings, SecureGARD achieves a 0% attack success rate across all three benchmarks while improving task utility under attack compared with existing baselines.
AI.conclusion: Explicit semantic governance can strengthen execution security without indiscriminate blocking.

title: PINR-ESI: Physics-Informed Self-Supervised Implicit Neural Representation Framework for EEG Extended-Source Imaging
summary: EEG extended-source imaging aims to localize active cortical regions and characterize their spatial extent, yet supervised inverse networks typically depend on synthetic EEG-source pairs and may be sensitive to synthetic-to-real mismatch. We propose a physics-informed self-supervised implicit neural representation (INR) framework for spatial source reconstruction without paired source labels or simulation-based supervised pretraining. The lead field matrix encodes the source-to-sensor volume-conduction model and constrains the INR through agreement between predicted and measured EEG. Cortical current density is modeled as a continuous coordinate-conditioned field. A classical inverse estimate provides warm initialization and spatial constraints on source activity, while patch-integrated projection maps the field to discrete source coefficients for forward modeling. Simulations with varying noise levels, source counts, and source extents showed the clearest advantage in identifying active cortical regions, particularly for multiple and larger sources. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations using real EEG recordings from epilepsy patients and intracranial stimulation experiments further supported the feasibility of the framework for source imaging. These findings suggest the potential of physics-informed self-supervised INR for extended-source imaging.

AI.tldr: PINR-ESI is a physics-informed, self-supervised implicit neural representation framework for EEG extended-source imaging that needs no paired source labels or simulation-based supervised pretraining, modeling cortical current density as a continuous coordinate-conditioned field.
AI.motivation: Supervised inverse networks typically depend on synthetic EEG-source pairs and may be sensitive to the mismatch between synthetic and real data.
AI.method: The lead field matrix encodes the source-to-sensor volume-conduction model and constrains the representation through agreement between predicted and measured EEG. A classical inverse estimate gives warm initialization and spatial constraints on source activity, and patch-integrated projection maps the field to discrete source coefficients for forward modeling.
AI.result: In simulations with varying noise levels, source counts and source extents, the clearest advantage was in identifying active cortical regions, particularly for multiple and larger sources. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations on real EEG from epilepsy patients and intracranial stimulation experiments supported the framework's feasibility for source imaging.
AI.conclusion: The findings suggest the potential of physics-informed self-supervised implicit neural representations for extended-source imaging.

title: Where It Breaks: Diagnosing Perception, Memory, and Decision Failures of a Vision-Language Agent in Pac-Man
summary: Training an agent to play Pac-Man with only up, down, left and right actions raises a basic question: when performance is poor, what should be improved? Difficulty can arise from reading the screen or from choosing actions over a long sequence. We examine these problems in a Qwen3.5-9B-based agent through separate perception checks and primitive-policy reinforcement-learning studies. In the policy study, which uses textual boards to remove image transcription from the decision interface, completion on eight held-out mazes increased from 0% before this optimization to 80.2% at a selected checkpoint, with three extra lives. The perception checks show that accurate static screenshot reading can coexist with errors during interaction. A separate policy comparison also shows that further optimization can accompany worse action choices. Together, these findings motivate concrete checks for post-training: evaluate perception in use, distinguish training success from full-game validation, and examine decisions and later performance rather than relying on one selected score. The study provides empirical lessons for improving future agent training and evaluation.

AI.tldr: Diagnoses where a Qwen3.5-9B-based vision-language agent fails in Pac-Man by separating perception errors from decision errors. The policy study with textual boards raises completion on eight held-out mazes from 0% to 80.2% at a selected checkpoint.
AI.motivation: Poor Pac-Man performance could come from reading the screen or from choosing actions over a long sequence, and these two sources need to be told apart before deciding what to improve.
AI.method: Separate perception checks on static screenshots, plus primitive-policy reinforcement-learning studies in which textual boards remove image transcription from the decision interface.
AI.result: Completion on eight held-out mazes rose from 0% to 80.2% at a selected checkpoint, with three extra lives. Accurate static screenshot reading coexisted with errors during interaction, and further optimization could come with worse action choices.
AI.conclusion: Post-training should evaluate perception in use, distinguish training success from full-game validation, and examine decisions and later performance rather than relying on one selected score.

title: Energy-Guided Transport for Projection-Free Physics-Informed Flow Matching
summary: Deep generative models, particularly Flow Matching frameworks, have emerged as powerful tools for synthesizing complex physical systems. However, standard architectures remain purely statistically driven and agnostic to the underlying governing equations, often violating fundamental physical constraints during inference. Existing zero-shot approaches designed to enforce these constraints typically rely on rigid algebraic projections. While effective for sparse boundary conditions, applying such discrete geometric corrections to dense, full-domain PDEs may disrupt the probability path, \rev{potentially deviating from the learned manifold and introducing substantial computational overhead}. To address these challenges, we introduce Energy-Guided Transport, a novel training-free framework that formulates non-linear physical constraints as a smooth potential energy landscape. Rather than interrupting the ODE integration, our method applies a continuous dissipative force directly to the intermediate generative states, steering them toward the physical manifold. By evaluating this force implicitly via reverse-mode automatic differentiation, our framework preserves the natural dynamics of the flow while maintaining an efficient $\mathcal{O}(N)$ algorithmic complexity. We extensively evaluate our framework across various 1D and 2D physical systems, including the chaotic Navier-Stokes equations. Our method achieves stable generation without structural divergence, significantly improves the stability-accuracy trade-off compared to state-of-the-art methods, and substantially accelerates inference with respect to exact projection strategies. Code available at: this https URL.

AI.tldr: Proposes Energy-Guided Transport, a training-free method that enforces nonlinear physical constraints in flow matching by applying a continuous force from a potential energy landscape during ODE integration.
AI.motivation: Flow matching generators often violate physical constraints at inference, and existing rigid algebraic projections can disrupt the probability path and add heavy overhead for dense, full-domain PDEs.
AI.method: A dissipative force computed from a smooth potential energy is applied to intermediate generative states, evaluated implicitly by reverse-mode automatic differentiation, with O(N) algorithmic complexity.
AI.result: Evaluated on 1D and 2D physical systems including chaotic Navier-Stokes equations, the method achieves stable generation without structural divergence, improves the stability-accuracy trade-off over state-of-the-art methods, and accelerates inference relative to exact projection strategies.
AI.conclusion: Steering the generative dynamics with an energy force during integration is a practical alternative to projection for enforcing physics in generative models.

title: Symmetry Breaking at the Edge of Stability via Central Flow Analysis
summary: Continuous symmetries in neural networks lead to conserved quantities that are invariant under gradient flow, such as layer balancedness in linear and ReLU networks. Finite-step gradient descent need not preserve these laws, particularly at the edge of stability (EOS), where the iterates oscillate around a smoother trajectory, which can be described by the central flow dynamics (Cohen et al., 2025). We study how gradient flow conservation laws evolve under the central flow description of this regime. We show that the curvature correction induces a finite-dimensional drift determined by the oscillation covariance along critical parameter directions. We thus take the first steps to analyse which conservation laws remain and are broken at the EOS according to the central flow dynamics by analysing a scalar two-layer model, two-layer matrix factorisation, and a two-layer ReLU network, where the known conservation laws are shown to be complete (Marcotte et al., 2023).

AI.tldr: Studies which conservation laws of gradient flow survive, and which are broken, at the edge of stability (EOS) under the central flow description of gradient descent.
AI.motivation: Finite-step gradient descent need not preserve the conservation laws of gradient flow, and at the EOS the iterates oscillate around a smoother trajectory, so the effect must be analysed separately.
AI.method: Analyses how the curvature correction of central flow induces a finite-dimensional drift determined by the oscillation covariance along critical parameter directions, on a scalar two-layer model, two-layer matrix factorisation and a two-layer ReLU network.
AI.result: The curvature correction produces a drift set by the oscillation covariance, and in the studied models the known conservation laws are shown to be complete.
AI.conclusion: This takes first steps toward identifying which conservation laws remain and which are broken at the edge of stability according to central flow dynamics.

title: Continual Classification Beyond the Kernel Regime: Harnessing the Sparsity Bias of L2 Regularization in Diagonal Linear Networks
summary: We study logistic regression for continual learning with linear predictors in a high-dimensional statistical setting. Existing theoretical work has largely focused on continual linear regression with variants of L2 regularization, motivated by their analytical simplicity and connection to the kernel regime of neural networks. We first derive the optimal L2 regularization strength for continual linear classification and characterize its generalization performance, recovering behavior analogous to prior results for continual linear regression. Next, we examine the effect of L2 regularization in deeper models using a minimal two-layer diagonal linear network. In the single-task setting, L2 regularization on the weights of such models is known to promote sparsity in the resulting predictor, yielding a rich, sparse feature-learning regime beyond the kernel regime (a similar effect arises in two-layer ReLU networks). However, in continual learning, where L2 regularization is typically centered on previous-task weights, this sparsity bias is no longer preserved. We therefore propose a weighted variant of L2 regularization that extends this beneficial sparsity bias to continual learning. We show theoretically and empirically that, for a sufficiently sparse teacher, our variant converges substantially faster than directly learning a linear predictor with conventional continual L2 or L1 regularization, trading some long-horizon bias for markedly improved performance over moderate task horizons.

AI.tldr: Derives the optimal L2 regularization strength for continual logistic regression and proposes a weighted L2 variant that keeps the sparsity bias of diagonal linear networks in continual learning.
AI.motivation: Continual L2 regularization centred on previous-task weights loses the sparsity bias that L2 gives single-task deep models, and earlier theory mainly covered continual linear regression.
AI.method: Derives the optimal L2 strength and generalization behaviour for continual linear classification, then studies a two-layer diagonal linear network and introduces a weighted L2 variant that extends the sparsity bias to continual learning.
AI.result: For a sufficiently sparse teacher, the weighted variant converges substantially faster than conventional continual L2 or L1 regularization over moderate task horizons, at the cost of some long-horizon bias.
AI.conclusion: Weighted regularization can carry the beneficial sparse feature-learning regime into continual learning, with clear gains over moderate horizons.

title: Uncertainty-Driven Efficient Communication for UAV-Based Collaborative Perception
summary: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV)-based collaborative perception enables multiple agents to share complementary perceptual information, overcoming limitations such as occlusion and limited sensing range. Communication efficiency is a critical bottleneck, as UAVs operate under stringent bandwidth and computational constraints. However, existing spatial selection methods focus predominantly on foreground regions to reduce missed detections, neglecting perceptually ambiguous regions and leaving false detections unresolved. We propose UCP, an uncertainty-driven framework that characterizes collaborative value through observational uncertainty, identifying sensor-limited regions, and discriminative uncertainty, capturing model-level ambiguity near the decision boundary. These estimates drive spatial request and supply maps for efficient inter-agent communication, and the received messages are aggregated via U-Fusion, an uncertainty-guided cross-attention module. Experiments on three benchmarks across 3D object detection and trajectory prediction demonstrate a superior performance-bandwidth trade-off with high interpretability and strong generalizability.

AI.tldr: Proposes UCP, an uncertainty-driven framework that decides which spatial regions UAVs share in collaborative perception, reaching a better performance-bandwidth trade-off.
AI.motivation: Existing spatial selection focuses on foreground regions to cut missed detections, which neglects perceptually ambiguous regions and leaves false detections unresolved under tight bandwidth.
AI.method: Observational uncertainty identifies sensor-limited regions and discriminative uncertainty identifies ambiguity near the decision boundary; these produce spatial request and supply maps, and received messages are aggregated by U-Fusion, an uncertainty-guided cross-attention module.
AI.result: Across three benchmarks for 3D object detection and trajectory prediction, UCP gives a superior performance-bandwidth trade-off with high interpretability and strong generalizability.
AI.conclusion: Uncertainty can guide efficient inter-agent communication for UAV-based collaborative perception.

title: Dynamical State-Space Diffusion for Spatiotemporal Prediction
summary: Diffusion models for temporal prediction typically corrupt each future frame with independent noise, leaving temporal dependence entirely to the denoiser. We propose Dynamical State-Space Diffusion (DSSD), which learns the temporal structure of the corruption process itself. DSSD builds a temporal kernel from the damped oscillatory modes of a stable diagonal state-space model, whose learned decay rates and frequencies let the corruption capture multiple timescales and oscillatory correlations, while the denoiser architecture remains unchanged. Running this model on a finite clip, however, requires the state before the first frame, which is unobserved; starting from a zero state leaves the early frames with less noise than the diffusion schedule prescribes. We avoid this by using the Cholesky factor of the model's stationary covariance as the temporal operator. We prove that this operator is causal, exactly invertible, keeps each frame's noise variance equal to that of standard diffusion, and reduces to the identity at the clean end of the process, and that it is exactly the Kalman innovations form of the state-space model. The denoiser is trained to predict the temporally correlated noise, and sampling removes and reapplies the temporal mixing at each step. On scientific-field and robot-video datasets, DSSD outperforms diffusion baselines that share its denoiser, and the evolution of its learned modes during training shows that the temporal operator adapts to each dataset.

AI.tldr: Introduces DSSD, a diffusion model for spatiotemporal prediction whose corruption process is temporally correlated through a damped oscillatory diagonal state-space model, with the denoiser architecture unchanged.
AI.motivation: Diffusion models for temporal prediction corrupt each future frame with independent noise and leave temporal dependence to the denoiser, and a state-space corruption on a finite clip needs an unobserved initial state.
AI.method: The temporal kernel is built from a stable diagonal state-space model, and the Cholesky factor of its stationary covariance serves as a causal, exactly invertible temporal operator. This keeps each frame's noise variance equal to standard diffusion and equals the Kalman innovations form; the denoiser predicts the correlated noise.
AI.result: On scientific-field and robot-video datasets, DSSD outperforms diffusion baselines that share its denoiser, and the learned modes adapt to each dataset during training.
AI.conclusion: Learning the temporal structure of the corruption process itself improves diffusion-based spatiotemporal prediction without changing the denoiser.

title: CardioDrift: Automatic Cardiac Motion Tracking on a 3D Atlas Mesh via Shape-aware Coherent Point Drift with Slice Shift Correction
summary: Automatic cardiac motion tracking from cine cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging is essential for quantifying myocardial motion abnormalities associated with cardiovascular disease. Existing methods fall into two groups: those that represent motion without anatomical correspondence across subjects and therefore limit inter-subject motion assessment; and those that represent motion with globally corresponding points, which typically require a time-consuming and error-prone semi-automatic step to fit a cardiac atlas to the subject space. To address these limitations, this study proposes CardioDrift, a fully automatic, atlas-based probabilistic framework that represents subject-specific cardiac motion on a 3D atlas mesh with globally corresponding points. The Coherent Point Drift (CPD) formulation is generalised to jointly register the atlas surfaces of multiple cardiac regions to the anatomically corresponding contours extracted from cine CMR segmentation maps throughout the cardiac cycle. Slice-shift correction is embedded in the same probabilistic model, estimating slice-wise translations that suppress the misalignment artefact limiting atlas-fitting accuracy. Evaluation on 1301 randomly selected UK Biobank subjects and the M&M dataset, CardioDrift attains Dice similarity coefficients (DSCs) of $92.23\pm8.70\%$, $82.11\pm7.56\%$, and $88.69\pm4.13\%$ for the left ventricle (LV), myocardium (Myo), and right ventricle (RV), exceeding the strongest baseline on every distance and overlap metric of both datasets.

AI.tldr: Presents CardioDrift, a fully automatic atlas-based probabilistic method that tracks subject-specific cardiac motion on a 3D atlas mesh from cine CMR, with globally corresponding points.
AI.motivation: Existing methods either lack anatomical correspondence across subjects, or need a time-consuming and error-prone semi-automatic step to fit a cardiac atlas to each subject.
AI.method: Generalises Coherent Point Drift to register the atlas surfaces of several cardiac regions jointly to contours from cine CMR segmentations across the cardiac cycle, with slice-shift correction embedded in the same probabilistic model.
AI.result: On 1301 UK Biobank subjects and the M&M dataset, Dice scores are 92.23 +/- 8.70% for the left ventricle, 82.11 +/- 7.56% for the myocardium and 88.69 +/- 4.13% for the right ventricle, exceeding the strongest baseline on every distance and overlap metric on both datasets.
AI.conclusion: Shape-aware probabilistic registration with slice-shift correction enables automatic cardiac motion tracking that supports inter-subject motion assessment.

title: Sekai: Incremental Event Memory for Generalized Reasoning Video Segmentation
comment: 20 pages, 6 figures. Code, example annotations, and evaluation scripts: this https URL
summary: Online reasoning video segmentation (Online RVS) requires a model to segment query-referred objects as a video streams in, using only the frames observed so far. Existing formulations largely assume a fixed target set throughout the video, overlooking a fundamental property of streaming reasoning: as new events occur, the objects that satisfy a query may change over time. To address this, we propose a new task, Generalized Reasoning Video Segmentation (GRVS), where the target set depends on query-relevant events accumulated over the observed video history. As new evidence accumulates, the target set can evolve from empty to one or multiple objects, requiring a model to continuously maintain target validity while localizing the valid objects currently in view. To evaluate GRVS, we build Isekai, a diagnostic benchmark of 60 videos and 197 queries across 11 temporal query families, with 12,569 scoring points whose target sets are causally annotated over time. We further propose Sekai, an online framework with two complementary components: an Event Memory Reasoner (EMR) that maintains query-relevant events and evolving target states in structured memory, and a Memory-Grounded Decoder (MGD) that identifies valid targets from this memory and localizes them in the current frame. Experiments show that Sekai significantly outperforms existing online RVS methods, achieving 50.33 J&F and improving over the strongest baseline by 3.2 points. Code, example annotations, and evaluation scripts are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Defines Generalized Reasoning Video Segmentation, where the target set changes as query-relevant events accumulate, and proposes Sekai, an online framework that reaches 50.33 J&F.
AI.motivation: Online reasoning video segmentation assumes a fixed target set, overlooking that the objects satisfying a query can change as new events occur in a streaming video.
AI.method: Builds the Isekai benchmark of 60 videos and 197 queries across 11 temporal query families, with causally annotated target sets. Sekai pairs an Event Memory Reasoner, which keeps query-relevant events and evolving target states in structured memory, with a Memory-Grounded Decoder that localizes valid targets in the current frame.
AI.result: Sekai achieves 50.33 J&F and improves over the strongest baseline by 3.2 points, significantly outperforming existing online RVS methods.
AI.conclusion: Structured event memory lets online segmentation track evolving query targets, and the benchmark gives a diagnostic test for this setting.

title: Agent-Driven Generative Priors for Pathology Image Synthesis and Segmentation
comment: Code available at: this https URL
summary: Deep learning methods for pathology are constrained by the limited availability and high cost of large-scale pixel-level annotations. Synthetic data can alleviate this limitation, but existing pipelines often lack reliable quality control and remain weakly connected to downstream analysis. To address these issues, we propose a three-stage framework that integrates automated data screening, generative representation learning, and efficient adaptation to downstream tasks. First, we develop a pathology agent system to assess image quality and filter samples, resulting in TCGA-200K, a dataset containing 217,030 pathology patches selected from the public TCGA repository. Second, we train a generative model on the screened data. In addition to image synthesis, its backbone learns structural and semantic representations that can be transferred to downstream tasks. Third, we adapt the pretrained generative backbone to semantic segmentation using a lightweight task-specific head. We further introduce PathSeg-380K, a semantic segmentation dataset with expert annotations for approximately 380,000 cells across 12 cell types. Experiments on multiple pathology datasets show that the proposed framework achieves state-of-the-art segmentation performance. Our code is publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Proposes a three-stage pathology framework that uses an agent to screen image quality, pretrains a generative model on the screened data, and adapts its backbone to cell segmentation.
AI.motivation: Deep learning for pathology is limited by the scarcity and cost of pixel-level annotations, and existing synthetic-data pipelines often lack reliable quality control and stay weakly connected to downstream analysis.
AI.method: A pathology agent filters TCGA patches into TCGA-200K, with 217,030 patches. A generative model is trained on the screened data, and its backbone is adapted to semantic segmentation with a lightweight task-specific head. PathSeg-380K, with expert annotations for about 380,000 cells across 12 cell types, is also introduced.
AI.result: The framework achieves state-of-the-art segmentation performance on multiple pathology datasets.
AI.conclusion: Agent-screened generative pretraining can yield representations that transfer to segmentation, which suggests a way to reduce dependence on pixel-level annotation.

title: Coupled Scene Graph Anticipation: When With-Constraint Recall Hides Structural Inconsistency
comment: Accepted at ICVGIP 2026 (Indian Conference on Computer Vision, Graphics, and Image Processing), December 21-24, 2026, Kolkata, India. 9 pages, 2 figures, 4 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Scene Graph Anticipation (SGA) predicts object relationships in future video frames. Continuous-time SGA models evolve each subject-object pair with an independent Neural ODE, so relationships sharing an entity cannot influence one another during integration, and nothing prevents mutually exclusive predictions, such as "sitting on" and "standing on", for the same pair. We introduce CoupledSGA, which links such relationships through a Relationship Interaction Graph with graph attention inside the ODE vector field, and adds a Structural Consistency Loss ($\mathcal{L}_{SC}$) based on a matrix of mutually exclusive predicates. Developing CoupledSGA revealed a limitation of the evaluation protocol. With-Constraint evaluation keeps one predicate per group for each subject-object pair, so its R@K and mR@K cannot capture the within-group violations targeted by $\mathcal{L}_{SC}$: we prove they are unchanged whenever each group's winning predicate and its score are held fixed. We further show that the gradient of $\mathcal{L}_{SC}$ depends on predicate scores rather than ground-truth labels: for two-predicate rules it amplifies the ordering the model already holds, and when all scores in a group are equal it suppresses predicates in more exclusion rules more strongly, explaining why the penalty can lower recall while improving consistency. On Action Genome, activating $\mathcal{L}_{SC}$ after two warm-up epochs reduces R@20 from 42.21% to 35.18% while lowering the No-Constraint contradiction rate from 45.92% to 4.07% (matched-budget R@20: 40.48% CoupledSGA vs. 44.78% SceneSayerODE). CoupledSGA is a testbed, not a state-of-the-art claim: With-Constraint recall captures the cost of enforcing structural consistency but not the improvement. We recommend reporting No-Constraint results alongside a contradiction rate for methods that constrain predicate co-activation.

AI.tldr: Introduces CoupledSGA, which couples relationships that share an entity in scene graph anticipation and adds a structural consistency loss, while showing that With-Constraint recall cannot see within-group violations.
AI.motivation: Independent per-pair Neural ODEs let mutually exclusive predicates such as sitting on and standing on coexist for the same pair, and the With-Constraint evaluation protocol cannot capture these violations.
AI.method: Relationships are linked through a Relationship Interaction Graph with graph attention inside the ODE vector field, and a Structural Consistency Loss is built from a matrix of mutually exclusive predicates. The paper proves that With-Constraint R@K and mR@K are unchanged whenever each group's winning predicate and score are held fixed.
AI.result: On Action Genome, activating the loss after two warm-up epochs lowers R@20 from 42.21% to 35.18% and cuts the No-Constraint contradiction rate from 45.92% to 4.07%. At matched budget, R@20 is 40.48% for CoupledSGA and 44.78% for SceneSayerODE.
AI.conclusion: CoupledSGA is a testbed rather than a state-of-the-art claim. The recall drop reflects the cost of enforcing consistency, and the authors recommend reporting No-Constraint results alongside a contradiction rate.

title: Benchmarking Fine-Grained Visual Reasoning for Remote Sensing in Urban Management
comment: Accepted by IEEE AP-GARSS 2026; 4 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables
summary: Fine-grained visual reasoning is essential for remote sensing in urban management, yet remains underexplored in the evaluation of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). We introduce UMBench, a fine-grained urban remote sensing benchmark built from unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) images for multiple urban management tasks such as traffic monitoring, urban construction, environmental quality, and disaster warning. Evaluations on UMBench reveal that current MLLMs often rely on scene-level priors and overlook fine-grained visual evidence. To address this issue, we further propose a novel evidence-first chain-of-thought method that directs models to inspect fine-grained visual evidence in a training-free manner. Experiments show that our method can improve the performance of both open-source and commercial MLLMs on UMBench.

AI.tldr: Introduces UMBench, a fine-grained UAV remote sensing benchmark for urban management, and a training-free evidence-first chain-of-thought method that improves MLLMs on it.
AI.motivation: Fine-grained visual reasoning for urban remote sensing is underexplored in MLLM evaluation, and current models often rely on scene-level priors instead of fine-grained visual evidence.
AI.method: UMBench is built from UAV images covering traffic monitoring, urban construction, environmental quality and disaster warning. The evidence-first chain-of-thought directs models to inspect fine-grained visual evidence without training.
AI.result: The method improves the performance of both open-source and commercial MLLMs on UMBench.
AI.conclusion: Directing models to inspect visual evidence first is a training-free way to improve fine-grained reasoning for urban remote sensing.

title: Semantic Residual Vector Quantization for Sign Language Generation
summary: Sign language generation (SLG) maps written sentences into signing motion while preserving both lexical content and fine-grained articulation. This requires a model to decide what signs should be expressed and to realize them through precise handshape, trajectory, facial expression and body coordination. Existing pose-based systems and reconstruction-only motion tokenizers often entangle these two decisions, leaving the generator without an explicit text-aligned intermediate target for what to sign before refining how to sign it. To address this issue, we introduce Semantic Residual Vector Quantization (SRVQ), a framework for SLG that frames generation as a two-level process moving from semantics to kinematics. The newly introduced SRV Quantizer learns a hierarchy in which the first residual level encodes sign content and subsequent levels refine pose, handshape, trajectory, and body coordination, all within a single quantizer and without separate semantic representations or external planning stages. Through word-aware conditioning for hierarchical code generation, a masked semantic generator predicts semantic codes and a kinematic generator completes the residual codes for full SMPL-X motion synthesis. We evaluate using retrieval and FID in a shared text-motion embedding space, alongside standard geometric metrics. On CSL-Daily and Phoenix-2014T, SRVQ achieves R@1 of 82.3 and 70.3, outperforming the previous SOTA by 30 and 46 points, respectively.

AI.tldr: Proposes SRVQ, a semantic residual vector quantizer for sign language generation that moves from semantics to kinematics, reaching R@1 of 82.3 on CSL-Daily and 70.3 on Phoenix-2014T.
AI.motivation: Pose-based systems and reconstruction-only motion tokenizers entangle what to sign with how to sign it, which leaves no explicit text-aligned intermediate target before refining the motion.
AI.method: A single SRV Quantizer learns a hierarchy in which the first residual level encodes sign content and later levels refine pose, handshape, trajectory and body coordination. A masked semantic generator predicts semantic codes, and a kinematic generator completes the residual codes for full SMPL-X motion synthesis.
AI.result: R@1 reaches 82.3 on CSL-Daily and 70.3 on Phoenix-2014T in a shared text-motion embedding space, outperforming the previous SOTA by 30 and 46 points respectively.
AI.conclusion: A hierarchical residual codebook gives an explicit semantic intermediate for sign language generation without separate semantic representations or planning stages.

title: VA-TDM: A Unified View for Improving Few-Step Diffusion Models by Velocity Adversarial Distillation
comment: Project Page: this https URL Code: this https URL
summary: Few-step distillation offers efficient generation with diffusion and flow models, but preserving quality with only a few sampling steps remains challenging. Distribution-matching methods via score distillation provide a strong foundation, yet they rely on accurately tracking the student's changing distribution. At intermediate generation steps in few-step sampling, student-score estimation can be difficult, and commonly used estimators may describe a different distribution from the one used to update the student. Flow matching allows a more flexible approach to supervision through velocity fields constructed from the student's sampling process. Building on this perspective, we introduce Velocity Adversarial Distillation (VAD), which uses a learned critic to compare student and teacher fields and turn their disagreement into feedback for learning. VAD unifies score distillation, Fisher-based matching, and moment matching, also explaining existing heuristic MMD updates and delivering new training objectives. We further develop VA-TDM, which follows trajectory distribution matching: providing supervision for partial denoising along the student trajectory. Beyond this, VA-TDM combines transition-aware online velocity learning and dual-form VAD supervision across intermediate student transitions. Extensive results show that VA-TDM is powerful for learning few-step generators, achieving state-of-the-art four-step performance in both text-to-image and text-to-video generation across various backbones and scaling effectively to 33B MiniMax-H3. In particular, our VA-TDM-H3 notably outperforms the few-step Fast-H3 and is closer to the original many-step H3 according to human preference.

AI.tldr: Proposes Velocity Adversarial Distillation (VAD) and VA-TDM for few-step diffusion and flow models, reaching state-of-the-art four-step text-to-image and text-to-video performance.
AI.motivation: Score distillation for few-step samplers depends on tracking the student's changing distribution, and the score estimators commonly used at intermediate steps can describe a different distribution from the one that updates the student.
AI.method: VAD uses a learned critic to compare student and teacher velocity fields and turns their disagreement into feedback. It unifies score distillation, Fisher-based matching and moment matching. VA-TDM follows trajectory distribution matching with transition-aware online velocity learning and dual-form VAD supervision across intermediate student transitions.
AI.result: VA-TDM achieves state-of-the-art four-step performance in text-to-image and text-to-video generation across various backbones and scales to a 33B model. Its 33B variant, VA-TDM-H3, outperforms the few-step Fast-H3 and is closer to the many-step H3 in human preference.
AI.conclusion: Velocity-based adversarial supervision gives a unified framework that yields stronger few-step generators.

title: Open-HumanScale: An Open Recipe for Scaling Human and Robot Experience for Embodied Foundation Models
comment: GitHub: this https URL Project website: this https URL
summary: Egocentric human video offers a scalable source of manipulation priors for robot learning, yet translating raw data scale into generalizable robot policies demands rigorous data curation and training recipes. We introduce Open-HumanScale, the first fully open recipe for scaling egocentric pretraining to 50,000 hours, anchored by Open-HumanScale-50K---a curated egocentric video corpus densely annotated with hand motion and natural language. Leveraging this corpus, we systematically investigate pure human pretraining via closed-loop simulation evaluations and uncover an empirical log-linear scaling law linking pretraining data hours to downstream robot success rates. Grounded in these findings, we develop HumanWAM-Vanilla, a world--action model pretrained exclusively on 50k hours of egocentric human video. Upon robot post-training, HumanWAM-Vanilla reaches 92.08% success on RoboTwin 2.0 Clean2Clean and 68.88% on Clean2Random, alongside a 14.17% mean success rate and a 19.00 mean progress score on RoboDojo. To push the capability frontier further, we explore joint human--robot pretraining with HumanWAM-Goal, a visual-goal-conditioned world--action model. Hybrid data scaling unlocks broad zero-shot generalization across both simulation and physical benchmarks, propelling post-trained RoboTwin 2.0 performance to new state-of-the-art levels: 92.70% on Clean2Clean and a substantial leap to 84.60% on Clean2Random. On physical robots, HumanWAM-Goal further exhibits emergent embodied in-context learning, dynamically adapting its manipulation behavior to unseen visual goals without parameter updates. To support reproducible scaling research in embodied AI, we open-source the Open-HumanScale-50K corpus, data curation and pretraining pipelines, alongside the pretrained and post-trained HumanWAM checkpoints, inference code, and simulation evaluation suites.

AI.tldr: Presents Open-HumanScale, an open recipe for scaling egocentric human video to 50,000 hours for embodied foundation models, and HumanWAM world-action models trained on it.
AI.motivation: Egocentric human video is a scalable source of manipulation priors for robot learning, but turning raw data scale into generalizable robot policies requires rigorous curation and training recipes.
AI.method: Curates Open-HumanScale-50K, a corpus densely annotated with hand motion and natural language. HumanWAM-Vanilla is pretrained only on human video, and HumanWAM-Goal, a visual-goal-conditioned model, is pretrained jointly on human and robot data.
AI.result: An empirical log-linear scaling law links pretraining hours to downstream robot success. HumanWAM-Vanilla reaches 92.08% on RoboTwin 2.0 Clean2Clean and 68.88% on Clean2Random, and HumanWAM-Goal reaches 92.70% and 84.60%, with zero-shot generalization and emergent in-context adaptation on physical robots.
AI.conclusion: Scaling egocentric human pretraining is effective, and the released corpus, pipelines and checkpoints support reproducible embodied AI scaling research.

title: Context-Aware Autoregressive Image Generation for Emerging Reasoning Properties
summary: Autoregressive image generation has recently emerged as a competitive visual generation paradigm, yet its generation order is often predefined or heuristic, such as next-patch prediction, random-order prediction, or one-step generation for specific scales. We observe that these strategies can cause models to overlook important structural dependencies in images, thereby limiting both structural robustness and reasoning capability. In this work, we propose a context-aware autoregressive generation framework, where the model dynamically determines the next token location based on global context and current local information. Rather than following a fixed or random order, our method allows the generation process to adapt to image structure and semantic dependencies. Extensive experiments show that context-aware generation significantly improves structural robustness across different image AR paradigms, including masked autoregressive and scale-wise autoregressive models. Beyond quantitative improvements, we further observe emerging reasoning properties: the model can better understand complex semantic instructions and generate images that more faithfully follow the given guidance. These findings suggest that generation order is a critical yet underexplored factor in image autoregressive modeling, and that context-aware decoding can unlock stronger reasoning-aware visual generation capabilities. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Proposes a context-aware autoregressive image generator that chooses the next token location from global context and local information, instead of a fixed or random generation order.
AI.motivation: Predefined or heuristic orders such as next-patch, random-order or scale-wise prediction can overlook structural dependencies in images, which limits structural robustness and reasoning capability.
AI.method: The model dynamically determines the next token location from global context and current local information. The framework is applied to masked autoregressive and scale-wise autoregressive models.
AI.result: Context-aware generation significantly improves structural robustness across these image AR paradigms. The authors also observe emerging reasoning properties, with generated images following complex semantic instructions more faithfully.
AI.conclusion: Generation order is a critical but underexplored factor in image autoregressive modelling, and context-aware decoding can unlock stronger reasoning-aware visual generation.

title: Same Layout, Different Count: What Number Words Do Past Ten in Text-to-Image Models
comment: 43 pages, including 32 pages of supplementary material; 14 figures, 44 tables
summary: Ask SD3.5-Medium for twelve of an object and then, from the same starting noise, for twenty-five. The picture keeps its layout, but the count changes about as much as it would under a new random seed, and in no consistent direction. We study what number words do once a request passes about ten objects, in five open text-to-image models. Holding the object and the starting noise fixed, we change one thing at a time, and people who never see the request count 3,088 of the images. Every model follows the number for small crowds, but only up to a point, its reach: SD3.5-M and FLUX.1-dev stop following it soon after ten, while FLUX.2 [klein] and Qwen-Image follow it loosely up to twenty-five. Beyond SD3.5-M's reach, the coarse part of the starting noise fixes the composition of the picture but not how many objects it holds: redrawing only the noise finer than an eighth of the image keeps the layout as well as a new number does, and already moves the count two-thirds as far. The number word still reaches the denoiser and acts in its first steps, but nothing we tried gives it a clear direction. Shown instead as a noised grid in the starting latent, the count is drawn: people find it in 59% of images, against 4% when it is only told. Past ten, an exact-match score barely separates a model that follows the number loosely from one that ignores it, and a relative-error score can even prefer a constant guess of sixteen. A same-noise test with a few requests per object tells them apart.

AI.tldr: Shows that number words above about ten barely control object counts in five open text-to-image models, and that the count is largely set by the starting noise rather than by the prompt.
AI.motivation: Models are often assumed to follow number words, but how counts beyond ten behave in generated images had not been measured.
AI.method: With the object and starting noise held fixed, one factor is changed at a time across five open text-to-image models, and 3,088 images are counted by people who never see the request. Noise-level tests and a noised-grid latent probe where the count is determined.
AI.result: Each model follows small counts only up to its reach: SD3.5-Medium and FLUX.1-dev stop soon after ten, while FLUX.2 [klein] and Qwen-Image follow loosely up to twenty-five. Beyond SD3.5-M's reach, redrawing only the finer noise moves the count two-thirds as far as a new number. A noised grid in the starting latent makes people find the count in 59% of images, against 4% when it is only told. Past ten, exact-match scores barely separate the models, and a relative-error score can prefer a constant guess of sixteen.
AI.conclusion: Past ten, a same-noise test with a few requests per object is needed to tell models apart, since the number word reaches the denoiser but gives no clear direction.

title: Where to Connect? Boosting MLLMs via Dynamic Gated Pathways across ALL ViT and LLM Layers
comment: 24 pages (10 pages main text + references + appendix), 15 figures. Accepted at the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)
summary: A central yet under-explored question in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) is where to connect---how visual information from a hierarchical vision encoder should be wired into the layer-wise semantics of a large language model. Mainstream MLLMs inject a fixed single-layer visual representation into the LLM and treat all LLM layers as a single consumer, ignoring that different layers demand different visual granularities. Recent multi-layer fusion methods either compress hierarchical features on the encoder side or rely on predefined sparse or hierarchical layer-to-layer connections, and therefore stop short of modeling adaptive cross-layer interactions between the ViT and LLM hierarchies. We address this gap with DGP (Dynamic Gated Pathways), a routing mechanism that establishes all-to-all connections between every ViT layer and every LLM layer, with each LLM layer dynamically gating its preference over visual layers conditioned on its own semantic state. Built on top of LLaVA-1.5-7B and 13B, DGP delivers consistent gains over the LLaVA-1.5-7B baseline (e.g., +4.2 on SQA$^{I}$, +3.3 on MM-Vet, +3.1 on VizWiz and LLaVA$^{W}$) and surpasses prior multi-layer visual fusion methods on most benchmarks. Layer-wise routing analyses further show that different LLM layers do select different visual granularities on demand, supporting both the effectiveness and interpretability of the proposed dynamic gated pathways. The code is available: this https URL.

AI.tldr: Proposes DGP (Dynamic Gated Pathways), a routing mechanism that connects every ViT layer to every LLM layer in an MLLM, with each LLM layer gating its preference over visual layers.
AI.motivation: MLLMs usually inject a single fixed visual layer into the LLM, and prior multi-layer fusion methods either compress features on the encoder side or rely on predefined sparse connections, missing adaptive cross-layer interaction.
AI.method: All-to-all connections link every ViT layer to every LLM layer, and each LLM layer dynamically gates its preference over visual layers based on its own semantic state. The method is built on LLaVA-1.5-7B and 13B.
AI.result: Over the LLaVA-1.5-7B baseline it gains +4.2 on SQA-I, +3.3 on MM-Vet, +3.1 on VizWiz and LLaVA-W, and it surpasses prior multi-layer fusion methods on most benchmarks. Routing analyses show different LLM layers select different visual granularities.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic gated routing across all layers is effective and interpretable for connecting ViT and LLM hierarchies.

title: Trainspotting: Learning Object-Centric 3D Reconstruction from Found Photos
summary: State-of-the-art feedforward reconstruction models perform poorly on in-the-wild object-centric photo collections. They are trained largely on single-session object captures whose images vary in viewpoint while the object and its environment remain nearly fixed. Public photo archives contain a different form of multi-view data. They hold found photos of the same object or design: photos taken independently by many people across years, environments, cameras, and sometimes physical units. In this work, we introduce Trainspotting, a dataset of 12,068 objects and 311,886 photos from Wikimedia Commons. We reconstruct each object to recover camera poses, multi-view stereo depth, and object masks. We categorize the objects into three regimes: objects fixed at one site, objects that move between sites, and designs shared by many physical units. Evaluating recent feedforward reconstruction models on Trainspotting shows that they fail most severely in the last two regimes. Fine-tuning VGGT-$\Omega$ on Trainspotting significantly improves camera pose, depth, and 3D geometry on held-out objects. We observe similar improvements on the independent NAVI in-the-wild benchmark, which contains photos of each object in different environments. Performance on conventional benchmarks remains largely unchanged.

AI.tldr: Introduces Trainspotting, a dataset of 12,068 objects and 311,886 Wikimedia Commons photos, for learning object-centric 3D reconstruction from found photos taken across years and environments.
AI.motivation: Feedforward reconstruction models perform poorly on in-the-wild object photo collections, because they are trained mostly on single-session captures in which the object and environment stay nearly fixed.
AI.method: Each object is reconstructed to recover camera poses, multi-view stereo depth and object masks. Objects are grouped into three regimes: fixed at one site, moving between sites, and shared designs across many physical units. VGGT-Omega is then fine-tuned on the dataset.
AI.result: Recent feedforward models fail most severely in the moving and shared-design regimes. Fine-tuning VGGT-Omega significantly improves camera pose, depth and 3D geometry on held-out objects, with similar improvements on the NAVI in-the-wild benchmark, while conventional benchmarks stay largely unchanged.
AI.conclusion: Found photo archives provide multi-environment, multi-unit training data that addresses failure cases which single-session data does not cover.

title: Visual Token Routing: Learning to keep tokens that matter
summary: Computer-use agents (CUAs) have recently achieved superhuman performance on several long-horizon benchmarks. However, their computational cost limits their use in long-horizon tasks and real-time domains such as video games. A key bottleneck is representing each screenshot as thousands of visual tokens, which accumulate into long contexts as agents reason over extended interaction histories. We observe that most of these visual tokens are either semantically irrelevant to the agent's next action or temporally redundant across screenshots. Building on this observation, we introduce Visual Token Routing (VTR), a joint training framework for learning sparse visual representations that preserve the information needed for action prediction. In VTR, we train the vision-language model together with a lightweight spatio-temporal router that examines each image region in the current and previous screenshots and decides whether its visual token enters the language model. We optimize the router using an adaptive loss to keep the number of visual tokens as small as possible while minimizing performance degradation. With just 2,000 training steps, VTR matches the performance of the full-resolution model on OSWorld, CUA-World, and video game action prediction, while using 2.5-5.8x fewer visual tokens. These savings reduce inference cost by up to 3.3x and speed up prefill by up to 2.9x. VTR also outperforms lowering the image resolution and other baselines for dropping tokens, by up to 12.8 points on OSWorld. Overall, VTR enables computer-use agents to process only the visual tokens they need, allowing them to be used in long-horizon tasks and real-time domains at a fraction of the computational cost. Code and models are available at this https URL

AI.tldr: Proposes Visual Token Routing (VTR), a jointly trained spatio-temporal router that keeps only the visual tokens a computer-use agent needs for action prediction, cutting visual tokens by 2.5-5.8x.
AI.motivation: Computer-use agents are costly because each screenshot becomes thousands of visual tokens, most of which are irrelevant to the next action or redundant across screenshots.
AI.method: A lightweight router examines each image region in the current and previous screenshots and decides whether its visual token enters the language model. It is trained with an adaptive loss that keeps the token count small while limiting performance degradation.
AI.result: After 2,000 training steps, VTR matches full-resolution performance on OSWorld, CUA-World and video game action prediction while using 2.5-5.8x fewer visual tokens. This reduces inference cost by up to 3.3x and speeds up prefill by up to 2.9x, and it beats lower resolution and other token-dropping baselines by up to 12.8 points on OSWorld.
AI.conclusion: Learned token routing lets computer-use agents process only the visual tokens they need, making long-horizon and real-time use practical at a fraction of the cost.

title: PixelSpline: Continuous Space-Time Video Super-Resolution via Endpoint-Anchored Shared Pixel Trajectories
summary: Existing continuous space-time video super-resolution methods often infer motion from only two endpoint frames and model the two motion directions independently, making them vulnerable to ambiguous correspondence and inconsistent trajectories. We introduce a continuous STVSR framework that combines long-context encoding, continuous HR feature lifting, and an endpoint-anchored PixelSpline. Long-range observations provide more reliable endpoint representations, while continuous upsampling constructs detailed appearance features directly on the requested HR grid. PixelSpline explicitly models each pixel's motion as a single continuous trajectory shared by both endpoints. Using this trajectory, our method warps endpoint colors into a coarse intermediate frame and aligns the HR features for residual reconstruction. Experiments across spatial and temporal upsampling settings demonstrate that the proposed framework offers a favorable quality--efficiency trade-off.

AI.tldr: Proposes PixelSpline, a continuous space-time video super-resolution framework that models each pixel's motion as one continuous trajectory shared by both endpoint frames.
AI.motivation: Existing methods infer motion from only two endpoint frames and model the two motion directions independently, which makes correspondence ambiguous and trajectories inconsistent.
AI.method: Combines long-context encoding, continuous high-resolution feature lifting and an endpoint-anchored PixelSpline. The shared trajectory warps endpoint colours into a coarse intermediate frame and aligns the high-resolution features for residual reconstruction.
AI.result: Experiments across spatial and temporal upsampling settings show a favourable quality-efficiency trade-off. The abstract reports no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Endpoint-anchored shared trajectories, supported by long-range observations, give a favourable quality-efficiency trade-off for continuous space-time super-resolution.

title: Procedural Adversarial Learning
summary: For many computer vision tasks, neural networks can be trained to produce a low average error, yet they still fail on seemingly simple scenes. Reducing these failures requires first finding them, but they may not be in a fixed dataset. We study procedural adversarial learning (PAL), a framework of minimax training and adversarial evaluation which searches the input space of a procedural generator for difficult instances. The procedural generator is an interpretable program mapping a low-dimensional vector of control parameters (e.g. layout, lighting, pose) to a rendered image and its label. We introduce the Simple-PAT algorithm, which uses zeroth-order optimization in the procedural generator's parameter space to propose adversarial training samples that are generated on demand. We also create PAL-Dojo, a collection of efficient procedural generators for surface normal estimation, image segmentation, and human pose estimation. Against a cross-model black-box adversary with 50M aggregate queries, Simple-PAT reduces worst-case error by a geometric mean of 3.15x compared to standard training and 2.63x compared to the strongest robust training baseline. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Proposes procedural adversarial learning, a minimax training scheme that searches the control-parameter space of a procedural generator for hard instances; the Simple-PAT algorithm cuts worst-case error by a geometric mean of 3.15x versus standard training and 2.63x versus the strongest robust baseline.
AI.motivation: Networks with low average error still fail on seemingly simple scenes, and these failures may not appear in any fixed dataset, so they must be actively searched for.
AI.method: Simple-PAT applies zeroth-order optimization over the low-dimensional control parameters (e.g. layout, lighting, pose) of an interpretable procedural generator to propose on-demand adversarial training samples; PAL-Dojo collects efficient generators for surface normal estimation, image segmentation and human pose estimation.
AI.result: Against a cross-model black-box adversary with 50M aggregate queries, Simple-PAT reduces worst-case error by a geometric mean of 3.15x compared with standard training and 2.63x compared with the strongest robust training baseline.
AI.conclusion: Searching the input space of procedural generators is a practical way to find and train on difficult cases that fixed datasets miss.

title: Motion-guided Contrastive Regularization For Latent World Models
summary: JEPA-style world models learn action-conditioned latent dynamics without reconstructing observations, but distributional regularization alone does not ensure that their representations preserve information needed for control. We identify static collapse, a failure mode in which the encoder preserves episode-specific static content while suppressing manipulation-relevant state changes. Because static content is temporally predictable yet diverse across episodes, this failure can persist despite regularizers such as SIGReg. A controlled study on OGBench-Cube shows that introducing randomized backgrounds substantially degrades planning performance while leaving the underlying manipulation task unchanged. To address this problem, we propose motion-guided contrastive regularization. Our approach compares predicted latent transitions with transitions to candidate observations from the same episode, reducing the usefulness of static background identity for distinguishing action outcomes. Optical-flow similarities provide soft contrastive targets, allowing candidates with similar motion to receive similar supervision. Combined with latent prediction and SIGReg, our objective encourages representations to preserve within-episode state distinctions and similarities between related transitions. Our method improves planning success over LeWorldModel (LeWM) from 52% to 78% on OGBench-Cube with randomized backgrounds and from 14% to 54% on LIBERO-Object, while maintaining comparable performance on four other visual-control benchmarks.

AI.tldr: Identifies static collapse in JEPA-style latent world models, where the encoder keeps episode-specific static content, and proposes motion-guided contrastive regularization using optical-flow similarity as soft targets; planning success rises from 52% to 78% on OGBench-Cube with randomized backgrounds and from 14% to 54% on LIBERO-Object.
AI.motivation: Distributional regularizers such as SIGReg do not ensure that latent representations keep the state information needed for control, and static background content can persist despite them, degrading planning under randomized backgrounds.
AI.method: The objective compares predicted latent transitions with transitions to candidate observations from the same episode, with optical-flow similarities giving soft contrastive targets so that candidates with similar motion receive similar supervision; it is combined with latent prediction and SIGReg.
AI.result: Planning success over LeWorldModel (LeWM) improves from 52% to 78% on OGBench-Cube with randomized backgrounds and from 14% to 54% on LIBERO-Object, while performance stays comparable on four other visual-control benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Motion-guided contrastive supervision counters static collapse by preserving within-episode state distinctions, which improves latent planning in world models.

title: From Pixels to Actions - Towards Native Vision-Language-Action Policies
summary: Vision-language-action models are typically built on a simple premise: perception is first compressed by visual encoders, and action reasoning begins only afterwards. Yet manipulation often hinges on precisely the visual signals most vulnerable to this abstraction, e.g., local geometry, boundaries, depth, and subtle state changes. This raises a fundamental question: should action policies inherit a fixed visual endpoint, or directly access evolving visual computation? We introduce NEO-VLA, a structurally encoder-free vision-language-action framework. Images are tokenized by lightweight patch convolutional layers and evolve jointly with language throughout the backbone, allowing a flow-matching action expert to draw from instruction-conditioned visual representations at different depths. This simple change reveals a consistent pattern. Native architectures outperform encoder-based counterparts under controlled comparisons; full fine-tuning reduces but does not erase the gap, and additional scale alone cannot recover it. More strikingly, layer-wise probing shows that the action-critical signals often peak well before the final visual representation. Across diverse manipulation settings and distribution shifts, NEO-VLA consequently achieves stronger and more robust control. Together, these results suggest that embodied control benefits from access to visual representations across the computational hierarchy, rather than a fixed encoder output.

AI.tldr: Proposes NEO-VLA, an encoder-free vision-language-action model that tokenizes images with lightweight patch convolutions and lets a flow-matching action expert read instruction-conditioned visual features at multiple depths; native architectures outperform encoder-based counterparts under controlled comparisons.
AI.motivation: Vision-language-action models first compress perception with a visual encoder, which can discard local geometry, boundaries, depth and subtle state changes that manipulation often depends on.
AI.method: Images are tokenized by lightweight patch convolutional layers and evolve jointly with language throughout the backbone, and a flow-matching action expert draws on visual representations at different depths.
AI.result: Under controlled comparisons native architectures beat encoder-based ones; full fine-tuning narrows but does not erase the gap, and scale alone does not recover it. Layer-wise probing shows action-critical signals often peak well before the final visual representation, and NEO-VLA achieves stronger and more robust control across manipulation settings and distribution shifts.
AI.conclusion: Embodied control benefits from access to visual representations across the computational hierarchy rather than only a fixed encoder output.

title: AgentCount: An Agentic Workflow for Traceable Colony Counting and Insight Generation from Agar Plate Images
summary: Colony counting is commonly used to evaluate microbial populations in food safety testing and microbiological studies. Despite its wide application, manual counting is time-consuming and operator-dependent, and the final count often lacks a record of the objects included in the measurement. To address these limitations, this study presents AgentCount, an open-source agentic workflow for colony counting and result interpretation from agar plate images. Plate photographs and plating metadata are processed through seven agents for image quality control, plate localisation, colony detection, counting, CFU calculation, validation, and reporting. Colony detection is performed using Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM 3) with multiple text prompts and morphology-based filtering. After that, replicate statistics are calculated and a large language model (LLM)-based agent is used to generate a results narrative. Intermediate outputs, including quality scores, segmentation masks, detections, and warnings, are retained to support review of the reported values. The workflow also extends to skill-guided analysis of archived microbial population data. In a retrospective comparison with two previously published studies, we benchmarked 241 published endpoints, including all 216 mean +- SD values of the meat-analogue pathogen tables; on the 168 endpoints with a complete n=6 replicate source, 164 (97.6%) agreed within 0.01 log10 units. Overall, AgentCount demonstrates the promising potential of agentic workflows for applications in applied microbiology.

AI.tldr: Presents AgentCount, an open-source agentic workflow for colony counting and result interpretation from agar plate images, using SAM 3 for detection and an LLM agent for the results narrative; 164 of 168 endpoints with a complete n=6 replicate source agreed with the published values within 0.01 log10 units.
AI.motivation: Manual colony counting is time-consuming and operator-dependent, and the final count often has no record of which objects were included.
AI.method: Seven agents handle image quality control, plate localisation, colony detection, counting, CFU calculation, validation and reporting; detection uses Segment Anything Model 3 with multiple text prompts and morphology-based filtering, replicate statistics are computed, and an LLM-based agent writes the narrative while quality scores, masks, detections and warnings are retained.
AI.result: In a retrospective comparison with two previously published studies, 241 endpoints were benchmarked, including all 216 mean +- SD values of the meat-analogue pathogen tables; on the 168 endpoints with a complete n=6 replicate source, 164 (97.6%) agreed within 0.01 log10 units. The workflow also extends to skill-guided analysis of archived microbial population data.
AI.conclusion: Agentic workflows show promising potential for applied microbiology, with retained intermediate outputs supporting review of the reported values.

title: When can multi-fragment 2D/3D registration be trusted? Calibrated certification and uncertainty-driven view planning for pelvic fracture fluoroscopy
summary: Registering a segmented CT to fluoroscopy can locate every fracture fragment but can guide surgery only when trusted. After each shot, our closed loop registers all fragments, bounds their errors with a calibrated sandwich covariance, flags implausible or ambiguous ones, and stops or plans the next view. On simulated fluoroscopy of 60 held-out fracture CTs with realistic image uncertainty, 95% bounds covered 83% of unflagged fragments and 91% of those within 5mm, but from the second view on 14% failed by over 5mm, a third with bounds of at most 2mm. A fragment's shift when a view was added separated tightly bounded failures best (exploratory; AUC 0.94, bound 0.81). Requiring that the newest view moved no fragment beyond its bound, preferred post hoc, lowered false stops at 2mm from 23% to 6% overall, with 345 instead of 362 correct ones but more trajectories uncertified; delaying the stop did not, and other signals at equal acceptance left 10-15% false. With a segmentation error shared by all views (median Dice 0.89), 21% of this rule's stops were false against 10% without it (15 cases; exploratory). Minimax planning certified sooner than the clinical protocol without the check (4.20 versus 4.72 shots, Holm p <0.001), but no criterion reached the pre-specified endpoint, a true 2mm error, significantly sooner, even in the true basin. On real fluoroscopy of five intact pelves no 2mm certificate was false. Trust takes evidence across views, not only a calibrated local bound.

AI.tldr: Proposes a closed-loop 2D/3D registration system for pelvic fracture fluoroscopy that bounds each fragment's error with a calibrated sandwich covariance, flags unreliable fragments, and stops or plans the next view; trust requires evidence across views, not only a calibrated local bound.
AI.motivation: Registering a segmented CT to fluoroscopy can locate every fracture fragment, but it can guide surgery only when its reliability is known.
AI.method: After each shot the system registers all fragments, bounds their errors with a calibrated sandwich covariance, flags implausible or ambiguous ones, and decides whether to stop or plan the next view; stopping rules compare shifts caused by adding a view against the bounds, and minimax view planning is compared with the clinical protocol.
AI.result: On simulated fluoroscopy of 60 held-out fracture CTs, 95% bounds covered 83% of unflagged fragments and 91% of those within 5 mm, but from the second view on 14% failed by over 5 mm. Requiring that the newest view move no fragment beyond its bound lowered false stops at 2 mm from 23% to 6% overall; minimax planning certified sooner than the clinical protocol (4.20 versus 4.72 shots, Holm p <0.001), but no criterion reached a true 2 mm error significantly sooner. On real fluoroscopy of five intact pelves no 2 mm certificate was false.
AI.conclusion: Trust in registration takes evidence accumulated across views, not only a calibrated local error bound.

title: Dual Flow: Joint Image-Measurement Flow for Inverse Problems
