comment: 17 pages, 8 figures. Our code is available at this https URL
summary: Existing generative model-based approaches to linear inverse problems typically use the acquired noisy measurement to condition or guide sampling in the image domain. In this work, we introduce Dual Flow, a novel joint flow model for solving linear inverse problems by jointly estimating the clean image and its corresponding noise-free measurement from the observation. Specifically, Dual Flow formulates image reconstruction and measurement denoising as a coupled estimation problem, using coupled flows in the image and measurement domains. The acquired noisy measurement $\mathbf{y}_0$ is used only to initialize the measurement state; thereafter, the image and measurement states are jointly updated based on their current values. By construction, the final image and measurement estimates are guaranteed to satisfy the underlying forward model. We derive the sampling updates for the joint flow and show that they are governed by the conditional mean of the clean image given the current joint state. We further derive a closed-form expression for a sufficient statistic of the joint state and show that the required conditional mean can be obtained by solving an image-domain Gaussian denoising problem involving operator-dependent, correlated noise. We train a velocity-prediction network using this formulation to estimate the conditional mean from the derived sufficient statistic. Dual Flow requires no hyperparameter tuning beyond selecting the number of inference steps and achieves substantially shorter reconstruction times than competing methods. Extensive experiments across various linear inverse problems and image datasets demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in both distortion metrics and perceptual quality. Additional analyses assess robustness to model mismatch, as well as the ability to generate diverse plausible reconstructions and characterize reconstruction uncertainty.

AI.tldr: Introduces Dual Flow, a joint image-measurement flow that estimates the clean image and its noise-free measurement together for linear inverse problems, so the final estimates satisfy the forward model by construction; it reports state-of-the-art distortion and perceptual quality with substantially shorter reconstruction times.
AI.motivation: Existing generative approaches use the noisy measurement to condition or guide image-domain sampling rather than estimating the image and measurement jointly.
AI.method: Coupled flows run in the image and measurement domains; the noisy measurement only initializes the measurement state, after which both states are updated jointly. The sampling updates are governed by the conditional mean of the clean image given the joint state, obtained by solving an image-domain Gaussian denoising problem with operator-dependent correlated noise, and a velocity-prediction network is trained on this formulation.
AI.result: Experiments across linear inverse problems and image datasets show state-of-the-art distortion metrics and perceptual quality, with substantially shorter reconstruction times than competing methods and no tuning beyond the number of inference steps; additional analyses cover robustness to model mismatch, diverse reconstructions and uncertainty.
AI.conclusion: Joint estimation of the image and its measurement gives a forward-model-consistent, faster solver for inverse problems.

title: Time-to-Goal: Learned Temporal Metrics for Long-Horizon Planning with JEPA World Models
summary: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) support planning by comparing predicted latent states with an encoded goal. For this comparison to guide temporal progress, states closer in time to the goal should receive lower costs. However, training representations for prediction and distribution regularization does not directly enforce this ordering. We examine this mismatch in flat LeWorldModel (LeWM) by analyzing how its Euclidean goal cost changes with temporal separation. Our analysis identifies conditions under which states at different long offsets receive similar average costs, weakening their temporal distinction. To learn the missing ordering explicitly, we introduce Time-to-Goal (T2G), a lightweight metric trained on latent triples from offline trajectories. A margin ranking loss encourages smaller distances for temporally nearer states, requiring no rewards or policy labels. The learned metric then replaces the Euclidean planning cost while the JEPA encoder and predictor remain frozen. Diagnostics on AntMaze and FourRoom show that T2G preserves stronger temporal contrast and improves near--far ranking at long offsets. Across four navigation and manipulation benchmarks, T2G improves the average planning success rate from 32.7\% (flat LeWM) to 63.0\% and approaches or even surpasses the performance of the hierarchical H-JEPA baselines. These results show that learning temporal ordering for the goal cost can substantially improve latent planning even with a flat world model.

AI.tldr: Proposes Time-to-Goal (T2G), a lightweight learned metric that orders latent states by temporal distance to the goal and replaces the Euclidean planning cost of a frozen JEPA world model; average planning success rises from 32.7% (flat LeWM) to 63.0% across four benchmarks.
AI.motivation: JEPA planning compares predicted latent states with the encoded goal under a Euclidean cost, but training for prediction and distribution regularization does not enforce that states closer to the goal in time receive lower costs, so states at different long offsets can get similar costs.
AI.method: A margin ranking loss trained on latent triples from offline trajectories encourages smaller distances for temporally nearer states, requiring no rewards or policy labels; the learned metric replaces the Euclidean cost while the JEPA encoder and predictor stay frozen.
AI.result: On AntMaze and FourRoom, T2G preserves stronger temporal contrast and improves near-far ranking at long offsets. Across four navigation and manipulation benchmarks, average planning success rises from 32.7% (flat LeWM) to 63.0% and approaches or surpasses the hierarchical H-JEPA baselines.
AI.conclusion: Learning temporal ordering for the goal cost can substantially improve latent planning even with a flat world model.

title: Cross-Modal Semantic Successive Refinement for Generative Image Communication over Underwater Acoustic Channels
summary: Underwater acoustic communication faces challenges such as limited available bandwidth and complex channel environments, which impose demanding requirements on efficient image transmission and reliable reconstruction. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a generative image communication framework based on cross-modal semantic successive refinement. At the transmitter, text descriptions, compact bottleneck features, and visual side information compressed by residual vector quantization are transmitted. At the receiver, text and bottleneck features are first fused to predict a base estimate of the intermediate visual representation. The received RVQ indices are then used to recover supplementary visual information and perform residual correction, followed by image reconstruction using a one-step Pixel Mean Flow model. During training, a CLIP-based text-image semantic consistency constraint is introduced to preserve the semantic correspondence between generated results and the original text descriptions. During transmission, protection resources are allocated according to the importance of different information branches and RVQ quantization stages. Simulations using COCO 2017 images and measured underwater acoustic channel records from Watermark show that text and bottleneck features provide complementary semantic and structural conditions, RVQ visual side information further improves reconstruction quality, and layered unequal error protection helps improve recovery at low SNRs. Code-rate allocation experiments reveal a tradeoff between the reliability of fundamental conditions and visual-detail reconstruction under a limited visual-feature coding budget, providing guidance for allocating protection resources in underwater acoustic image transmission.

AI.tldr: Proposes a generative image communication framework for underwater acoustic channels that sends text, compact bottleneck features and RVQ-compressed visual side information, and reconstructs images with a one-step Pixel Mean Flow model; layered unequal error protection helps recovery at low SNR.
AI.motivation: Underwater acoustic communication has limited bandwidth and complex channels, which make efficient and reliable image transmission difficult.
AI.method: The transmitter sends text descriptions, bottleneck features and residual-vector-quantized visual side information; the receiver fuses text and bottleneck features into a base estimate of the intermediate visual representation, refines it with the received RVQ indices, and reconstructs with a one-step Pixel Mean Flow model. Training uses a CLIP-based text-image semantic consistency constraint, and protection resources are allocated by branch importance and RVQ stage.
AI.result: Simulations on COCO 2017 images and measured Watermark channel records show that text and bottleneck features are complementary, RVQ side information further improves reconstruction quality, and layered unequal error protection improves recovery at low SNRs; code-rate experiments reveal a tradeoff between reliable fundamental conditions and visual detail under a limited coding budget.
AI.conclusion: The work gives guidance for allocating protection resources in underwater acoustic image transmission.

title: UniLoop: Unified Loop Closure Detection from Retrieval to Geometric Verification and Relative Pose Estimation
summary: Loop closure detection conventionally cascades separate models for global retrieval, geometric verification, and relative pose estimation, leading to redundant computation and disconnected visual representations. We propose UniLoop, a unified framework that reuses the hierarchical representations of the pretrained geometric foundation model throughout this pipeline. A shared image encoder produces features for compact global descriptors; the same features are passed to the cross-view decoder for pairwise verification; and the original geometric predictions provide relative camera constraints for pose-graph optimization. Experiments on place recognition, loop verification, and relative pose estimation show that UniLoop improves loop-closure robustness and accuracy while reducing redundant backbone computation relative to modular pipelines. UniLoop achieves the best Recall@10 on MSLS (96.6) and Pitts30k (99.3) among the compared methods, while its verification branch reaches 95.63 AP and 96.29 ROC-AUC, surpassing the existing geometric verification baselines.

AI.tldr: Proposes UniLoop, which runs loop closure detection (global retrieval, geometric verification and relative pose estimation) on shared features from a pretrained geometric foundation model, and reports the best Recall@10 on MSLS (96.6) and Pitts30k (99.3) among the compared methods.
AI.motivation: Conventional loop closure cascades separate models for retrieval, verification and pose estimation, causing redundant computation and disconnected visual representations.
AI.method: A shared image encoder produces compact global descriptors; the same features feed a cross-view decoder for pairwise verification; the foundation model's geometric predictions supply relative camera constraints for pose-graph optimization.
AI.result: On place recognition, loop verification and relative pose estimation, UniLoop improves loop-closure robustness and accuracy while reducing redundant backbone computation; its verification branch reaches 95.63 AP and 96.29 ROC-AUC, surpassing the existing geometric verification baselines.
AI.conclusion: Reusing one pretrained geometric backbone across the whole loop closure pipeline gives both efficiency and accuracy gains over modular pipelines.

title: TOP: Transmission-Oriented Remote Sensing Pansharpening
summary: Pansharpening has been extensively studied as a fundamental image fusion task in remote sensing. However, most existing methods focus on improving fusion quality under the implicit assumption that high-resolution observations have already been fully downlinked to the ground. As a result, existing models are highly vulnerable to perturbations introduced by lossy compression used for downlink transmission. To address this limitation, we present, to the best of our knowledge, the first transmission oriented pansharpening (TOP) framework, which unifies compact latent coding, onboard pansharpening, and efficient downlink transmission within a single satellite-toground pipeline. TOP encodes remote-sensing observations into a compact binary latent space, where a lightweight onboard fusion module can efficiently predict the fused binary latent code. Since only the compact fused code is downlinked, the transmission payload is substantially reduced. Overall, TOP enables low-payload downlink and lightweight onboard processing while maintaining high fusion quality under severe bandwidth constraints. Experiments across multispectral and hyperspectral settings show that TOP consistently achieves superior fusion quality at higher compression ratios than representative pansharpening methods paired with standard lossy codecs. For example, on GaoFen-2, TOP attains a fusion PSNR of 31.4 dB at a downlink compression ratio of 50x. This design also points toward transmissionoriented processing for other remote-sensing tasks. The code will be made available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Proposes transmission-oriented pansharpening (TOP), which encodes observations into a compact binary latent space, predicts the fused code onboard and downlinks only that code; on GaoFen-2 it reaches a fusion PSNR of 31.4 dB at a 50x downlink compression ratio.
AI.motivation: Existing pansharpening assumes full-resolution observations are downlinked intact, so its fusion quality is vulnerable to perturbations introduced by lossy downlink compression.
AI.method: A compact binary latent space encodes the observations, a lightweight onboard fusion module predicts the fused binary latent code, and only this compact code is transmitted to the ground.
AI.result: Across multispectral and hyperspectral settings, TOP achieves higher fusion quality at higher compression ratios than representative pansharpening methods paired with standard lossy codecs; on GaoFen-2 it attains 31.4 dB PSNR at 50x.
AI.conclusion: TOP enables low-payload downlink and lightweight onboard processing under tight bandwidth, and the design points toward transmission-oriented processing for other remote-sensing tasks.

title: Beyond Infraction Scores: Failure-Boundary Profiles for Closed-Loop Evaluation of Driving and Robot Navigation Agents
comment: 16 pages, 12 figures, 3 tables. Code: this https URL. Data: this https URL
summary: Closed-loop driving benchmarks in CARLA rank agents by a driving score that multiplies route completion by an infraction penalty. This score does not distinguish an agent that stops in front of an obstacle from one that pushes past it. In a corridor closed by two parked cars, for example, one agent that drives through with contact averages 52.2 on the blocked widths, while the agents that stop average between 37.8 and 40.6. We propose failure-boundary profiles, an evaluation in which each scenario family varies one measured factor, such as corridor width or the time gap in oncoming traffic, and each variant is certified from measurement as one where the agent should proceed or one where it should stop. Along this axis we estimate two curves per agent, commitment (the probability of attempting the passage) and competence (the probability of passing without contact), and locate where each crosses one half, with intervals that account for the simulator's run-to-run variance. The certified labels also give a summary metric, decision accuracy, which credits clean passes on passable variants and stops on blocked ones. We evaluate seven driving agents on seven CARLA families. The rule-based expert reaches a decision accuracy of 0.74 and TFv6, the highest-scoring learned agent, 0.60. Agents with similar driving scores fail in different ways, and agents that reliably stop at a blocked corridor still rarely wait for a gap in oncoming traffic. We also apply the method, unchanged, to a warehouse robot in Isaac Sim. The navigation policy we test stops at blocked gaps in only one of three families, and two fine-tuned versions of it pass more gaps cleanly but no longer stop at all.

AI.tldr: Proposes failure-boundary profiles for closed-loop evaluation of driving and robot navigation agents, estimating commitment and competence curves per scenario family; the rule-based expert reaches 0.74 decision accuracy and the best learned agent, TFv6, reaches 0.60.
AI.motivation: The CARLA driving score multiplies route completion by an infraction penalty, so it cannot tell an agent that stops before an obstacle from one that pushes past it.
AI.method: Each scenario family varies one measured factor (e.g. corridor width or the oncoming time gap), and each variant is certified from measurement as one where the agent should proceed or should stop; per agent, commitment (probability of attempting the passage) and competence (probability of passing without contact) are estimated with intervals that account for run-to-run variance, and decision accuracy credits clean passes on passable variants and stops on blocked ones.
AI.result: Across seven agents and seven CARLA families, the rule-based expert reaches 0.74 decision accuracy and TFv6 0.60; agents with similar driving scores fail in different ways, and agents that reliably stop at a blocked corridor still rarely wait for a gap in oncoming traffic. Applied unchanged to a warehouse robot in Isaac Sim, the tested navigation policy stops at blocked gaps in only one of three families.
AI.conclusion: Driving-score rankings hide distinct decision failures that failure-boundary profiles expose, and the method transfers across driving and robot navigation domains.

title: Object-independent evaluation of small-data astronomical image classifiers: architecture, representation, and acquisition shortcuts
summary: Reported performance in small astronomical image datasets can reflect object reuse, field-of-view differences, acquisition settings, and catalogue-derived properties as well as astronomical morphology. We designed \dataset{} to measure these effects in a four-class task comprising galaxies, globular clusters, nebulae, and open clusters. The dataset contains 370 catalogue-supported physical objects, each represented by three Digitised Sky Survey FITS bands, and uses a group-constrained split of 222 training, 75 validation, and 73 test objects. We compared a custom CNN--Transformer trained from scratch with ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50 and ViT-B/16 under an adaptive full-field representation, a common angular field, and two central-region-masked controls, using three fixed seeds. In the one-pass object-independent test, mean balanced accuracy on the adaptive view was $0.773\pm0.014$, $0.874\pm0.054$, and $0.866\pm0.023$ for the custom model, ResNet-50, and ViT-B/16, respectively. No primary architecture contrast rejected its null after Holm correction; ResNet-50 and ViT-B/16 differed by 0.007 balanced-accuracy points (95\% cluster-bootstrap interval $[-0.048,0.062]$). Controls based on acquisition and catalogue metadata reached 0.721--0.735, and central-region-masked adaptive views reached 0.731--0.800. These results demonstrate generalisation to unseen physical objects, but also show that image context, acquisition settings, and catalogue-derived object properties carry substantial class information. In this regime, high accuracy cannot be interpreted as evidence that a classifier learned target morphology, and the comparison does not isolate architecture from pretraining.

AI.tldr: Shows that accuracy on a small four-class astronomical image dataset (galaxies, globular clusters, nebulae, open clusters) reflects image context, acquisition settings and catalogue-derived properties as well as morphology, so high accuracy cannot be read as learned morphology.
AI.motivation: Reported performance on small astronomical image datasets can reflect object reuse, field-of-view differences, acquisition settings and catalogue-derived properties rather than astronomical morphology.
AI.method: The dataset has 370 catalogue-supported physical objects, each with three Digitised Sky Survey FITS bands, split by group constraint into 222 training, 75 validation and 73 test objects; a custom CNN-Transformer trained from scratch is compared with ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50 and ViT-B/16 under an adaptive full-field view, a common angular field and two central-region-masked controls, over three fixed seeds.
AI.result: On the adaptive view, mean balanced accuracy is 0.773 +- 0.014 for the custom model, 0.874 +- 0.054 for ResNet-50 and 0.866 +- 0.023 for ViT-B/16; no primary architecture contrast rejected its null after Holm correction, and ResNet-50 and ViT-B/16 differ by 0.007 points (95% cluster-bootstrap interval [-0.048, 0.062]). Metadata-based controls reach 0.721 to 0.735 and central-region-masked adaptive views reach 0.731 to 0.800.
AI.conclusion: Models generalise to unseen physical objects, but image context, acquisition settings and catalogue properties carry substantial class information, and the comparison does not isolate architecture from pretraining.

title: Systolic Linear Attention: Co-Designing Tile-Grouped Gated Delta Attention for TPUs
summary: Gated-delta linear attention layers such as Gated DeltaNet (GDN), Kimi Delta Attention (KDA), and GDN-2 are tuned for GPUs, where small tensor-core tiles and fast vector registers make per-channel decay rescaling and sequential in-block solves cheap. On Google TPUs, which concentrate compute in wide $256 \times 256$ systolic matrix units backed by a slower vector unit, porting these layers directly leaves half of each matrix tile empty and bottlenecks on vector operations. We present \textbf{Systolic Linear Attention (SLA)}, which reshapes gated delta attention around the matrix unit by widening keys to $256$ with grouped value heads, grouping decay gates into four $64$-channel tiles, and computing the chunk solve entirely with block matrix products in a single fused kernel. On TPU v7x, a full \texttt{SLA-R4} layer runs $1.6\times$--$2.5\times$ faster than the open-source Tokamax KDA kernel ($1.4\times$--$2.4\times$ with exact chunk inversion), driven primarily by head sharing and kernel fusion. Across a $2{,}048$-chip TPU v7x pre-training study of sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models from $6.5\text{B}$ to $63.1\text{B}$ parameters, SLA trains $11\%$--$24\%$ faster than KDA at similar perplexity, and reaches slightly lower perplexity than KDA in smaller matched-seed runs.

AI.tldr: Proposes Systolic Linear Attention (SLA), a gated delta attention design reshaped for the 256x256 matrix units of TPU v7x, running 1.6x to 2.5x faster than the open-source Tokamax KDA kernel and training sparse MoE models 11% to 24% faster than KDA at similar perplexity.
AI.motivation: Gated-delta linear attention layers such as GDN, KDA and GDN-2 are tuned for GPUs; ported directly to TPUs they leave half of each matrix tile empty and bottleneck on the slower vector unit.
AI.method: SLA widens keys to 256 with grouped value heads, groups decay gates into four 64-channel tiles, and computes the chunk solve entirely with block matrix products inside a single fused kernel.
AI.result: On TPU v7x a full SLA-R4 layer runs 1.6x to 2.5x faster than the Tokamax KDA kernel (1.4x to 2.4x with exact chunk inversion), driven mainly by head sharing and kernel fusion; in a 2,048-chip pre-training study of sparse MoE models from 6.5B to 63.1B parameters, SLA trains 11% to 24% faster than KDA at similar perplexity and reaches slightly lower perplexity in smaller matched-seed runs.
AI.conclusion: Co-designing linear attention around the hardware's matrix unit yields substantial TPU speedups at similar model quality.

title: Navigating Disagreement Among Criteria for Evaluating Explanation Faithfulness
summary: Faithfulness requires that algorithmic explanations accurately reflect the model's behavior. Yet existing operationalizations of faithfulness can disagree about whether the same explanation is faithful, leaving developers and auditors to choose among conflicting evaluations. In this paper, we investigate disagreement among evaluation criteria and offer a practical path forward for evaluating explanation faithfulness. We first identify how operationalizations of faithfulness differ. We introduce a faithfulness functional that locates their disagreements in what an explanation claims about the model, which comparisons bear on that claim, and how agreement across those comparisons should be aggregated, and we reconstruct existing evaluation criteria within it. We argue these reconstructions support understanding faithfulness as a common though incompletely specified relation between the model and explanation, so the differences reflect choices left open by the general requirement. Justifying an operationalization then comes down to justifying these choices, which, on our view, draws on explanatory, institutional, and normative considerations. We support this argument with a case study of adverse action notices, reconstructing the evaluation implicit in an industry-proposed procedure and identifying which of its choices the setting justifies and which remain open. Our work gives auditors and practitioners a way to navigate disagreeing evaluations of faithfulness. It also explains why the literature should expect multiple operationalizations, while showing how concrete settings can narrow the choice among them. More broadly, our analysis shows how a shared requirement of faithfulness can support contextually justified evaluations despite disagreement among existing metrics.

AI.tldr: Analyses why evaluation criteria for explanation faithfulness disagree, introduces a faithfulness functional that locates these disagreements, and argues that the differences reflect choices a shared requirement leaves open, to be justified by context; an adverse action notice case study illustrates this.
AI.motivation: Existing operationalizations of faithfulness can disagree about whether the same explanation is faithful, leaving developers and auditors to choose among conflicting evaluations.
AI.method: A faithfulness functional locates disagreements in what an explanation claims about the model, which comparisons bear on that claim, and how agreement across comparisons is aggregated; existing criteria are reconstructed within it, and a case study reconstructs the evaluation implicit in an industry-proposed procedure for adverse action notices.
AI.result: The reconstructions support understanding faithfulness as a common but incompletely specified relation between model and explanation; the case study identifies which of the procedure's choices the setting justifies and which remain open.
AI.conclusion: Justifying an operationalization comes down to justifying its choices on explanatory, institutional and normative grounds, which explains why multiple operationalizations are expected and how concrete settings can narrow the choice among them.

title: Adaptive Multi Mode: Budget-Aware Routing of Optimizers By Online Landscape Probes
comment: 29 pages, 8 figures, 19 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: The best classical optimizer for a continuous black-box problem depends on its budget and landscape. Existing routers decide from the dimension and budget, past improvement or features fitted to one benchmark, and few test an optimizer's implicit assumptions online. AMM (Adaptive Multi Mode) routes a known budget among quasi-Newton, trust-region, coordinate, multistart and evolution-strategy optimization engines with online probes of curvature, plateaus, separability, kinks, basins and fractal structure. Each probe has a default, a dimension-by-budget validity range and a cost charged to the budget. In its pre-registered development loop on bbob, 32 of 36 predictions held over the last 16 confirmations. AMM was then tested once on held-out bbob instances 101-110 (D=2-40, 10*D-1000*D) against up to seven competitors. It has the highest target share in 382 of 600 function-dimension-budget cells (236 outright, 146 tied) and, by a descriptive posterior rule, is credibly behind in 35, mostly at 10*D and 30*D. At every budget it also leads the controls built from its own engines (the best engine alone, the best engine per dimension and budget, and a greedy schedule), narrowly at 10*D and 30*D, and nevergrad's NgIohTuned. In pre-registered runs its lead over IPOP-CMA-ES holds under affine and box transformations, on box-constrained bbob and, pooled, on rotated f2-f4, but rotating the separable f3 and f4 removes most of the lead there. On held-out MA-BBOB its final share at 2000*D is level with IPOP-CMA-ES's and its anytime area lower. We published AMM as an open-source Python package (pip install amm-optimizer; this https URL).

AI.tldr: Presents AMM, which routes a known budget among five continuous optimizers using online landscape probes; on held-out bbob instances it has the highest target share in 382 of 600 function-dimension-budget cells and is credibly behind in 35, and it is released as an open-source Python package.
AI.motivation: The best classical optimizer depends on budget and landscape, but existing routers use dimension, budget, past improvement or features fitted to one benchmark, and few test an optimizer's implicit assumptions online.
AI.method: AMM routes a known budget among quasi-Newton, trust-region, coordinate, multistart and evolution-strategy engines using online probes of curvature, plateaus, separability, kinks, basins and fractal structure; each probe has a default, a dimension-by-budget validity range and a cost charged to the budget, and the design was developed in a pre-registered loop on bbob.
AI.result: Tested once on held-out bbob instances 101 to 110 (D=2 to 40) against up to seven competitors, AMM has the highest target share in 382 of 600 cells (236 outright, 146 tied) and is credibly behind in 35, mostly at 10*D and 30*D; it leads the controls built from its own engines and nevergrad's NgIohTuned at every budget, and its lead over IPOP-CMA-ES holds under affine and box transformations but is largely removed on rotated separable f3 and f4. On held-out MA-BBOB its final share at 2000*D is level with IPOP-CMA-ES's and its anytime area is lower.
AI.conclusion: Budget-aware routing driven by online probes of optimizer assumptions can match or beat strong single optimizers and controls, though the lead depends on function structure.

title: Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement
summary: The introduction of generalist robot policies has enabled a single, large model to learn to perform a variety of tasks from a vast pre-training corpus. While these models often exhibit powerful zero-shot generalization capabilities, they typically require an adaptation phase to achieve sufficient performance in deployment. Iterated self-improvement via reinforcement learning (RL) has demonstrated promise in enabling this adaptation, yet such approaches have been largely explored in single-task settings - where the goal is to simply improve on a narrow deployment task - which lies in stark contrast to the multi-task capabilities of the base policy. In this work we ask whether generalist robot policies are capable of multi-task, generalist improvement in deployment - targeting many diverse tasks simultaneously - and what algorithmic recipe enables this. To answer this question, we first develop a set of structured evaluations to test generalist improvement capabilities, and systematically evaluate algorithmic and practical design choices regarding value estimation, policy extraction and resource allocation. We show that not only can generalist policies be improved online across diverse tasks, but that the right recipe can enable generalization and increase performance on tasks not considered during online training. We characterize when this generalization occurs and show that both the training task distribution and the use of value-based RL are critical. To the best of our knowledge, this is among the first evidence for online generalist improvement for robot foundation models.

AI.tldr: Shows that generalist robot policies can be improved online across many diverse tasks at once with reinforcement learning, and that the right recipe can also raise performance on tasks absent from online training, with both the training task distribution and value-based RL found critical.
AI.motivation: Iterated RL self-improvement has mostly been studied on a single narrow deployment task, whereas generalist policies have multi-task capabilities, so multi-task generalist improvement in deployment was an open question.
AI.method: The authors build structured evaluations of generalist improvement and systematically test algorithmic and practical design choices for value estimation, policy extraction and resource allocation.
AI.result: Generalist policies can be improved online across diverse tasks, and the right recipe enables generalization that increases performance on tasks not considered during online training; the authors characterize when this generalization occurs.
AI.conclusion: This is, to the authors' knowledge, among the first evidence for online generalist improvement of robot foundation models.

title: BIOTRAM: Biochemistry-informed Transformer for Relative Abundance via Metabarcoding
summary: Arthropod monitoring at scale begins with metabarcoding of bulk samples: trap collections of hundreds to thousands of specimens processed as one unit, extraction of DNA from the bulked specimens, then sequencing of the DNA from all specimens together. Metabarcoding reveals which taxa such a sample contains, but due to factors such as differing DNA amplification rates and body sizes, its read counts do not neatly correspond to how abundant the different taxa are relative to one another. This lack of relative abundance limits the data's utility for the multitude of ecological analyses that depend on it. We propose BIOTRAM: a neural network that estimates per-taxon specimen counts by dividing the observed read counts by a learned read yield per specimen, which it factors into the DNA each specimen contributes and how efficiently that DNA is amplified. On a paired dataset of 1,188 bottles (800 k specimens) processed both by metabarcoding and by comprehensive individual barcoding for ground-truthing, BIOTRAM reduces the Jensen-Shannon divergence between the estimated and the true composition from 0.3586 for raw read proportions (the usual proxy for abundance) to 0.1200. Trained on the same objective and inputs as four generic deep architectures, all with tuned loss weights, it reaches a count error 3.2% below that of the strongest of them and the lowest composition divergence. It also generalizes to out-of-domain data better, beating all baselines on bottles from unseen regions, later collection dates and unseen sequencing batches, and transferring to data from an unseen laboratory. Structuring the mapping from reads to counts around the steps of the experimental pipeline thus yields more accurate abundance estimates than leaving that mapping unconstrained.

AI.tldr: Proposes BIOTRAM, a neural network that estimates per-taxon specimen counts from metabarcoding read counts by dividing them by a learned read yield per specimen; the Jensen-Shannon divergence to the true composition drops from 0.3586 for raw read proportions to 0.1200.
AI.motivation: Metabarcoding read counts do not neatly correspond to relative abundance because of differing DNA amplification rates and body sizes, which limits the data's use in ecological analyses.
AI.method: The learned read yield per specimen is factored into the DNA each specimen contributes and how efficiently that DNA is amplified, so the mapping from reads to counts follows the steps of the experimental pipeline.
AI.result: On 1,188 bottles (800k specimens) with individual barcoding as ground truth, BIOTRAM reduces the Jensen-Shannon divergence from 0.3586 (raw read proportions) to 0.1200; compared with four generic deep architectures trained on the same objective and inputs, its count error is 3.2% below that of the strongest and it has the lowest composition divergence, and it beats all baselines on bottles from unseen regions, later collection dates, unseen sequencing batches and an unseen laboratory.
AI.conclusion: Structuring the read-to-count mapping around the experimental pipeline yields more accurate abundance estimates than an unconstrained mapping.

title: HLA-Net: A Physics-Guided Skeleton-Based Framework for Automatic Gravitational Arc Detection in Astronomical Images
comment: 16 pages, 2 figures, planning to submit: The Open Journal of Astrophysics
summary: Gravitational arcs produced by strong gravitational lensing provide a unique approach for investigating dark matter distribution, galaxy cluster mass reconstruction and the structure of the Universe. Automated detection remains challenging because gravitational arcs are rare, often faint and morphologically similar to elongated this http URL this paper, we propose \textbf{HLA-Net (Hybrid Lens Arc Network)}, an interpretable multi-stage framework for automatic gravitational arc detection that explicitly exploits both the geometric morphology and physical characteristics of gravitational lensing without requiring manually annotated training this http URL proposed framework was evaluated on astronomical FITS images containing complex galaxy cluster structures. Starting from 169 initial arc candidates extracted from ordered skeleton representations, the multi-stage verification pipeline reduced the search space to 83 geometrically consistent candidates, while robust circle fitting successfully modelled 113 candidate arc structures. The results demonstrate that HLA-Net effectively suppresses false-positive detections while preserving physically reasonable lens candidates through an interpretable and modular verification strategy.

AI.tldr: Proposes HLA-Net, an interpretable multi-stage framework that detects gravitational arcs in astronomical FITS images without manually annotated training data; from 169 initial candidates, verification leaves 83 geometrically consistent ones, and robust circle fitting models 113 candidate arc structures.
AI.motivation: Gravitational arcs are rare, faint and morphologically similar to other elongated structures, which makes automated detection hard even though arcs matter for dark matter and cluster mass studies.
AI.method: HLA-Net exploits both the geometric morphology and the physical characteristics of lensing; candidates extracted from ordered skeleton representations pass through a multi-stage verification pipeline that includes robust circle fitting.
AI.result: On FITS images containing complex galaxy cluster structures, the pipeline reduces 169 initial candidates to 83 geometrically consistent ones, models 113 candidate arc structures with robust circle fitting, and suppresses false positives while keeping physically reasonable lens candidates.
AI.conclusion: The modular, interpretable verification strategy effectively suppresses false-positive arc detections.

title: Classical training of conditional instantaneous quantum polynomial-time Born machines
summary: Instantaneous quantum polynomial-time (IQP) Born machines are attractive quantum generative models, as certain IQP circuit families are conjectured to be hard to sample, yet they can be trained classically. Previously proposed conditional IQP Born machines make the parameters of the diagonal layer condition dependent. We introduce conditional IQP Born machines, in which the condition is encoded in the input state and a single IQP unitary is shared across conditions. Efficient sampling and amplitude-ratio evaluation for the reference state entering the diagonal layer suffice to obtain unbiased classical estimates of a conditional maximum mean discrepancy objective and its gradients. We show that input conditioning can represent conditional families that no diagonally conditioned IQP model with the same number of qubits can reproduce. For the sixteen-qubit Curie-Weiss spin model, a single conditional model captures the magnetization transition at held-out temperatures. Its mean total variation distance is six times lower than that of diagonal conditioning under the same protocol and comparable to that of classical generative models with up to seven times as many parameters. We also train conditional models classically with up to 2048 qubits, which reproduce the mean squared magnetization of the target away from the crossover. These results extend classically trained IQP Born machines to conditional generation.

AI.tldr: Introduces conditional IQP Born machines, in which the condition is encoded in the input state and one IQP unitary is shared across conditions, trained classically through unbiased estimates of a conditional maximum mean discrepancy objective; on a sixteen-qubit Curie-Weiss model its mean total variation distance is six times lower than that of diagonal conditioning.
AI.motivation: Previously proposed conditional IQP Born machines make the parameters of the diagonal layer condition-dependent, and the authors seek a classically trainable conditional generative model.
AI.method: The condition is encoded in the input state and a single IQP unitary is shared across conditions; efficient sampling and amplitude-ratio evaluation for the reference state entering the diagonal layer give unbiased classical estimates of the conditional MMD objective and its gradients.
AI.result: Input conditioning represents conditional families that no diagonally conditioned IQP model with the same number of qubits can reproduce; on the sixteen-qubit Curie-Weiss spin model a single conditional model captures the magnetization transition at held-out temperatures, with mean total variation distance six times lower than diagonal conditioning and comparable to classical generative models with up to seven times as many parameters; classically trained models with up to 2048 qubits reproduce the mean squared magnetization away from the crossover.
AI.conclusion: The work extends classically trained IQP Born machines to conditional generation through input-state conditioning.

title: Ctrl-F: Force as an Interface for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
summary: Humanoid motion tracking has scaled to general policies that reproduce diverse human motion, but the resulting behavior is in free-space: the tracker knows where the body should be, not how it should interact with the environment. Other work makes the object part of the objective, yet abstracts that interaction to contact or geometry, which leaves the demanding cases under-explored. We argue that force is a natural command channel between motion imitation and object interaction, one that specifies not just where to make contact but how hard. We present Ctrl-F, a hierarchical motion-force framework that augments motion tracking with an explicit force command, a 3-D force at each designated contact body such as a hand or a foot. The hierarchical framework comprises: (1) A unified motion-force controller tracks the reference motion while applying the commanded force to the world. (2) A high-level force planner that issues a force command online based on object state and proprioception observations. In simulation and on hardware, Ctrl-F completes loco-manipulation that demands large, sustained interaction force and adjusts its command online as the load changes, both out of reach of a force-blind tracker. On hardware, Ctrl-F demonstrates hand-based dragging, pushing, and lifting, as well as foot-based kicking, successfully manipulating boxes weighing up to 20kg in pushing and kicking tasks where the force-blind baseline fails, while adapting online to additional loads introduced mid-task.

AI.tldr: Proposes Ctrl-F, a hierarchical motion-force framework that adds a 3-D force command at designated contact bodies such as a hand or foot to motion tracking, enabling a humanoid to perform loco-manipulation with large sustained forces, including pushing and kicking boxes up to 20 kg.
AI.motivation: Humanoid motion trackers reproduce motion in free space, knowing where the body should be but not how it should interact with the environment, while existing object-aware work abstracts interaction to contact or geometry and leaves demanding cases under-explored.
AI.method: A unified motion-force controller tracks the reference motion while applying the commanded force to the world, and a high-level force planner issues force commands online from object state and proprioception.
AI.result: In simulation and on hardware, Ctrl-F completes loco-manipulation that demands large sustained interaction force and adjusts its command as the load changes, tasks out of reach of a force-blind tracker; on hardware it performs hand-based dragging, pushing and lifting and foot-based kicking, succeeding with boxes up to 20 kg in pushing and kicking where the force-blind baseline fails, and adapting to loads added mid-task.
AI.conclusion: Force is a natural command channel between motion imitation and object interaction, specifying not only where to make contact but how hard.

title: Learning vs. Optimizing Players in Budgeted Games
summary: We study repeated general games over $T$ rounds between a utility-maximizing optimizer and a learning agent, where budget constraints couple the players' decisions across rounds. Without budgets, low swap regret simultaneously guarantees the learner sublinear regret and caps the optimizer at its Stackelberg value. Budgets break this picture: adversarial no-regret becomes impossible, so the natural goals are non-manipulability---no adaptive optimizer earns more than $\mathtt{BSE} \cdot T + o(T)$, where $\mathtt{BSE}$ is its Budgeted Stackelberg Equilibrium value---and low stochastic regret when the optimizer plays a fixed mixed strategy. We give an efficient, budget-feasible learning algorithm that achieves both goals in every budgeted game: any adaptive optimizer, budgeted or not, earns at most $\mathtt{BSE} \cdot T + O(\sqrt{T})$ in expectation, and if the optimizer plays a fixed mixed strategy on each of a constant number of intervals, the learner has $O(\sqrt{T})$ regret on each such interval. Our learner best responds to forecasts of the optimizer's play that are calibrated in two novel senses, since under budgets the calibration that prevents manipulation no longer yields low stochastic regret. Response calibration, which conditions on the learner's own mixed response by embedding its continuous mixing weight as a step function in $L^2([-1,1])$, prevents manipulation without discretizing responses; dual-weighted Lagrangian calibration ensures low regret. Although low calibration error requires randomized forecasts---distributions over a continuous space that need not have a succinct representation or be directly computable---we construct such forecasts in polynomial time by simulating online gradient ascent.

AI.tldr: Studies repeated games between a budget-constrained optimizer and a learning agent, and gives an efficient budget-feasible learner that prevents manipulation and has low stochastic regret. Any adaptive optimizer earns at most BSE*T + O(sqrt(T)) in expectation.
AI.motivation: Without budgets, low swap regret caps the optimizer at its Stackelberg value, but budgets make adversarial no-regret impossible, and the calibration that prevents manipulation no longer yields low stochastic regret.
AI.method: The learner best responds to forecasts calibrated in two novel senses: response calibration, which embeds the learner's continuous mixing weight as a step function in L2([-1,1]), and dual-weighted Lagrangian calibration for low regret. Randomized forecasts are built in polynomial time by simulating online gradient ascent.
AI.result: Any adaptive optimizer, budgeted or not, earns at most BSE*T + O(sqrt(T)) in expectation. If the optimizer plays a fixed mixed strategy on each of a constant number of intervals, the learner has O(sqrt(T)) regret on each interval.
AI.conclusion: Budgeted games admit an efficient learner that resists manipulation while still achieving low regret against fixed strategies.

title: Distinguishing Initial-Condition and Model Error Using Machine-Learning Weather Models
summary: Gated and ungated optimizations evaluated in GraphCast and Pangu-Weather. The first panel (upper-left) shows the mean over the 36 dates; remaining panels show first-of-month 12 UTC optimization descents from January-November 2017. The y-axis metric is the summed day 1-10 Z500 RMSE verified against ERA5, expressed as percent change from each model's date-matched control. The gated arm optimizes the initial conditions jointly with a LoRA weight correction; its GraphCast curve uses the initial conditions alone (LoRA removed), the same state Pangu receives. Stars and diamonds mark the lowest Pangu errors in the 5- and 10-day windows, respectively. Percentages above each panel show the best Pangu improvement relative to control for gated (green) and ungated (red) optimization. Ungated outperforms gated on half of dates when stopped early. Gating does not guarantee a better Pangu performance, but it does produce more comparable GraphCast and Pangu-Weather improvements on all 36 cases.

AI.tldr: The supplied abstract is actually a figure caption, describing gated and ungated optimization of initial conditions in GraphCast and Pangu-Weather, where the gated arm also learns a LoRA weight correction.
AI.motivation: The text does not state a problem or existing gap; it is a caption describing the experimental panels.
AI.method: Optimizes the initial conditions by descent, comparing ungated and gated variants; the gated arm adds a LoRA weight correction, and the GraphCast curve uses initial conditions alone. The metric is summed day 1-10 Z500 RMSE against ERA5, as percent change from a date-matched control, over 36 dates.
AI.result: Ungated optimization outperforms gated on half of the dates when stopped early. Gating does not guarantee better Pangu-Weather performance, but it gives more comparable GraphCast and Pangu-Weather improvements on all 36 cases.
AI.conclusion: Gating yields more consistent improvements across the two models, though it does not reliably beat ungated optimization for Pangu-Weather.

title: Neural networks and games
summary: Hopfield neural networks and noncooperative games provide seemingly different approaches to understanding how collective outcomes emerge from local interactions. In a neural network, individual units adjust their states according to local signals; in a game, players choose actions to maximise individual payoffs. I establish an exact equivalence between symmetric binary Hopfield networks and binary-action games that admit a quadratic potential. The equivalence identifies stable network configurations with pure-strategy Nash equilibria, and asynchronous neural updating with best-response dynamics. More broadly, the storage and retrieval of memories in neural networks correspond, respectively, to the design and selection of equilibria in games.

AI.tldr: Establishes an exact equivalence between symmetric binary Hopfield networks and binary-action games with a quadratic potential, mapping stable network states to pure-strategy Nash equilibria.
AI.motivation: Hopfield networks and noncooperative games are usually treated as separate ways of explaining how collective outcomes emerge from local interactions.
AI.method: Shows that symmetric binary Hopfield networks and binary-action games admitting a quadratic potential are exactly equivalent. Stable configurations correspond to pure-strategy Nash equilibria, and asynchronous neural updating corresponds to best-response dynamics.
AI.result: Memory storage and retrieval in neural networks correspond, respectively, to the design and selection of equilibria in games.
AI.conclusion: Games give a unified view of neural memory, in which storing memories is equilibrium design and retrieving them is equilibrium selection.

title: Timing is Everything: Inferring Temporal Membership in Continually Updated Models
summary: Continual model updating has become a common practice in the deployment of machine learning systems. However, the dynamic training behaviors give rise to new risks not sufficiently addressed by existing studies. In this paper, we present the first systematic study of temporal privacy risk in continually updated deep learning models. We formalize the notion of temporal membership in continually updated models. We then define the temporal membership inference attack, which seeks to infer whether and when individual samples were involved in model training, at both timestamp-level and interval-level granularities. To this end, we propose TMIA, a novel black-box attack that leverages bidirectional LSTMs to infer temporal membership from model outputs observed across successive updates. Through extensive experiments on three language models and three image classification models, we show that TMIA is highly effective and significantly outperforms existing baselines. Finally, we evaluate three potential defenses, revealing the trade-off between privacy protection and model utility.

AI.tldr: Presents the first systematic study of temporal privacy risk in continually updated models and proposes TMIA, a black-box attack that uses bidirectional LSTMs to infer whether and when samples were used in training.
AI.motivation: Continual model updating creates new privacy risks from dynamic training behavior, which existing membership inference studies do not address.
AI.method: Formalizes temporal membership and defines temporal membership inference at timestamp and interval granularity. TMIA uses bidirectional LSTMs over model outputs observed across successive updates.
AI.result: TMIA is highly effective across three language models and three image classification models and significantly outperforms existing baselines. Three potential defenses reveal a trade-off between privacy protection and model utility.
AI.conclusion: Continual updates leak temporal membership information, and the defenses tested trade privacy against utility.

title: ZipDrift: Generating Multimodal Short-Horizon MPC Costs with One-Step Drifting Models
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures, 4 tables. Preliminary simulation study
summary: Short-horizon model predictive control (MPC) is fast but myopic. ZipMPC compensates by learning a context-dependent correction of the short-horizon cost that imitates a long-horizon expert. We observe that the optimal correction is often multimodal: when a slower opponent can be passed on either side, good corrections of opposite sign coexist, and the expert's choice between them hinges on tiny cost differences. Deterministic regression then averages modes or inherits inconsistent expert tie-breaking. We propose ZipDrift, which trains a one-step drifting generator over MPC cost corrections, tilted toward low closed-loop cost and learned only from cost evaluations of candidate corrections, without differentiating through the optimiser. A few generated candidates are ranked by a learned critic, and the model-based MPC then enforces dynamics and constraints. In a kinematic overtaking benchmark derived from ZipMPC, 53% of contexts are bimodal and the manual short-horizon MPC crashes in 28.5% of test episodes. With an eight-dimensional stagewise correction, ZipDrift is collision-free in all 600 test episodes and matches the best evaluated candidate, whereas an idealised ZipMPC-style regressor crashes in 4.0% (16.0% with inconsistent expert labels) and critic-ranked random candidates with the same budget in 2.0%.

AI.tldr: Proposes ZipDrift, which trains a one-step drifting generator over multimodal MPC cost corrections, and a learned critic ranks the candidates before model-based MPC enforces dynamics and constraints.
AI.motivation: Short-horizon MPC is myopic, and corrections that imitate a long-horizon expert are often multimodal, so deterministic regression averages modes or inherits inconsistent expert tie-breaking.
AI.method: The generator learns only from cost evaluations of candidate corrections, tilted toward low closed-loop cost, without differentiating through the optimiser. A learned critic ranks a few generated candidates.
AI.result: In a kinematic overtaking benchmark where 53% of contexts are bimodal, manual short-horizon MPC crashes in 28.5% of test episodes. With an eight-dimensional correction, ZipDrift is collision-free in all 600 test episodes and matches the best evaluated candidate, while an idealised ZipMPC-style regressor crashes in 4.0% (16.0% with inconsistent expert labels) and critic-ranked random candidates crash in 2.0%.
AI.conclusion: Generating multimodal corrections and ranking them with a critic gives collision-free control in the benchmark, where deterministic regression fails.

title: Item Representations Matter: Bridging Hard Semantic IDs and Soft Prototype Mixtures for Generative Retrieval
summary: Modern recommender systems rely on generative retrieval techniques to predict the next item either as discrete codes or as a continuous vector. On the one hand, Semantic IDs (SIDs) give discrete models shared parameters and pretrained semantic structure, but discretizing items into hard codes discards some information from the original content embeddings. On the other hand, continuous models avoid quantization, yet typically use flat item lookup tables with no explicit parameter tying across items. We ask whether a continuous recommender can introduce shared structure without making it a discrete bottleneck. We propose CAP-Mix, a flow recommender that represents each item as a soft mixture of shared prototypes plus an item-specific vector. The assignments, prototypes, and item vectors are trained jointly, and the soft representation is retained at inference. Pretrained information is optional: SID responsibilities can serve as a prior over assignments, while a full content embedding can initialize the item-specific vector without changing the initial flat table. In matched comparisons on three datasets, CAP-Mix improves over a flat table on the two sparse Amazon datasets and yields a small gain on Steam when trained without pretrained information. Given only an offline SID, it outperforms a hard table built from the same tokenizer by 4.45-14.90% in HR@5. Given the full content embedding, it matches or improves a strong flat table while hard assignments regress on the sparse Amazon datasets. Overall, averaged across six benchmarks, CAP-Mix improves HR@5 and NDCG@5 by 6.9% and 13.6% relative to the best evaluated baseline for each dataset and metric, while delivering 1.4-161x the inference throughput of the discrete baselines in our experiments.

AI.tldr: Proposes CAP-Mix, a continuous flow recommender that represents each item as a soft mixture of shared prototypes plus an item-specific vector, avoiding hard semantic-ID discretization.
AI.motivation: Semantic IDs share parameters but discard information through hard quantization, while continuous models avoid quantization yet use flat lookup tables with no explicit parameter tying across items.
AI.method: Assignments, prototypes and item vectors are trained jointly, and the soft representation is kept at inference. SID responsibilities can serve as a prior over assignments, and a full content embedding can initialize the item-specific vector; both are optional.
AI.result: Given only an offline SID, CAP-Mix beats a hard table built from the same tokenizer by 4.45-14.90% in HR@5. Given the full content embedding it matches or improves a flat table, where hard assignments regress on sparse Amazon datasets. Averaged over six benchmarks it improves HR@5 and NDCG@5 by 6.9% and 13.6% relative to the best baseline, with 1.4-161x the inference throughput of discrete baselines.
AI.conclusion: Shared soft structure can be added to a continuous recommender without a discrete bottleneck, improving accuracy and inference throughput over discrete baselines.

title: When Is One Query per Template Enough? Adapting Learned Cost Models to New Hardware
comment: 13 pages, 2 figures, 10 tables. Code and data: this https URL
summary: A learned cost model that predicts query runtimes is trained on measurements from one machine. When the database moves to other hardware, its plans stay the same but their runtimes change, each by its own factor. We ask how to adapt such a model from k queries measured on the new machine: which queries to run, how to use their runtimes, and how many are enough. On PostgreSQL we timed the same plans of 1,162 TPC-H and TPC-DS queries in six environments: a laptop and a server, each with all its processors or pinned to one, the server also pinned to two, and the laptop also with a small buffer pool. No single factor describes the slowdown between two environments: most of its variance lies between query templates, so a speed factor stops improving after a few queries. A correction that fits separate lines for serial and parallel plans and adds an offset for every measured template brings the moved model, with one measured query per template, to an error (geometric mean over templates of the median Q-error) of 1.10 on TPC-H and 1.19 on TPC-DS, close to the same correction on a model trained on the new machine; fine-tuning a DACE-style neural cost model on the same queries gains at most 2%. On templates never measured, no correction we tried is on average more than 2% better than the speed factor. We then fixed hypotheses and timed new data. On TPC-H at ten times the scale the errors follow these results, but two of five repeated tests miss. On the Join Order Benchmark, whose queries differ widely within a template, the model errs by 2.36 even when retrained on the new machine, no correction gains much, and only the test on new templates holds; boosted trees and a neural model fit these queries better, and correcting the neural model works as well as fine-tuning it. We report every test as registered.

AI.tldr: Studies how to adapt a learned query cost model to new hardware from k measured queries, finding that one measured query per template with a per-template offset and separate serial and parallel lines works best on TPC-H and TPC-DS.
AI.motivation: Moving a database to new hardware changes each query's runtime by its own factor, and it is unclear which queries to measure and how many are enough.
AI.method: On PostgreSQL, the same plans of 1,162 TPC-H and TPC-DS queries were timed in six environments. A speed factor was compared with a correction that fits separate lines for serial and parallel plans and adds an offset per measured template, and with fine-tuning a DACE-style neural cost model. Every test is reported as registered.
AI.result: With one measured query per template, the correction reaches a geometric-mean median Q-error of 1.10 on TPC-H and 1.19 on TPC-DS, close to a model trained on the new machine; fine-tuning gains at most 2%. On unseen templates no correction is more than 2% better than the speed factor. On the Join Order Benchmark the model errs by 2.36 even when retrained, and boosted trees or a neural model fit better.
AI.conclusion: Per-template offsets help for measured templates, but gains are small on unseen templates and on the Join Order Benchmark, and the TPC-H ten-times-scale test only partly held.

title: Retrieval Supersedes Scale: Efficient Log Level Prediction via Multiplex Socio-Technical Context
summary: Developers insert logging statements in source code to record its execution, and the resulting logs are essential for detecting and troubleshooting system anomalies. A key part of these statements is the log level (e.g., DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR), which determines whether a message is recorded. Choosing it is a trade-off: levels set too low mask important information in production, while levels set too high create noisy logs and extra I/O and storage overhead. Recent work uses Large Language Models (LLMs) with In-Context Learning (ICL) to predict log levels, but typically augments the prompt with randomly sampled examples. We argue that this overlooks the socio-technical nature of logging, where conventions vary by component and development team. Off-the-shelf LLMs using random examples are reported to achieve median AUCs of only 0.56 to 0.76, leaving room for improvement without fine-tuning. In this paper, we propose a retrieval approach for LLM-powered log level prediction that prioritizes context relevance over random selection and basic similarity. Our method retrieves logging examples relevant along two socio-technical dimensions: (i) functionality (code performing similar operations) and (ii) ownership (code maintained by the same developers). Evaluating four LLMs across ten popular Java projects, we find that this retrieval improves AUC over random baselines by 0.07 (median), and combining both signals yields median AUCs of 0.83 to 0.97. Our ablation studies show that each signal improves on random retrieval, and that combining them outperforms the stronger of the two on all ten projects. Our results also significantly exceed state-of-the-art supervised predictors (e.g., DeepLV) by a median AUC of 0.12 to 0.19. Our findings highlight the importance of socio-technical signals such as code functionality and ownership for LLM-powered log level prediction.

AI.tldr: Proposes retrieving logging examples by functionality and code ownership for LLM in-context log level prediction, reaching median AUCs of 0.83 to 0.97 across ten Java projects.
AI.motivation: LLM log level prediction typically uses random examples, which give median AUCs of only 0.56 to 0.76, and it ignores that logging conventions vary by component and development team.
AI.method: Retrieves examples along two socio-technical dimensions, functionality (code performing similar operations) and ownership (code maintained by the same developers), and combines both signals. Four LLMs were evaluated, with ablation studies.
AI.result: Retrieval improves AUC over random baselines by 0.07 (median). Combining both signals yields median AUCs of 0.83 to 0.97, outperforming the stronger single signal on all ten projects, and exceeds the supervised predictor DeepLV by a median AUC of 0.12 to 0.19.
AI.conclusion: Socio-technical signals such as code functionality and ownership are important for LLM-powered log level prediction.

title: Improved approximation algorithms for capacitated cluster editing
summary: We study the minimum-disagreement cluster editing problem that, from a complete edge-signed graph, where a positive edge represents two vertices agreeing to each other while a negative represents a disagreement, constructs disjoint cliques of upper bounded size such that the total number of negative edges inside cliques and positive edges outside cliques is minimized. When the sizes of the candidate cliques are unbounded, the problem is NP-hard and APX-hard, and many approximation algorithms with improving ratios have been proposed in the literature and the state-of-the-art approximation ratio of $\alpha = 1.3865 + \epsilon$. The capacitated variant, in which the candidate cliques have sizes no greater than a given $k$, is less studied and the best approximation ratio is $5.37$. In this paper, we study the latter problem. We first present a downsizing procedure that achieves an approximation ratio of $\alpha_k = 2 \alpha + 1$, based on any $\alpha$-approximation algorithm for the uncapacitated problem. Secondly, we propose a hybrid of cluster-LP sampling and pivoting and show that for every fractional capacitated cluster-LP solution of cost $L$, the hybrid using ordinary pivoting has an expected cost at most $\frac 95 L + \frac 1{10} \OPT_k$, and the hybrid using conditional pivoting has an expected cost at most $\frac {306}{203} L + \frac {50}{203} \OPT_k$. A cardinality-constrained adaptation of the approximate dual-separation framework of García-Soriano and Schohn supplies the required fractional solution and yields a randomized $(1.9 + \epsilon)$-approximation algorithm and a randomized $(1.7537 + \epsilon)$-approximation algorithm, respectively.

AI.tldr: Gives improved approximation algorithms for capacitated cluster editing, with a downsizing procedure achieving ratio 2*alpha + 1 and randomized (1.9+eps) and (1.7537+eps) approximations from cluster-LP sampling with pivoting.
AI.motivation: The capacitated variant, where cliques have size at most k, is less studied, and its best known approximation ratio is 5.37, compared with 1.3865+eps for the uncapacitated problem.
AI.method: A downsizing procedure built on any alpha-approximation for the uncapacitated problem; a hybrid of cluster-LP sampling and pivoting, using either ordinary or conditional pivoting; and a cardinality-constrained adaptation of the approximate dual-separation framework of Garcia-Soriano and Schohn to supply the fractional solution.
AI.result: Ordinary pivoting gives expected cost at most (9/5)L + OPT_k/10, and conditional pivoting gives (306/203)L + (50/203)OPT_k, where L is the cost of the fractional cluster-LP solution. These yield randomized (1.9+eps) and (1.7537+eps) approximation algorithms.
AI.conclusion: The capacitated problem admits substantially better approximation than the previous 5.37 bound.

title: Diversity-Aware Experience Replay via Statistical Leverage Scores
summary: Off-policy deep reinforcement learning trains on random samples from a replay buffer of past experience. In physical robot settings, that buffer is dominated by routine: thousands of near-identical transitions from normal operation, while the rare events that define the edges of the task are rarely sampled. We propose scoring every stored transition by its statistical leverage, which measures how unusual it is relative to the buffer's own data, computed from the stored numbers alone, with no labels, rewards, or value network. We draw each mini-batch from a mixture of this score and uniform sampling. First, the natural way to build the score along the directions where the data varies most turns out to be blind when actions are stored as one-hot indicators, because indicator columns always win the variance ranking; we instead select the feature columns with the heaviest tails (largest kurtosis) where small far-away populations are revealed. Second, the importance weights that prioritized replay uses to keep gradients unbiased cancel the method exactly: with full correction, training matches uniform sampling, so we drop the correction and deliberately optimize the rebalanced objective. Third, when the rare situations of a log are relational, visible only in how a stretch of behavior relates to its goal, not in any single stored coordinate-per-transition scores are blind; applying the same tail rule to short trajectory windows described relative to their goal restores the signal, and on a three-joint arm that must push an object around an obstacle it raises the rare-task success from 0.49 to 0.69 against a labeled-oracle ceiling of 0.74.

AI.tldr: Proposes scoring replay buffer transitions by statistical leverage computed from stored numbers alone, mixed with uniform sampling, which raises rare-task success on a three-joint robot arm from 0.49 to 0.69.
AI.motivation: Robot replay buffers are dominated by near-identical routine transitions, so the rare events that define the task edges are seldom sampled.
AI.method: Scores transitions by leverage, selecting the heaviest-tailed (largest kurtosis) feature columns, since one-hot action indicators dominate variance rankings. The importance-weight correction is dropped because it cancels the method. For rare relational situations, the same tail rule is applied to short trajectory windows described relative to their goal.
AI.result: On a three-joint arm that must push an object around an obstacle, rare-task success rises from 0.49 to 0.69, against a labeled-oracle ceiling of 0.74.
AI.conclusion: Leverage-based mixed sampling recovers most of the gap to a labeled oracle without labels, rewards, or a value network.

title: A Controlled Experimental Evaluation of Configuration and Cache Architecture in LLM Serving Engines
comment: 29 pages, 14 figures, 7 tables. Artifact: this https URL
summary: Multi-agent LLM applications repeat most of their prompt tokens across requests, and serving engines reuse the cached state of shared prefixes. vLLM and SGLang reuse it at different granularities, and benchmarks of their default deployments report large performance gaps, usually credited to the cache. Such comparisons rarely control for other configuration differences. One of them, whether a long prompt is prefilled in chunks, is set by each engine's defaults from the hardware and the release, and it confounds the comparison. We built a reproducible testbed on Kubernetes and a seeded multi-agent workload generator, and compared the two engines under vendor defaults and with chunked prefill matched. SGLang's configuration is the same in both arms, which makes it an internal control across independently provisioned deployments. Under defaults, vLLM's median time to first token is up to 64x SGLang's. Matching one setting removes 78% of the capacity gap where that gap is largest and 30 to 67% of the latency gap. Near saturation the remaining latency gap reflects queue growth. A fluid queue model driven only by a 4.4% throughput shortfall reproduces it, and shows that such a gap scales with the length of the benchmark run. What survives matching is a tail-latency advantage of 2.4 to 6.4x at equal throughput, consistent with cache-aware ordering of waiting requests. We derive six recommendations for comparing serving engines.

AI.tldr: A controlled comparison of vLLM and SGLang finds that large default-configuration latency gaps are largely driven by chunked-prefill settings; after matching that setting, a tail-latency advantage of 2.4 to 6.4x at equal throughput remains.
AI.motivation: Benchmarks of default deployments report large gaps credited to the cache, but they rarely control for other configuration differences, such as chunked prefill, which each engine's defaults set from the hardware and release.
AI.method: A reproducible Kubernetes testbed and a seeded multi-agent workload generator. The engines were compared under vendor defaults and with chunked prefill matched, with SGLang's configuration unchanged across arms as an internal control. A fluid queue model driven by throughput shortfall explains the residual latency gap.
AI.result: Under defaults, vLLM's median time to first token is up to 64x SGLang's. Matching the setting removes 78% of the capacity gap where it is largest and 30 to 67% of the latency gap. The residual gap is reproduced by a fluid queue model with a 4.4% throughput shortfall and scales with benchmark length.
AI.conclusion: Default-configuration comparisons overstate the cache's role; six recommendations are derived for comparing serving engines.

title: Do Search-Augmented Recommenders Use the Latest Search Episode?
comment: Accepted at WSDM 2027. Code: this https URL
summary: Search-augmented recommenders can use the latest search episode and earlier searches. We introduce FocalSwap to test how these inputs contribute to the next recommendation. For each recommendation, it changes the latest search slot or all search inputs while holding the target, candidates, pre-search history, and scorer fixed. It compares neutral masks with matched observed-search replacements, recording rank changes, RR gains relative to each control, and preference for the true focal search. A planted signal and GenSAR's current-query task confirm that the audit detects known input dependence. We evaluate behavioral and lexical evidence on KuaiSAR and Qilin, and recommendation checkpoints trained using the released SESRec and UniSAR implementations. Across three independently trained UniSAR checkpoints, the estimated all-source benefit depends on the control. On the same 66,139 rows, replacing all search inputs with a neutral ID yields a positive signed contribution, whereas replacing them with category/profile-matched observed search sequences gives smaller estimates, with an interval below zero for one checkpoint. The paired RR gaps range from $+2.770 \times 10^{-3}$ to $+6.604 \times 10^{-3}$, and every adjusted interval is above zero. Neutral masks change 59.7-61.7% of target ranks, while matched replacements change 44.1-44.8%. The control contrast persists across five alternative donor assignments per checkpoint. Under the primary neutral-mask and category-matched controls, positive latest-slot contribution is not established in SESRec or UniSAR. These results show why masking evidence should be compared with observed-search replacements when attributing a benefit to broader search state or the latest episode.

AI.tldr: Introduces FocalSwap, an audit that perturbs search inputs in search-augmented recommenders and finds that, under category-matched observed-search controls, a positive latest-slot contribution is not established in SESRec or UniSAR.
AI.motivation: Attributing a recommendation benefit to the latest search episode requires comparing masking with observed-search replacement, since masking evidence can overstate the effect.
AI.method: For each recommendation, the latest search slot or all search inputs are replaced with neutral masks or with matched observed-search replacements, holding the target, candidates, pre-search history and scorer fixed. The audit is checked with a planted signal and GenSAR's current-query task, on KuaiSAR and Qilin with released SESRec and UniSAR implementations.
AI.result: Across three independently trained UniSAR checkpoints the estimated all-source benefit depends on the control. Paired RR gaps range from +2.770e-3 to +6.604e-3. Neutral masks change 59.7-61.7% of target ranks, while matched replacements change 44.1-44.8%, and the contrast persists across five alternative donor assignments.
AI.conclusion: Masking overstates the benefit of search evidence, so attributing gains to the latest search episode needs observed-search replacement controls.

title: Impact of Negative Weights on Performance in Reservoir Computing
summary: Reservoir computing provides an efficient framework for time-series prediction because only the readout layer is trained while the recurrent reservoir remains fixed. In this study, we examine how the negative sign ratio of a signed Erdos-Renyi reservoir affects the internal dynamics and forecasting performance of an echo state network on the Mackey-Glass benchmark. To characterize the reservoir responses, we use two Shannon-entropy-based observables, namely node-state entropy and node-frequency entropy, as empirical proxies for the diversity of reservoir states and temporal activation patterns.
